In corank zero, Burungale–Tian’s theorem covers every rational CM elliptic curve at every prime, without a reduction restriction (A. A. Burungale and Tian 2026, Theorem 1.1) <a id="pm-cite-35"></a>[[BurungaleTian2026](#ref-BurungaleTian2026)]. Combined with Smith’s unrestricted distribution, it therefore already gives the analytic-rank-zero half for every CM twist family. Their Theorem 1.2 gives rank zero for almost all positive squarefree $n\equiv1,2,3\pmod8$ in the congruent-number family $ny^2=x^3-x$. Kriz’s preprint states a converse for curves with CM by the full ring of integers at the unique ramified prime of the CM field, and derives analytic densities for restricted CM families, including congruent-number curves (Kriz 2022, Theorems 1.1 and 10.17) <a id="pm-cite-36"></a>[[Kriz2022](#ref-Kriz2022)]. Its dyadic pointwise statement concerns the CM fields $\mathbb Q(i)$ and $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-2})$. Together with Smith’s distribution theorem, the stated dyadic converse would yield both half-density conclusions for quadratic twists of every curve with CM by either of these maximal orders. Theorem <a href="#thm:main-converse" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:main-converse">1</a> treats the full $2$-power Selmer corank for every rational elliptic curve, in both ranks zero and one.

<a id="pm-h-6"></a>
#### Proof strategy

Fix the curve under consideration. We construct finite binary families of twists $$h_x=\prod_{q\in\mathcal Q}(q^*)^{\lambda_q(x)},\qquad
 q^*=(-1/q)q,\qquad x\in\mathbb F_2^b,$$ where $\mathcal Q$ is a finite set of distinct good odd primes and the $\lambda_q$ are linear forms. The parameter at $x=0$ is $1$. The families have the same local twisting classes at every fixed bad place. Their nonzero vertices have analytic order zero or one, according to the corank of the fixed curve. A scalar determinant coordinate attached to the relevant class and Selmer complex has a nonzero central specialization there, with uniformly bounded $2$-adic valuation. Bounded integral interpolation then recovers nonvanishing at the missing vertex $0$.

At corank zero, the interpolated class is a Beilinson–Kato class and its central specialization detects $L(E,1)$ (Kato 2004) <a id="pm-cite-37"></a>[[Kato2004](#ref-Kato2004)]. At corank one, it is a Heegner class over an imaginary quadratic field $K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt{k})$, whose height detects $$\left[L(E,s)L(E^{(k)},s)\right]'_{s=1}.$$ An analytically nonvanishing companion $E^{(k)}$ makes the Selmer corank over $K$ equal to one. The argument retains integral Kummer conditions at $2$ and every bad prime. The rational Iwasawa input is used in its stated scope; the uniform integral estimates at $2$ are proved in Sections <a href="#sec:heegner-interpolation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:heegner-interpolation">13</a> and <a href="#sec:cy:interpolation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:cy:interpolation">12</a>. The Heegner construction is related to Howard’s Kolyvagin-system framework (Howard 2004) <a id="pm-cite-38"></a>[[Howard2012](#ref-Howard2012)]; the integral bounds required here are established with the local conditions and uniformity stated in this paper.

The finite families are built from modular coefficients. Waldspurger’s formula supplies the even-sign coefficients (Waldspurger 1981) <a id="pm-cite-39"></a>[[Waldspurger1981](#ref-Waldspurger1981)]. In odd sign, reductions of genus Heegner sums give weighted ternary theta coefficients at increasing finite precisions. A uniform lower bound allows a least normalized valuation to be selected. In the even case this is a minimum among the coefficients of one form. In the odd case it is a minimum over bounded-weight sequences as the precision increases; each finite collection of tests is then realized at a sufficiently high actual precision. A test attaining the minimum detects the required analytic order and gives a uniform upper bound. Weight-two Hecke traces turn these coefficient tests into contraction and deletion rules for finite configurations of primes.

There are two exhaustive residual cases. If $E[2]$ is reducible, its invariant line is a rational point of order two. Graphs encode prescribed quadratic residue symbols between auxiliary primes. The resulting finite construction makes two separate coefficient tests nonzero together at every nonzero binary vertex. The odd argument fixes one companion field before the dimension grows. In this branch, the even construction first supplies the lower bound needed to normalize the odd coefficient test. If $E[2]$ is irreducible, local Selmer equations give matrices over $\mathbb F_2$. Subtracting a correction determined by finitely many local types makes these matrices symmetric; their nullities still give a lower bound on the Selmer dimension up to a fixed cost. Removing one selected prime or pair of primes, or retaining it with either of two allowed local choices, gives three configurations. Their coefficient tests satisfy the same sum-zero relation as the corresponding matrix determinants. This relation does not identify the coefficient test with the determinant. We group the configurations into blocks and arrange that the matrix entries between distinct blocks vanish. A nonzero coefficient test bounds the matrix kernel, and hence the number of singular blocks in the finite configuration. Fixing a configuration with a maximal number of such blocks lets us arrange nonzero tests at every nonzero binary vertex. An additional alternating-matrix construction supplies a companion with uniformly bounded prime count and Selmer length.

Two parts of the argument have uses beyond this assembly. The interpolation algebra clears denominators through a bounded complex, so the required congruence precision is independent of the number of new primes. The graph construction treats the coefficient tests as polynomials in prescribed residue symbols and makes separately nonzero tests nonzero together. Its proof retains squared variables until after multiplying their highest-degree parts. Neither construction presupposes the desired nonvanishing at the base.

<a id="pm-h-7"></a>
###### Organization.

Section <a href="#sec:preliminaries" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:preliminaries">2</a> records the rank implications and local conventions. Section <a href="#sec:transfer-criteria" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:transfer-criteria">3</a> states the two arithmetic transfer criteria, the lower bounds needed to normalize coefficients, and auxiliary nonvanishing with prescribed local conditions. Sections <a href="#cs:coefficient-systems" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="cs:coefficient-systems">4</a> and <a href="#sec:trace-calculus" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:trace-calculus">5</a> turn analytic nonvanishing into coefficient tests and prime-substitution identities. Section <a href="#gr:section" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="gr:section">6</a> develops the graph construction used in the rational-torsion converse of Section <a href="#pw:section" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="pw:section">7</a>. Section <a href="#sec:lm:local-matrices" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:lm:local-matrices">8</a> supplies the Selmer matrices for the irreducible converse in Section <a href="#sec:sa:saturation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:sa:saturation">9</a>. The remaining main-text sections prove the arithmetic inputs: Section <a href="#sec:auxiliary-nonvanishing" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:auxiliary-nonvanishing">10</a> establishes auxiliary nonvanishing, Section <a href="#sec:binary-algebra" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:binary-algebra">11</a> develops the common finite-complex and binary transfer arguments, and Sections <a href="#sec:cy:interpolation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:cy:interpolation">12</a> and <a href="#sec:heegner-interpolation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:heegner-interpolation">13</a> construct the cyclotomic and Heegner determinant coordinates and prove their integral bounds. Finally, Section <a href="#sec:conclusions" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:conclusions">14</a> assembles the unrestricted result and its density and finite-descent consequences.

<a id="sec:preliminaries"></a>
### Selmer ranks and local conventions

We first record the arithmetic implications used to pass between curves and to interpret the final analytic nonvanishing. They apply to every elliptic curve over $\mathbb Q$.

Throughout, we use Mordell–Weil finite generation and the positive definiteness of the canonical height modulo torsion over number fields (Milne 2021, chap. IV, finite-basis theorem, Theorem 4.7, Remark 4.12, and Theorem 6.1) <a id="pm-cite-40"></a>[[MilneEC2021](#ref-MilneEC2021)].

<a id="stmt-pr-ranks"></a>
<div id="pr:ranks" class="lemma">

**Lemma 4** (Ranks and the forward implication). *For an elliptic curve $A/\mathbb Q$ there is an exact sequence $$0\longrightarrow A(\mathbb Q)\otimes\mathbb Q_2/\mathbb Z_2
 \longrightarrow\mathop{\mathrm{Sel}}_{2^\infty}(A/\mathbb Q)
 \longrightarrow\mathop{\mathrm{Sha}}(A/\mathbb Q)[2^\infty]\longrightarrow0.$$ In particular $$c_2(A)=r(A)+\mathop{\mathrm{corank}}_{\mathbb Z_2}\mathop{\mathrm{Sha}}(A/\mathbb Q)[2^\infty].$$ If $a(A)\le1$, then $r(A)=a(A)$, the whole group $\mathop{\mathrm{Sha}}(A/\mathbb Q)$ is finite, and $c_2(A)=a(A)$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-pr-ranks"><summary>Proof of stmt-pr-ranks</summary>

*Proof.* The finite Kummer exact sequences are $$0\longrightarrow A(\mathbb Q)/2^nA(\mathbb Q)
 \longrightarrow\mathop{\mathrm{Sel}}_{2^n}(A/\mathbb Q)
 \longrightarrow\mathop{\mathrm{Sha}}(A/\mathbb Q)[2^n]\longrightarrow0.$$ Their direct limit gives the displayed sequence; taking coranks gives the identity. The last assertion is the Gross–Zagier–Kolyvagin forward theorem (Gross and Zagier 1986; Kolyvagin 1990) <a id="pm-cite-41"></a>[[GrossZagier1986](#ref-GrossZagier1986), [Kolyvagin1990](#ref-Kolyvagin1990)]; see also its unrestricted formulation in Skinner (2020, sec. 1) <a id="pm-cite-42"></a>[[Skinner2020](#ref-Skinner2020)]. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-prop-selmer-parity"></a>
<div id="prop:selmer-parity" class="lemma">

**Lemma 5** (Parity and change of curve). *<span id="pr:invariance" label="pr:invariance"></span> For every elliptic curve $A/\mathbb Q$ with root number $\varepsilon(A)$, $$(-1)^{c_2(A)}=\varepsilon(A).$$ A rational isogeny preserves $a(A)$, $r(A)$ and $c_2(A)$. For a quadratic field $K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt{k})$, $$\mathop{\mathrm{corank}}_{\mathbb Z_2}\mathop{\mathrm{Sel}}_{2^\infty}(A/K)
       =c_2(A)+c_2(A^{(k)}).$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-prop-selmer-parity"><summary>Proof of stmt-prop-selmer-parity</summary>

*Proof.* The parity statement is the $p=2$ case of Dokchitser and Dokchitser (2010, Theorem 1.4, equivalently Theorem 4.19) <a id="pm-cite-43"></a>[[DokchitserDokchitser2010](#ref-DokchitserDokchitser2010)]. At $p=2$ this is Monsky’s theorem (Monsky 1996) <a id="pm-cite-44"></a>[[Monsky1996](#ref-Monsky1996)]. Isogenies and their duals induce maps respecting every local Kummer condition; their composites are multiplication by their fixed degree. After rationalization these maps preserve ranks and coranks. Their $L$-functions agree by isogeny invariance.

Restriction to $K$ and the two conjugation projections $1+c$ and $1-c$ give maps between $\mathop{\mathrm{Sel}}_{2^\infty}(A/K)$ and the sum of the Selmer groups of $A$ and $A^{(k)}$ over $\mathbb Q$, with composites multiplication by $2$. They respect local Kummer images, so rationalization gives the corank identity. An integral direct sum is not needed. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-pr-residual-cases"></a>
<div id="pr:residual-cases" class="lemma">

**Lemma 6** (The residual alternatives). *The representation $E[2]$ is reducible over $\mathbb F_2$ if and only if $E(\mathbb Q)[2]\ne0$. In that case it is an extension of two trivial $\mathbb F_2$-representations. Otherwise its image is $C_3$ or $S_3$ in $\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}_2(\mathbb F_2)$. Quadratic twisting leaves this representation unchanged.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-pr-residual-cases"><summary>Proof of stmt-pr-residual-cases</summary>

*Proof.* An invariant line over $\mathbb F_2$ has a unique nonzero vector, which must be fixed. Conversely a rational point of order two spans an invariant line. Both that line and the one-dimensional quotient are trivial, since $\mathbb F_2^\times=\{1\}$. The irreducible subgroups of $\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}_2(\mathbb F_2)\simeq S_3$ are $C_3$ and $S_3$. Finally a quadratic character reduces to $1$ modulo $2$. ◻

</details>

The distinction here is irreducibility over $\mathbb F_2$, rather than absolute irreducibility: the cyclic cubic case is included. In the rational-torsion case we may first replace the curve by a rationally isogenous one with full rational two-torsion, if such a curve exists. Otherwise, for any chosen rational two-isogeny $E\to E'$, both $\mathbb Q(E[2])$ and $\mathbb Q(E'[2])$ are quadratic. Lemma <a href="#pr:invariance" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="pr:invariance">[pr:invariance]</a> justifies this choice before any constructions.

<a id="pm-h-9"></a>
#### Finite lengths and twisting data

All valuations above $2$ are normalized by $v(2)=1$, with $v(0)=+\infty$. For a finite $\mathbb Z_2$-module $M$, its length is $\log_2\#M$. The corank of a cofinitely generated discrete $\mathbb Z_2$-module is the rank of its Pontryagin dual. Its quotient by the maximal divisible subgroup is finite. This finite quotient must be distinguished from finiteness of the original group.

A fixed support $S$ is a finite set of primes containing $2$ and all primes of bad reduction; it is enlarged explicitly when necessary. Write $N$ for the conductor of $E$. A local filter specifies a real sign and unit squareclasses at $S$ for a variable odd fundamental discriminant prime to $S$. The empty discriminant $h=1$ denotes the untwisted curve. We also write $E^{(h)}$ for twisting by a rational squareclass. For an odd prime $p$, the signed prime discriminant is $p^*=(-1/p)p$. Products of distinct $p^*$ are odd fundamental discriminants, with the empty product interpreted as $1$.

For an odd fundamental discriminant $h$ prime to $2N$, the coprime-twist root-number formula is $$\varepsilon(E^{(h)})=\varepsilon(E)\chi_h(-N)$$ (Radziwiłł and Soundararajan 2015, sec. 1) <a id="pm-cite-45"></a>[[RadziwillSoundararajan2015](#ref-RadziwillSoundararajan2015)]. Thus matching unit squareclasses at the primes dividing $2N$ and opposite real signs give opposite functional signs: the values of $\chi_h(N)$ agree, whereas $\chi_h(-1)=\operatorname{sgn}(h)$. This verifies the sign condition when choosing the auxiliary partners below.

Put $T=T_2(E)$ and $V=E[2]$. Frobenius is arithmetic, and $a_p(E)=p+1-\#E(\mathbb F_p)$ at a good prime. For $h$ prime to $S$, set <a id="eq:h:weights"></a>$$\label{eq:h:weights}
 t_p=\dim_{\mathbb F_2}V^{\mathop{\mathrm{Fr}}_p},\qquad
 w(h)=\frac12\sum_{p\mid |h|}t_p.$$ The residual identity, a transposition and a rotation of order three have $t_p=2,1,0$, respectively. We call these split, simple and root primes; their weights are $1,1/2,0$. Only types present in the residual image are used. Quadratic residue symbols written additively take the values $0,1\in\mathbb F_2$, corresponding to $+1,-1$.

Whenever its group is finite, write $$s(h)=\mathop{\mathrm{length}}_{\mathbb Z_2}\mathop{\mathrm{Sha}}(E^{(h)}/\mathbb Q)[2^\infty].$$ This includes every twist already proved to have analytic rank zero or one. It also includes a base of Selmer corank zero, since its full $2$-primary Selmer group is then finite. We make no whole-Sha finiteness assertion at such a base until analytic nonvanishing has been established.

<a id="eq:h:algebraic-value"></a>
Let $\Omega_E^+$ be a positive real period and let $\Omega_E^-$ be the positive magnitude of a nonzero anti-invariant period. Put $$\label{eq:h:algebraic-value}
 \mathcal L(h)=
 \frac{\sqrt{|h|}\,L(E^{(h)},1)}{\Omega_E^{\operatorname{sgn}(h)}}.$$ Valuations refer to this algebraic period-normalized value at a chosen place above $2$. Changes of the fixed period, modular parametrization or isogeny affect valuations by bounded constants. All parametrizations send the cusp $\infty$ to the origin. Replacing Equation <a href="#eq:h:algebraic-value" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:h:algebraic-value">[eq:h:algebraic-value]</a> by the central value divided by a Néron real period of $E^{(h)}$ changes a finite valuation by $O_E(1)$: the differential changes by the usual twisting factor, and there are only finitely many twisting classes at $2$.

Every uniform bound below specifies its fixed data. Constants may depend on the curve, a chosen fixed twist and finite local preparation; they may not depend on the subsequent cube dimension or the number of new primes. At finite precision, the sizes of primes realizing a specified configuration may depend on that entire configuration. A limiting construction will only be used through its finite realizations.

<a id="stmt-pr-finite-descent"></a>
<div id="pr:finite-descent" class="lemma">

**Lemma 7** (Finite descent and corank). *Let $F$ be the quotient of $\mathop{\mathrm{Sha}}(E/\mathbb Q)[2^\infty]$ by its maximal divisible subgroup. Then $$d_2(E)=c_2(E)+\dim_{\mathbb F_2}F[2],
 \qquad \dim_{\mathbb F_2}F[2]\text{ is even}.$$ Thus $d_2(E)\in\{0,1\}$ implies $c_2(E)=d_2(E)$ and $F=0$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-pr-finite-descent"><summary>Proof of stmt-pr-finite-descent</summary>

*Proof.* The finite Kummer sequence at $n=1$ gives $d_2(E)=r(E)+\dim_{\mathbb F_2}\mathop{\mathrm{Sha}}(E/\mathbb Q)[2]$. The divisible subgroup is a direct sum of copies of $\mathbb Q_2/\mathbb Z_2$ and splits as an abstract abelian subgroup. Its $2$-torsion dimension is its corank. Lemma <a href="#pr:ranks" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="pr:ranks">4</a> therefore gives the displayed identity. The Cassels–Tate pairing on $F$ is perfect. For an elliptic curve, the rational divisor $[O]$ defining its principal polarization makes the pairing alternating (Milne 2006, chap. I, Remark 6.10(b) and Theorem 6.13(a)) <a id="pm-cite-46"></a>[[MilneADT2006](#ref-MilneADT2006)]. A finite abelian $2$-group with such a pairing is an orthogonal sum of pairs of cyclic groups of equal order: choose an element of maximal order, pair it with an element detecting that order, split off their nondegenerate plane, and continue. Hence its $2$-rank is even. A finite $2$-group with zero $2$-rank is zero, proving the last assertion. ◻

</details>

<a id="sec:transfer-criteria"></a>
### Arithmetic estimates for finite twist families

The pointwise converse will follow by placing the given curve at the zero vertex of a large finite family of twists. We arrange analytic nonvanishing at every other vertex, together with an upper bound on a normalized valuation. The estimates in this section explain which normalization is needed and what must be uniform as the family grows. Their proofs occupy Sections <a href="#sec:binary-algebra" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:binary-algebra">11</a>, <a href="#sec:cy:interpolation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:cy:interpolation">12</a> and <a href="#sec:heegner-interpolation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:heegner-interpolation">13</a>.

Fix $E/\mathbb Q$ of conductor $N$ and retain the local weights $w(h)$, finite Sha lengths $s(h)$, and period-normalized values $\mathcal L(h)$ of Section <a href="#sec:preliminaries" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:preliminaries">2</a>. In particular $s(h)$ is defined at a corank-zero base and at every twist already known to have analytic rank zero or one. All valuations satisfy $v(2)=1$.

A binary family has the form $$h_x=h_0\prod_{q\in\mathcal Q}(q^*)^{\lambda_q(x)},
 \qquad x\in\mathbb F_2^b,\qquad q^*=(-1/q)q,$$ where the new primes are distinct and prime to $2Nh_0$, and each $\lambda_q$ is linear. The old factors of $h_0$ remain at every vertex; no new factor is present at zero. We will hold the required local squareclasses fixed while $b$ grows. Both the set of primes and their sizes may depend on $b$.

Here is the common transfer mechanism. For families satisfying the hypotheses of the transfer theorems below, the arithmetic proofs attach power series $$u_x(t)\in\mathbb Z_2[[t]][1/2]$$ to the vertices, using a common family of cochain models and compatible trivializations of the determinant lines. The differences of these coordinates therefore have a fixed meaning. Their constant terms detect the central value in rank zero or a Heegner point in rank one. If the analytic nonvanishing sought at the base fails, then $u_0(0)=0$. The nonzero vertices instead satisfy $v(u_x(0))\le B_1$ with $B_1$ independent of $b$. The denominator analysis proves that, for every fixed integer $m$ and sufficiently large $b$, some $x\ne0$ satisfies $$v\bigl(u_x(0)-u_0(0)\bigr)\ge m.$$ Taking $m>B_1$ contradicts these two assertions. The work is to obtain this congruence with a dimension threshold independent of the number of new primes. Section <a href="#sec:binary-algebra" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:binary-algebra">11</a> does so after the new local blocks have been eliminated from the Selmer complex: a clearing factor for the remaining bounded complex makes finitely many coefficient congruences sufficient. Only that clearing factor needs a uniform pole bound; the numerator may involve the whole prime set.

<a id="pm-h-11"></a>
#### Transfer of a central value

<a id="eq:transfer-normalized-value"></a>
For a twist with nonzero central value, put $$\label{eq:transfer-normalized-value}
                  D(h)=v(\mathcal L(h))-2w(h)-s(h).$$ The subtraction records the local contributions of the ramified primes and the finite Selmer contribution. In the cyclotomic proof, Kato’s class and the invariant line at the real place form the determinant coordinate $u_x$. Its central valuation differs from $D(h_x)$ by a fixed bounded amount. Thus an upper bound on $D$ is exactly the arithmetic input to the preceding contradiction.

<a id="stmt-thm-cyclotomic-interpolation"></a>
<div id="thm:cyclotomic-interpolation" class="theorem">

<a id="eq:cy:cube"></a>
<a id="eq:cy:prime-bound"></a>
<a id="eq:cy:transferred-bound"></a>
**Theorem 8** (Cyclotomic missing vertex). *There is a constant $C_E$, depending only on $E$, with the following property. Fix an odd fundamental discriminant $h_0$, prime to $2N$, with $c_2(E^{(h_0)})=0$. Suppose that for arbitrarily large $b$ there is a family $$\label{eq:cy:cube}
 h_x=h_0\prod_{q\in\mathcal Q}(q^*)^{\lambda_q(x)},
 \qquad x\in\mathbb F_2^b,\qquad \lambda_q\in(\mathbb F_2^b)^*,$$ where $\mathcal Q$ consists of distinct primes outside $2Nh_0$, $q^*=(-1/q)q$, and every $h_x$ has the same sign and the same local squareclasses at $2N$. Assume that a constant $B$, independent of $b$, satisfies <a id="eq:cy:punctured-bound"></a>$$\label{eq:cy:punctured-bound}
 L(E^{(h_x)},1)\ne0,\qquad D(h_x)\le B\qquad(x\ne0).$$ If $E[2]$ is irreducible, assume also that some $L$, independent of $b$, satisfies $$\label{eq:cy:prime-bound}
 v_2(q^2-1)\le L\qquad(q\in\mathcal Q).$$ Then $L(E^{(h_0)},1)\ne0$ and $$\label{eq:cy:transferred-bound}
 D(h_0)\le B+C_E.$$ The necessary dimension may depend on $h_0$, its finite Selmer group, and the bound in Equation <a href="#eq:cy:prime-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:cy:prime-bound">[eq:cy:prime-bound]</a>; $C_E$ does not.*

</div>

The final constant $C_E$ bounds the specialization error. The finite Selmer group of the base and, in the irreducible case, the bound on $v_2(q^2-1)$ affect how large a cube is needed, but not this transferred error. We shall construct the nonzero vertices so that $v(\mathcal L(h_x))\le2w(h_x)+C$; since $s(h_x)\ge0$, this supplies the hypothesis on $D(h_x)$.

<a id="sec:h:statements"></a>
#### Transfer of a Heegner point

In corank one the coordinate comes from a Heegner point. The family must also carry a companion twist whose central value is nonzero. We first specify the two Heegner constructions whose indices enter the estimates.

Let $K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt{k})$, where $k<0$ is an odd fundamental discriminant and every prime dividing $2N$ splits in $K$. We omit the two fields with extra units and, if $E$ has complex multiplication, its CM field. Fix a nonzero modular parametrization $X_0(N)\to E$, translated so that the cusp $\infty$ maps to the origin, and compatible orientations of the Heegner points $y_c\in E(H_c)$, where $H_c$ is the ring class field of conductor $c$. The Manin–Drinfeld theorem makes the images of cusp differences torsion (Drinfeld 1973, sec. 1) <a id="pm-cite-47"></a>[[Drinfeld1973](#ref-Drinfeld1973)]. Since the modular curve and parametrization are fixed, one integer kills all these images and removes cuspidal ambiguities.

If $\chi_e|_{G_K}$ is a primitive ring class character of conductor $c$, write $P_c(e)$ for the character *sum* of $y_c$. Equivalently, twist over $H_c$ and trace to $E^{(e)}(K)$. If this latter group has rank one, $j(P_c(e))$ is the valuation of its index on the free rank-one lattice. Passing between this lattice and the rank-one lattice of the contributing curve among $E^{(e)}(\mathbb Q)$ and $E^{(ek)}(\mathbb Q)$ changes the index by a bounded amount: restriction and addition or subtraction of conjugates have composites multiplication by $2$.

We use two choices of data: $$\begin{aligned}
 \text{genus data:}\quad& k=h h_*,\quad (h,h_*)=1,
                         \quad e=h_*,\quad c=1,
                         \quad h_*\text{ fixed};\\
 \text{ring data:}\quad& (k,h)=1,\quad e=h,\quad c=|h|.
\end{aligned}$$ The character in genus data is unramified. In ring data, restriction at each $q\mid h$ has conductor exponent one: this follows by pulling the quadratic character back under the local norm. Thus these are the asserted primitive ring class conductors.

<a id="stmt-prop-heegner-comparison"></a>
<div id="prop:heegner-comparison" class="proposition">

<a id="eq:h:height"></a>
**Proposition 9** (Comparison of the two Heegner constructions). *For either set of data, $$\label{eq:h:height}
 \widehat h(P_c(e))
 =C_E\,c\sqrt{|k|}\,
       \left[L(E^{(e)},s)L(E^{(ek)},s)\right]'_{s=1},$$ with a fixed nonzero constant determined by the parametrization and height conventions. In particular, a simple zero of the product gives total Mordell–Weil rank one and finite Shafarevich–Tate groups.*

<a id="eq:h:index-comparison"></a>
<a id="eq:h:reverse-comparison"></a>
*Suppose $h$ has analytic rank one, and use genus data with a fixed partner $h_*$ of analytic rank zero and ring data with a possibly varying $k$, where $L(E^{(hk)},1)\ne0$. Then $$\label{eq:h:index-comparison}
 2j(P_{|h|}(h))-2j(P_1(h_*))
       =v(\mathcal L(hk))+O_{E,h_*}(1).$$ Here the two points are formed in their respective quadratic fields. If instead $h_*$ has analytic rank one and $L(E^{(h)},1)\ne0$, genus data give $$\label{eq:h:reverse-comparison}
 2j(P_1(h_*))=v(\mathcal L(h))+O_{E,h_*}(1).$$*

</div>

The genus construction varies the quadratic field $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{hh_*})$ while holding $h_*$ fixed. It is the construction detected by the odd coefficients below. Interpolation instead uses the ring construction: within one binary family the field $K$ is common to every vertex. Equation <a href="#eq:h:index-comparison" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:h:index-comparison">[eq:h:index-comparison]</a> converts a genus-index estimate and an even central-value estimate into the ring-index estimate needed for transfer. The field $K$ may change when a new family is chosen.

<a id="stmt-thm-heegner-interpolation"></a>
<div id="thm:heegner-interpolation" class="theorem">

**Theorem 10** (Heegner interpolation). *Fix $E$ and an initial discriminant $h_0$. Consider families $h_x$, $x\in\mathbb F_2^b$, obtained from $h_0$ by adjoining new prime factors with linear activation functions on $\mathbb F_2^b$. No old factor is removed; the signed factor belonging to an odd prime $q$ is $q^*=(-1/q)q$. Suppose the local twisting classes at $2N$ are constant. For each family let $k$ define an imaginary field satisfying the standing Heegner conditions, with $(k,h_x)=1$ for every $x$. Each new prime must either split in $K$ or satisfy $t_q=0$.*

*Assume that the following bounds are fixed independently of $b$:*

1.  *a bound for $\omega(k)$;*

2.  *a bound for the length of the finite quotient of $\mathop{\mathrm{Sel}}_{2^\infty}(E^{(h_0)}/K)$ by its divisible subgroup;*

3.  *a constant $B$.*

<a id="eq:h:interpolation-hypothesis"></a>
*Assume this base Selmer group has corank one. Suppose, for every $x\ne0$, the product $L(E^{(h_x)},s)L(E^{(h_xk)},s)$ has a simple zero and $$\label{eq:h:interpolation-hypothesis}
 2j(P_{|h_x|}(h_x))-4w(h_x)-s(h_x)-s(h_xk)\le B.$$ Then, for sufficiently large $b$, the base product has a simple zero. The dimension threshold depends only on the fixed base and the displayed bounds, not on the number or sizes of the new primes. The field $K$ may vary with the family.*

</div>

In these ring data, the relevant normalized quantity is $$2j(P_{|h|}(h))-4w(h)-s(h)-s(hk).$$ We use the theorem to prove nonvanishing at the base. In our applications, the genus-index and even central-value estimates will give $2j(P_{|h_x|}(h_x))\le4w(h_x)+C$ at every nonzero vertex. Subtracting the nonnegative Sha lengths supplies the required upper bound.

The finite-quotient condition allows two uses of the theorem. The rational-two-torsion argument fixes $K$ before increasing $b$. The irreducible argument lets $K$ vary and verifies the following criterion.

<a id="stmt-lem-h-base-selmer-bound"></a>
<div id="lem:h:base-selmer-bound" class="lemma">

**Lemma 11**. *The finite-quotient bound in Theorem <a href="#thm:heegner-interpolation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:heegner-interpolation">10</a> holds if $K$ belongs to a fixed finite collection. It also holds if $E^{(h_0)}$ is fixed with Selmer corank one, the curves $E^{(h_0k)}$ have analytic rank zero with bounded $s(h_0k)$, and $\omega(k)$ is bounded.*

</div>

<a id="pm-h-13"></a>
#### Lower bounds and the coefficient constructions

The transfer criteria ask for upper bounds at a well-chosen set of twists. To find those twists, we first need lower bounds on all the normalized coefficients under consideration. In even sign a least normalized valuation can then be selected, and a coefficient attaining it gives both analytic nonvanishing and an upper bound with a constant independent of the prime support. In odd sign the coefficients come at increasing finite precision: the minimum is defined through bounded-weight sequences, and each use is realized on a finite collection of indices.

For the even coefficient construction, Section <a href="#cs:coefficient-systems" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="cs:coefficient-systems">4</a> relates twice a coefficient valuation to $v(\mathcal L(h))$ up to a fixed constant. For the odd construction it relates the coefficient valuation to the genus index. The following three lower estimates supply the normalizations, with different roles in the two residual cases.

When $E[2]$ is reducible, the cyclotomic argument supplies the even lower estimate directly. By Lemma <a href="#pr:residual-cases" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="pr:residual-cases">6</a>, the representation is then an extension of two trivial modules.

<a id="stmt-thm-cyclotomic-bound"></a>
<div id="thm:cyclotomic-bound" class="theorem">

**Theorem 12** (Cyclotomic lower bound). *Suppose that $E[2]$ is an extension of two trivial $\mathbb F_2$-modules. There is a constant $C_E$ such that every odd fundamental discriminant $h$ prime to $2N$ with $L(E^{(h)},1)\ne0$ satisfies <a id="eq:cy:lower-bound"></a>$$\label{eq:cy:lower-bound}
 v(\mathcal L(h))\ge 2w(h)+s(h)-C_E.$$ The constant is independent of the number and sizes of the primes that divide $h$.*

</div>

When $E[2]$ is irreducible, the genus construction supplies the lower estimate for either sign. With an analytic-rank-zero fixed partner, it bounds the odd genus index. With an analytic-rank-one fixed partner, Equation <a href="#eq:h:reverse-comparison" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:h:reverse-comparison">[eq:h:reverse-comparison]</a> turns it into the even central-value bound.

<a id="stmt-thm-heegner-genus-bound"></a>
<div id="thm:heegner-genus-bound" class="theorem">

<a id="eq:h:genus-bound"></a>
**Theorem 13** (Genus bound). *In genus data, suppose the product in Equation <a href="#eq:h:height" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:h:height">[eq:h:height]</a> has a simple zero and $E[2]$ is irreducible. Then, uniformly in $h$, $$\label{eq:h:genus-bound}
 2j(P_1(h_*))\ge 2w(h)+s(h)-O_{E,h_*}(1).$$ In proving the uniform estimate, one may omit the finitely many $h$ for which $K$ meets $\mathbb Q(E[2])$ nontrivially.*

</div>

The remaining case is the odd coefficient construction with rational two-torsion. Here the genus estimate just stated is unavailable. We use instead the following ring estimate, whose residual representation is unrestricted.

<a id="stmt-thm-heegner-ring-bound"></a>
<div id="thm:heegner-ring-bound" class="theorem">

<a id="eq:h:ring-bound"></a>
**Theorem 14** (Ring bound). *In ring data, suppose the product in Equation <a href="#eq:h:height" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:h:height">[eq:h:height]</a> has a simple zero, every $q\mid h$ splits in $K$, and $\omega(k)\le a$, where $\omega$ counts distinct prime factors. Then $$\label{eq:h:ring-bound}
 2j(P_{|h|}(h))\ge
       4w(h)+s(h)+s(hk)-O_{E,a}(1).$$ There is no irreducibility assumption on $E[2]$.*

</div>

The passage from this ring estimate to an odd genus estimate is part of Proposition <a href="#prop:rational-odd-bound" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:rational-odd-bound">42</a>. The even coefficient construction first provides, for each already rank-one twist $h$ in the positive filter, a companion parameter $k'$ satisfying the ring-bound hypotheses: it is negative, odd fundamental, coprime to $2Nh$, a local square at every prime of $2Nh$, and defines a nonexceptional imaginary field. Its prime count is bounded, and the companion obeys $L(E^{(hk')},1)\ne0$ and $$v(\mathcal L(hk'))\le2w(hk')+s(hk')+C.$$ Substitute this upper bound into Equation <a href="#eq:h:index-comparison" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:h:index-comparison">[eq:h:index-comparison]</a> and the ring lower bound. Since $w(hk')=w(h)+w(k')$ and $w(k')$ is bounded, the result is $$2j(P_1(h_*))\ge2w(h)+s(h)-C'.$$ Only then is the odd coefficient system normalized in the reducible branch. Thus the lower-bound dependencies are $$\begin{array}{c@{\quad\longrightarrow\quad}l}
 \text{irreducible genus bound}&\text{even and odd coefficient bounds},\\[2pt]
 \text{reducible cyclotomic bound}&\text{even coefficients, then bounded companions},\\[2pt]
 \text{ring bound and those companions}&\text{reducible odd coefficient bound}.
 \end{array}$$ The reducible odd normalization is therefore available after the even companion construction. The all-split hypothesis belongs to the ring lower bound used here. The Heegner transfer criterion retains its stated alternative for new primes with $t_q=0$.

<a id="pm-h-14"></a>
#### Auxiliary twists in prescribed local classes

The coefficient constructions also require an auxiliary twist with specified local classes. For even sign the number of its prime factors must remain bounded as the local conditions vary. The following nonvanishing result supplies both kinds of partner; its proof is given in Section <a href="#sec:auxiliary-nonvanishing" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:auxiliary-nonvanishing">10</a>.

<a id="stmt-nv-local-witness"></a>
<div id="nv:local-witness" class="proposition">

**Proposition 15** (Auxiliary nonvanishing). *<span id="prop:rough-nonvanishing" label="prop:rough-nonvanishing"></span><span id="nv:rough" label="nv:rough"></span>Let $E/\mathbb Q$ have conductor $N$, and let $S$ be a finite set of primes containing the prime divisors of $2N$. Prescribe a real sign $\sigma\in\{1,-1\}$ and a unit squareclass $c_p\in\mathbb Z_p^\times/\mathbb Z_p^{\times2}$ for each $p\in S$. Suppose that these data are realized by an odd fundamental discriminant, and that twists in this filter have root number $\varepsilon$. For every finite set $B$ of primes there are odd fundamental discriminants $D$ of arbitrarily large absolute value such that $$\operatorname{sign}(D)=\sigma,\qquad [D]_p=c_p\quad(p\in S),\qquad
 p\nmid D\quad(p\in B),$$ Moreover:*

1.  *If $\varepsilon=1$, they can be chosen with $L(E^{(D)},1)\ne0$ and $\omega(|D|)\le5$.*

2.  *If $\varepsilon=-1$, they can be chosen with $L'(E^{(D)},1)\ne0$, so the central zero is simple.*

*The bound five in <span class="upright">(i)</span> is independent of $E,S,B$ and the prescribed classes. In either case, every prime factor of $D$ can be required to exceed any previously fixed bound.*

</div>

<a id="cs:coefficient-systems"></a>
### Coefficients that detect analytic rank

The interpolation theorems require nonvanishing with a uniform valuation bound at the nonzero vertices of a cube. We encode both requirements in one binary coefficient: it is one when a modular coefficient has the least normalized valuation. Waldspurger’s formula supplies the even-sign coefficients; reduction of genus Heegner sums supplies the odd-sign coefficients at finite precision. We prove their modular and arithmetic properties separately before choosing this normalization.

<a id="pm-h-16"></a>
#### Filters and prime weights

Fix $E/\mathbb Q$ and a finite set $S$ containing the primes of $2N$ and the ramification set of $F=\mathbb Q(E[2])$. Additional fixed primes may be included. A *filter* consists of a sign $\sigma\in\{1,-1\}$ and unit squareclasses at the primes in $S$, imposed on positive squarefree integers $D$ prime to $S$, so that $$h=\sigma D$$ is an odd fundamental discriminant and the functional sign of $E^{(h)}$ is constant. Multiplication by squares of units preserves the local conditions. We impose these conditions on all Fourier indices, not only on squarefree ones. Projections onto the required unit squareclasses are finite combinations of quadratic coefficient twists and coprimality projections; they enlarge the level only at $S$.

For $p\notin S$, the action on $V=E[2]$ has the following three types: $$\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\text{type}&\mathop{\mathrm{Fr}}_p|_V&\text{weight}\\ \hline
\text{split}&1&1\\
\text{simple}&\text{an element of order }2&1/2\\
\text{root}&\text{an element of order }3&0.
\end{array}$$ Thus $w(D)=\frac12\sum_{p\mid D}\dim_{\mathbf F_2}V^{\mathop{\mathrm{Fr}}_p}=w(h)$. The fractional part of $w(D)$ is constant on a filter: it is determined by the quadratic discriminant character of the residual representation. For an arbitrary squarefree set of primes we use the same additive weight. Signs are encoded by $p^*=(-1/p)p$, so that $h=\prod_{p\mid D}p^*$.

We use the ordinary theta multiplier cubed in weight $3/2$. A finite idele unit character and its Dirichlet character are related by the reciprocal convention: if a finite Schwartz function obeys $f(ux)=\alpha(u)f(x)$, its scalar classical character on the lower-right entry is associated to $\alpha^{-1}$. All valuations satisfy $v(2)=1$.

<a id="pm-h-17"></a>
#### The even coefficient system

<a id="stmt-co-even"></a>
<div id="co:even" class="proposition">

**Proposition 16** (Even coefficients). *<span id="prop:even-coefficients" label="prop:even-coefficients"></span>Fix a nonempty filter with even functional sign. There are a holomorphic weight-$3/2$ cusp form $$g=\sum_{n\geq1}a(n)q^n$$ of level supported on $S$, after enlarging exponents at those primes, and finite-order characters $\psi,\eta$ of $2$-power order, with $\psi/\eta$ quadratic, having the following properties.*

<a id="cs:hecke-recurrence"></a>
1.  *The coefficients vanish off the filter and, for $p\notin S$, $$a(p^2n)=\bigl(\eta(p)a_p(E)-\psi(p)(-n/p)\bigr)a(n)
                       -p\eta(p)^2a(n/p^2).
    \label{cs:hecke-recurrence}$$ As usual a coefficient with a nonintegral index is zero.*

<a id="cs:even-ratio"></a>
<a id="cs:even-value"></a>
2.  *After normalizing at one nonzero squarefree index, every squarefree coefficient in the filter is a rational number times a root of unity of $2$-power order. For a fixed nonzero squarefree index $D_0$, $$2v\left(\frac{a(D)}{a(D_0)}\right)
     =v\left(\frac{\mathcal L(\sigma D)}{\mathcal L(\sigma D_0)}\right)
     \quad\text{whenever }a(D)\ne0.
    \label{cs:even-ratio}$$ Equivalently, there is a constant $c_g$, independent of $D$, such that $$2v(a(D))=v\bigl({\cal L}(h)\bigr)+c_g.
    \label{cs:even-value}$$ In particular $a(D)\ne0$ if and only if $L(E^{(h)},1)\ne0$.*

<a id="cs:even-lower-bound"></a>
3.  *After the fixed auxiliary exclusions described below, there is a constant $C_g$ such that, at every nonzero squarefree coefficient, $$v(a(D))\geq w(D)+\tfrac12s(h)-C_g.
    \label{cs:even-lower-bound}$$ The constants depend on the fixed curve, filter and auxiliary choices, and not on $D$ or its number of prime factors.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-co-even"><summary>Proof of stmt-co-even</summary>

*Proof.* We first choose the packet member and its local characters. We then establish the rationality up to phase needed for valuation comparisons, apply the coefficient-square formula, and deduce the uniform lower bound from the interpolation estimates.

Use the Shimura packet attached to the integral-weight newform of $E^{(-\sigma)}$. In the classical convention its positive Fourier index $D$ tests the twist by $\chi_{-D}$, hence the curve $E^{(\sigma D)}$. The packet and Fourier coefficient results of Waldspurger (1980, 1981) <a id="pm-cite-48"></a>[[Waldspurger1980](#ref-Waldspurger1980), [Waldspurger1981](#ref-Waldspurger1981)] apply to the cuspidal packet orthogonal to unary theta series. Their local uniqueness and global multiplicity assertions are summarized in (Waldspurger 1984, sec. 3.1 and 5.1) <a id="pm-cite-49"></a>[[Waldspurger1983](#ref-Waldspurger1983)]. A nonzero central value in the filter exists by Proposition <a href="#prop:rough-nonvanishing" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:rough-nonvanishing">[prop:rough-nonvanishing]</a>. It selects a globally occurring packet member with nonzero Fourier functional at that index. At good odd primes choose spherical vectors; at infinity choose the holomorphic vector of weight $3/2$.

We explain the choices at a prime of $S$. Let $\lambda_D$ be a nonzero local Fourier functional and start with a vector on which it is nonzero. Average upper-unipotent translates against the inverse additive character of frequency $D$. If the averaging compact subgroup is sufficiently large, its translate by a unit scale $u$ can contribute only when $u^2$ is sufficiently close to $1$. The surviving scales are consequently small neighborhoods of $1$ and $-1$. Local constancy then permits projection onto a unit character which matches the forced action of $-1$, without killing the Fourier value: the contributions of the two neighborhoods add. Such a character may be chosen to have $2$-power order. Indeed only its parity is prescribed, and the $2$-primary quotient of the unit group realizes either possible parity. Upper averaging at integral frequency gives period one, and lower-unipotent invariance holds at sufficiently large depth. These vectors therefore give a classical form at a level supported on $S$. The parity conditions combine correctly by automorphy. The subsequent squareclass projections preserve its character. Write that character as $\psi$.

In the theta-multiplier convention the good eigenvalues of the packet are $\psi(p)$ times those of $E^{(-\sigma)}$. Set $\eta=\psi\chi_{-\sigma}$. Then $\psi/\eta$ is quadratic and the weight-$3/2$ Hecke formula gives Equation <a href="#cs:hecke-recurrence" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="cs:hecke-recurrence">[cs:hecke-recurrence]</a>.

We need more than algebraicity of the coefficients. After normalization at one squarefree index, their nonzero squarefree valuations must be integers, so that a strict valuation inequality gains a full factor of $2$, even when the character field is ramified. We prove this by showing that every such coefficient is rational up to a phase of $2$-power order. At the fixed level, the weight-$3/2$ cusp space with character $\psi$ has a basis over the field of character values, and coefficient conjugation changes $\psi$ to its conjugate (Shimura 1981, sec. 2, Lemma 4(3)–(4), pp. 658–659) <a id="pm-cite-50"></a>[[Shimura1981CriticalValues](#ref-Shimura1981CriticalValues)]. The good Hecke equations and the vanishing of coefficients off the filter are linear equations over $\mathbb Q(\psi,\eta)$. In a finite-dimensional space, finitely many of these equations cut out their full common kernel. The constructed complex vector has a nonzero coefficient at a squarefree index $D_0$ of the filter, so this coefficient functional is nonzero on some algebraic vector in that kernel. Choose such a vector. It remains orthogonal to unary theta series: at good primes their eigenvalues have absolute value $p+1$, whereas the prescribed eigenvalues have absolute value at most $2\sqrt p$ by Hasse’s bound (Purkait 2013, sec. 2, Lemma 2.1, and Corollary 5.2) <a id="pm-cite-51"></a>[[Purkait2012](#ref-Purkait2012)].

We use Waldspurger (1981, Corollary 2, pp. 483–484) <a id="pm-cite-52"></a>[[Waldspurger1981](#ref-Waldspurger1981)] to compare Fourier coefficients. Its hypothesis (H1) holds for every nonzero classical eigenspace used here, by Proposition 2 of that paper. The final paragraph of the corollary’s proof removes (H2) when the indices lie in the same local squareclass at every level prime. Our filters retain this condition at $2$ as well as at the odd primes.

Let $u$ be an automorphism of $\overline\mathbb Q$ acting by an odd power $e$ on the $2$-power characters, and put $\nu=\eta^{(e-1)/2}$. The coefficient conjugate $g^u$ and coefficient twist $g\otimes\nu$ have exactly the same character and good Hecke system, since $$\psi\nu^2=\psi\eta^{e-1}=\psi^e,
                 \qquad \eta\nu^2=\eta^e.$$ They may be compared at a common level supported on $S$, in the same good Hecke eigenspace $W$, and both have a nonzero $D_0$-coefficient. Let $\ell_n:W\to\mathbb C$ denote the $n$th Fourier-coefficient functional. Waldspurger’s corollary applies to every $f\in W$ and gives $$\ell_D(f)^2=C_D\ell_{D_0}(f)^2,$$ where $C_D$ is independent of $f$. If $C_D=0$, then $\ell_D=0$. Otherwise choose $c_D\in\mathbb C$ with $c_D^2=C_D$ and factor the identity as $$(\ell_D-c_D\ell_{D_0})(\ell_D+c_D\ell_{D_0})=0.$$ The polynomial ring on $W$ is an integral domain, so one factor vanishes identically. Thus the two coefficient functionals are proportional on the whole space, including oldvectors and linear combinations. In particular the two forms have the same ratio of their $D$- and $D_0$-coefficients.

It follows, for $\xi=a(D)/a(D_0)$, that $$u(\xi)=\nu(D/D_0)\xi.$$ The local squareclass conditions imply $\eta(D/D_0)=z^2$ for a value $z$ in the group of values of $\eta$. Consequently $u(\xi/z)=\xi/z$ for every $u$, so $\xi/z\in\mathbb Q$. This proves the phase assertion.

With our characters and period normalization, its identity of *coefficient squares* is <a id="cs:even-square-ratio"></a>$$\left(\frac{a(D)}{a(D_0)}\right)^2
 =\psi(D/D_0)\,
   \frac{\mathcal L(\sigma D)}{\mathcal L(\sigma D_0)}.
 \label{cs:even-square-ratio}$$ Here $\psi(D/D_0)=\psi(D)\psi(D_0)^{-1}$ has valuation zero; the factor $\sqrt{D/D_0}$ in the classical central-value comparison is incorporated in $\mathcal L$. The local unit squareclasses at $S$ agree; at a good prime the spherical squarefree factor is one at both valuations zero and one (Waldspurger 1981, sec. I.3, pp. 377–378) <a id="pm-cite-53"></a>[[Waldspurger1981](#ref-Waldspurger1981)]. There is consequently no extra product over the prime factors of $D$. Taking valuations gives Equation <a href="#cs:even-ratio" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="cs:even-ratio">[cs:even-ratio]</a>, hence Equation <a href="#cs:even-value" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="cs:even-value">[cs:even-value]</a>. The same identity, compared with the nonzero coefficient at $D_0$, gives the asserted equivalence of vanishing. The corresponding rational-square statement for central values is Vignéras’s rationality theorem, recalled in Waldspurger (1984, sec. 6.3, Theorem 6) <a id="pm-cite-54"></a>[[Waldspurger1983](#ref-Waldspurger1983)].

If $E[2]$ is an extension of trivial modules, combine Equation <a href="#cs:even-value" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="cs:even-value">[cs:even-value]</a> with Theorem <a href="#thm:cyclotomic-bound" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:cyclotomic-bound">12</a>. If $E[2]$ is irreducible, choose a fixed odd fundamental discriminant $h_*$ of opposite infinite sign, of analytic rank one, whose local characters agree with those of $h$ at $2N$. Proposition <a href="#prop:rough-nonvanishing" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:rough-nonvanishing">[prop:rough-nonvanishing]</a> supplies such a choice. Exclude its prime factors from the filter and choose its support to avoid the finitely many exceptional genus fields. The reverse genus comparison in Proposition <a href="#prop:heegner-comparison" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:heegner-comparison">9</a> and Theorem <a href="#thm:heegner-genus-bound" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:heegner-genus-bound">13</a> give the same lower bound. These are fixed exclusions and constants, proving Equation <a href="#cs:even-lower-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="cs:even-lower-bound">[cs:even-lower-bound]</a> in both cases. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-18"></a>
#### Odd coefficients from reduction of Heegner traces

The odd construction combines reduction of Heegner points with the ternary quadratic forms attached to definite quaternion orders. We use Deuring’s reduction correspondence in the oriented form of Cornut–Jetchev, together with the Eichler-order and ternary-form description of Jetchev–Kane (Deuring 1941; Cornut and Jetchev 2013; Jetchev and Kane 2011) <a id="pm-cite-55"></a>[[Deuring1941](#ref-Deuring1941), [CornutJetchev2013](#ref-CornutJetchev2013), [JetchevKane2011](#ref-JetchevKane2011)]. The weights below retain the genus character and the local orientations, so that the resulting Fourier coefficients recover the reduced genus sum at finite precision.

Fix now a nonempty filter of odd functional sign. Choose an odd fundamental $h_*$ of opposite infinite sign, with $L(E^{(h_*)},1)\ne0$, whose local characters agree with those of $h$ at $2N$. Exclude its primes. We may choose $|h_*|>3$ and include in its support a prime outside the exceptional imaginary quadratic discriminants. Thus all genus fields below have only the units $\{1,-1\}$ and avoid the CM field of $E$. Write $$k=hh_*<0,\qquad K_D=\mathbb Q(\sqrt{k}),\qquad
          P_D=P_1(h_*).$$ The point $P_D$ is the character *sum* of the conductor-one Heegner point for $K_D$. We fix the modular parametrization $\varphi$ with $\varphi(\infty)=0$, so the constants in its Hecke and Atkin–Lehner relations are torsion. At a simple zero of $E^{(h)}$, its free line is that of $E^{(h)}$, up to the fixed-degree identifications in Proposition <a href="#prop:heegner-comparison" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:heegner-comparison">9</a>. Below, the product derivative means the derivative at $s=1$ of $L(E^{(h)},s)L(E^{(h_*)},s)$.

<a id="stmt-co-odd"></a>
<div id="co:odd" class="proposition">

<a id="cs:odd-bound-hypothesis"></a>
**Proposition 17** (Odd coefficients under a genus-index bound). *<span id="prop:odd-coefficients" label="prop:odd-coefficients"></span>Assume that a constant $C_*$ satisfies $$j(P_D)\geq w(D)+\tfrac12s(h)-C_*
\label{cs:odd-bound-hypothesis}$$ for every $h$ in the filter with a simple zero. There are arbitrarily large precisions $M$, good odd primes $\ell$ outside the fixed support, and holomorphic weight-$3/2$ forms $g_M=\sum a_M(n)q^n$, of level supported on $S\cup\{\ell\}$, with the following properties.*

<a id="cs:detecting-prime"></a>
1.  *The additional filter at $\ell$ is $$(h_*/\ell)=-\sigma,\qquad (h/\ell)=\sigma,
                   \qquad \rho_T(\mathop{\mathrm{Fr}}_\ell)\equiv C\pmod{2^M},
    \label{cs:detecting-prime}$$ where $C$ is the action of a complex conjugation. In particular $\ell\equiv-1\pmod{2^M}$.*

2.  *After a fixed harmless decrease in the working precision, the forms satisfy Equation <a href="#cs:hecke-recurrence" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="cs:hecke-recurrence">[cs:hecke-recurrence]</a> modulo that precision, with characters $\eta_M,\psi_M$ of $2$-power order and quadratic ratio. Their squarefree coefficients have the form of a $2$-power phase times an integer modulo $2^M$.*

<a id="cs:odd-detection"></a>
<a id="cs:odd-lower-bound"></a>
3.  *If a coefficient is visible, meaning $v(a_M(D))<M$, then $E^{(h)}$ has a simple zero and $$j(P_D)\leq v(a_M(D))+C_1.
    \label{cs:odd-detection}$$ For every admissible $D$ the coefficient lower bound is $$v(a_M(D))\geq
           \min\{M,\,w(D)+\tfrac12s(h)-C_2\}
    \label{cs:odd-lower-bound}$$ when the product derivative is nonzero; if it is zero, the coefficient is zero modulo $2^M$. Here $C_1,C_2$ are independent of $\ell,M,D$.*

4.  *A fixed squarefree witness $D_w$ in the original filter is admissible at every chosen $\ell$ and has $v(a_M(D_w))$ bounded as $M\to\infty$.*

*For irreducible $E[2]$, the hypothesis is Theorem <a href="#thm:heegner-genus-bound" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:heegner-genus-bound">13</a>. For rational two-torsion, the positive filters used in the pointwise argument have this bound by Proposition <a href="#prop:rational-odd-bound" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:rational-odd-bound">42</a>, using only the even source. An arbitrary twist is first absorbed into the fixed curve, so only these positive filters are needed there.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-co-odd"><summary>Proof of stmt-co-odd</summary>

*Proof.* The proof has three stages. A reduction map detects one fixed nonzero genus point at arbitrarily high precisions. Weighted theta series then supply holomorphic forms with the required Hecke recurrence. Finally, an exact comparison with genus sums transfers point divisibility and the assumed lower bound to their squarefree coefficients.

<a id="pm-h-19"></a>
###### The reduction map and a detecting sequence.

Choose a nonzero integral row $b$ with $bC=\sigma b$. Under Equation <a href="#cs:detecting-prime" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="cs:detecting-prime">[cs:detecting-prime]</a>, finite-field Kummer theory gives $$\kappa_M:E(\mathbf F_{\ell^2})\longrightarrow
 H^1(\mathbf F_{\ell^2},E[2^M])
       =E[2^M]/(\mathop{\mathrm{Fr}}_\ell^2-1)E[2^M]=E[2^M].$$ The last identification is evaluation at arithmetic Frobenius squared. Put $\lambda_M=b\kappa_M$. This map has Frobenius sign $\sigma$.

Choose $h_w=\sigma D_w$ in the original filter with a simple zero, using Proposition <a href="#prop:rough-nonvanishing" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:rough-nonvanishing">[prop:rough-nonvanishing]</a>. A fixed multiple of its genus point is a nonzero point on the rational curve $E^{(h_w)}$. Its division cocycle has open translation image on the kernel of the Tate action, even after fixed finite auxiliary fields have been adjoined. Here is the relevant argument. The translation image is a Galois-stable $\mathbb Z_2$-submodule of the Tate module. Its rational span is nonzero: otherwise the point’s Kummer class would factor through the Tate image; that image has a central nonidentity scalar, which kills its rational first cohomology, contradicting Kummer injectivity. The rational Tate representation is irreducible by Serre (1968, chap. IV, Section 2.1, pp. IV-9–IV-10) <a id="pm-cite-56"></a>[[Serre1968](#ref-Serre1968)], since $\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb Q}(E)=\mathbb Z$. This includes curves with geometric complex multiplication, whose nonreal endomorphisms are not defined over $\mathbb Q$. The scalar Lie-algebra assertion of Bogomolov (1981, sec. 2, Theorem 3, p. 62) <a id="pm-cite-57"></a>[[Bogomolov1981](#ref-Bogomolov1981)], followed by local logarithm and exponential, supplies the required nonidentity scalar. The nonzero stable span is therefore the whole Tate module. The translation image consequently contains a full lattice. Passing to a finite-index subgroup preserves this fact.

Take an element acting as $C$ on $T$ and as complex conjugation on the fixed quadratic character fields, and modify it by such a translation. On the twisted module for $h_w$ its action is $\sigma C$; at its square the cocycle includes $1+\sigma C$. Projection by $b$ is twice the corresponding nonzero row. We can therefore arrange nonzero detection with a fixed finite valuation. Chebotarev, applied at successive finite precisions to this fixed compatible Galois element and its division data, supplies arbitrarily large primes satisfying Equation <a href="#cs:detecting-prime" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="cs:detecting-prime">[cs:detecting-prime]</a>, also with $h=h_w$, and the asserted bounded detection. A congruence on the target curve’s Frobenius is all that is required. The supersingular objects used next are points of the modular curve, not an additional reduction hypothesis on $E$.

<a id="pm-h-20"></a>
###### Supersingular values and local weights.

Let $B$ be the quaternion algebra ramified at $\ell$ and infinity, and let $R$ be an Eichler order of level $N$. Supersingular pairs on $X_0(N)$ are parametrized by $$B^\times\backslash\widehat B^\times/
                  \widehat R^\times.$$ They are defined over $\mathbf F_{\ell^2}$. The reduction and Eichler order description apply to arbitrary $N$ prime to $\ell$; see (Jetchev and Kane 2011, secs. 1.1–1.2 and 2.5) <a id="pm-cite-58"></a>[[JetchevKane2011](#ref-JetchevKane2011)]. For a representative $z$ write $R_z=B\cap z\widehat Rz^{-1}$ and let $P_M(z)$ be the reduced modular-parametrization value followed by $\lambda_M$. The cusp differences have torsion image by Drinfeld (1973, sec. 1) <a id="pm-cite-59"></a>[[Drinfeld1973](#ref-Drinfeld1973)]. Multiply the parametrization once by a fixed integer $L$ killing the cuspidal constants in its Hecke and Atkin–Lehner relations and the bounded-degree torsion occurring in genus sums. This choice is independent of $D,\ell,M$.

The resulting $P_M$ has good Brandt eigenvalues $a_p(E)$, level Atkin–Lehner eigenvalues $w_{p^e}$ for $p^e\Vert N$, and eigenvalue $\sigma$ for the right uniformizer at $\ell$. These identities hold modulo $2^M$. Choose integer representatives of its values when making an ordinary characteristic-zero theta series.

On $B^0$, the trace-zero subspace, use the positive definite quadratic form $Q(x)=-x^2=\mathop{\mathrm{Nrd}}(x)$. Our aim is to make the squarefree coefficient $a_M(D)$ equal, modulo $2^M$ and up to a phase of $2$-power order, to a fixed integer multiple of $$\lambda_M\bigl(\operatorname{red}_{\ell}(L P_D)\bigr).$$ We will identify its terms with optimal embeddings of $\mathcal O_{K_D}$. Their local orientations give several copies of the genus sum. The weights must make those copies contribute equally, while their unit-scaling law must give a scalar modular character. The weighted trace calculation below will determine the exact multiplier.

Define a finite compactly supported, locally constant weight $f=\prod f_p$ as follows; a value not satisfying a listed condition is zero.

1.  Away from $2Nh_*\ell$, require order integrality and put $f_p=1$.

2.  At $2$, require $(1+x)/2$ to be integral and $x^2$ to be a split fundamental unit squareclass. At $p^e\Vert N$, require the split fundamental unit type and its order embedding. The cyclic Eichler level line selects one of the two eigenroots $r$ of $x$; weight it by a $2$-power unit character $\eta_p(r)$ with $$\eta_p(-1)=w_{p^e}\chi_{h_*}(p)^e.$$ If $p=2$, use the selected summand of $(1+x)/2$, whose eigenvalues $(1+r)/2$ and $(1-r)/2$ differ by the odd unit $r$. Scaling by an odd $u$ sends this operator to $u(1+x)/2+(1-u)/2$ and preserves that summand; its selected root for $ux$ is $ur$. Thus the weight changes by $\eta_2(u)$, even when the two eigenvalue parities interchange. If $2\nmid N$, impose only the stated integrality restriction.

3.  At $p\mid h_*$ require integral $x$ with determinant of valuation one. Its reduction is nonzero nilpotent. On that orbit use the sign which transforms by $(\det u/p)$ under conjugation by $u\in\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}_2(\mathbf Z_p)$. This sign exists because the stabilizer of a nonzero nilpotent has the form $aI+bX$ and determinant $a^2$. Scaling $x$ by a unit $u$ changes this sign by $(u/p)$.

4.  At $\ell$ require integral unit norm and the unramified quadratic type. Choose a basis of the trace-zero line in $\mathbf F_{\ell^2}$ and weight the nonzero residue on that line by its Legendre symbol relative to the basis.

All these conditions may be imposed at finite depth. They are stable under unit scaling. Right order-unit conjugation changes $f$ by the inverse of $\chi_{h_*}\circ\mathop{\mathrm{Nrd}}$, exactly canceling the norm character below. At $\ell$, order units commute on the residue field, while a uniformizer negates its trace-zero line. Since $\ell\equiv-1\pmod4$, the latter weight changes by $-1$.

Write $\alpha_B=\prod_p\alpha_p$ for the finite unit-scaling character, so that $f(ux)=\alpha_B(u)f(x)$. Define the classical Dirichlet character $\eta_B$ by $$\eta_B(d)=\prod_p\alpha_p(d)
 \qquad\text{for integers }d\text{ prime to the support}.$$ The associated finite idele character restricts to $\alpha_B^{-1}$ on the ramified unit groups, in accordance with our reciprocal convention. Both characters are even. Indeed their value on $-1$ is $$\left(\prod_{p^e\Vert N}w_{p^e}\chi_{h_*}(p)^e\right)
                      \chi_{h_*}(-1)(-1)=1,$$ by the even functional sign of $E^{(h_*)}$. The characters have $2$-power order.

<a id="pm-h-21"></a>
###### Transformation and good Hecke relation.

<a id="cs:weighted-theta"></a>
Choose a fixed positive integer $c_0$ divisible by the orders of all unit groups which occur. Such a choice is uniform: a unit group of a rational definite quaternion order has bounded order. Form $$H_M(n)=c_0\sum_z\frac{P_M(z)\chi_{h_*}(\mathop{\mathrm{Nrd}}z)}{|R_z^\times|}
             \sum_{\substack{x\in B^0\\-x^2=n}}f(z^{-1}xz),
 \qquad H_M(\tau)=\sum_{n\geq1}H_M(n)q^n.
\label{cs:weighted-theta}$$ The norm character is trivial on rational $B^\times$, since its rational reduced norms are positive. The right transformation just checked makes Equation <a href="#cs:weighted-theta" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="cs:weighted-theta">[cs:weighted-theta]</a> independent of the representatives.

For scalar modularity, apply the Weil representation of $(B^0,Q)$ to $f$ and the Gaussian at infinity (Weil 1964) <a id="pm-cite-60"></a>[[Weil1964](#ref-Weil1964)]. At a finite prime, with the additive character of conductor $\mathbb Z_p$, the local formulas are (Pal and Vera-Piquero 2019, sec. 4.3, pp. 1965–1966) <a id="pm-cite-61"></a>[[PalDeVeraPiquero2019](#ref-PalDeVeraPiquero2019)] $$\begin{aligned}
 \omega(n(b))f_p(x)&=\mathbf e_p(bQ(x))f_p(x),\\
 \omega(m(u))f_p(x)&=\gamma_p(u)|u|_p^{3/2}f_p(ux),
 &\omega(w)f_p&=\gamma_p\widehat f_p.
 \end{aligned}$$ Here $n(b)=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&b\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, $m(u)=\operatorname{diag}(u,u^{-1})$, and $w$ is the Weyl element. Integral $b$ fixes $f_p$, since $Q$ is integral on its support. Choose a lattice of translation invariance for $f_p$; its dual contains the support of $\widehat f_p$. For sufficiently large $a_p$, the form $p^{a_p}Q$ is integral on that dual lattice. Thus $n(p^{a_p}b)$ fixes $\widehat f_p$, and conjugation by $w$ proves invariance under sufficiently deep lower unipotents. This argument also works at $2$ and at arbitrary finite character depth.

Compare with the threefold ordinary-theta reference line, using the same additive character and lifts. In a presentation $B=(-a,-b)$, the quadratic form is $aX^2+bY^2+abZ^2$. The ratio of its diagonal Weil factor to the reference factor is $$(a,u)_p(b,u)_p(ab,u)_p=((ab)^2,u)_p=1.$$ This calculation holds also over $\mathbb Q_2$. The remaining local diagonal scalar is therefore $\alpha_p(u)$. Upper unipotents, diagonal units, and sufficiently deep lower unipotents generate the required local $\Gamma_0$ subgroup: explicitly, for $a$ a unit, $$\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}
 =n^-(c/a)m(a)n(b/a).$$ Choose the depths also to serve the ordinary-theta reference line and the character conductors. The central ambiguity of the metaplectic lifts cancels in the comparison, since both representations have the same odd central action. At the chosen depth, $a$ is congruent to $d^{-1}$ modulo the character conductor, so the local right eigenvalue is $\alpha_p(d)^{-1}$. Classical restriction uses the inverse finite component and consequently gives the character $\eta_B(d)$. Conjugation by $z$ preserves $Q$ and commutes with the Weil action, so all summands have this same level and scalar character. At good odd primes the lattice is spherical. The Gaussian gives weight $3/2$, and positive definiteness gives holomorphy at every cusp. Thus $H_M$ is a classical form of level supported on $2Nh_*\ell$.

At a prime $p\nmid 2Nh_*\ell$, the neighbor relation has Hecke eigenvalue $$\eta_B(p)\chi_{h_*}(p)a_p(E).$$ The factor $\chi_{h_*}(p)$ comes from the reduced norm of a Brandt neighbor and $\eta_B(p)$ from scaling at the other primes.

The multiplicities can be read directly in a matrix order. Put $y=px$. If $y$ is primitive and $Q(y)$ is divisible by $p^2$, its nonzero nilpotent reduction has a unique invariant line; in a basis adapted to that line the other off-diagonal entry is divisible by $p^2$, so exactly one neighbor makes $y/p$ integral. If $y/p$ is integral, its reduction has $1+(-Q(y/p)/p)$ invariant lines, except that a zero reduction has a further $p$ lines. These are precisely the middle and last terms of the weight-$3/2$ Hecke recurrence. The factors $|R_z^\times|^{-1}$ are the orbit-stabilizer factors making the Brandt transfer valid. Since the eigenrelation for $P_M$ holds modulo $2^M$, so does this relation for $H_M$.

Put $d=|h_*|$. The weights force $Q(x)$ to be divisible by $d$. Before the final filter projections, the series with coefficients $a_M(n)=H_M(dn)$ is the same weighted theta sum for $Q/d$. Its ternary determinant changes by $d^{-3}$, whose squareclass is $d$; hence the scalar character acquires $(d/\cdot)$. Substitution of $dn$ in the good-prime recurrence leaves $\eta_B\chi_{h_*}$ unchanged. Now apply the filter projections. Extraction of these multiples changes the character to $\psi_M=\eta_B( |h_*|/\cdot)$, while $\eta_M=\eta_B\chi_{h_*}$ is the good eigenvalue character. Their quotient is quadratic. The neighbor relation therefore becomes Equation <a href="#cs:hecke-recurrence" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="cs:hecke-recurrence">[cs:hecke-recurrence]</a>. Every operation has level supported on $S\cup\{\ell\}$.

<a id="pm-h-22"></a>
###### The weighted trace identity.

The form and its recurrence are now constructed. We next identify a squarefree coefficient with the reduction of the original genus sum, keeping the orientation multiplicities and unit stabilizers explicit.

For a squarefree $D$ in the filter, put $n=|h_*|D=-k$. An $x$ counted in Equation <a href="#cs:weighted-theta" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="cs:weighted-theta">[cs:weighted-theta]</a> is exactly an optimal embedding of the full order $\mathcal O_{K_D}$ into $R_z$, by sending $\sqrt{k}$ to $x$. At $2$ the generator is $(1+\sqrt{k})/2$, which is why the integrality condition above is necessary. At a split level prime there are two choices of cyclic level orientation, and at $\ell$ there are two choices of unramified quadratic orientation. There is one local orbit at the remaining primes. The split-level assertion follows by decomposing a stable lattice into its two idempotent summands: a cyclic quotient of order $p^e$ forces all of that quotient into one summand. The division-prime assertion follows from the two reduced-norm parity cosets. At primes outside $2Nh_*\ell$, stable lattices are the fractional ideals of the quadratic order, giving the single local orbit.

Fix one orientation tuple and a rational embedding $x_0$. The corresponding global optimal-embedding orbits are parametrized by $\mathop{\mathrm{Pic}}(\mathcal O_{K_D})$. Explicitly, once one adelic representative $z_0$ is fixed, the representatives are $z_{\mathfrak a}=a z_0$ with $a\in\widehat K_D^\times$; changing $a$ by $K_D^\times$ or $\widehat{\mathcal O}_{K_D}^{\times}$ gives exactly the same class. Because $a$ commutes with $x_0$, the Schwartz factor is constant along this class-group orbit. Its remaining relative weight is $$\chi_{h_*}(\mathop{\mathrm{Nrd}}a)
              =\chi_{h_*}(\operatorname{Norm}_{K_D/\mathbb Q}a),$$ the unramified genus character. This computation establishes the weighted identity, rather than merely an unweighted correspondence.

For completeness the stabilizer factor is also exact. Each orbit of embeddings in a given $R_z$ has $|R_z^\times|/|\mathcal O_{K_D}^\times|=|R_z^\times|/2$ elements. Thus its contribution after division by $|R_z^\times|$ is one half of the corresponding class-group term. These are oriented embeddings, not conjugate pairs: $x$ and $-x$ have opposite orientations at $\ell$ and cannot be conjugate by an order unit, whose residue conjugation on $\mathbf F_{\ell^2}$ is trivial. CM reduction at the inert prime identifies these terms with the reductions of the Heegner points and commutes with ideal action; the cyclic subgroup carries the selected level orientation. Fixing the residue-field identification at $\ell$ retains its orientation in the reduction-to-embedding correspondence of Deuring (1941) <a id="pm-cite-62"></a>[[Deuring1941](#ref-Deuring1941)]; see (Cornut and Jetchev 2013, arXiv version 1, Theorem 3.1, Corollary 3.2, and Section 3.6, Remark 1) <a id="pm-cite-63"></a>[[CornutJetchev2013](#ref-CornutJetchev2013)] and (Jetchev and Kane 2011, secs. 2.4–2.6 and 4.1) <a id="pm-cite-64"></a>[[JetchevKane2011](#ref-JetchevKane2011)]. The former remark explains that forgetting this identification identifies conjugate embeddings. Here both orientations remain in the theta sum.

<a id="cs:weighted-trace-identity"></a>
Choose the initial orientation to agree with the Heegner point defining $P_D$. The constant weight on its orbit is a phase $\zeta_M(D)\in\mu_{2^\infty}$, since all its local weights are units. Changing orientation at $p^e\Vert N$ multiplies the Schwartz factor by $w_{p^e}\chi_{h_*}(p)^e$, and multiplies the norm-character-weighted parametrization value by the same sign. At $\ell$ both signs are $-1$, since $\sigma\chi_{h_*}(\ell)=-1$. Hence every one of the $2^{\omega(N)+1}$ orientation tuples contributes the same term. With the fixed multiplier $L$ already incorporated into $P_M$, the comparison is consequently $$a_M(D)=c_0\,2^{\omega(N)}\zeta_M(D)\,
           \lambda_M\bigl(\operatorname{red}_{\ell}(L P_D)\bigr)
                           \pmod{2^M}.
\label{cs:weighted-trace-identity}$$ The initial basis at $\ell$ and initial orientation affect only $\zeta_M(D)$. Formula <a href="#cs:weighted-trace-identity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="cs:weighted-trace-identity">[cs:weighted-trace-identity]</a> specifies the normalization using a character sum, with no class-number denominator. All rational multipliers are fixed independently of $D$ and $\ell$.

If the product derivative is zero, Gross–Zagier makes $P_D$ torsion. The fixed multiplier kills it: genus sums and their twist comparisons are defined over biquadratic fields. The torsion of a fixed elliptic curve in degree at most four is uniformly bounded, as one sees by reducing its prime-to-residue-characteristic torsion at two fixed good primes of distinct residue characteristic; the residue degrees are at most four. Thus the coefficient is zero at the stated precision. If the derivative is nonzero, write the point against the free twist line. Division by $2^{j(P_D)}$ on that line implies the same divisibility after reduction and $\lambda_M$, up to the fixed-degree comparison and the fixed multiplier. Conversely, a visible image bounds $j(P_D)$ above by its visible valuation plus a fixed constant. Equation <a href="#cs:weighted-trace-identity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="cs:weighted-trace-identity">[cs:weighted-trace-identity]</a> proves Equations <a href="#cs:odd-detection" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="cs:odd-detection">[cs:odd-detection]</a> and <a href="#cs:odd-lower-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="cs:odd-lower-bound">[cs:odd-lower-bound]</a>, using Equation <a href="#cs:odd-bound-hypothesis" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="cs:odd-bound-hypothesis">[cs:odd-bound-hypothesis]</a>. Gross–Zagier–Kolyvagin then gives the simple zero and finite $\mathop{\mathrm{Sha}}$ when the coefficient is visible. The detecting construction for $D_w$ supplies the final assertion. Fixed denominators or multipliers only reduce $M$ by a fixed amount; reindexing the precisions gives the formulation stated. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-23"></a>
#### The least normalized depth

We now minimize the coefficient valuation after subtracting the prime weight $w(D)$. This normalization is fixed before any prime array is chosen. Attainment of the minimum will detect analytic rank and bound the finite Selmer contribution; for the odd source this is interpreted through the bounded-weight sequences and finite realizations below.

For the even source, first rescale $g$ so that $a(D_0)=1$ at one nonzero squarefree index. Its nonzero squarefree valuations are then integers by Proposition <a href="#prop:even-coefficients" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:even-coefficients">[prop:even-coefficients]</a>. Set <a id="cs:even-symbol"></a>$$\delta=\min_D\{v(a(D))-w(D)\},\qquad
 A(D)=\begin{cases}
 1,&v(a(D))=\delta+w(D),\\
 0,&\text{otherwise},
 \end{cases}
\label{cs:even-symbol}$$ with $A(D)=0$ off the filter. The minimum exists: the lower bound is uniform, visible valuations are integers after normalization, the fractional part of the weight is fixed, and a nonzero witness exists.

For the odd source fix a nonprincipal ultrafilter $\mathcal U$ on its sequence of precisions. Consider all sequences $D_M$ of admissible indices for which $w(D_M)$ is bounded and $v(a_M(D_M))$ is visible on an ultrafilter-large set. For each such sequence, its normalized depth has a lower bound in a discrete set. Let $\delta$ be the least depth attainable on an ultrafilter-large set. This least depth exists and is attained: the uniform lower bound bounds it below, discreteness gives a least value, and the fixed witness bounds the possible minimum above. For a bounded-weight admissible sequence $\mathbf D=(D_M)$, define $$A(\mathbf D)=1
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \{M:v(a_M(D_M))=\delta+w(D_M)\}\in\mathcal U,$$ and set $A(\mathbf D)=0$ otherwise. We suppress the sequence notation when discussing finite configurations; each application uses their simultaneous finite realizations, as proved below.

For the odd source, a least weight supporting a unit symbol is minimized among the same bounded-weight sequences that attain depth $\delta$. After restricting to an ultrafilter-large set, the weight of such a sequence may be held constant, since it lies in a bounded subset of $\tfrac12\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$. The set of these constant weights is nonempty and has a least element $m$. If unit symbols of weight below $m$ occurred on an ultrafilter-large set of stages, choosing one such index at each stage would contradict the definition of $m$.

<a id="stmt-cs-fixed-weight-uniformity"></a>
<div id="cs:fixed-weight-uniformity" class="lemma">

**Lemma 18** (Uniformity at a fixed weight bound). *For every fixed $W$, on an ultrafilter-large set of sufficiently high precisions, $$v(a_M(D))\geq\delta+w(D)$$ for every admissible index with $w(D)\leq W$, with valuations truncated at the working precision. Any finite list of stabilized symbol assertions of bounded weight is realized simultaneously at such precisions. The definition allows arbitrarily many weight-zero root factors.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-cs-fixed-weight-uniformity"><summary>Proof of stmt-cs-fixed-weight-uniformity</summary>

*Proof.* If the first assertion failed on an ultrafilter-large set, choose a violating $D_M$ at each of those levels. Their weights are bounded by $W$ and their normalized depths lie in a fixed bounded discrete range. After selecting one depth on an ultrafilter-large set, they contradict the definition of $\delta$. For a finite collection of stabilized bits, intersect their ultrafilter-large realization sets. A bound on weight, rather than on the number or size of primes, is all that this argument uses. At weights beyond the chosen bound, the truncated lower estimate of Proposition <a href="#prop:odd-coefficients" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:odd-coefficients">[prop:odd-coefficients]</a> still supplies any prescribed bounded-depth divisibility test once the weight is sufficiently large. No claim of one finite level valid for all unbounded weights is made. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-prop-unit-symbol-detection"></a>
<div id="prop:unit-symbol-detection" class="proposition">

**Proposition 19** (Detection by a unit symbol). *For either coefficient source, $A(D)=1$ implies the prescribed analytic order: zero in the even case and one in the odd case. At every such index, <a id="cs:even-sharp"></a><a id="cs:odd-sharp"></a><a id="cs:unit-selmer-bound"></a>$$\begin{aligned}
 v({\cal L}(h))&\leq2w(D)+C &&\text{in the even case},
 \label{cs:even-sharp}\\
 j(P_D)&\leq w(D)+C &&\text{in the odd case},
 \label{cs:odd-sharp}\\
 s(h)&\leq C,\qquad \dim_{\mathbf F_2}\mathop{\mathrm{Sel}}_2(E^{(h)}/\mathbb Q)\leq C.
 \label{cs:unit-selmer-bound}
\end{aligned}$$ The constants are fixed after choosing the original curve, filter, coefficient normalization and genus partner. For the odd source they are independent of the detecting prime and the working precision, and of the number and size of active primes. Statements about its symbols are used through finite realizations as in Lemma <a href="#cs:fixed-weight-uniformity" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="cs:fixed-weight-uniformity">18</a>.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-prop-unit-symbol-detection"><summary>Proof of stmt-prop-unit-symbol-detection</summary>

*Proof.* In the even case substitute $v(a(D))=\delta+w(D)$ into Equations <a href="#cs:even-value" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="cs:even-value">[cs:even-value]</a> and <a href="#cs:even-lower-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="cs:even-lower-bound">[cs:even-lower-bound]</a>.
