In the odd case use a precision greater than the finitely many tested depths and apply Equations <a href="#cs:odd-detection" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="cs:odd-detection">[cs:odd-detection]</a> and <a href="#cs:odd-lower-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="cs:odd-lower-bound">[cs:odd-lower-bound]</a>. The constant $\delta$ is fixed and the comparison constants are uniform, proving the first inequalities and the bound on $s(h)$. At these indices the analytic order is established, so Gross–Zagier–Kolyvagin gives the same algebraic rank and finite $\mathop{\mathrm{Sha}}$ (Gross and Zagier 1986; Kolyvagin 1990) <a id="pm-cite-65"></a>[[GrossZagier1986](#ref-GrossZagier1986), [Kolyvagin1990](#ref-Kolyvagin1990)]. The exact sequence for $2$-Selmer then bounds its dimension by that rank, the fixed bound on rational $2$-torsion, and the $2$-primary length of $\mathop{\mathrm{Sha}}$. This proves the final assertion without making any finiteness assumption at an index where the analytic order has not yet been detected. ◻

</details>

<a id="sec:trace-calculus"></a>
### Trace identities and prime substitutions

We now turn the least-depth coefficients into rules for replacing, contracting, and deleting primes. The input is a coefficient system from Section <a href="#cs:coefficient-systems" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="cs:coefficient-systems">4</a>, with fixed support $S$, characters $\eta,\psi$, expansion $g=\sum_{n\ge1}a(n)q^n$, minimum depth $\delta$, and symbol $A(D)\in\mathbb F_2$, extended by zero off its filter. The coefficient lower bounds and the rational leading units proved there are essential hypotheses. A unit symbol has the analytic interpretation of Proposition <a href="#prop:unit-symbol-detection" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:unit-symbol-detection">19</a>.

Put $F=\mathbb Q(E[2])$. A prime outside $S$ is called split, simple, or a root according as its action on $E[2]$ is the identity, a transposition, or an element of order three; its weight is respectively $1$, $1/2$, or $0$. The same terminology will be used for Galois elements, according to their image in $\mathop{\mathrm{Gal}}(F/\mathbb Q)$. A nonroot is an element of either of the first two types. A finite set of primes and its squarefree product will occasionally be denoted by the same letter. Thus $U/p$ means deletion of $p$ from $U$, not deletion of a prime power from an arbitrary integer.

An oriented Frobenius label in an extension $L$ of $F$ means a *rational* arithmetic Frobenius lift in $\mathop{\mathrm{Gal}}(L/\mathbb Q)$, with a chosen place and its residual image in $\mathop{\mathrm{Gal}}(F/\mathbb Q)$ retained. At a simple prime this is the lift $g$ of the transposition, not only the Frobenius $g^2$ of the residue-degree-two place of $F$.

For the odd source, fix the finite operator patterns, their weight bounds, and all integer divisions required by the intended tests before choosing an actual stage. The primes realizing those patterns may depend on the stage. The lemma below distinguishes the sharp estimate on a prescribed bounded range of squarefree weights from integrality at every Fourier index. Both are needed to form the integral weight-two trace lattice. At a chosen stage the detecting prime belongs to $S$, and the level, coefficient field, and characteristic-zero lift are fixed. Recurrences hold modulo the working precision before division.

<a id="pm-h-25"></a>
#### Normalized coefficient operators

Let $U$ be a finite set of nonroot primes outside $S$. Write $$\mathsf U_p\!\left(\sum_n c(n)q^n\right)=\sum_n c(pn)q^n,
 \qquad
 \mathsf V_p\!\left(\sum_n c(n)q^n\right)=\sum_n c(n)q^{pn},$$ and define <a id="tc:normalized-operator"></a>$$B_U=2^{-\lceil\delta+w(U)\rceil}
             \prod_{p\in U}(\mathsf U_p-\eta(p)\mathsf V_p)g,
 \qquad
 e_U=\lceil\delta+w(U)\rceil-\delta-w(U).
 \label{tc:normalized-operator}$$ The factors commute. We say that $U$ has matching parity if $\delta+w(U)$ is integral, and opposite parity otherwise. Equivalently, $w(U)$ has, or does not have, the fractional part prescribed by the filter. Consequently $e_U=0$ or $1/2$, respectively.

<a id="tc:transformed-recurrence"></a>
These operations increase the level at a newly introduced $p$ only to exponent one. In fact, $\mathsf V_p$ changes the character by $(p/\cdot)$ and raises the level by $p$, while on that raised level $\mathsf U_p=\mathsf U_{p^2}\mathsf V_p$. We denote the resulting character of $B_U$ by $\psi_U$. At a good prime $q\notin S\cup U$ the coefficient recurrence remains $$B_U[q^2n]
 =\bigl(\eta(q)a_q(E)-\psi_U(q)(-n/q)\bigr)B_U[n]
       -q\eta(q)^2B_U[n/q^2].
 \label{tc:transformed-recurrence}$$ For the odd source, Equation <a href="#tc:transformed-recurrence" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tc:transformed-recurrence">[tc:transformed-recurrence]</a> is read modulo $2^{M-\lceil\delta+w(U)\rceil}$ when $M$ is the working recurrence precision before normalization. As usual, a coefficient with nonintegral index is zero. The equality of the good eigenvalue before and after $\mathsf V_p$ can also be seen directly: its new middle character contains $(p/q)$, which cancels the factor $(p/q)$ arising from the change of coefficient index.

<a id="stmt-tc-shell-bound"></a>
<div id="tc:shell-bound" class="lemma">

**Lemma 20** (Coefficient bound and first shell). *Write an index prime to $S$ uniquely as $$n=Jr m^2,
 \qquad J\subseteq U,
 \qquad r\text{ squarefree},\quad (r,U)=1,$$ and put $D=(U/J)r$.*

*For the even source, $B_U$ has integral coefficients and satisfies the following assertions at every index. For the odd source, fix bounds on $w(U)$ and on the squarefree weights to be tested, and fix an integer $K\ge0$. There is a larger cutoff $W$ and an ultrafilter-large set of arbitrarily high stages at which $B_U$ is integral at every index, the assertions below hold whenever $w(D)\le W$, and $$v(B_U[n])\ge K\qquad\text{if }w(D)>W.$$ These choices are uniform over prime realizations with the prescribed weight bounds.*

<a id="tc:coefficient-bound"></a>
<a id="tc:shell-factor"></a>
*The coefficient $B_U[n]$ is zero unless $D$ belongs to the filter. Within the range just specified, it satisfies $$v(B_U[n])\geq
       w(r)+\frac{\#\{p\in J:p\text{ simple}\}}2-e_U.
 \label{tc:coefficient-bound}$$ At a split prime $p\in J$, the factor contributed by the difference operator, after removing its character phase and one factor of $2$, is $$c_p(D)=
 \frac{a_p(E)-(\psi/\eta)(p)(-D/p)-1}{2}\pmod 2.
 \label{tc:shell-factor}$$ This is independent of the exponent of $p$ in $m$. At a simple prime $p\in J$, Equation <a href="#tc:shell-factor" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tc:shell-factor">[tc:shell-factor]</a> holds for the first shell, that is, when $p\nmid m$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-tc-shell-bound"><summary>Proof of stmt-tc-shell-bound</summary>

*Proof.* The good-prime recurrence of Section <a href="#cs:coefficient-systems" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="cs:coefficient-systems">4</a> expresses every relevant coefficient in terms of the squarefree coefficient $a(D)$. After removing the factor $\eta(p)^s$, the multipliers for powers $p^{2s}$ are determined by $$b_0=1,\qquad
 b_1=a_p(E)-(\psi/\eta)(p)(-D/p),\qquad
 b_{s+1}=a_p(E)b_s-pb_{s-1}.$$ If $p\mid D$, the Legendre symbol in $b_1$ is zero. The recurrences at different primes commute and their multipliers multiply.

For $p\in U/J$ the difference operator contributes $b_s-b_{s-1}$, with $b_{-1}=0$. Here $p\mid D$, so $b_1=a_p(E)$ is even. Modulo $2$ the sequence alternates between $1$ and $0$, and every such difference is odd. For $p\in J$ we have $p\nmid D$; now $b_0$ and $b_1$ are odd and every $b_s$ is odd. The difference $b_{s+1}-b_s$ is therefore even.

For the more precise assertion at a split prime put $a=a_p(E)$ and $\kappa=(\psi/\eta)(p)(-D/p)\in\{1,-1\}$. Since $E[2]$ is rational over $\mathbf F_p$, $a\equiv p+1\pmod4$. If $\Delta_s=b_{s+1}-b_s$, the recurrence gives $$\Delta_{s+1}=a\Delta_s-p\Delta_{s-1}\quad(s\geq1).$$ Every $\Delta_s$ is even, whence $\Delta_{s+1}\equiv\Delta_{s-1}\pmod4$. Directly, $$\Delta_1-\Delta_0
 =a^2-a\kappa-2a+2\kappa+1-p\equiv0\pmod4.$$ Thus $\Delta_s/2\equiv(a-\kappa-1)/2\pmod2$ for every $s$. For a simple prime this last formula is still the defining calculation at $s=0$, which is all that will be required.

Put $d_U=\lceil\delta+w(U)\rceil$. Whenever the sharp squarefree bound $v(a(D))\ge\delta+w(D)$ is available, the factors just computed give at least one further factor of $2$ for each $p\in J$. Hence $$v(B_U[n])\ge \delta+w(D)+\#J-d_U
 =w(r)+\frac{\#\{p\in J:p\text{ simple}\}}2-e_U.$$ For an allowed squarefree class this expression is integral, since $\delta+w(D)$ is integral. Its only possible negative value before this parity condition is imposed is $-1/2$, so it is nonnegative. For the even source the sharp bound holds at every squarefree index, which proves all-index integrality and the displayed estimate.

For the odd source, let $u_0$ bound $w(U)$. Every prime in $U$ is a nonroot, so $\#U\le2u_0$ and the normalizing exponents $d_U$ are bounded. Proposition <a href="#prop:odd-coefficients" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:odd-coefficients">[prop:odd-coefficients]</a> gives a constant $C$ such that at every admissible squarefree index $$v(a_M(D))\ge\min\{M,w(D)-C\}.$$ This includes the case of zero product derivative, when the coefficient vanishes modulo $2^M$. Choose $W$ above the prescribed tested weights and so large that $W-C-d_U>K$ for all permitted $U$. By Lemma <a href="#cs:fixed-weight-uniformity" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="cs:fixed-weight-uniformity">18</a>, on an ultrafilter-large set of stages the sharp squarefree bound holds simultaneously for every $D$ with $w(D)\le W$. Take an arbitrarily high stage in this set, with precision exceeding all the fixed normalizations, the first-shell tests, and $\delta+W+2u_0$, and such that $M-d_U\ge K$ for every permitted $U$.

The recurrences and operator identities for this source hold modulo the working precision. Their multipliers are integral, so iteration through any square exponent leaves errors in the same precision ideal. After dividing by $2^{d_U}$, the possible error has valuation at least $M-d_U$. Thus the sharp calculation above is valid throughout the bounded range. Outside that range the same calculation with the coarse squarefree bound gives $$v(B_U[n])\ge
 \min\{M-d_U,\,w(D)-C+\#J-d_U\}\ge K.$$ This proves integrality at every index of the actual form, while asserting the sharp estimate only on the specified bounded range. There is no restriction on the number of weight-zero root factors. Coefficients excluded by the filter are zero. Every removed phase is a value of $\eta$, hence a unit reducing to $1$ at the chosen prime above $2$. ◻

</details>

At equality, the normalized leading coefficient is $A(D)$ times the displayed shell factors. In particular it is zero when $A(D)=0$. For the odd source this assertion is used for the finite stabilized symbol evaluations realized at the chosen stage. All omitted-prime comparisons use the same source $g$ and minimum $\delta$.

In later coefficientwise divisions, choose $K$ to cover the largest additional division and the desired final divisibility. If a least-weight argument also requires all lower-weight symbols to vanish, that condition holds simultaneously on an ultrafilter-large set: a failure would select a bounded-weight sequence contradicting the stabilized minimum. Intersect that set with the one in the lemma. The bounded range then supplies the sharp calculation and any required zero symbols; the coefficients beyond the cutoff already have all the necessary factors of $2$. Consequently all coefficientwise divisions and vanishings used below hold on actual integral forms at one chosen stage for each finite collection of tests. No stage is required to work for every unbounded configuration.

<a id="pm-h-26"></a>
#### Removing unary coefficients

The coefficient bound identifies the terms that can survive at the lowest valuation. For matching $U$ in the rational-torsion case, these lie on finitely many square classes. Subtracting the corresponding unary theta series will permit one further integral division by $2$.

<a id="tc:unary-subtraction"></a>
Suppose first that $E(\mathbb Q)[2]\ne0$. There are then no root primes. For matching $U$, define $$\begin{split}
 \Theta_J&=
    \sum_{\substack{m>0\\(m,\prod_{s\in S}s)=1}}
       \eta(m)\chi_{-4}(m)^i m\,q^{Jm^2},\\
 H_U&=\frac12\left(B_U-
       \sum_{\substack{J\subseteq U\\J\text{ split only}}}
                    B_U[J]\Theta_J\right),
 \end{split}
 \label{tc:unary-subtraction}$$ where $i\in\{0,1\}$ is chosen so that $\eta\chi_{-4}^i$ is odd. For opposite $U$, set $H_U=B_U$. Except where a further division is explicitly made in Lemma <a href="#tc:minimum-transfer" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="tc:minimum-transfer">28</a>, in the irreducible case we also set $H_U=B_U$.

<a id="stmt-tc-unary-integrality"></a>
<div id="tc:unary-integrality" class="lemma">

**Lemma 21**. *The form in Equation <a href="#tc:unary-subtraction" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tc:unary-subtraction">[tc:unary-subtraction]</a> is integral. Each $\Theta_J$ is a weight-$3/2$ unary theta form with character $$\eta\chi_{-4}^i(-J/\cdot),$$ whose new level primes are the primes of $J$, each to exponent one. Its character differs from $\psi_U$ by a quadratic character.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-tc-unary-integrality"><summary>Proof of stmt-tc-unary-integrality</summary>

*Proof.* In matching parity the right side of Equation <a href="#tc:coefficient-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tc:coefficient-bound">[tc:coefficient-bound]</a> can be zero only if $r=1$ and $J$ consists of split primes. At these indices Equation <a href="#tc:shell-factor" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tc:shell-factor">[tc:shell-factor]</a>, together with the odd squared-index multipliers at primes outside $U$, gives $$B_U[Jm^2]\equiv B_U[J]\eta(m)\pmod2.$$ The coefficient of $\Theta_J$ at $Jm^2$ has precisely this residue: the common phase $\eta(m)$ is retained on both sides, while $\chi_{-4}(m)^i m$ is an odd integer. Thus this is divisibility by $2$, not merely by $\mathfrak m$ in a ramified coefficient ring. Different squarefree $J$ have disjoint such supports. The numerator in Equation <a href="#tc:unary-subtraction" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tc:unary-subtraction">[tc:unary-subtraction]</a> is consequently divisible by $2$ coefficientwise.

Put $\beta=\eta\chi_{-4}^i$, and let $\beta_0$ be its primitive inducing character, of conductor $r$ supported on $S$. The unary theta transformation (Purkait 2013, sec. 2, p. 2) <a id="pm-cite-66"></a>[[Purkait2012](#ref-Purkait2012)] gives $$\Theta_J^0=\sum_{m>0}\beta_0(m)m q^{Jm^2}
 \in S_{3/2}\bigl(4r^2J,\beta_0(-4J/\cdot)\bigr).$$ Removing the terms with $s\mid m$ applies $1-s\beta_0(s)\mathsf V_{s^2}$, where $\mathsf V_{s^2}=\mathsf V_s^2$. Thus $$\Theta_J=\prod_{s\in S}
       \bigl(1-s\beta_0(s)\mathsf V_{s^2}\bigr)\Theta_J^0.$$ Writing $P_S=\prod_{s\in S}s$, every term in this product has theta parameter $Jd^2$ for some $d\mid P_S$. The same transformation formula places all terms at level $4r^2JP_S^2$, with character $\beta_0(-4J/\cdot)$ on the units of that level. This is the displayed character $\eta\chi_{-4}^i(-J/\cdot)$. Since $J$ is prime to $S$, each fresh prime in $J$ still occurs in the level to exponent one. Finally $\psi_U/\eta$ is quadratic, as is $\chi_{-4}^i(-J/\cdot)$, proving the last assertion. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-27"></a>
#### Weight-two traces

We next express coefficient tests as traces of Galois representations. The trace identities will give relations among the tests; the level-prime identity will compare a test with the one obtained by omitting a prime.

Multiply the integral half-integral-weight form under consideration by $$\theta=1+2\sum_{m\geq1}q^{m^2}.$$ This produces a weight-two modular form with the same reduced expansion. Choose a finite extension of $\mathbb Q_2$ containing all coefficient fields and character values needed at the fixed level, and denote its ring of integers and maximal ideal by $\mathcal O$ and $\mathfrak m$.

The characteristic-zero decomposition by the Hecke operators away from the level supplies commuting operators $$t(u),\ d(u),\qquad u\in G_{\mathbb Q},$$ by taking the traces and determinants of the corresponding two-dimensional Galois representations. For cuspidal systems these are the weight-two representations of Deligne; for Eisenstein systems they are the sums of the two defining characters. At a good arithmetic Frobenius, $t(\mathop{\mathrm{Fr}}_q)$ is the ordinary weight-two $T_q$, and the determinant is the cyclotomic character times the diamond character. We use the existence and good-prime compatibility of these representations in their characteristic-zero form (Deligne 1971, secs. 3, (3.9)–(3.12), and Theorem 4.9) <a id="pm-cite-67"></a>[[Deligne1969](#ref-Deligne1969)], and local-global compatibility (Carayol 1986, Theorem (A), §0.7) <a id="pm-cite-68"></a>[[Carayol1986](#ref-Carayol1986)]. We take the contragredients of the cohomological representations in these references, so arithmetic Frobenius has trace $a_q$ and determinant $q$ times the diamond eigenvalue.

Here is a precise integral framework for the reductions that follow. Take the finite-dimensional sum of these characteristic-zero systems, retaining their multiplicity spaces, that contains the vector under consideration and its diamond transforms. Its integral Fourier lattice is finite over $\mathcal O$: finitely many coefficients already give an injective map of this space, and the lattice embeds in the corresponding finite free $\mathcal O$-module. Good Hecke operators preserve integral expansions. Diamonds do so as well. For the subtracted vector this last claim follows from the formula $$\langle u\rangle H_U
 =\psi_U(u)H_U+
 \frac12\sum_J B_U[J]
       \bigl(\psi_U(u)-\eta(u)\chi_{-4}(u)^i(-J/u)\bigr)\Theta_J:$$ each parenthesis is zero or twice a unit. The same observation applies after multiplying by $\theta$.

Traces at arbitrary Galois elements are limits of good Frobenius traces on this finite lattice. Indeed, continuity gives a common finite quotient at any prescribed accuracy, and Chebotarev gives a good prime in each required conjugacy class. Its size is unrestricted, and it may avoid any specified finite list of indices and primes. This proves integrality of all the traces and determinants used below, not only of the good Hecke operators with which the construction began.

Let $\mathcal T$ be the resulting commutative operator algebra on the reduced orbit of the vector. Equality means equality of every Fourier coefficient after any further indicated operator products. We retain this algebra, including its possible nilpotents.

<a id="stmt-co-traces"></a>
<div id="co:traces" class="lemma">

<a id="tc:trace-identities"></a>
**Lemma 22** (Trace identities and fresh-prime tests). *<span id="tc:trace-algebra" label="tc:trace-algebra"></span>In this reduced operator algebra, $$d(u)t(v)=t(v),\qquad
 t(u)t(v)=t(uv)+t(uv^{-1}),\qquad t(1)=0.
 \label{tc:trace-identities}$$ A coefficient of a product of traces can be tested by replacing its arguments with Frobenius elements at distinct fresh primes avoiding the coefficient index. If the index is $n$ and those primes are $q_1,\ldots,q_a$, the test is the reduced coefficient at $nq_1\cdots q_a$. Determinants may be applied first.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-co-traces"><summary>Proof of stmt-co-traces</summary>

*Proof.* For a weight-two form $f$, the good-prime formula is $$(T_qf)[n]=f[qn]+q(\langle q\rangle f)[n/q].$$ When $q\nmid n$ the second term is absent. Choosing the successive test primes distinct and avoiding $n$ proves the coefficient assertion. Chebotarev and continuity, on the finite lattice just described, allow these choices for arbitrary trace arguments at any required accuracy.

All the diamond characters are of $2$-power order. On a form with one character its determinant therefore reduces to the identity. For a subtracted vector the displayed diamond formula leaves, in addition, only unary contributions $\Theta_J\theta$. A fresh trace kills each such contribution modulo $\mathfrak m$: its coefficient test has index $nq$ with $q\nmid nJ$, and cannot have the squarefree part $J$. The same argument applies after any further tests. This proves $d(u)t(v)=t(v)$.

For two invertible $2$-by-$2$ matrices the characteristic-zero identity is $$\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(A)\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(B)=\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(AB)+\det(B)\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(AB^{-1}).$$ Apply it to every characteristic-zero system and use the determinant identity just proved. Finally, $t(1)=2$ before reduction. ◻

</details>

The bounds of Lemma <a href="#tc:shell-bound" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="tc:shell-bound">20</a> are particularly well suited to these tests: an added prime contributes its nonnegative weight, and additional root primes contribute no weight. A zero established by one of these bounds consequently remains zero after all the further tests used here. In the moving-precision case all the preceding constructions are made at the actual fixed level of the chosen stage. The required divisibility is uniform at the specified weight cutoff; continuity is used only in a finite-dimensional space at that stage.

The only level-prime identity we need is the following. We distinguish the weight-two operator $\mathsf U_p^{(2)}$ from the earlier half-integral-weight notation, although both extract $p$-multiples in their respective Fourier expansions.

<a id="stmt-co-inertia"></a>
<div id="co:inertia" class="lemma">

<a id="tc:exact-level-identity"></a>
**Lemma 23** (Inertia and a level operator). *<span id="tc:inertia-identity" label="tc:inertia-identity"></span>For $p\in U$, choose a place over $p$, an inertia element $\tau_p$ on which the ramified quadratic character is $-1$, and a corresponding arithmetic Frobenius lift $\phi_p$. On the characteristic-zero space under consideration, before reduction, one has $$\mathsf U_p^{(2)}
       \bigl(t(g\tau_p\phi_p)-t(g\phi_p)\bigr)
 =d(\phi_p)\bigl(t(g\tau_p)-t(g)\bigr).
 \label{tc:exact-level-identity}$$ The identity commutes with further good traces. After reduction it therefore evaluates a difference at coefficient $1$ by the corresponding difference at coefficient $p$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-co-inertia"><summary>Proof of stmt-co-inertia</summary>

*Proof.* At $p$ the summands in question are either old from a level omitting $p$, or have conductor exponent one and primitive ramified quadratic diamond character. For the former the representation is unramified, so both trace differences are zero, irrespective of the action of $\mathsf U_p^{(2)}$ on the old multiplicity space.

For the latter, local-global compatibility identifies the local representation with a principal series with one unramified and one ramified character; its monodromy is zero. In a basis of these two lines write $$\rho(\tau_p)=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 \rho(\phi_p)=\begin{pmatrix}\lambda&0\\0&\mu\end{pmatrix}.$$ The level eigenvalue is $\lambda$, the Frobenius eigenvalue on the unramified line, and $d(\phi_p)=\lambda\mu$. If the lower-right entry of $\rho(g)$ is $z$, the two trace differences are $-2z\mu$ and $-2z$, respectively. Both sides of Equation <a href="#tc:exact-level-identity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tc:exact-level-identity">[tc:exact-level-identity]</a> are $-2z\lambda\mu$. The Eisenstein calculation is the identical calculation on its pair of characters. Copies old at other primes do not change it.

These are all the possibilities: the new level has exponent one at $p$, with ramified quadratic determinant, so the Steinberg case with unramified determinant does not enter. A unary summand with $p\notin J$ is old from a level omitting $p$; with $p\in J$ it has the same ramified quadratic local character. Thus the preceding classification also covers Equation <a href="#tc:unary-subtraction" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tc:unary-subtraction">[tc:unary-subtraction]</a>.

Finally apply Equation <a href="#tc:trace-identities" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tc:trace-identities">[tc:trace-identities]</a> to remove the determinant from the right side after reduction. Taking coefficient $1$ on the left is taking coefficient $p$ before $\mathsf U_p^{(2)}$. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-28"></a>
#### Rules when there is rational two-torsion

We now apply the common trace identities to the rational-torsion case. The coefficient bounds first restrict the Galois data on which a symbol can depend. The level-prime identity then determines how the symbol changes when one of those data is varied.

An elementary extension of a number field means a compositum of quadratic extensions. Whenever a ramification support is specified, only extensions unramified outside that support are included. For finite support the resulting elementary extension is finite. Labels below are Frobenius specifications in these extensions, with a chosen place when an orientation over $F$ is needed. They always include the fixed rational local conditions that specify the filter.

<a id="stmt-tc-rational-rules"></a>
<div id="tc:rational-rules" class="proposition">

**Proposition 24** (Rational trace and contraction rules). *Suppose $E(\mathbb Q)[2]\ne0$.*

1.  *For matching $U$, on the subtracted vector $H_U$, $$t(g)t(u)=0\quad(u\text{ split}).$$ The trace on split elements factors through the elementary extension of $F$ supported on $S\cup U$. For opposite $U$, on $B_U$, every product of two traces is zero, and traces factor through the rational elementary extension supported there.*

2.  *If $U\cup\{q\}$ has the parity of the filter, its symbol is read at coefficient $1$ by $t(\mathop{\mathrm{Fr}}_q)$ on $H_U$ for split $q$, and on $B_U$ for simple $q$.*

<a id="tc:rational-contraction"></a>
3.  *Fix $p\in U$ and put $g=\mathop{\mathrm{Fr}}_q$. Replacing $g$ by $g\tau_p$ changes the symbol, additively in $\mathbf F_2$, by $$A\bigl((U/p)\cup\{q'\}\bigr),
           \qquad \mathop{\mathrm{Fr}}_{q'}\sim g\phi_p,
     \label{tc:rational-contraction}$$ if $p$ and $q$ are not both simple. The label of $q'$ is required only away from the omitted primes and carries their product labels. The replacement uses the original source with level support $S\cup(U/p)$: the *whole rational prime* $p$ is omitted, including both places over it if $p$ splits in $F$. If both endpoints are simple, the change is zero.*

4.  *A split vertex with trivial label relative to the level with that vertex omitted has symbol zero.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-tc-rational-rules"><summary>Proof of stmt-tc-rational-rules</summary>

*Proof.* For matching $U$, two fresh tests, one of them split, add weight at least $3/2$ to Equation <a href="#tc:coefficient-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tc:coefficient-bound">[tc:coefficient-bound]</a>. The allowed valuation is integral, so the numerator has valuation at least $2$. After the division in Equation <a href="#tc:unary-subtraction" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tc:unary-subtraction">[tc:unary-subtraction]</a> it still vanishes modulo $\mathfrak m$; fresh tests kill its unary terms. For opposite $U$, two nonroot tests add weight at least $1$, leaving at least $1/2$ after subtracting $e_U$, and hence at least $1$ at an allowed coefficient. This proves the two product vanishings on the entire reduced orbit.

The trace identities show why these vanishings give the stated elementary quotients. If $u$ is split, apply the identity to $t(gu)t(u)$ to obtain $t(gu^2)=t(g)$. The subgroup generated by squares in $G_F$ has elementary quotient, since a group of exponent two is abelian. In the opposite case the same calculation applies to every $u\in G_\mathbb Q$. Ramification outside the level is absent from the characteristic-zero representations and remains absent in the quotient.

For a split $q$, its added weight is $1$: at coefficient $q$ the division by $2$ in $H_U$ places the coefficient exactly at the normalized detection depth. There is no unary term at that index. For simple $q$, $e_U=1/2$ already gives that depth on $B_U$. The character phases reduce to $1$, proving (ii).

For (iii), apply Lemma <a href="#tc:inertia-identity" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="tc:inertia-identity">[tc:inertia-identity]</a> at coefficient $1$, so that its left side is a coefficient-$p$ test. Replace its trace arguments by fresh primes with Frobenius $g\tau_p\phi_p$ and $g\phi_p$. Put $V=U/p$. For $X=U,V$, set $n_X=\lceil\delta+w(X)\rceil$ and let $m_X$ be one in matching parity and zero otherwise. After a fresh trace kills the unary terms, the shell multiplier relative to the omitted-source test is $$2^{1+n_V-n_U-m_U+m_V}c_p(D'),
 \qquad D'=Vq',\quad \mathop{\mathrm{Fr}}_{q'}\sim g\phi_p.$$ The exponent is zero for split $p$, and also for simple $p$ with matching $U$. It is one for simple $p$ with opposite $U$, precisely the simple–simple case. This checks all integer divisions in the contraction rule. For simple $p$ only the first shell is used. The change $\psi_U/\psi_V=(p/\cdot)$ is already included in that shell calculation; all remaining phases reduce to one.

In the first three cases the shell is therefore $c_p(D')A(D')$. Both fresh Frobenius elements have the same image in the omitted source: that source is built from the original modular form, the same $\eta,\psi,\delta$, and the operators at $V$, so it is unramified at the entire rational prime $p$. Inertia at either place over $p$ acts trivially on its symbol. The ramified quadratic coordinate of $\tau_p$ reverses the Legendre sign in $c_p$, whose additive change is one. The difference of the two shell values is consequently $A(D')$, proving Equation <a href="#tc:rational-contraction" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tc:rational-contraction">[tc:rational-contraction]</a>.

If both primes are simple, their residual images are the same transposition, so $g\phi_p$ is split. The shell now has positive valuation after normalization and contributes zero. Finally (iv) is (ii) with $t(\mathop{\mathrm{Fr}}_q)=t(1)=0$ in the relevant elementary quotient. ◻

</details>

The contraction rules control changes in existing vertices. The next calculation gives a way to add two simple vertices while preserving the symbol.

<a id="stmt-tc-simple-twins"></a>
<div id="tc:simple-twins" class="proposition">

**Proposition 25** (Insertion of a pair of simple primes). *Suppose $E(\mathbb Q)[2]\ne0$ and $U$ has matching parity. Let a rational elementary label, relative to $S$ and all existing split vertices, be realized by a simple prime $q$ with $$\#E(\mathbf F_q)\equiv2\pmod4.$$ Inserting two fresh simple primes with this same label leaves $A(U)$ unchanged. Their mutual simple-edge label, and their labels against other simple vertices, do not affect this assertion.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-tc-simple-twins"><summary>Proof of stmt-tc-simple-twins</summary>

*Proof.* First test $t(\mathop{\mathrm{Fr}}_q)^2$ on matching $H_U$. The weight-two Hecke formula at coefficient $1$ gives, after reduction, $$H_U[q^2]+q(\langle q\rangle H_U)[1].$$ Only the $J=1$ unary term can contribute at $1$ or $q^2$. Write $b=B_U[1]$, $\epsilon=\chi_{-4}(q)$, and $\kappa=(\psi_U/\eta)(q)$. Substituting Equation <a href="#tc:transformed-recurrence" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tc:transformed-recurrence">[tc:transformed-recurrence]</a> and the two characters in Equation <a href="#tc:unary-subtraction" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tc:unary-subtraction">[tc:unary-subtraction]</a>, the preceding expression is the reduction of <a id="tc:twin-calculation"></a>$$b\,\frac{\eta(q)}2
 \left(a_q(E)+\kappa(q-\epsilon)
                 -q\epsilon^i(1+\epsilon)\right).
 \label{tc:twin-calculation}$$ For $q\equiv3\pmod4$ the parenthesis divided by $2$ is $a_q(E)/2$ modulo $2$. For $q\equiv1\pmod4$ it is $a_q(E)/2+1$. In either case it equals $(q+1-a_q(E))/2=\#E(\mathbf F_q)/2$ modulo $2$. Since $b$ reduces to $A(U)$, this proves that the squared trace has coefficient $(\#E(\mathbf F_q)/2)A(U)$.

By Lemma <a href="#tc:trace-algebra" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="tc:trace-algebra">[tc:trace-algebra]</a>, replace the two copies of this trace by distinct fresh primes realizing the same operator tests. Their product coefficient reads the symbol with the two primes inserted. To pass to any other pair with the labels in the statement, vary one prime at a time. After omitting that simple prime the opposite-parity test of Proposition <a href="#tc:rational-rules" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="tc:rational-rules">24</a> depends only on rational elementary labels. Its changes against other simple primes are zero by the simple–simple case of the same proposition. Thus only the fixed support and existing split labels need be matched. Fresh intermediate primes can match both old and new finite specifications, so that no collision of vertices is required. The assumed odd value of $\#E(\mathbf F_q)/2$ completes the proof. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-29"></a>
#### An elementary character on root elements

Assume now that $E[2]$ is irreducible. Its image is either cyclic of order three or $S_3$. The reduced trace algebra need not be a field: the order-two units below can have nontrivial nilpotent parts. We therefore retain the algebra, rather than replacing it by its residue field.

<a id="stmt-tc-root-character"></a>
<div id="tc:root-character" class="lemma">

**Lemma 26** (Root character). *On matching $B_U$ one has $t(u)=0$ for every nonroot $u$. On opposite $B_U$ one has $t(u)=0$ for split $u$ and $t(g)t(u)=0$ for two simple elements. In either parity, $$t(u)^2=1\quad(u\text{ a root}).$$ The traces factor through an extension of $\mathop{\mathrm{Gal}}(F/\mathbb Q)$ by an elementary kernel over $F$. Moreover, there is a multiplicative character $\alpha:G_\mathbb Q\longrightarrow\mathcal T^\times$ into the reduced trace algebra, unramified outside $S\cup U$, such that $$\alpha(u)^2=1\quad\text{for all }u,
 \qquad       t(u)=\alpha(u)\quad(u\text{ a root}).$$ In particular $\alpha$ factors through a rational elementary extension with that ramification support.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-tc-root-character"><summary>Proof of stmt-tc-root-character</summary>

*Proof.* The trace vanishings follow from Equation <a href="#tc:coefficient-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tc:coefficient-bound">[tc:coefficient-bound]</a>. In matching parity, one nonroot test adds at least $1/2$ and hence gives an integral valuation at least $1$. In opposite parity, either a split test or two simple tests add at least $1$, again leaving positive integral valuation after the loss $e_U=1/2$.

For a root test, use the same fresh prime $q$ twice, avoiding the coefficient index, rather than two distinct primes. The weight-two Hecke formula and Equation <a href="#tc:transformed-recurrence" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tc:transformed-recurrence">[tc:transformed-recurrence]</a> give the identity operator modulo $\mathfrak m$: $a_q(E)$ is odd, and the middle quadratic-character term cancels the diamond term modulo $2$. This proves $t(u)^2=1$ by continuity for every root $u$. For completeness, it suffices to check indices prime to the chosen $q$; each particular index permits such a choice of $q$ with the prescribed finite trace data.

Since split traces vanish in both parities, $t(gu^2)=t(g)$ for $u\in G_F$. Thus the traces factor through the quotient by the squares of $G_F$. At any fixed accuracy the trace action is on a finite lattice modulo $\mathfrak m$, so we may work in a finite quotient $$1\longrightarrow H\longrightarrow\Gamma
          \longrightarrow\mathop{\mathrm{Gal}}(F/\mathbb Q)\longrightarrow1$$ with $H$ elementary abelian. Choose an order-three lift $R$ of a rotation. Such a lift exists because the inverse image of the order-three subgroup is an extension by a finite $2$-group. The trace identity with the identity element gives $t(R)=t(R^{-1})=t(R^2)$. Applying it to $R,R^2$ gives $t(R)t(R^2)=t(1)+t(R^{-1})=t(R)$; the left side is $1$. Hence $$t(R)=t(R^2)=1.$$

For $a\in H$ set $$\alpha(a)=t(aR)=t(aR^2).$$ The equality follows from $t(a)=0$ and the trace identity with $R$. Conjugacy invariance by an element $b\in H$ implies that $\alpha$ is unchanged on multiplying its argument by $bR(b)^{-1}$. It therefore factors through the coinvariants $H/[H,R]$. Also it is invariant under conjugation by $R$. The trace product now gives $$\alpha(a)\alpha(b)
   =t(aR)t(bR)
   =t\bigl(aR(b)R^2\bigr)+t(ab^{-1})
   =\alpha\bigl(aR(b)\bigr)
   =\alpha(ab).$$ The last equality uses the coinvariant invariance just proved; the split term is zero. Since $aR$ is a root, $\alpha(a)^2=1$.

For cyclic residual image, this already extends to $\Gamma$ by setting $\alpha(R)=1$. For $S_3$, choose a transposition lift $s$ normalizing $\langle R\rangle$. It can be obtained from any transposition lift by conjugating its order-three complement by an element of $H$. Thus $sRs^{-1}=R^{-1}$ and $s^2\in H$. Conjugacy of traces shows that $\alpha$ on $H$ is invariant under $s$. In both parities we have $t(s)t(sR)=0$, either because each factor is zero or by the two-simple product rule. Its trace identity reads $$0=\alpha(s^2)+t(R)=\alpha(s^2)+1.$$ Therefore the extension defined by $\alpha(s)=1$ respects the relation for $s^2$, as well as conjugation and the relations in $\langle R\rangle$. It is the required multiplicative order-two character, and agrees with the trace on both root cosets. At the fixed stage, choose one common finite quotient through which the traces and residual representation factor, and pull back the character constructed there. No canonical choice across quotients is needed. Unramifiedness outside the level is preserved. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-30"></a>
#### Irreducible deletion rules and minimal labels

The root character replaces products of root traces by a single multiplicative value. We now combine that fact with the level-prime identity to compute changes at nonroot vertices. The last lemma applies these rules at the least weight where a symbol is nonzero.

The *total root label* is the product of the rational elementary labels of all root primes being used. It includes the fixed-support conditions and the rational quadratic labels against the active nonroot vertices. Its discriminant coordinate is trivial in the quadratic quotient of $S_3$; for cyclic residual image there is no such coordinate.

<a id="stmt-tc-irreducible-rules"></a>
<div id="tc:irreducible-rules" class="proposition">

**Proposition 27** (Irreducible substitution rules). *Suppose $E[2]$ is irreducible.*

1.  *On matching $B_U$, coefficient $1$ of a product of root traces reads $A$ on the union of $U$ and those roots. It depends on the roots only through their total rational elementary label relative to $S\cup U$. Any finite collection of roots, including the empty collection, may be replaced in this test by one virtual root with that label.*

2.  *Changing the Legendre bit of that root against a split vertex $p$ has additive derivative equal to deletion of $p$, with its rational labels away from $p$ transferred to the total root label. Changing the root bit against a simple vertex has derivative zero.*

3.  *To vary a simple vertex $q$, omit it and use opposite $B_V$, retaining the other root probes. At another simple vertex $p$, choose Frobenius lifts $g$ and $\phi_p$ for $q$ and $p$. If their transposition images are different, the derivative under $g\mapsto g\tau_p$ deletes both $p$ and $q$ and transfers their rational labels to the root total. If their transposition images are equal, the derivative is zero.*

4.  *In the test in (iii), variation at a split $p$ is given by the first-shell factors $c_p$ times symbols of merged configurations whose weight is one less. It consequently vanishes whenever all symbols of that lower weight vanish.*

*All these assertions preserve every specified label at the other vertices, and use the chosen place for inertia and Frobenius.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-tc-irreducible-rules"><summary>Proof of stmt-tc-irreducible-rules</summary>

*Proof.* Root primes have weight zero. Thus the fresh-prime tests at coefficient $1$ of matching $B_U$ are precisely the normalized coefficients defining $A$. Lemma <a href="#tc:root-character" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="tc:root-character">26</a> makes the product of root traces equal to the value of $\alpha$ on their total elementary label. A rotation survives every compatible elementary specification: an elementary quotient cannot eliminate the order-three subgroup, and in the $S_3$ case the only compatibility condition is its trivial image in the quadratic quotient. Chebotarev therefore supplies the claimed single virtual root, even for the empty total label.

For (ii), apply Lemma <a href="#tc:inertia-identity" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="tc:inertia-identity">[tc:inertia-identity]</a> with $g$ a root. If $p$ is split then $g\phi_p$ is a root. The coefficient with $J=\{p\}$ has zero cost in Equation <a href="#tc:coefficient-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tc:coefficient-bound">[tc:coefficient-bound]</a>; its first shell is $c_p$ times the symbol with $p$ deleted. The latter is unramified at $p$ and is the same in the two tests, while $c_p$ changes by $1$. Multiplication of Frobenius labels by $\phi_p$ is exactly the transfer of the deleted vertex’s rational labels to the root. If $p$ is simple, $g\phi_p$ is simple, and its weight $1/2$ plus the $1/2$ contributed by $J$ puts the shell above the testing depth. The derivative is then zero.

For (iii), $e_V=1/2$. When the two transpositions differ, $g\phi_p$ is a rotation, and the $1/2$ contribution from the simple prime in $J=\{p\}$ exactly cancels $e_V$. The shell again equals $c_p$ times the omitted-$p$ symbol, now with both simple vertices removed and their product represented by a root. The Legendre flip proves the asserted derivative. For equal transpositions their product is split; its additional weight $1$ forces the shell to vanish.

Finally, if $p$ is split and $g$ simple, then $g\phi_p$ is simple. The $p$-shell is at the first-shell depth and is expressed by Equation <a href="#tc:shell-factor" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tc:shell-factor">[tc:shell-factor]</a> with $D'=(V/p)q'$ and the retained root probes. Its nonroot weight is $$w(V)-1+\frac12
                  =\left(w(V)+\frac12\right)-1.$$ This is one less than the original weight. In particular both shell terms vanish when symbols of that weight vanish. The comparison omitting $p$ is unramified there. Root probes can be matched on the rational elementary support throughout, which proves the final label assertion as well. ◻

</details>

At the least nonzero weight, every lower-weight term in the preceding rules vanishes. This removes the dependence on internal edge labels; the remaining assertion keeps both the fixed-support labels and the total root label.

<a id="stmt-tc-minimum-transfer"></a>
<div id="tc:minimum-transfer" class="lemma">

**Lemma 28** (Transfer at the least nonzero weight). *Suppose $E[2]$ is irreducible, and let $m$ be the least weight of an index on the filter with nonzero symbol. At weight $m$, the dependence on each nonroot vertex is only through its oriented rational Frobenius lift in the Galois group over $\mathbb Q$ of the maximal elementary extension of $F$ unramified outside $S$, together with the requirement on the total root label. In particular, replacing the nonroot vertices by fresh vertices with those same fixed-support labels preserves the symbol, irrespective of their internal edge labels, provided the root total is matched. The assertion allows simultaneous changes using disjoint intermediate configurations.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-tc-minimum-transfer"><summary>Proof of stmt-tc-minimum-transfer</summary>

*Proof.* Every symbol of weight less than $m$ is zero. For a simple vertex, Proposition <a href="#tc:irreducible-rules" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="tc:irreducible-rules">27</a> therefore makes its inertia derivatives at every other active nonroot vertex zero: different transpositions give a lower-weight deletion, equal transpositions give zero directly, and a split vertex gives a lower-weight merged configuration. Its labels against root vertices are immaterial by the simple case of the root derivative rule. These statements hold for conjugates of inertia too, because the Frobenius and inertia calculation is made at a chosen place and may be conjugated. Starting with the elementary extension over $F$ supported on $S\cup V$, killing the inertia at the active vertices leaves exactly fixed-support elementary labels. This proves the assertion for a simple vertex.

For a split vertex $q$, let $V$ be the other nonroot vertices, so $w(V)=m-1$ and $V$ still has matching parity. We first claim that $B_V$ is divisible by $2$ integrally. In Equation <a href="#tc:coefficient-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tc:coefficient-bound">[tc:coefficient-bound]</a>, an entry of cost zero has $r$ consisting only of roots and $J$ consisting only of split primes. Its underlying squarefree class has weight $$w(V)-\#J<m.$$ Its symbol is zero. The shell formula at every split prime, valid at all exponents, therefore adds one more factor of $2$ to the normalized coefficient. All other allowed entries already have positive integral cost. This proves the claim, including at arbitrarily large coefficient indices.

Use now $H_V=B_V/2$. Two split traces give zero on $H_V$: their added weight $2$ in Equation <a href="#tc:coefficient-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tc:coefficient-bound">[tc:coefficient-bound]</a> still leaves one factor of $2$ after this division. The trace restricted to split elements consequently factors through the elementary kernel over $F$, by the same square-invariance argument as before. Coefficient $1$ with the new split trace and the retained root probes reads the symbol at weight $m$.

Apply Lemma <a href="#tc:inertia-identity" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="tc:inertia-identity">[tc:inertia-identity]</a> at $p\in V$ to this divided vector. The element $g\phi_p$ has the type of $p$, because $g$ is split. Its $p$-shell is $c_p$ times a symbol of weight $m-1$, whether $p$ is split or simple; for a simple $p$ only the first shell is used. For a simple $p$ the normalization can be checked directly: $J=\{p\}$ and the new simple probe contribute $1/2+1/2=1$ to Equation <a href="#tc:coefficient-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tc:coefficient-bound">[tc:coefficient-bound]</a>. Writing $n_V=\delta+w(V)$, the divided shell is $$\frac{2c_p(D')a(D')}{2^{n_V+1}}
 =c_p(D')\frac{a(D')}{2^{n_V}},\qquad w(D')=w(V)=m-1.$$ The omitted set $V/p$ has opposite parity, but its ceiling normalization is still $n_V$. Thus this is exactly its unit-symbol test, with no fractional loss. Both compared values are zero. Every such inertia derivative therefore vanishes, leaving only the fixed-support elementary label.

No character $\alpha$ on this further divided vector is needed. Use actual matched root probes in both tests. At weight $m$, their changes against a split vertex are already zero by the split root-deletion rule, because its deletion has weight $m-1$. They can therefore be matched while the nonroot vertex is moved. Moving vertices successively, using fresh intermediate copies when necessary, proves the joint assertion without imposing old internal edge labels.

For a moving coefficient system, minimality is used on a fixed bounded weight range. A failure of the required lower-weight vanishing on an ultrafilter-large set of stages would give a bounded-weight sequence contradicting the stabilized minimum. Choose the actual stage as in Lemma <a href="#tc:shell-bound" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="tc:shell-bound">20</a>, with the additional division by $2$ included among its fixed division bounds. Its coarse estimate controls all larger weights, and its integral square-index recurrences control every shell. Thus the preceding coefficientwise arguments apply to the actual forms at that stage. The argument does not require $m$ to be integral. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-31"></a>
#### Summary and finite realization

We collect the rules in the form used to construct finite prime arrays. The analytic meaning of a nonzero symbol is unchanged; this section has established which substitutions preserve it or compute its change.

<a id="stmt-co-symbol-interface"></a>
<div id="co:symbol-interface" class="theorem">

**Theorem 29** (Symbol rules). *<span id="thm:symbol-rules" label="thm:symbol-rules"></span>For either coefficient source of Propositions <a href="#prop:even-coefficients" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:even-coefficients">[prop:even-coefficients]</a> and <a href="#prop:odd-coefficients" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:odd-coefficients">[prop:odd-coefficients]</a>, assume its stated coefficient lower bound and use its normalized symbol and filter. Then the following rules hold for finite configurations of primes outside the level support.*

1.  *With rational two-torsion, the elementary-label factorizations, contraction except in the simple–simple case, and isolation by a trivial split label are those of Proposition <a href="#tc:rational-rules" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="tc:rational-rules">24</a>. A pair of identical simple labels realized with $\#E(\mathbf F_q)/2$ odd can be inserted without changing the symbol, as in Proposition <a href="#tc:simple-twins" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="tc:simple-twins">25</a>.*

2.  *With irreducible $E[2]$, all root probes combine into one total rational elementary label. A root-bit derivative at a split vertex deletes that vertex, while at a simple vertex it is zero. The derivative between two simple vertices deletes both when their transposition images are different, and is zero when they are equal. The remaining simple–split shell has weight one less. These are the rules of Proposition <a href="#tc:irreducible-rules" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="tc:irreducible-rules">27</a>.*

3.  *At the least weight supporting a nonzero symbol in the irreducible case, each nonroot may be moved with only its fixed-support elementary Frobenius label prescribed; internal edges impose no further condition on the value, subject to matching the total root label. This is Lemma <a href="#tc:minimum-transfer" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="tc:minimum-transfer">28</a>.*

*The analytic and finite-Selmer consequences of a nonzero symbol remain those of Proposition <a href="#prop:unit-symbol-detection" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:unit-symbol-detection">19</a>. In the odd source the rules mean finite tests at arbitrarily high stages chosen in the ultrafilter-large sets of the prescribed stabilization.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-co-symbol-interface"><summary>Proof of stmt-co-symbol-interface</summary>

*Proof.* The preceding propositions prove the assertions. For one application, put the finitely many Galois modules and operator tests in a common finite quotient at the required precision. Chebotarev then gives simultaneously fresh Frobenius representatives. The omitted source is unramified at the whole omitted prime, whereas its ramified rational quadratic coordinate is exactly the Legendre flip in the shell formula. These are therefore substitutions with all other labels held fixed.

The arithmetic compatibility of an entire array is addressed in the following sections. The present assertions concern each finite array; in the odd case choose a sufficiently high actual stage in the required ultrafilter-large intersection. Arbitrarily many weight-zero roots cause no additional depth loss, because the coefficient bound is uniform at a fixed weight and their traces combine through one total elementary label. ◻

</details>

<a id="gr:section"></a>
### Prime graphs and simultaneous unit coefficients

The coefficient symbols will now be regarded as functions of finitely many quadratic residue bits. We first identify the arithmetic data that those bits record and explain how the trace calculation becomes a finite difference. This gives polynomials whose derivatives contract prime labels. We then adjoin auxiliary vertices so that one or two nonzero coefficient polynomials take the value $1$ at every nonzero address of a binary cube.

The two-polynomial case is needed for the odd converse: the odd symbol tests $h$, while an even symbol tests a quadratic companion $kh$. Separate nonzero polynomials need not have a common unit evaluation; for example, $z$ and $1+z$ do not. The auxiliary vertices change the polynomials by controlled contraction operators. The arithmetic input is the rational contraction and isolation rules of Theorem <a href="#thm:symbol-rules" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:symbol-rules">[thm:symbol-rules]</a>, including omission of an entire rational prime. The same argument applies to any coefficient test with these rules, such as the restricted even test constructed in Section <a href="#pw:split-section" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="pw:split-section">7.5</a>.

Encoding quadratic residue symbols by graphs has a precedent in the congruent-number problem: Feng–Xiong express descent conditions through prime graphs and the ranks of their binary Laplacians (Feng and Xiong 2004, sec. 2, Definitions 2.1 and 2.3 and Lemma 2.2) <a id="pm-cite-69"></a>[[FengXiong2004](#ref-FengXiong2004)]. Here the graphs record coefficient-symbol rules, and their oriented contractions produce simultaneous unit values.

<a id="pm-h-33"></a>
#### Prime labels and their realization

Let $F$ be $\mathbf Q$ or a quadratic field. The applications use $F=\mathbf Q(E[2])$ when this field is quadratic, and also an auxiliary quadratic field when $E[2]$ is rational. Fix a finite set $S$ of rational primes containing $2$ and the ramification support of the fixed data. Enlarge $S$ so that prime ideals above it generate the class group of $F$, and let $S_F$ include these places and the infinite places. Set $$V_S(F)=\{\alpha\in F^\times/F^{\times2}:
       v_{\mathfrak p}(\alpha)\equiv0\pmod2
       \text{ for }\mathfrak p\notin S_F\}.$$ The valuation sequence expresses this as an extension of the squareclasses of $S_F$-units by a subgroup of the $2$-torsion of the $S_F$-class group; in particular, it is finite-dimensional over $\mathbf F_2$ (Milne 2020a, Theorems 4.4 and 5.11) <a id="pm-cite-70"></a>[[MilneANT2020](#ref-MilneANT2020)]. Write $F_S^{(2)}=F(\sqrt{V_S(F)})$.

<a id="gr:norm"></a>
A *split vertex* is a rational prime $p\notin S$ split in $F$, with an *orientation* $\mathfrak p\mid p$ when $F$ is quadratic. Choose a generator $\pi_{\mathfrak p}$ whose divisor outside $S_F$ is $\mathfrak p$; this is possible by the class-group condition. Use its conjugate for the other orientation. Then $$\label{gr:norm}
 N_{F/\mathbf Q}(\pi_{\mathfrak p})=p u_{\mathfrak p},
 \qquad u_{\mathfrak p}\text{ a signed rational }S\text{-unit}.$$ For $F=\mathbf Q$, use the generator $p$. In the quadratic case an inert rational prime is a *simple vertex*, with rational generator $p$. A split vertex has its fixed Frobenius label on $F_S^{(2)}$; a simple vertex has rational fixed-support labels. A *type* may also specify local squareclasses, support valuation parities, real signs, and finite ray conditions on its generator. Prescribed types must be compatible and individually realizable. A *filter* fixes the total rational labels and sign of the signed-prime product, where $p^*=(-1/p)p$.

Write quadratic residue symbols additively in $\mathbf F_2$. Between two split vertices in the quadratic case there are two independent forward bits: the residues of $\pi_{\mathfrak p}$ and $\overline{\pi_{\mathfrak p}}$ at the chosen place of the other vertex. Hilbert reciprocity and the types determine the reverse bits. Their sum, with the fixed correction in <a href="#gr:norm" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="gr:norm">[gr:norm]</a>, gives the rational norm bit. If an endpoint is simple, or if $F=\mathbf Q$, there is one rational forward bit. Vertices, types, and these bits form an *arithmetic graph*; there is no self-residue datum.

For the coefficient symbols, the vertices are the prime factors of the Fourier index. Their types fix the support and elementary Frobenius conditions, while the edge bits record the remaining quadratic residue tests. Varying an edge leaves those types and the total filter unchanged. The next calculation explains the resulting contraction rule.

<a id="gr:first-contraction"></a>
For the standard rational-two-torsion symbol of Proposition <a href="#tc:rational-rules" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="tc:rational-rules">24</a>, take split primes $p,q$ and let $U$ contain $p$ but not $q$, with matching parity. Write $V=U/p$ and $g=\mathop{\mathrm{Fr}}_q$. By Proposition <a href="#tc:rational-rules" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="tc:rational-rules">24</a>, $$A(Uq)=\bigl[t(g)H_U\bigr][1].$$ Changing one residue bit from $p$ to $q$ replaces $g$ by $g\tau_p$, where $\tau_p$ is the corresponding inertia element. The level identity <a href="#tc:exact-level-identity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="tc:exact-level-identity">[tc:exact-level-identity]</a> moves the difference to the coefficient at $p$. Its two first-shell values are $$c_p(D')A(D'),\qquad (c_p(D')+1)A(D'),
 \qquad D'=Vq',\quad \mathop{\mathrm{Fr}}_{q'}\sim g\phi_p.$$ The omitted source is unramified at the whole prime $p$, so its value $A(D')$ is the same in the two terms. Their sum is $A(D')$. Thus, if $z$ is the changed edge bit, $$\label{gr:first-contraction}
 A\big|_{z=0}+A\big|_{z=1}=A(Vq').$$ Here $q'$ is a fresh prime carrying the product labels of $p$ and $q$; it replaces two vertices by one. Its integer value is not the product $pq$.

In the quadratic field, the two choices of oriented bit correspond to using $\pi_{\mathfrak p}\pi_{\mathfrak q}$ or $\pi_{\mathfrak p}\overline{\pi_{\mathfrak q}}$ as a product template, up to the choice of output orientation. The template adds the support labels and the external residue bits in the indicated orientations. There is no internal residue attached to the new vertex. Omitting $p$ removes both places above that rational prime from the source, so a second difference in the other oriented bit gives zero. Split–simple contraction has the same interpretation with rational product data; a simple–simple difference is zero.

To use these formulas on arbitrary arrays of bits, we must know that the arrays and the product templates have prime representatives, and that different representatives give the same symbol. The following lemma supplies both facts.

<a id="stmt-gr-realization"></a>
<div id="gr:realization" class="lemma">

**Lemma 30** (Finite realization and product labels). *Fix finitely many old vertices and individually realizable new types. Every choice of independent forward bits is realized by distinct fresh primes, avoiding any given finite set. Further fixed local tests may be included in $S$.*

*A split cluster may be represented by the product of its oriented generators, with conjugations prescribed along a contraction tree; its support types and external bits are the corresponding sums. A cluster containing one simple vertex has the corresponding rational product data. These products may be replaced by fresh prime representatives. For a symbol satisfying the omitted-vertex dependence of Theorem <a href="#thm:symbol-rules" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:symbol-rules">[thm:symbol-rules]</a>, the graph data determine its value, and these replacements preserve the contracted symbol.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-gr-realization"><summary>Proof of stmt-gr-realization</summary>

*Proof.* The displayed generators account for every relevant radical. Let $U$ be a finite set of new rational primes and $U_F$ the places above them. From a squareclass with even valuations outside $S_F\cup U_F$ subtract the generators at the primes of $U_F$ where its valuation is odd. The remainder lies in $V_S(F)$. At an inert prime its rational generator has valuation one at the unique place of $F$. Thus the fixed labels and residue bits determine every elementary Frobenius test with this ramification support.

For a new split vertex, start with a template $\pi_0$ of its type, at a prime ideal $\mathfrak p_0$ away from the old vertices. Weak approximation gives $a\in F^\times$ sufficiently close to $1$ at $S_F$, positive at the specified real places, and with residues at the old prime ideals chosen so that $a\pi_0$ has the prescribed quadratic residues. Use a ray modulus containing deep enough powers of $S_F$, all old prime ideals, and the real places. A prime ideal $\mathfrak q$ in the ray class of $(a)\mathfrak p_0$ satisfies $$\mathfrak q=(ab)\mathfrak p_0,\qquad
 b\equiv1\pmod{\text{ray modulus}}.$$ Then $ab\pi_0$ has the desired divisor and type. The prime ideals in this ray class have positive Dirichlet density (Milne 2020b, chap. V, Theorem 2.5) <a id="pm-cite-71"></a>[[MilneCFT2020](#ref-MilneCFT2020)]. For $s>1$, the sum of $(N\mathfrak q)^{-s}$ over prime ideals of residue degree greater than one is at most $2\sum_p p^{-2s}$, which stays bounded as $s\downarrow1$. The corresponding sum over the ray class diverges. Hence that class contains infinitely many degree-one primes. Outside the fixed ramification support these give split rational primes, and finite exclusions remove finitely many choices.

At an old inert prime, prescribe instead the norm of the residue in $\mathbf F_{p^2}^\times$. Its norm onto $\mathbf F_p^\times$ is surjective. For a new simple vertex all conditions are rational congruences, including the inert class in $F$; the Chinese remainder theorem and Dirichlet’s theorem apply. Successive selection realizes the whole graph. Reciprocity determines reverse bits, since the support Hilbert symbols are fixed and only the two endpoint residues remain. Taking norms gives <a href="#gr:norm" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="gr:norm">[gr:norm]</a>, with no extra independent condition.

The same construction applies to a product template. It preserves its support data and its residues at every remaining vertex; no internal residue is imposed on the replacement. For a simple cluster use rational congruences for the norm labels. To check the rational filter in a split cluster, write $\pi=\prod_i\pi_i$ and $\pi'=ab\pi$ for its replacement. The multiplier $ab$ is a square unit at $S_F$ and positive at real places. Consequently $$N\pi=(\prod_i p_i)u,\qquad N\pi'=q u$$ have the same signed rational $S$-unit $u$: its valuations and sign agree. Thus $q/\prod_i p_i=N(ab)$ is locally square at the rational support. The condition at $2$ also identifies $q^*$ with $\prod_i p_i^*$ in the fixed tests. This verifies preservation of the norm correction.

Finally, compare two disjoint realizations of the same graph. Insert fresh bridge vertices with matching bits to both realizations and replace vertices one at a time. The omitted-vertex Frobenius tests agree by the radical description above, so the symbol values agree. A preliminary bridge removes any overlap. This proves both graph dependence and invariance under the product replacements. ◻

</details>

Consequently, fixing the vertex types gives a well-defined function $A_{\mathcal G}$ of the independent forward edge bits: choose any prime realization of the graph $\mathcal G$ and evaluate its coefficient symbol. Lemma <a href="#gr:realization" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="gr:realization">30</a> makes the result independent of that choice. We will write its unique multilinear polynomial as $P$. Equation <a href="#gr:first-contraction" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="gr:first-contraction">[gr:first-contraction]</a> says that a derivative of $P$ evaluates the contracted graph.

A split vertex is *primary* if its generator is a square unit at every finite place of $S_F$ and positive at every real place. The principal ray class realizes such types. Reciprocity makes their fixed radical labels trivial, and their signed rational contributions are squares in the fixed tests. Including stationary vertex primes in those tests makes primary incidences to them neutral. Including the support of a quadratic discriminant $k$ ensures that every primary prime splits in $\mathbf Q(\sqrt{k})$.

Two symbols may use different fixed-support tests or read only rational norm labels from this same graph. We call these *compatible projections* when they forget fixed-label coordinates or take norm data, preserve primary vertices, and commute with the omitted-vertex product substitution. In the norm projection either oriented-bit toggle changes the rational bit once. Thus one physical edge difference induces the specified difference for each symbol; it need not give the same polynomial for both symbols.

<a id="stmt-gr-partitionable"></a>
<div id="gr:partitionable" class="definition">

**Definition 31** (Witnesses and permitted partitions). A *witness* is a finite graph with symbol $1$. A graph is *partitionable* if it admits a partition into nonempty clusters, each containing at most one simple vertex, and oriented contraction trees whose contracted graph is a witness. The contraction trees are part of the data; this definition makes no assertion about a Selmer group.

</div>

For a two-isogenous curve with quadratic field $F'=\mathbf Q(E'[2])$, a simple vertex is *good* if it is inert in both $F$ and $F'$. A *donor* is split in $F$ and inert in $F'$. Attaching a donor turns a simple vertex split in $F'$ into a good one. These are conditions on finite labels; their supply will be established in the arithmetic application.

<a id="pm-h-34"></a>
#### Forests as finite-difference operators

For an edge bit $z$, put $\Delta_z f=f|_{z=0}+f|_{z=1}$. Every function on a finite binary cube has a unique multilinear polynomial over $\mathbf F_2$; $\Delta_z$ is its formal derivative. Differences therefore commute and satisfy $\Delta_z^2=0$.

<a id="stmt-gr-forest"></a>
<div id="gr:forest" class="lemma">

**Lemma 32** (Oriented forests). *Assume the contraction, isolation, and omitted-prime assertions of Theorem <a href="#thm:symbol-rules" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:symbol-rules">[thm:symbol-rules]</a>. Differentiation along a tree contracts it, adding product labels and external incidences; the result is zero if the tree contains two simple vertices. A collection of edge variables containing a cycle has zero derivative, including when its orientations are incompatible. The two oriented variables on one pair form a cycle of length two.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-gr-forest"><summary>Proof of stmt-gr-forest</summary>

*Proof.* The one-edge rule is the symbol contraction identity, with product replacement supplied by Lemma <a href="#gr:realization" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="gr:realization">30</a>. Induction contracts a tree: split–split mergers remain split, split–simple mergers remain simple, and merging two simple components gives zero. A root orientation determines all relative orientations along the tree. Its product template uses support types and external bits, not the differentiated internal bits.

For the two variables on a split pair $p,q$, differentiate first in one inertia bit over $p$. The resulting symbol omits the *entire rational prime* $p$, so its elementary extension is unramified at both places over $p$. The derivative in the other oriented bit is zero. Repeated use of the same variable gives zero by $\Delta_z^2=0$.

For a longer cycle, contract a spanning path. The closing edge becomes internal to one cluster and changes neither its support label nor an incidence to a remaining vertex. The omitted-endpoint argument just given therefore kills its derivative. Conjugating the product only changes its orientation; it does not restore the omitted endpoint or create a self-residue.

For example, after contracting aligned edge $12$, the two bits from its product to vertex $3$ are $t_0=z_{13}^0+z_{23}^0$ and $t_1=z_{13}^1+z_{23}^1$, up to fixed type corrections. An aligned edge $23$ differentiates $t_0$. The closing edge $31$ differentiates either $t_0$ again, giving zero, or $t_1$, giving the omitted-endpoint zero. Every longer cycle reduces to these cases. Further differences commute with this zero derivative. ◻

</details>

Call the original vertices *terminals*; any stationary external vertices retain their types and incidences. Fix their vertex types and a realizable baseline graph. Write $z=(z_e)$ for the independent toggles of the terminal–terminal bits, and let $P(z)$ be the terminal symbol. A *network* adjoins primary vertices and specified incidences involving them. It adds no terminal–terminal edge: the original bits $z$ remain parameters. All unspecified primary incidences are neutral. Within each network fix a consistent orientation at each terminal. Different networks may use different alignments.

Write $y=(y_e)$ for the bits on the added incidences, and let $f(z,y)$ be the symbol of the enlarged graph. We shall express $f(z,\mathbf1)$ as a finite-difference operator applied to $P(z)$. The differences in $y$ first contract the added graph; the forest rule then expresses each surviving term as differences in the original variables $z$.

For example, join one primary vertex $r$ to two permitted terminals $a,b$, in a fixed alignment. Expanding in its two added incidences gives four terms. The term with no difference is zero because $r$ is isolated. Each one-edge difference contracts $r$ onto one terminal and leaves the original symbol $P$, so these two terms cancel in $\mathbb F_2$. The two-edge tree contracts the terminal pair and gives $\Delta_{z_{ab}}P$. Thus this path acts exactly as the terminal difference $\Delta_{z_{ab}}$. The path has two added edges, but its operator has contraction degree one. In general, a component meeting $t$ terminals has terminal contraction degree $t-1$.

<a id="gr:grounding-dictionary"></a>
The lowest two operator degrees can be read from a matrix. Index the internal primary vertices by $I$, let $e_{ij}$ be their internal edge bits, and let $c_a$ be the incidence column from them to terminal $a$. The grounded Laplacian is the symmetric matrix over $\mathbb F_2$ with $$Q_{ij}=e_{ij}\quad(i\ne j),\qquad
 Q_{ii}=\sum_{j\ne i}e_{ij}+\sum_a(c_a)_i.$$ Equivalently, $$\label{gr:grounding-dictionary}
                         Q\mathbf1=\sum_a c_a.$$ Thus prescribed off-diagonal entries and terminal columns realize a given symmetric $Q$ precisely when this row-sum identity holds. For the one-primary-vertex path above, $Q=(0)$ and $c_a=c_b=(1)$.

The coefficients below are instances over $\mathbb F_2$ of the all-minors matrix-tree theorem (Chaiken 1982, sec. 1, Equation (2)) <a id="pm-cite-72"></a>[[Chaiken1982](#ref-Chaiken1982)]; we include the incidence-matrix proof needed here.

<a id="stmt-gr-network"></a>
<div id="gr:network" class="lemma">

**Lemma 33** (Network expansion). *A network satisfies $f(z,\mathbf1)=\mathcal N P(z)$, where $\mathcal N$ is a sum of terminal finite-difference operators indexed by forests. In each surviving forest term, every component containing an internal primary vertex meets a terminal. A component meeting $t$ terminals has contraction degree $t-1$; a component containing two simple terminals acts as zero. Networks with disjoint internal vertices and no edges between them multiply as operators on the same $P$. In particular, degree greater than $\deg P$ annihilates it.*

<a id="gr:forest-coefficients"></a>
*For the grounded Laplacian $Q$ and terminal columns $c_a$ defined above, the constant and the pair-contraction coefficients are $$\label{gr:forest-coefficients}
 \det Q,\qquad c_a^{\mathsf t}\operatorname{adj}(Q)c_b\quad(a\ne b).$$ The latter multiplies the terminal difference in the selected alignment; a prohibited pair multiplies the zero operator.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-gr-network"><summary>Proof of stmt-gr-network</summary>

*Proof.* For the set $E_0$ of added incidences, keep the terminal variables $z$ fixed and expand in the variables $y$: $$f(z,\mathbf1)=\sum_{T\subseteq E_0}(\Delta_T^y f)(z,\mathbf0).$$ Lemma <a href="#gr:forest" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="gr:forest">32</a> removes cycles. A component meeting no terminal contracts to an isolated primary vertex, so isolation removes it, including an untouched primary vertex. In a surviving component the primary labels and external primary bits are trivial. Its contracted label and external incidences are thus exactly those obtained by contracting its terminals in the original graph. A terminal tree with the same relative orientations gives that operator, of degree $t-1$.

Expanding two disjoint networks gives composition: product labels agree in either order, and any resulting cycle vanishes. Polynomial differentiation then proves the degree bound. This reasoning also verifies compatibility with projections at every degree. Norms commute with oriented products, primary norm corrections are neutral, and either oriented toggle induces its rational toggle on the original terminal polynomial. Repeated projected differences or prohibited simple mergers give zero. Forgetting fixed-label coordinates commutes with the same products.

For the coefficients, write the Laplacian of the added network as $L=DD^{\mathsf t}$, where each incidence column has ones at its edge endpoints. Let $I$ and $A$ be the internal and terminal sets. Cauchy–Binet for $Q=L_{I,I}$ counts edge sets whose incidence matrix becomes invertible after deleting the terminal rows. They are exactly forests with one terminal in each component: cycles give dependent columns, a component with no deleted row gives dependent rows, and a tree with one row deleted is invertible by leaf removal. These are the degree-zero terms.

Apply Cauchy–Binet instead to row set $I\cup\{a\}$ and column set $I\cup\{b\}$. Each component must contain one root from each of $A\setminus\{a\}$ and $A\setminus\{b\}$. Thus $a,b$ lie together and every other terminal lies in its own component. The corresponding minor is $$\det\begin{pmatrix}Q&c_b\\c_a^{\mathsf t}&0\end{pmatrix}
   =c_a^{\mathsf t}\operatorname{adj}(Q)c_b.$$ The corner is zero because there is no added terminal–terminal edge. Signs disappear in characteristic two, and the adjugate identity remains valid when $Q$ is singular. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-35"></a>
#### Selecting one address

An *address* is $x\in\mathbf F_2^b$, where $b\ge1$. A vertex with activation $\lambda\in(\mathbf F_2^b)^*$ is present when $\lambda(x)=1$. Fix a nonzero target $x_*$ and an edge bit $z$ joining terminals $a_0,a_1$ active there. Either all terminals are always present, or all have nonzero linear activations with at least one terminal for each nonzero linear form. For one symbol we need a derivative as the leading term at $x_*$ and a constant term $1$ elsewhere. For two symbols we must also account for a derivative allocated to just one factor; the second network includes a binary parameter for this purpose. We construct these two networks by prescribing their constant and degree-one terms; the final degree count will remove every higher term.

Choose a dual basis $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_b$ with $\lambda_i(x_*)=1$ for every $i$. Indeed, start with $\lambda_1(x_*)=1$ and add it to a basis of the annihilator of $x_*$. Make $b$ groups of three primary vertices, with all three vertices in group $i$ activated by $\lambda_i$. The physical coordinate vectors index these actual vertices. In each three-dimensional coordinate space choose a computational basis $(e_i,u_i,v_i)$ with $e_i=(1,1,1)$. Prescribe a symmetric form $Q$ by making the $e_i$ orthonormal and orthogonal to all $u_j,v_j$, and using on the remaining coordinates <a id="gr:H"></a>$$\label{gr:H}
 H(T,B)=\begin{pmatrix}0&T\\T^{\mathsf t}&B\end{pmatrix}.$$ Convert this form to its matrix in the physical vertex coordinates, which we also denote by $Q$. Write $Q_J$ for the restriction to the physical coordinates in groups $J$.

The column $h_i=Qe_i$ represents the covector dual to $e_i$. Since the coordinate changes do not mix groups, $h_i$ is supported on group $i$; it is independent of $T,B$. Attach this incidence column to a terminal of activation $\lambda_i$, or to any fixed terminal in the stationary case. When the active groups are $J$, the sum of these anchor columns is $$\sum_{i\in J}h_i|_J=Q_J\mathbf1_J,$$ since $\mathbf1_J=\sum_{i\in J}e_i$. Use the off-diagonal physical entries of $Q$ as the internal edge bits. Equation <a href="#gr:grounding-dictionary" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="gr:grounding-dictionary">[gr:grounding-dictionary]</a> then gives the prescribed diagonal as well: the anchors make the actual grounded Laplacian equal to $Q_J$ at every address, even after groups have disappeared.

Also attach the same column $c$ to $a_0,a_1$. If their moving activations $\alpha,\beta$ differ, attach it to a terminal of activation $\alpha+\beta$ as well. The additional column sum is always zero: $$\bigl(\alpha(x)+\beta(x)+(\alpha+\beta)(x)\bigr)c=0.$$ The third terminal is absent at $x_*$. Equal activations, or two stationary terminals, require only the first two columns. Coincident terminal roles mean addition of columns. Hence these attachments preserve the grounding at every restriction.

Write $O_{\ge d}$ for a sum of contraction operators of degrees at least $d$. This denotes a filtration, not a numerical estimate. Figure <a href="#gr:selector-figure" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="gr:selector-figure">1</a> depicts the group-level cycle and path used in the two programs when $b=4$.

<a id="stmt-gr-programs"></a>
<div id="gr:programs" class="lemma">

**Lemma 34** (Two address programs). *With these activations and grounding, there are the following networks:*

1.  *A singular program $\mathcal S$ such that $$\mathcal S_{x_*}=\Delta_z+O_{\ge2},\qquad
     \mathcal S_x=1+O_{\ge1}\quad(x\ne x_*).$$*

2.  *Two nonsingular programs on the same sites, indexed by $\varepsilon\in\mathbf F_2$, such that $$\mathcal N_x^{(\varepsilon)}=1+O_{\ge1},\qquad
     \mathcal N_x^{(1)}+\mathcal N_x^{(0)}
     =\begin{cases}\Delta_z+O_{\ge2},&x=x_*,\\
     O_{\ge2},&x\ne x_*.
     \end{cases}$$*

*All new sites have nonzero activation and are absent at $0$. Unspecified incidences, including those to stationary external vertices, may remain neutral.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-gr-programs"><summary>Proof of stmt-gr-programs</summary>

*Proof.* For the first program, take $T=I+P$, with $P$ the cyclic permutation matrix, and let $B$ be diagonal with exactly one nonzero entry. Every proper principal restriction of $P$ is a union of directed paths, hence nilpotent. Thus $T_J$ and $H(T_J,B_J)$ are invertible for proper $J$, including the empty restriction, whose determinant is $1$.

On all groups, $\ker T$ and $\ker T^{\mathsf t}$ are spanned by $\mathbf1$.
