A radical vector of $H$ has $v=t\mathbf1$; summing $T^{\mathsf t}u+Bv=0$ gives $t=0$, since $\mathbf1^{\mathsf t}B\mathbf1=1$. Hence $Q$ has radical generated by $r=\sum_i u_i$. Its adjugate is $rr^{\mathsf t}$: it is nonzero of rank one, symmetry identifies its factors with the kernel, and the only nonzero scalar in $\mathbf F_2$ is $1$.

Take $c$ dual to $u_1$, so $c^{\mathsf t}r=1$. All anchors annihilate $r$. At $x_*$ the only terminal columns pairing nontrivially with $r$ are therefore those of $a_0,a_1$. Formula <a href="#gr:forest-coefficients" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="gr:forest-coefficients">[gr:forest-coefficients]</a> gives constant zero and precisely $\Delta_z$ in degree one. Every other address has a proper group subset and constant $1$, since the activation forms form a basis. For $b=1$, $T=0$ and $B=(1)$ give the same radical.

For the second program take $T=I+L$, where $L$ is the consecutive lower shift, and $B_\varepsilon=\varepsilon E_{bb}$. Every group restriction of $T$ is invertible, and <a id="gr:inverse"></a>$$\label{gr:inverse}
 H(T,B)^{-1}=
 \begin{pmatrix}T^{-\mathsf t}BT^{-1}&T^{-\mathsf t}\\
 T^{-1}&0\end{pmatrix}.$$ Again take $c$ dual to $u_1$. On groups $J$, the change in $c^{\mathsf t}Q_J^{-1}c$ is $((T_J^{-1})_{b1})^2$, interpreted as zero if an endpoint is absent. The expansion $(I+L_J)^{-1}=I+L_J+L_J^2+\cdots$ shows that this is $1$ exactly when the entire path $1,\ldots,b$ survives, namely at $x_*$. Pairings with anchors do not change, since $Q_J^{-1}h_i=e_i$ and $e_i,h_i,c$ are independent of $\varepsilon$. At the target the balancing terminal is absent, leaving only the changed pair $a_0,a_1$. All determinants are $1$. Lemma <a href="#gr:network" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="gr:network">33</a> proves the assertion, also for the single-vertex path $b=1$. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-36"></a>
#### Simultaneous units on a punctured cube

The preceding programs control only two degrees of their operators. To make this sufficient, at each address we spend exactly the degree of a chosen top monomial. Any additional contraction then vanishes. For two symbols, the same accounting uses the ordinary product of their top homogeneous parts. The multiplication is performed before imposing the Boolean relation $z^2=z$, so one occurrence of $z$ in each factor remains two contraction requirements.

<a id="stmt-gr-address"></a>
<div id="gr:address" class="theorem">

**Theorem 35** (Address lemma). *Assume the contraction, isolation, and whole-prime omission rules of Proposition <a href="#tc:rational-rules" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="tc:rational-rules">24</a>, or the same rules for another symbol, together with the realization freedoms of Lemma <a href="#gr:realization" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="gr:realization">30</a>. Let $b\ge1$ and consider either of the following terminal arrangements:*

1.  *One symbol on a nonempty set of always active terminals, whose polynomial in the independent pair bits is nonzero.*

2.  *One or two symbols on terminals with nonzero linear activations, including a terminal for every nonzero linear form. At each $x\ne0$, each symbol separately is a nonzero polynomial in the active bits. The symbols may have stationary external data and may read compatible projections of a common graph.*

*At every $x\ne0$, assume that the active terminal data and the stationary external data obey each required filter. Then finitely many primary auxiliaries with nonzero linear activations, and one realizable assignment of graph bits, make all the symbols $1$ at every $x\ne0$. No auxiliary is present at $0$. All may satisfy fixed splitting and neutral-incidence conditions included in their primary type.*

*A nonzero evaluation or a nonzero iterated edge difference suffices for the polynomial hypothesis. In particular, a partition as in Definition <a href="#gr:partitionable" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="gr:partitionable">31</a> suffices in the stationary case.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-gr-address"><summary>Proof of stmt-gr-address</summary>

*Proof.* Fix a common realizable baseline for the terminal bits and regard their toggles as variables; omit variables invisible to a symbol. A nonzero iterated difference implies a nonzero polynomial, while every nonzero polynomial has a top monomial with coefficient $1$. By Lemma <a href="#gr:forest" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="gr:forest">32</a>, this also proves the assertion about partitions.

For one symbol, let $P_x$ have degree $d_x$ at $x\ne0$ and choose a monomial of degree $d_x$ with coefficient $1$. For each of its variables adjoin a separate singular program targeted at $x$, all with disjoint internal vertices. At address $x$, its own $d_x$ programs have zero constant, so they consume at least $d_x$ contraction degrees. Any extra degree from any program kills $P_x$. Only the selected degree-one terms of these programs and the constants of the others survive, giving the chosen coefficient $1$. A nonzero constant polynomial needs no program. Stationary anchors give the same argument for always active terminals.

For two symbols, write their polynomials at $x$ as $P_x,R_x$, of degrees $d_x,e_x$. Multiply their top homogeneous parts in the ordinary ring $\mathbf F_2[z_1,\ldots,z_m]$, before imposing Boolean relations. This ring is a domain, so choose a coefficient $1$ at a monomial <a id="gr:chosen-monomial"></a>$$\label{gr:chosen-monomial}
 M_x=\prod_z z^{\nu_{xz}},\qquad
 \nu_{xz}\in\{0,1,2\},\qquad
 \sum_z\nu_{xz}=d_x+e_x.$$ For each exponent two add one singular program targeted at $x$; for each exponent one add one nonsingular program, with its own parameter $\varepsilon_{xz}\in\mathbf F_2$. Keep all internal sets disjoint. Let $$\Phi(\varepsilon)=\prod_{x\ne0}
    (\text{final value of }P_x)(\text{final value of }R_x).$$ We show that $\sum_\varepsilon\Phi(\varepsilon)=1$, which implies that one choice makes every factor $1$.

Expand the operators by contraction degree. At its target a singular program has zero constant in both factors, so it consumes at least one degree in each. A nonsingular program has constant $1$ independent of its parameter. Summing that parameter cancels a term using only its constants everywhere; a surviving term must consume at least one degree somewhere for that program. The total of these minimum costs is <a id="gr:budget"></a>$$\label{gr:budget}
 D=\sum_{x\ne0}(d_x+e_x).$$ A nonzero term cannot consume more, since some factor would then be differentiated beyond its degree. Every surviving term therefore uses each minimum cost exactly.

Thus a singular program contributes precisely $\Delta_z$ in each factor at its target and constants elsewhere. A nonsingular program contributes degree one in exactly one factor. Summing its parameter kills that contribution away from its target and gives $\Delta_z$ at the target; every other occurrence contributes the common constant $1$. In particular, no higher forest coefficient remains.

At one address put $Z_i=\{z:\nu_{xz}=i\}$ for $i=1,2$, and write $z_J=\prod_{z\in J}z$. The surviving allocation sum is $$\sum_{J\subseteq Z_1}
 [z_{Z_2}z_J]P_x^{\rm top}\,
 [z_{Z_2}z_{Z_1\setminus J}]R_x^{\rm top}
   =[M_x](P_x^{\rm top}R_x^{\rm top})=1.$$ Wrong-degree coefficients are zero. Since the total degree is $D$ and no factor exceeds its degree, each factor receives its full degree; its derivative is exactly the displayed coefficient, independent of the baseline. Allocations at distinct addresses are independent, so their product is $1$. This covers constant factors too. For instance, if both top forms are $z$, their ordinary product is $z^2$: a singular program differentiates each once. Boolean reduction would lose that allocation.

Choose parameters with $\Phi=1$ and realize the resulting finite graph by Lemma <a href="#gr:realization" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="gr:realization">30</a>. Primary types preserve the filters and the stipulated neutral incidences and splitting conditions. Nonzero linear activations ensure that no new vertex appears at $0$. ◻

</details>

For a stabilized symbol this is a finite construction at each dimension. First choose $b$, the terminal data, and all networks; their weights and coefficient tests then have a finite bound. Select an actual stage where the numerical bounds and the finitely many stabilized symbol evaluations hold for that range. The required precision may grow with $b$. The unit-valuation constant, however, is the constant of the coefficient construction and must be independent of $b$; the forest argument supplies no additional uniformity assertion.

<a id="pw:section"></a>
### The converse with rational two-torsion

We prove the pointwise converse for curves with $E(\mathbb Q)[2]\ne0$. The finite graph construction supplies binary families with a unit coefficient at every nonzero address. Cyclotomic interpolation settles the even case. For the odd case we first establish the missing lower bound for the moving coefficient system, then keep one nonvanishing quadratic companion fixed throughout the interpolation.

Fix such a curve $E/\mathbb Q$. We use the prime weights $w(h)$, normalized values $\mathcal L(h)$, and finite $2$-primary Shafarevich–Tate lengths $s(h)$ from the preceding sections. The corank $c_2(E^{(h)})$ is a different quantity: a corank-zero base has finite $s(h)$ before analytic nonvanishing is known. All new primes are odd primes of good reduction. A filter fixes the real sign and the local unit squareclasses at a finite support containing $2N$, and may exclude any further fixed finite set.

<a id="pw:even-unit-interface"></a>
<a id="pw:odd-unit-interface"></a>
For a signed parameter $h$, write $A(h)$ for the symbol at the positive index $|h|$ on its chosen filter. We will use two bounds attached to a unit coefficient: $$\begin{aligned}
 A(h)=1\text{ in the even system}\quad&\Longrightarrow\quad
 L(E^{(h)},1)\ne0,\qquad v(\mathcal L(h))\le 2w(h)+C,
 \label{pw:even-unit-interface}\\
 A(h)=1\text{ in the odd system}\quad&\Longrightarrow\quad
 a(E^{(h)})=1,\qquad j(P_h)\le w(h)+C.
 \label{pw:odd-unit-interface}
\end{aligned}$$ Here $P_h$ is the genus Heegner sum with a fixed analytic-rank-zero partner $h_*$, and $j(P_h)$ is its free-line index valuation. The first bound is available from the even coefficient construction and Theorem <a href="#thm:cyclotomic-bound" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:cyclotomic-bound">12</a>. We use the second only after Proposition <a href="#prop:rational-odd-bound" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:rational-odd-bound">42</a> has supplied the arithmetic lower bound required to normalize the odd system. The contraction and isolation identities are those of Theorem <a href="#thm:symbol-rules" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:symbol-rules">[thm:symbol-rules]</a>; their finite graph consequences were proved in Section <a href="#gr:section" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="gr:section">6</a>.

<a id="pw:ring-lower-interface"></a>
Write $j_h(k)=j(P_{|h|}(h))$ for the ring-class index over $K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt{k})$. Theorem <a href="#thm:heegner-ring-bound" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:heegner-ring-bound">14</a> states that, if $k<0$ is an odd fundamental discriminant with $(k,2Nh)=1$, has at most $A$ prime factors, is square at $2Nh$, and defines a nonexceptional imaginary field, and the twists $h,hk$ have analytic orders one and zero, then $$\label{pw:ring-lower-interface}
 2j_h(k)\ge4w(h)+s(h)+s(hk)-C_{E,A}.$$ All coefficient and interpolation constants depend on the fixed curve, its parametrization, and fixed local data. A bound on $\omega(k)$ may enter $C_{E,A}$; the sizes of its primes do not. The finite networks, required coefficient precision, and prime sizes may depend on the binary dimension. The unit bounds in Equations <a href="#pw:even-unit-interface" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="pw:even-unit-interface">[pw:even-unit-interface]</a> and <a href="#pw:odd-unit-interface" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="pw:odd-unit-interface">[pw:odd-unit-interface]</a> may not.

By Lemma <a href="#pr:invariance" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="pr:invariance">[pr:invariance]</a>, an isogeny preserves analytic rank and Selmer corank. If the isogeny class contains a curve with full rational two-torsion, we use that curve. Otherwise choose a rational two-isogeny $E\to E'$ and write $F=\mathbb Q(E[2])$, $F'=\mathbb Q(E'[2])$; both fields are quadratic. A prime split in $F$ is called split, and one inert in $F$ is called simple. Their weights are respectively $1$ and $1/2$. A simple prime is good if it is also inert in $F'$. At such a prime <a id="pw:good-simple"></a>$$\label{pw:good-simple}
 \#E(\mathbb F_p)\equiv2\pmod4.$$ Indeed there is exactly one nonzero rational two-torsion point in the reduction. If the group order were divisible by four, its two-primary subgroup would contain a rational point of order four. Its image under the two-isogeny would supply on $E'$ a rational two-torsion point different from the dual kernel, contradicting inertness in $F'$. Thus the good-twin rule applies. When $F=F'$, every simple prime is good.

<a id="pw:seeds-section"></a>
#### Seeds and finite supplies

The word “label” below means an individually realizable fixed-support elementary Frobenius label, with orientations when required. It does not include a self-residue of a prime generator. All contractions and comparisons are those of Theorem <a href="#thm:symbol-rules" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:symbol-rules">[thm:symbol-rules]</a> and Lemma <a href="#gr:forest" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="gr:forest">32</a>.

<a id="stmt-pw-minimum-seeds"></a>
<div id="pw:minimum-seeds" class="lemma">

**Lemma 36** (Minimum seeds).

1.  *In an all-split alphabet, suppose a unit symbol has a nonempty witness. At the least positive vertex count $r$ of such a witness, all mutual edge bits are immaterial. The symbol is determined by the individual fixed-support labels. This remains true if the empty configuration is a unit, provided no contraction to the empty configuration is used.*

2.  *In the quadratic case, suppose the symbol has a nonzero witness, the alphabet is closed under the allowed contractions, and it contains the good twin operations. There are $r\ge0$ and $s_1\ge1$ such that for every $s\ge s_1$ of the permitted simple parity, the minimum split count of a unit with $s$ simple vertices is $r$. At these counts all edge bits are immaterial. A chosen minimum seed may be padded by arbitrarily many good twin pairs.*

*The assertions also hold for a stabilized moving odd symbol, with every particular finite list of uses made at a sufficiently advanced stage.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-pw-minimum-seeds"><summary>Proof of stmt-pw-minimum-seeds</summary>

*Proof.* For the first assertion, a derivative in an edge of an $r$-vertex graph is a symbol on $r-1$ vertices. If $r\ge2$, this graph remains nonempty and has value zero by minimality. If $r=1$, there is no edge. The omitted-vertex description then leaves exactly the fixed-support labels.

For the second assertion let $r(s)$ be the minimum split count at simple count $s$, with value $+\infty$ when no witness exists. Once a finite value occurs, good-twin insertion gives $r(s+2)\le r(s)$. A nonincreasing sequence of nonnegative integers stabilizes. Choose $s_1\ge1$ in that range. A derivative of an edge with a split endpoint reduces the split count and preserves the simple count; it is therefore zero at the minimum. A simple–simple derivative is zero by the symbol rule. Twin insertion gives the last assertion.

For the moving system, take the minimum and the nonincreasing sequence in the stabilized profile. Each comparison just used involves bounded vertex counts. A failure on an ultrafilter-large set of stages at any one such bound would produce a bounded-weight sequence contradicting that minimum. Thus any fixed finite collection holds on an ultrafilter-large intersection of stages, from which an arbitrarily high stage may be chosen. No assertion about every sufficiently high stage, or about all unbounded counts at one stage, is needed. ◻

</details>

Recall that a list is partitionable when a permitted contraction forest has a unit symbol as its output. Its terminal polynomial is then nonzero, since the indicated iterated finite difference is nonzero.

<a id="stmt-pw-reserves"></a>
<div id="pw:reserves" class="lemma">

**Lemma 37** (Finite label reserves). *Fix a minimum seed and a finite label alphabet.*

1.  *In the all-split rational alphabet, a list with the same total label as the seed and sufficiently many copies of its labels is partitionable.*

<a id="pw:donor-balance"></a>
2.  *In the quadratic alphabet, retain $r$ split anchors with the seed labels. Suppose there are sufficiently many simple vertices of the required parity and sufficiently many split reserves of each realizable rational shift. If $F\ne F'$, also suppose $$\label{pw:donor-balance}
     \begin{aligned}
     \Delta={}&\#\{p:\ p\text{ split in }F\text{ and inert in }F'\}\\
           &-\#\{p:\ p\text{ inert in }F\text{ and split in }F'\}>C_0.
     \end{aligned}$$ Here $C_0$ depends only on the anchors and the reserves. Then all other split vertices can be attached to simple vertices so that the result is the minimum seed and good twin pairs. The twins may match a prescribed finite enrichment of the rational labels. The base simple labels may be specified on any projection on which the required total agrees.*

*All reserve requirements depend only on the finite alphabets, seed, and projection. They do not depend on the original list length.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-pw-reserves"><summary>Proof of stmt-pw-reserves</summary>

*Proof.* In the first case retain the first $r-1$ seed labels and merge all other vertices to the last cluster. Sufficient copies ensure that this cluster is nonempty. Its label is forced by the total, hence is the last seed label. Lemma <a href="#pw:minimum-seeds" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="pw:minimum-seeds">36</a> makes its unknown edges immaterial.

For the second case, the rational labels of split attachments form the subgroup with trivial $F$-coordinate. They act transitively on the simple coset, so every prescribed change of a simple label has a realizable split shift. Reserve sufficiently many representatives of every such shift. Remove these reserves and the anchors from the donor pool. If $F\ne F'$, <a href="#pw:donor-balance" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="pw:donor-balance">[pw:donor-balance]</a>, with $C_0$ exceeding the number removed, leaves a distinct donor for each bad simple vertex. Attach these donors; every simple vertex is now good. If $F=F'$, this operation was unnecessary.

Pair equal enriched good labels. By withholding a bounded number of pairs, leave between $s_1$ and $s_1+C_1$ unpaired vertices, with the correct parity; $C_1$ depends only on the number of enriched labels. Use reserved shifts to turn the excess unpaired vertices into good pairs and to set the first $s_1-1$ base positions to the desired seed labels. The seed labels themselves need not all be good. Attach every remaining nonanchor split vertex to the last base position. Its projected label is forced by the total, the anchors, the other base positions, and the twin pairs. It is the required last seed label. Each cluster contains one simple vertex, so every contraction is permitted. Only a bounded number of reserve shifts was used.

When incidences to a retained split anchor are needed only to remove twins, they can be prescribed after the contracted labels are fixed, by the independent terminal-edge realization. Fixed stationary vertices instead enter the finite label enrichment from the outset. These two uses do not increase the number of label types with the original list length. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-pw-packets"></a>
<div id="pw:packets" class="lemma">

**Lemma 38** (Neutral packets). *For any of the finite reserve problems above with prescribed rational total zero, one can choose a finite packet of terminal labels with rational total zero such that every nonempty union of copies of the packet has the required supplies. In the quadratic case with $F\ne F'$, its donor surplus may be made arbitrarily large. Compatible fixed splitting conditions may be included whenever the needed individual labels and shifts remain realizable.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-pw-packets"><summary>Proof of stmt-pw-packets</summary>

*Proof.* Choose ample copies of every required label, including anchors and shifts. When the quadratic fields $F,F'$ are distinct, add enough donors to exceed all the losses from the other labels and the prescribed reserve margin. When $F=F'$, every simple vertex is already good. Duplicate every full label in the resulting list. Duplication gives total zero in every rational elementary coordinate and preserves any strict donor surplus. Choose the margins so that after reserving the finitely many anchors in any one packet, the union of any positive number of packets still meets the reserve requirements. All labels are realized by distinct fresh primes; duplication never means repeating an actual prime factor. ◻

</details>

<a id="pw:lower-section"></a>
#### The even converse and its uniform estimate

<a id="stmt-pw-even-base"></a>
<div id="pw:even-base" class="proposition">

**Proposition 39** (Even original base). *If $c_2(E)=0$, then $a(E)=0$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-pw-even-base"><summary>Proof of stmt-pw-even-base</summary>

*Proof.* Parity gives even functional sign. Fix an even symbol on the filter of $1$, including all auxiliary class-group tests. If its value at $1$ is a unit, analytic nonvanishing is already detected. Otherwise use a nonempty minimum seed in the full-torsion case, or a stabilized quadratic seed in the other case.

For each $b$, assign a neutral packet from Lemma <a href="#pw:packets" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="pw:packets">38</a> to every nonzero linear form on $\mathbb F_2^b$, and activate its primes by that form. At every nonzero address at least one packet is active; their union satisfies the reserve problem and has a nonzero terminal polynomial. At zero no terminal is active. The single-symbol case of Theorem <a href="#gr:address" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="gr:address">35</a> adds primary auxiliaries and makes the symbol a unit at every nonzero address. All local classes remain those of $1$. Equation <a href="#pw:even-unit-interface" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="pw:even-unit-interface">[pw:even-unit-interface]</a> gives the uniform bound at all nonzero vertices. Theorem <a href="#thm:cyclotomic-interpolation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:cyclotomic-interpolation">8</a>, applied at the original corank-zero base, now gives $a(E)=0$. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-pw-partitionable-even"></a>
<div id="pw:partitionable-even" class="proposition">

<a id="pw:partitionable-bound"></a>
**Proposition 40** (Partitionable even estimate). *Fix an even unit symbol on a prescribed filter. For every partitionable parameter $h$ on its filter with $c_2(E^{(h)})=0$, $$\label{pw:partitionable-bound}
 \mathcal L(h)\ne0,\qquad v(\mathcal L(h))-2w(h)-s(h)\le C.$$ The constant depends only on the symbol and fixed local data.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-pw-partitionable-even"><summary>Proof of stmt-pw-partitionable-even</summary>

*Proof.* If the parameter has no prime factors, the only contraction is the identity, so partitionability means that the empty symbol itself is a unit. Equation <a href="#pw:even-unit-interface" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="pw:even-unit-interface">[pw:even-unit-interface]</a> then proves the assertion directly. Otherwise the stationary terminal set is nonempty. Keep the prime factors of $h$ stationary. The iterated edge difference along the defining contraction forest is $1$, so their terminal polynomial is nonzero. The stationary one-symbol case of Theorem <a href="#gr:address" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="gr:address">35</a> gives arbitrarily large binary cubes based at $h$, with only primary new primes, whose other addresses have unit symbol. Equation <a href="#pw:even-unit-interface" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="pw:even-unit-interface">[pw:even-unit-interface]</a> and $s(h_x)\ge0$ give the uniform upper bound required by the cyclotomic transfer. The base corank is zero, so Theorem <a href="#thm:cyclotomic-interpolation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:cyclotomic-interpolation">8</a> gives <a href="#pw:partitionable-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="pw:partitionable-bound">[pw:partitionable-bound]</a>. A base-dependent dimension threshold does not affect the asserted constant. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-40"></a>
#### The lower bound needed for odd coefficients

The even estimate also supplies the arithmetic hypothesis of Proposition <a href="#prop:odd-coefficients" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:odd-coefficients">[prop:odd-coefficients]</a>. For an already analytic-rank-one parameter $h$, we choose a companion $k'=k'(h)$ with boundedly many prime factors and estimate the central value at $hk'$. Comparing the ring and genus Heegner sums then bounds $j(P_h)$ from below. The companion in this argument may vary with $h$; the odd coefficient system has not yet been normalized.

<a id="pw:isogeny-weight-comparison"></a>
To compare the two fixed isogenous curves $E,E'$, add subscripts to $s,w,\mathcal L$. At a parameter $h$ already known to have analytic rank zero, both twists have finite Tate–Shafarevich groups by the forward theorem. Cassels’s isogeny formula for the arithmetic BSD quotient (Cassels 1965) <a id="pm-cite-73"></a>[[Cassels1965](#ref-Cassels1965)], as explained in Tate (1966, Theorem 2.1 and the following discussion) <a id="pm-cite-74"></a>[[Tate1966](#ref-Tate1966)], gives $$\label{pw:isogeny-weight-comparison}
 s_E(h)+2w_E(h)=s_{E'}(h)+2w_{E'}(h)+O_{E,E'}(1).$$ Indeed, at an active odd good prime the component-group valuation is $t_p$ for the corresponding curve, so the active Tamagawa valuations sum to twice its weight. At the fixed support only finitely many local twisting classes occur. Differential, period, and torsion ratios are bounded by the fixed isogeny and its reverse, and the rank-zero regulator is $1$. These account for the bounded error in <a href="#pw:isogeny-weight-comparison" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="pw:isogeny-weight-comparison">[pw:isogeny-weight-comparison]</a>. The isogeny identity applies to the known finite groups and does not assume the BSD value formula.

The two twists have the same $L$-function. Their fixed normalizing periods therefore give $v(\mathcal L_E(h))-v(\mathcal L_{E'}(h))=O_{E,E'}(1)$, uniformly in $h$. Combining this with <a href="#pw:isogeny-weight-comparison" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="pw:isogeny-weight-comparison">[pw:isogeny-weight-comparison]</a> shows that $v(\mathcal L(h))-2w(h)-s(h)$ changes by a uniformly bounded amount. Consequently <a href="#pw:partitionable-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="pw:partitionable-bound">[pw:partitionable-bound]</a> transfers in either direction with one constant, even when the choice between the two fixed isogeny orientations depends on $h$.

<a id="stmt-pw-rough-companion"></a>
<div id="pw:rough-companion" class="lemma">

**Lemma 41** (A bounded companion for a varying odd parameter). *Fix a positive odd-sign filter and a negative genus partner $h_*$ with $L(E^{(h_*)},1)\ne0$, chosen using Proposition <a href="#prop:rough-nonvanishing" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:rough-nonvanishing">[prop:rough-nonvanishing]</a> and then excluded from the variable parameters. There are constants $A,C$ such that every $h$ on this filter of analytic order one admits a negative odd fundamental discriminant $k'$ for which*

1.  *$(k',2Nh)=1$, $k'$ is a square at every place of $2Nh$, and $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{k'})$ is nonexceptional;*

2.  *$\omega(k')\le A$;*

<a id="pw:rough-bound"></a>
3.  *$L(E^{(hk')},1)\ne0$ and $$\label{pw:rough-bound}
     v(\mathcal L(hk'))\le 2w(hk')+s(hk')+C.$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-pw-rough-companion"><summary>Proof of stmt-pw-rough-companion</summary>

*Proof.* Choose the class-group support and all other fixed label tests before varying $h$. Prepare an even negative-index symbol for each possible total type at this support, and for both isogeny orientations if needed. There are finitely many such preparations. The positive index $|hk'|$ has nonzero total rational type: its negative-discriminant parity is already nontrivial among the tests at $2$. Thus in the full-torsion case a unit seed has positive count. In the quadratic case use the stabilized seed of Lemma <a href="#pw:minimum-seeds" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="pw:minimum-seeds">36</a>.

When $F\ne F'$, interchanging the isogeny orientation interchanges the two counts in <a href="#pw:donor-balance" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="pw:donor-balance">[pw:donor-balance]</a>. Select the orientation with initial balance at least zero. The existing donors can then pay for arbitrarily many existing bad simples. They do not have to be supplied by new primes.

Let $R$ be the absolute prime-count bound in Proposition <a href="#prop:rough-nonvanishing" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:rough-nonvanishing">[prop:rough-nonvanishing]</a>. Insert in $k'$ a finite dummy supply that meets the anchors, minimum simple count, and reserve requirements for every one of the finitely many prepared symbols. When the quadratic fields $F,F'$ are distinct, add donor slack paying for every reserved loss, the new dummy bad simples, and a further possible loss of $R$ from the later rough factor. Add a fresh ramified prime if needed to exclude the exceptional imaginary fields. The number of dummy primes is bounded independently of $h$. Their labels and initial incidences may be chosen by Lemma <a href="#gr:realization" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="gr:realization">30</a>.

Absorb $h$ and the dummy product into the curve. Apply Proposition <a href="#prop:rough-nonvanishing" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:rough-nonvanishing">[prop:rough-nonvanishing]</a> to complete $k'$ by a squarefree factor coprime to all primes already used. Prescribe its sign and its local unit classes so that the final $k'$ is an odd negative fundamental discriminant, is a square at $2Nh$, and has the required original local classes at $2N$. These conditions are reduced congruences at the level of the absorbed curve. Additional fixed primes may be excluded. The lemma makes the central value at $hk'$ nonzero with at most $R$ new factors. Its size threshold may depend on $h$ and all these congruences; $R$ does not.

No particular resulting unit class at the auxiliary class-group support was assumed in advance: dummy supplies were prepared for every possible total there. For the actual total, Lemma <a href="#pw:reserves" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="pw:reserves">37</a> makes $hk'$ partitionable. Analytic nonvanishing gives Selmer corank zero by the forward theorem. Proposition <a href="#pw:partitionable-even" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="pw:partitionable-even">40</a> therefore gives <a href="#pw:rough-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="pw:rough-bound">[pw:rough-bound]</a>, with the isogeny comparison above if the other orientation was used. The finite preparation and the bound on dummy and rough factors give $A,C$ independent of $h$. ◻

</details>

<a id="pw:height-ratio"></a>
Proposition <a href="#prop:heegner-comparison" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:heegner-comparison">9</a> compares the genus sum $P_h$ with the ring-class sum over $K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt{k})$: $$\label{pw:height-ratio}
 2j_h(k)-2j(P_h)=v(\mathcal L(hk))+O(1)$$ whenever the two twists have analytic orders one and zero. The error is uniform in $h$ for fixed $k$, and uniform in $h,k$ when $\omega(k)$ is bounded and the prescribed local classes are retained. Thus the same comparison applies to the bounded companions just constructed.

<a id="stmt-prop-rational-odd-bound"></a>
<div id="prop:rational-odd-bound" class="proposition">

**Proposition 42** (Uniform lower bound for the odd detector). *<span id="pw:odd-lower" label="pw:odd-lower"></span>Every analytically rank-one $h$ in the fixed positive filter satisfies <a id="pw:odd-lower-bound"></a>$$\label{pw:odd-lower-bound}
 2j(P_h)\ge 2w(h)+s(h)-C.$$ In particular $j(P_h)\ge w(h)-C$ uniformly in $h$ and its prime count.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-prop-rational-odd-bound"><summary>Proof of stmt-prop-rational-odd-bound</summary>

*Proof.* Choose $k'$ by Lemma <a href="#pw:rough-companion" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="pw:rough-companion">41</a>. Combine <a href="#pw:ring-lower-interface" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="pw:ring-lower-interface">[pw:ring-lower-interface]</a>, <a href="#pw:height-ratio" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="pw:height-ratio">[pw:height-ratio]</a>, and <a href="#pw:rough-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="pw:rough-bound">[pw:rough-bound]</a>. Since the factors are coprime, $w(hk')=w(h)+w(k')$, and $w(k')\le\omega(k')\le A$. Hence $$\begin{aligned}
 2j(P_h)
 &\ge 4w(h)+s(h)+s(hk')-v(\mathcal L(hk'))-C\\
 &\ge 2w(h)+s(h)-2w(k')-C\\
 &\ge 2w(h)+s(h)-C'.
\end{aligned}$$ Only even symbols and independently nonvanishing companions were used. Thus this proof precedes, and does not assume, the odd minimum-depth normalization. ◻

</details>

<a id="pw:fixed-companion-section"></a>
#### A fixed companion for the odd converse

Suppose the functional sign is odd. By Proposition <a href="#pw:odd-lower" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="pw:odd-lower">[pw:odd-lower]</a>, the odd coefficient system can now be normalized on the positive filter of $1$. Fix its old support and genus partner $h_*$. Its moving detecting prime $\ell$ has not become an extra fixed support requirement.

Choose a separate even symbol for negative discriminants square at $2N$, excluding the fixed odd support, the relevant torsion ramification, and the exceptional imaginary fields. Choose a unit $k$ of that symbol. Then $L(E^{(k)},1)\ne0$. Fix this $k$ and $K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt{k})$ for the rest of the construction, before choosing any cube dimension. Its fresh ramification makes it independent of the old fixed label extensions. At sufficiently advanced stages $\ell$ avoids $k$. The intrinsic odd label tests continue to omit the primes of $k$. When the odd symbol already detects the base, the converse follows directly. We henceforth consider the remaining case, in which the odd symbol has the nonempty seed described above.

For the moving odd source, fix its stabilized minimum depth and seed profiles before constructing packets. A bounded-weight seed has boundedly many vertices here, since every prime has weight at least $1/2$. For each fixed field used in the labels, permitting ramification above the one moving prime $\ell$ adds only boundedly many dimensions to its elementary squareclass space. Identify these spaces compatibly with their fixed projections and stabilize the finitely many seed and label profiles. The reserve bounds of Lemma <a href="#pw:reserves" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="pw:reserves">37</a> are uniform over these profiles, so the packet constructions below have a fixed size. They are finite tables of labels; their prime representatives will be chosen at an actual coefficient stage after the networks and their weight bounds have been specified.

Our remaining task is to construct, for every binary dimension, a family in which the odd test at $h$ and an even test at $hk$ are simultaneously units away from the zero address. Every new prime will split in this single field $K$. For quadratic $F$, the good-twin rule makes the unit at $k$ a nonzero even test on additional prime configurations. With full rational two-torsion, the restriction to $K$-split primes can instead leave only the empty configuration at the original minimum depth. The next construction supplies a nonempty witness in exactly that case; its extra division changes the valuation estimate by a fixed constant.

<a id="pw:split-section"></a>
#### A nonempty witness with full rational two-torsion

<a id="stmt-pw-recurrence"></a>
<div id="pw:recurrence" class="lemma">

**Lemma 43** (Recurrence congruences). *Let $p$ be odd, $a\equiv p+1\pmod4$, and let $$b_0=1,\quad b_1=a-\kappa,\quad
 b_{s+1}=ab_s-pb_{s-1}.$$ If $\kappa=\pm1$, then $b_{s+1}-b_s$ is even and $$\frac{b_{s+1}-b_s}{2}\equiv\frac{a-\kappa-1}{2}\pmod2
 \quad(s\ge0).$$ If $\kappa=0$, put $b_{-1}=0$; then $b_s-b_{s-1}$ is odd for every $s\ge0$. Finally, for $\kappa=1$, if $a\equiv p+1\pmod{2^m}$ then $b_s\equiv p^s\pmod{2^m}$ for every $s\ge0$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-pw-recurrence"><summary>Proof of stmt-pw-recurrence</summary>

*Proof.* Modulo $2$ the recurrence is $b_{s+1}=b_{s-1}$. Its initial values prove the parity assertions. For $d_s=b_{s+1}-b_s$, the recurrence for $d_s$ is the same. Directly, $d_1-d_0\equiv(p-1)(p-\kappa)\equiv0\pmod4$ when $\kappa=\pm1$. Thus $d_s/2$ is constant modulo $2$. The last assertion follows by substituting the sequence $p^s$ in the recurrence and checking its first two terms. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-pw-split-witness"></a>
<div id="pw:split-witness" class="lemma">

**Lemma 44** (Nonempty $K$-split witness). *Suppose $E[2]$ is rational. Choose a negative unit $k$ of a fixed even symbol for $E$, prime to all previous fixed support and to the ramification support of $E[8]$. Put $K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt{k})$, chosen nonexceptional. Let $S_0$ contain $2N$, the primes of $k$, and primes generating the class group of $K$. On the positive filter of $1$ square at $S_0$, there is an even unit test on nonempty products of primes split in $K$ with these properties:*

1.  *it has a nonempty witness;*

2.  *it satisfies the oriented split contraction and primary-isolation rules over $K$, for contractions with nonempty output;*

<a id="pw:split-unit-bound"></a>
3.  *a unit at $D$ implies $$\label{pw:split-unit-bound}
     L(E^{(kD)},1)\ne0,\qquad v(\mathcal L(kD))\le 2\omega(D)+C_k.$$*

*The proof uses Lemmas <a href="#tc:trace-algebra" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="tc:trace-algebra">[tc:trace-algebra]</a> and <a href="#tc:inertia-identity" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="tc:inertia-identity">[tc:inertia-identity]</a> to construct a further divided coefficient test.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-pw-split-witness"><summary>Proof of stmt-pw-split-witness</summary>

<a id="pw:split-basic-depth"></a>
*Proof.* Let $a_0(n)$ be the coefficients of the original negative-index form for $E$. Since $k$ attains its least normalized depth, $v(a_0(|k|D)/a_0(|k|))\ge\omega(D)$ whenever $kD$ lies on its filter. Use the ordinary even coefficient form for $E^{(k)}$, normalized by $a(1)=1$, on the positive filter of $1$ square at $S_0$. The two exact comparisons in Equation <a href="#cs:even-ratio" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="cs:even-ratio">[cs:even-ratio]</a> give $$2v(a(D))
 =v\!\left(\frac{\sqrt D\,L(E^{(kD)},1)}{L(E^{(k)},1)}\right)
 =2v\!\left(\frac{a_0(|k|D)}{a_0(|k|)}\right).$$ Indeed, the period and the factor $\sqrt{|k|}$ cancel in the old ratio, and the new period cancels in the new ratio. Enlarging $S_0$ only restricts the allowed $D$, so the original minimum still gives $$\label{pw:split-basic-depth}
 v(a(D))\ge\omega(D)$$ at every allowed squarefree $D$.

<a id="pw:split-extra-depth"></a>
If equality holds at a nonempty product of $K$-split primes, use the usual even bit, projected from oriented $K$-labels to rational labels. It has all the required properties by Theorem <a href="#thm:symbol-rules" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:symbol-rules">[thm:symbol-rules]</a>. We therefore assume for the rest of the proof that equality never occurs there. By the rational-phase assertion in Proposition <a href="#prop:even-coefficients" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:even-coefficients">[prop:even-coefficients]</a>, normalization by $a(1)=1$ makes each nonzero squarefree coefficient a rational number times a root of unity. Its valuation is an integer, not just an element of the possibly ramified coefficient field’s discrete value group. Thus strict inequality implies $$\label{pw:split-extra-depth}
 v(a(D))\ge\omega(D)+1
 \quad\text{for every nonempty allowed all-$K$-split }D.$$

Write $g=\sum a(n)q^n$ for the form. Its characters satisfy $\psi/\eta=\chi_{-4}$; since the scalar character $\psi$ is even, $\eta$ is odd. For a set $U$ of $K$-split primes put $$B_U=2^{-|U|}\prod_{p\in U}(U_p-\eta(p)V_p)g,
 \qquad
 \Theta_J=\sum_{m>0,\ (m,S_0)=1}\eta(m)m q^{Jm^2}.$$ All expansions retain the prescribed support sieves. The ordinary divided form is $$H_U=\frac12\left(B_U-\sum_{J\subseteq U}B_U[J]\Theta_J\right).$$ Here $B_U[J]$ denotes its coefficient at the squarefree index $J$.

<a id="pw:split-mod8"></a>
*The mod-$8$ consequence.* We first prove $$\label{pw:split-mod8}
 a_p(E^{(k)})\equiv p+1\pmod8
 \quad\text{for every allowed good }p\text{ split in }K.$$ Put $f=H_{\{p\}}\theta$ and apply its trace at a Frobenius lift $\phi_p$, testing coefficient $p^2$. The terms $B_{\{p\}}\theta$ and $\Theta_{\{p\}}\theta$ have the same character, whose $p$-part is primitive quadratic. Thus they have no $p$-old constituent. On their conductor-one ramified principal-series constituents the identity is $$U_p^2t(\phi_p)=U_p^3+d(\phi_p)U_p.$$ The remaining term $\Theta_\varnothing\theta$ is unraised, and obeys the ordinary good-prime coefficient identity. Consequently $$(t(\phi_p)f)[p^2]=f[p^3]+(d(\phi_p)f)[p].$$ Replace the trace by a fresh split prime $p'$ with the same finite data, including every support-unit test. At each rational quadratic character unramified outside $S_0$, a Frobenius lift at $p$ has the character value of $p$. Hence the matched $p'$ has the same value, and $pp'$ has value $1$. Equivalently, $p'$ has the same unit squareclasses as $p$ at all places of $S_0$, so their product is square at all of them, including $2$. Since $\phi_p\in G_K$, the new prime is also split in $K$. Its coefficient on the left tests $pp'$; by <a href="#pw:split-extra-depth" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="pw:split-extra-depth">[pw:split-extra-depth]</a> it is zero modulo the maximal ideal after the two divisions. To check the determinant term, let $d_1,d_0$ be the determinant scalars on the raised and unraised character spaces. Then $$d(\phi_p)f
 =d_1f+\frac{B_{\{p\}}[1]}2(d_1-d_0)
                  \Theta_\varnothing\theta.$$ The character difference $(d_1-d_0)/2$ is integral. Also $f[p]\equiv H_{\{p\}}[p]=0$ modulo the maximal ideal, since $\Theta_{\{p\}}[p]=1$, whereas $(\Theta_\varnothing\theta)[p]\equiv\Theta_\varnothing[p]=0$ because $\theta\equiv1$ and $p$ is nonsquare. Thus $(d(\phi_p)f)[p]=0$ after reduction. This cancellation uses the two character spaces together.

On the right, the indices $p$ and $p^3$ in $B_{\{p\}}$ have underlying squarefree index $1$; they involve only $a(1),a(p^2),a(p^4)$. The $J=\varnothing$ unary term has no coefficient at either nonsquare index. Thus no other squarefree coefficient contributes there. For $a=a_p(E^{(k)})$, the phase-free square coefficients are $1,a-1,a(a-1)-p$. Hence the remaining coefficient is, up to a unit, $$H_{\{p\}}[p^3]
 =\frac{a^2-2a-p+1-p(a-2)}4
 =\frac{(a-1)(a-p-1)}4.$$ This quotient is rational. Its vanishing in the residue field therefore gives a positive integral $2$-adic valuation, so it is divisible by $2$. Full rational two-torsion makes $a$ even, so $a-1$ is odd; this proves <a href="#pw:split-mod8" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="pw:split-mod8">[pw:split-mod8]</a>. No individual total filter condition on $p$ was needed: its matched prime $p'$ makes $pp'$ lie on the filter, and the square-index terms on the right come from $1$.

<a id="pw:four-divided-form"></a>
<a id="pw:shell-valuation"></a>
*One further division by $2$.* Define $$\label{pw:four-divided-form}
 \widetilde H_U=\frac14
 \left(B_U-\sum_{J\subseteq U}B_U[J]\Theta_J\right).$$ We verify integrality at every coefficient. Write a test index uniquely as $Jrm^2$, where $J\subseteq U$ and $r$ is squarefree and disjoint from $U$. The underlying squarefree coefficient is at $D=(U/J)r$. Removing the unit phases, a prime of $U/J$ contributes an odd factor $b_s-b_{s-1}$ with $\kappa=0$, and a prime of $J$ contributes $b_{s+1}-b_s$ with $\kappa=(D/p)$. Thus $$\label{pw:shell-valuation}
 v(B_U[Jrm^2])\ge\omega(r)$$ by <a href="#pw:split-basic-depth" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="pw:split-basic-depth">[pw:split-basic-depth]</a>, with one additional unit of valuation when $D$ is nonempty and all its primes split in $K$.

If $r\ne1$ and all primes of $D$ split in $K$, the last inequality is at least $\omega(r)+1\ge2$. If $D$ contains an inert prime, then $r$ contains at least two: the total rational $K$-character is trivial on the filter, and all primes of $U$ split. Then <a href="#pw:shell-valuation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="pw:shell-valuation">[pw:shell-valuation]</a> is again at least $2$. No unary term has this squarefree part. This proves divisibility by $4$ for $r\ne1$.

Suppose $r=1$ and $J\ne U$. Then $D=U/J$ is nonempty and all split, so $B_U[J]$ is even. This cancellation can be checked without dividing by a leading multiplier, which may be zero. Factor from both shell coefficients the common phase and the scalar $2^{-|U|+|J|}a(U/J)$, whose valuation is at least $1$ by <a href="#pw:split-extra-depth" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="pw:split-extra-depth">[pw:split-extra-depth]</a>. The remaining factors are the odd differences at $U/J$, the integral divided differences at $J$, and the ordinary square-index factors outside $U$. By Lemma <a href="#pw:recurrence" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="pw:recurrence">43</a>, their product is congruent modulo $2$ to the product of their leading values, even when one of those values is zero modulo $2$. Since $m$ is odd, multiplication by $m$ preserves this congruence. The common scalar supplies the second factor $2$. Retaining the phase $\eta(m)$ therefore gives $$B_U[Jm^2]\equiv B_U[J]\eta(m)m\pmod4.$$ This is exactly the cancellation with $B_U[J]\Theta_J$.

Finally let $J=U$, so $D=1$. At a prime outside $U$ the recurrence gives $b_s\equiv p^s\pmod4$. At a prime of $U$, <a href="#pw:split-mod8" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="pw:split-mod8">[pw:split-mod8]</a> gives $b_s\equiv p^s\pmod8$, and hence $$\frac{b_{s+1}-b_s}{2}
 \equiv \frac{a_p-2}{2}\,p^s\pmod4.$$ Multiplying these congruences, again retaining the phases, gives $B_U[Um^2]\equiv B_U[U]\eta(m)m\pmod4$. This proves integrality in the last case and establishes <a href="#pw:four-divided-form" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="pw:four-divided-form">[pw:four-divided-form]</a>. Diamonds preserve this lattice: when $J\ne U$, $B_U[J]$ is even and the quadratic character difference supplies another factor $2$; when $J=U$, the characters agree exactly.

*The new symbol and its witness.* Multiply <a href="#pw:four-divided-form" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="pw:four-divided-form">[pw:four-divided-form]</a> by ordinary theta and use the integral trace operators. Two fresh traces in $G_K$ give zero after reduction at every coefficient. To see this, start with an arbitrary test index $Jrm^2$ and choose the two fresh primes outside that index and the level. The filter imposes $\chi_K(D)=1$; since $U$ is all split, the number of inert factors in $r$ is either zero or at least two. The fresh traces replace $r$ by $rq_1q_2$, with both $q_i$ split. In the first case the valuation after division by $4$ is at least $\omega(r)+2+1-2=\omega(r)+1\ge1$. In the second case it is at least $\omega(r)+2-2=\omega(r)\ge2$. The unary terms disappear under these fresh tests. Additional fresh $G_K$ traces only improve these estimates, so vanishing holds on the entire reduced trace orbit. The trace identity therefore gives $$t(gu^2)=t(g)\qquad(g,u\in G_K)$$ on this reduced trace orbit. Thus the tests factor through the elementary extension of $K$ unramified off the level.

<a id="pw:deeper-bit"></a>
A single fresh $K$-split trace at coefficient $1$ reads the bit $$\label{pw:deeper-bit}
 \widetilde A(D)=
 \left(2^{-\omega(D)-1}a(D)\text{ with its phase removed}\right)\bmod2$$ for a nonempty all-split configuration. The contraction rule follows from the same integral local identity as in Lemma <a href="#tc:inertia-identity" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="tc:inertia-identity">[tc:inertia-identity]</a>. For completeness its first shell, with $p\in U$ and a fresh trace $q$, has underlying configuration $D'=(U/p)q$, which is still nonempty, and its reduction is $$c_p(D')\widetilde A(D'),\qquad
 c_p(D')=\frac{a_p-(D'/p)-1}{2}\bmod2.$$ Changing the oriented inertia bit changes $c_p$ once. The omitted-prime identity gives the product label and removes the entire rational prime $p$ from the new ramification support. Consequently its repeated contraction has precisely the forest interpretation of Lemma <a href="#gr:forest" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="gr:forest">32</a>. An omitted-vertex label equal to the identity has trace zero, which is primary isolation. No contraction to the empty configuration has occurred.

It remains to prove that this deeper test has a witness. Fresh ramification gives $K\not\subseteq\mathbb Q(E[8])$. By Chebotarev there is a good prime $p$ inert in $K$ and trivial on the original $E[8]$. Then $$p\equiv1\pmod8,\qquad a_p(E^{(k)})\equiv-2\pmod8.$$ On $\widetilde H_\varnothing$, whose coefficient at $1$ is zero, test $t(u)^2$ at coefficient $1$, where $u=\operatorname{Fr}_p$. The square coefficient and matching unary character give, up to a unit, $$\frac{a_p(E^{(k)})-1-p}{4}\bmod2=1.$$ The determinant term at coefficient $1$ cancels. In characteristic two, $t(u^2)=t(u)^2$, so a single trace in $G_K$ is nonzero. A fresh prime realizing this finite trace test is split in $K$. Moreover $u^2$ is trivial on every rational quadratic character, so the prime lies on the required total rational filter. It is a nonempty witness for <a href="#pw:deeper-bit" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="pw:deeper-bit">[pw:deeper-bit]</a>. Finally the exact coefficient ratio gives <a href="#pw:split-unit-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="pw:split-unit-bound">[pw:split-unit-bound]</a>, with the additional depth at most one. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-pw-coinvariants"></a>
<div id="pw:coinvariants" class="lemma">

**Lemma 45** (Orientation correction). *Let $K$ be imaginary quadratic, let $S_0$ contain $2$ and its ramification support, and let $V_0$ be the elementary label space over $K$ unramified off $S_0$. Complex conjugation acts on $V_0$ by $c$. If the rational total of an oriented prime configuration is zero on every rational quadratic character unramified off $S_0$, then its oriented total belongs to $(1+c)V_0$. A reserved supply containing every label allows its orientations to be flipped to realize any prescribed change in $(1+c)V_0$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-pw-coinvariants"><summary>Proof of stmt-pw-coinvariants</summary>

*Proof.* Complex conjugation has order two outside $G_K$, so $G_{\mathbb Q}=G_K\rtimes\langle c\rangle$. A $c$-invariant quadratic character of $G_K$ extends by giving $c$ value zero. At a rational prime outside $S_0$, inertia lies in $G_K$ and the character is trivial there; thus its extension remains unramified outside $S_0$. The assumed total therefore annihilates $(V_0^*)^c$.

For a finite vector space with involution, the annihilator of $\ker(1+c^*)=(V_0^*)^c$ is $\operatorname{im}(1+c)$. This proves the first assertion. Flipping a vertex of label $v$ changes its oriented label from $v$ to $cv$, and hence changes the total by $(1+c)v$. Reserve one representative for every preimage needed to express the desired element of the image. Their independent flips give the second assertion. These flips preserve every rational norm label. ◻

</details>

<a id="pw:assembly-section"></a>
#### Common packets and rank-one interpolation

<a id="stmt-pw-fixed-companion-families"></a>
<div id="pw:fixed-companion-families" class="proposition">

**Proposition 46** (Families with a fixed companion). *With the fixed odd coefficient system and companion $k$ chosen in Section <a href="#pw:fixed-companion-section" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="pw:fixed-companion-section">7.4</a>, suppose the odd symbol at $1$ is zero. There is a constant $C$ with the following property. For every $b\ge1$ there are distinct primes outside $2Nk$ and the fixed supports of both coefficient tests, with nonzero linear activations, such that their signed products $h_x$, $x\in\mathbb F_2^b$, satisfy $h_0=1$. Every $h_x$ is positive and has the fixed local classes of $1$, and every new prime splits in $K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt{k})$. The primes also avoid the detecting prime of the actual odd coefficient stage. In particular $(h_x,k)=1$ for every $x$. For every $x\ne0$, $$a(E^{(h_x)})=1,\qquad L(E^{(h_xk)},1)\ne0,$$ and $$j(P_{h_x})\le w(h_x)+C,\qquad
 v(\mathcal L(h_xk))\le 2w(h_x)+C.$$ The constant $C$ and the discriminant $k$ are independent of $b$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-pw-fixed-companion-families"><summary>Proof of stmt-pw-fixed-companion-families</summary>

*Proof.* We construct common terminal packets, individually split in $K$, such that the odd terminal polynomial and an even terminal polynomial testing $hk$ are separately nonzero at each nonzero address.

First suppose $F,F'$ are quadratic. Keep the original even symbol evaluated on $hk$, treating the vertices of $k$ as stationary external data. Enrich the rational labels of the $h$-vertices by the primes of $k$. Their total there and at the even support is required to be zero. Let $V$ be the resulting rational elementary label space, including the $F,F'$ and $K$ coordinates and all relations among these characters. The allowed simple labels form the affine set $\{v\in V:\chi_F(v)=1,\ \chi_K(v)=0\}$, in additive notation. The difference of any two of its elements belongs to $\ker\chi_F\cap\ker\chi_K$, precisely the realizable rational labels of the permitted split attachments. Translation by this subgroup is therefore transitive. The fields $F,F'$ are unramified outside the old support, whereas $K$ has a fresh ramified prime; thus $K$ is independent of their compositum. When $F\ne F'$, this realizes both the good-simple pattern $(1,1,0)$ and the donor pattern $(0,1,0)$ in their three coordinates. When $F=F'$, all simple labels are good.

For the old odd projection, take a normal closure of its finite label extension, including the moving prime $\ell$ at any stage realizing the stabilized profile. It is unramified outside the old support and $\ell$. Once $\ell$ avoids $k$, a prime ramified in $K$ remains outside that set. Hence $K$ has trivial intersection with this normal closure, and every old odd label can be realized together with splitting in $K$. This applies also to oriented split anchors over $F$. The added stationary $k$ coordinates may have relations, but they are already included in $V$; they do not impose extra requirements on the omitted odd projection.

Use packets with the required simple supply and reserves in this kernel, and with sufficiently large donor slack when $F\ne F'$. For the even test, take no split anchors. Correct all bad simples to good ones, pair equal enriched labels, and retain a nonempty good base pair. Use reserves to match the pair and the remaining good pairs, and attach every leftover split vertex to the last base position. Its label is forced by total zero. The output is a collection of good twin pairs, each matching also at every split vertex of $k$. Twin insertion into the unit at $k$ proves that this output has even symbol one. Thus the even terminal polynomial is nonzero.

For the odd test, project away the newly added tests at $k$. The same packets contain enough split anchors, simple vertices and reserve shifts to contract to the stabilized odd seed and good pairs, by Lemma <a href="#pw:reserves" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="pw:reserves">37</a>. Its total on that projection is the prescribed zero total. Incidences between the retained anchors and the good pairs can be set after contraction, by independent edge choices. The odd polynomial is therefore nonzero as well. This odd test does not include the stationary vertices of $k$.

Now suppose the curve has full rational two-torsion. Use the even test of Lemma <a href="#pw:split-witness" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="pw:split-witness">44</a>, with $K$-oriented labels on its support $S_0$, and let $v_1,\ldots,v_r$ be a minimum nonempty witness. Its oriented total $v_1+\cdots+v_r$ lies in $(1+c)V_0$, by Lemma <a href="#pw:coinvariants" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="pw:coinvariants">45</a>. Choose packets containing ample copies of every needed even label, all odd seed labels on their rational projection, and orientation-shifting reserves. In the common compositum, restriction to the even label extension is surjective, so each even label has a lift. Each intrinsic odd label also has a lift fixing $K$: fresh ramification gives $K\cap L_{\rm odd}=\mathbb Q$, and the moving odd prime avoids $k$. Extending these elements to the common compositum gives the required lifts. Take sufficiently many lifts for each projection separately, without prescribing their other projection. Duplicate each full label, so the packet has rational total zero.

For the even contraction, retain anchors with labels $v_1,\ldots,v_{r-1}$. After reserving these anchors, use orientation flips to make the total equal to $\sum v_i$; this is possible by Lemma <a href="#pw:coinvariants" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="pw:coinvariants">45</a>. Merge all remaining vertices into the last cluster. Its label is $v_r$. The cluster is nonempty, and the minimum nonempty count makes the output a unit independently of its mutual edges. For the odd contraction, use its rational projection. Every odd seed label lifts to a $K$-split prime because $K$ was freshly ramified outside its intrinsic support. Retain all but the last odd seed label and merge the remainder. Total zero gives the last label, so this is also a unit. Orientation correction is conjugation over $\mathbb Q$, which preserves every rational quadratic label, including those at the moving odd prime. Adding $k$ to the common support has not added it to the intrinsic odd projection.

In both cases put a sufficient common packet at every nonzero linear form on $\mathbb F_2^b$. Each nonzero address has two separately nonzero terminal polynomials. Theorem <a href="#gr:address" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="gr:address">35</a> supplies primary auxiliaries split in $K$ (and $F$ in the quadratic case), neutral at the stationary primes of $k$, and makes both symbols one at every nonzero address. The auxiliary generators are primary at every support coordinate used by either projection. Thus the odd and even graph identities remain identities on the same common terminal polynomial data. All active products $h$ are positive and square at the fixed tests, and all their primes split in $K$.

For each fixed $b$, the terminal tables and networks now give a finite list of coefficient tests and a maximum weight. Choose the working precision after these bounds are fixed. Finer ray neighborhoods affect prime realization but do not enlarge the elementary label alphabet. Lemma <a href="#cs:fixed-weight-uniformity" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="cs:fixed-weight-uniformity">18</a> and Theorem <a href="#thm:symbol-rules" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:symbol-rules">[thm:symbol-rules]</a> realize the required divisibilities and symbol identities on an ultrafilter-large intersection of stages. At an arbitrarily high actual stage in that intersection, realize the finite graphs by distinct primes. The unit-depth constants and the companion $k$ were fixed before $b$ was chosen, and therefore remain uniform in these realizations.

At each nonzero address the odd unit detects analytic rank one and gives $j(P_h)\le w(h)+C$. The even unit detects $L(E^{(hk)},1)\ne0$ and gives $v(\mathcal L(hk))\le2w(hk)+C$, or the bound <a href="#pw:split-unit-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="pw:split-unit-bound">[pw:split-unit-bound]</a> in the full-torsion case. The fixed quantity $2w(k)$ is absorbed into $C$. These are the asserted estimates. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-pw-odd-base"></a>
<div id="pw:odd-base" class="proposition">

**Proposition 47** (Odd original base). *If $c_2(E)=1$, then $a(E)=1$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-pw-odd-base"><summary>Proof of stmt-pw-odd-base</summary>

*Proof.* Parity gives odd functional sign. Proposition <a href="#pw:odd-lower" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="pw:odd-lower">[pw:odd-lower]</a> therefore permits the odd normalization used above. If its symbol at $1$ is a unit, it already gives $a(E)=1$. Otherwise apply Proposition <a href="#pw:fixed-companion-families" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="pw:fixed-companion-families">46</a> for arbitrarily large $b$. At every nonzero address its estimates and Proposition <a href="#prop:heegner-comparison" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:heegner-comparison">9</a>, with the fixed $k$, give $$2j_h(k)\le4w(h)+C.$$ The finite Sha lengths there are nonnegative. Hence $2j_h(k)-4w(h)-s(h)-s(hk)\le C$, as required for Heegner interpolation.

At address zero, $L(E^{(k)},1)\ne0$ gives $c_2(E^{(k)})=0$ by Lemma <a href="#pr:ranks" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="pr:ranks">4</a>. Lemma <a href="#pr:invariance" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="pr:invariance">[pr:invariance]</a> gives $$\mathop{\mathrm{corank}}_{\mathbb Z_2}\mathop{\mathrm{Sel}}_{2^\infty}(E/K)
 =c_2(E)+c_2(E^{(k)})=1.$$ Since $K$ is fixed, the finite quotient of this base Selmer group has a fixed length. Theorem <a href="#thm:heegner-interpolation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:heegner-interpolation">10</a> makes $L(E,s)L(E^{(k)},s)$ have a simple zero. Its second factor is nonzero at $1$, so $a(E)=1$. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-thm-rational-converse"></a>
<div id="thm:rational-converse" class="theorem">

**Theorem 48** (The rational-two-torsion converse). *Let $E/\mathbb Q$ satisfy $E(\mathbb Q)[2]\ne0$ and $c_2(E)=\operatorname{corank}_{\mathbb Z_2}\mathop{\mathrm{Sel}}_{2^\infty}(E/\mathbb Q)\in\{0,1\}$, with the local Kummer conditions at every place. Then $$\operatorname{ord}_{s=1}L(E,s)=c_2(E).$$ There is no restriction on the rational isogeny configuration, complex multiplication, or reduction at $2$ or at the bad primes.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-thm-rational-converse"><summary>Proof of stmt-thm-rational-converse</summary>

*Proof.* The initial isogeny choice preserves both quantities and covers both rational two-torsion configurations. Proposition <a href="#pw:even-base" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="pw:even-base">39</a> proves the corank-zero case. In the corank-one case, Proposition <a href="#prop:rational-odd-bound" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:rational-odd-bound">42</a> supplies the coefficient normalization, and Proposition <a href="#pw:odd-base" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="pw:odd-base">47</a> proves analytic rank one using a companion fixed before the binary dimension grows. ◻

</details>

<a id="sec:lm:local-matrices"></a>
### Selmer matrices and three-state relations

Assume that $V=E[2]$ is irreducible, and write $F=\mathbb Q(V)$ and $G=\mathop{\mathrm{Gal}}(F/\mathbb Q)\in\{C_3,S_3\}$. The symbol rules will be useful because a unit symbol bounds the $2$-Selmer dimension. We now express local Selmer conditions by a binary matrix and make that bound constrain the number of singular blocks. The second half of the section develops the elementary matrix operations needed to apply this constraint.

Write the Weil pairing additively, and choose a basis of $V$ in which its matrix is $$J=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.$$ Fix a finite set $S$ containing $2$, $3$, the bad primes, all auxiliary exclusions, and rational primes whose prime ideals generate the class groups of every subfield of $F$. Local specifications at $S$ will also include the archimedean places. The detecting prime $\ell$ for an odd coefficient system is kept separate: all generators below have valuation zero there. This separation keeps the set of support types finite as $\ell$ varies. We shall apply the construction to a fixed curve, after absorbing any initial quadratic twist into $E$.

<a id="pm-h-45"></a>
#### Global classes and local equations

<a id="eq:lm:generator-class"></a>
At a split prime $p$, choose a place of $F$ and put $H_p=1$. At a simple prime, choose a place with Frobenius a specified transposition $c$ and put $H_p=\langle c\rangle$. Set $$F'_p=F^{H_p},\qquad V_p=V^{H_p}.$$ Thus $V_p$ has dimension two or one, respectively. The chosen place lies above a degree-one prime $P_p$ of $F'_p$. By the choice of $S$, there is $\pi_p\in(F'_p)^\times$ whose divisor away from $S$ is $P_p$. For $x\in V_p$ define $$\label{eq:lm:generator-class}
 C_p(x)=\mathop{\mathrm{cor}}_{F'_p/\mathbb Q}(\chi_{\pi_p}x)\in H^1(\mathbb Q,V).$$ Here $\chi_{\pi_p}$ is the quadratic Kummer character; its product with $x$ is a cocycle because $H_p$ fixes $x$.

The inertia coordinate of $C_p(x)$ at $p$ is $x$, and all its other inertia coordinates outside $S$ vanish. Indeed, local restriction–corestriction has exactly one ramified summand, at the degree-one place where $\pi_p$ has valuation one. These coordinates therefore make the classes for distinct $p$ independent. A root prime has $V^{\mathop{\mathrm{Fr}}_p}=0$ and contributes no coordinates.

Let $h$ be a twist containing the active nonroot primes in its discriminant. At a good odd prime $p$ ramified in $h$, inertia identifies the local Kummer condition with $V_p$. To see surjectivity, halve a Frobenius-fixed two-torsion point over the maximal unramified extension. The ramified twisting involution negates its half, so the resulting Kummer inertia is that two-torsion point. The Kummer condition has dimension $\dim V_p$ by local duality, giving the asserted isomorphism.

Fix arithmetic Frobenius lifts $\phi_p$. A second local coordinate is unramified evaluation at $\phi_p$, modulo Frobenius coboundaries. Let $K_p(x)(\phi_p)$ be this coordinate for the Kummer lift of inertia $x$. It is determined by $E[4]$ and the local twisting squareclass. Define the block matrix $B$ by <a id="eq:lm:raw-matrix"></a>$$\label{eq:lm:raw-matrix}
 B_{qp}(y,x)=\langle C_p(x)(\phi_q),y\rangle
 -\mathbf1_{p=q}\langle K_p(x)(\phi_p),y\rangle,
 \qquad x\in V_p,\quad y\in V_q.$$ Thus $Bx=0$ is exactly the collection of active-prime Selmer equations for $\sum_p C_p(x_p)$. Changing the unramified unit part of the twist adds $J$ to a split diagonal block. On a simple line it changes nothing, since the Weil pairing restricts to zero on a one-dimensional space.

<a id="eq:lm:symmetry-defect"></a>
Record in the *type* $\mathfrak h_p$ the subgroup $H_p$ and the squareclasses of $\pi_p$ at the places over $S$, including signatures. Only finitely many types occur. Finer generator neighborhoods will be used to reproduce self entries, but they are not part of this type alphabet and do not enter its codimension cost. Global reciprocity gives $$\label{eq:lm:symmetry-defect}
 B_{qp}+B_{pq}^{t}=b(\mathfrak h_q,\mathfrak h_p),$$ where $b$ is the sum of the local cup pairings at $S$. Indeed, at an active prime decompose each class into its Kummer lift and its unramified difference. Both planes are isotropic, and the cross pairing is unramified evaluation paired with inertia. The terms at $p$ and $q$ give the left side; the sum over all places is zero. Elsewhere outside $S$ the classes are unramified, so the local pairing vanishes. This includes $\ell$, where the generators have unit valuation. The same calculation shows that $b(\mathfrak h,\mathfrak h)$ is alternating.

<a id="pm-h-46"></a>
#### Prescribing the matrix entries

We next prove that the off-diagonal entries and the rational Legendre bits can be varied independently. The latter bits will control split diagonals without disturbing the other blocks. The class-field inputs are ray-class reciprocity, the Hilbert product formula, and Chebotarev (Neukirch 1999, vol. 322, chap. VI, Sections 7–8, and Chapter VII, Section 13) <a id="pm-cite-75"></a>[[Neukirch1999](#ref-Neukirch1999)]; see also Milne (2020b, chap. V, Theorems 3.23, 5.3 and 5.5, and Example 5.4) <a id="pm-cite-76"></a>[[MilneCFT2020](#ref-MilneCFT2020)].

<a id="stmt-lem-lm-arithmetic-realization"></a>
<div id="lem:lm:arithmetic-realization" class="lemma">

**Lemma 49** (Realization of finite matrix prescriptions). *Fix finitely many individually admissible oriented prime templates, including generator neighborhoods at $S$, any additional finite places, and oriented Frobenius on $E[4]$ and fixed quadratic-radical extensions unramified outside that support. At arbitrarily fresh primes these templates admit the following simultaneous prescriptions.*

1.  *Between distinct vertices, one direction of the double-coset residue bits is free and reciprocity determines the reverse direction. The available matrix blocks are all binary matrices for two split vertices in the $S_3$ case, and $J\mathbb F_4$ in the $C_3$ case, with the rotation algebra identified with $\mathbb F_4$. For split–simple vertices the full vector space is available, and for simple–simple vertices the scalar entry is available.*

2.  *The rational Legendre bit between the absolute primes is independent of the matrix block, subject to rational reciprocity in the reverse direction.*

3.  *Repeating a template fixes its simple self entry and its split self block modulo a scalar multiple of $J$. A sufficiently primary split template with trivial $E[4]$-Frobenius has self block in $\mathbb F_2J$.*

*Here *primary* means sufficiently close to $1$ at the finite places of $S$ and totally positive at the real places. New cross-bit prescriptions are made outside the support. All assertions concern finite configurations; an additional moving prime $\ell$ may be included among the prescribed places.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-lm-arithmetic-realization"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-lm-arithmetic-realization</summary>

<a id="eq:lm:double-coset"></a>
*Proof.* *Off-diagonal entries.* Restriction–corestriction in Equation <a href="#eq:lm:generator-class" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:lm:generator-class">[eq:lm:generator-class]</a> gives, for distinct vertices, $$\label{eq:lm:double-coset}
 B_{qp}(y,x)=
 \sum_{g\in H_q\backslash G/H_p}
 e_{pq}(g)\langle gx,y\rangle.$$ The bit $e_{pq}(g)$ is the quadratic residue of $g\pi_p$ at the oriented $q$-place in $F^{H_q\cap gH_pg^{-1}}$. Indeed, pair local transfer with the $H_q$-invariant vector $y$; the orbit length $[H_q:H_q\cap gH_pg^{-1}]$ is precisely the residue degree in the norm calculation. In this intermediate field, each of $\pi_q$ and $g\pi_p$ has its off-support divisor at a single prime: its oriented Frobenius generates the subgroup fixing the generator. Hilbert reciprocity therefore relates $e_{pq}(g)$ to $e_{qp}(g^{-1})$, with correction only at $S$.

For a new vertex the independent forward bits are residue conditions at distinct primes of its own field $F'_p$. Move an initial template away from the old primes and choose a degree-one prime in the ray class whose quotient generator has the prescribed neighborhoods at $S$, real signs, and nonzero residues at those old primes. Multiplying the template generator by this quotient gives the required new generator. These conditions also preserve the admissible fixed Frobenius data: changes by local units at old primes are trivial on the intersection with extensions unramified outside the fixed support. Chebotarev thus imposes the ray and fixed-label conditions simultaneously. Prime ideals of degree greater than one over $\mathbb Q$ have density zero among prime ideals of $F'_p$, so requiring degree one loses no admissible class. The same argument permits additional finite support, including $\ell$. Reverse bits are then determined by reciprocity. Rational norm bits at already chosen root primes may be imposed as additional residue conditions in the ray modulus: finite-field norm maps are surjective, and these primes contribute no matrix coordinates.

*Matrix span and the norm bit.* The norm to $\mathbb Q$ writes the rational absolute-prime Legendre bit as the sum of the double-coset bits, plus a fixed support-unit correction. For two split vertices the matrices in Equation <a href="#eq:lm:double-coset" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:lm:double-coset">[eq:lm:double-coset]</a> are $Jg$. They span $\operatorname{Mat}_2(\mathbb F_2)$ for $S_3$ and $J\mathbb F_4$ for $C_3$. A nontrivial rotation satisfies $1+R+R^2=0$: changing these three bits fixes the matrix and changes their sum. For split–simple vertices, the three nonzero vectors or dual vectors likewise span the full space and have the same odd relation. For two simple vertices, the matching double coset has zero pairing and the other has nonzero pairing. The first bit changes the norm bit alone. This proves <span class="upright">(i)</span> and <span class="upright">(ii)</span>.

*Self entries.* The nonidentity double cosets in self-transfer are unramified at the oriented prime. The identity term is a scalar times the pairing and is therefore zero on a simple line. At a split vertex the two rotation terms have fixed sum by reciprocity; changing both alters the block only by a scalar multiple of $J$. Every other term has an involution representative $\tau$ exchanging the oriented place with another one. For a simple vertex this includes a transposition other than $c$ representing the nonmatching self double coset.

Work in $F^\tau$ and put $$\alpha=\pi_p\tau\pi_p,\qquad
 \beta=\pi_p+\tau\pi_p,\qquad
 F=F^\tau(\sqrt{D_\tau}).$$ The distinct divisors of $\pi_p$ and $\tau\pi_p$ ensure $\beta\ne0$. If $v_0$ is the place below the oriented prime, the residue symbol of $\tau\pi_p$ there is $(\alpha,\beta)_{v_0}$: $\alpha$ has valuation one and $\beta$ is a unit with the required residue. Outside $S\cup\{v_0\}$, $\alpha$ is a unit. When $\beta$ is a unit, both $(\alpha,\beta)_v$ and $(-D_\tau,\beta)_v$ vanish. When $\beta$ has positive valuation, put $\gamma=(\pi_p-\tau\pi_p)/\sqrt{D_\tau}\in F^\tau$. The identity $$\beta^2-4\alpha=D_\tau\gamma^2$$ shows that $\alpha$ has residue squareclass $-D_\tau$; the two symbols are again equal. At $v_0$, $(-D_\tau,\beta)_{v_0}=0$. Reciprocity applied to both symbols gives, in additive notation, <a id="eq:lm:self-spin"></a>$$\label{eq:lm:self-spin}
 (\alpha,\beta)_{v_0}
 =\sum_{v\in S}\bigl((\alpha,\beta)_v+(-D_\tau,\beta)_v\bigr).$$

At finite support places the right side is locally constant in a sufficiently small neighborhood of the template. At a real place where $F/F^\tau$ is complex, $\alpha$ and $-D_\tau$ are positive. At a split real place, opposite signs of $\pi_p$ and $\tau\pi_p$ make the two terms cancel; equal signs determine their sum. Thus signatures suffice, without archimedean size restrictions. For a primary template, $\alpha$ is a square at the finite support places and $\beta$ has the squareclass of $2$. The support sum becomes $\sum_{v\in S}(-D_\tau,2)_v=0$, since the terms outside $S$ vanish. The involution terms are therefore zero. Together with the local Kummer lift determined by $E[4]$, this proves <span class="upright">(iii)</span>. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-47"></a>
#### Symmetrization and the Selmer bound

The realization lemma supplies the allowable matrix blocks. We now remove their fixed-support reciprocity defect and compare the resulting kernels with actual Selmer classes. The fixed support types, stationary environment and additional local conditions will account for the loss in dimension.

Choose a matrix rule $L(\mathfrak h,\mathfrak h')$ in the available block spans such that <a id="eq:lm:type-correction"></a>$$\label{eq:lm:type-correction}
 L(\mathfrak h,\mathfrak h')+
 L(\mathfrak h',\mathfrak h)^t=b(\mathfrak h,\mathfrak h').$$ For distinct types, choose either direction using Equation <a href="#eq:lm:symmetry-defect" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:lm:symmetry-defect">[eq:lm:symmetry-defect]</a>. For equal types, the right side is alternating. It is a matrix plus its transpose in the full span; in the rotation span use $R+R^{-1}=1$ after multiplication by $J$. On a simple line it is zero. Choose $L=0$ when one type is primary and trivial at $S$, since then its support pairings vanish. Define, on every pair including the diagonal, $$M_{qp}=B_{qp}-L(\mathfrak h_q,\mathfrak h_p).$$ The matrix $M$ is symmetric. Lemma <a href="#lem:lm:arithmetic-realization" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:lm:arithmetic-realization">49</a> allows zero cross-$M$ entries between prescribed blocks independently of their internal entries.

A *stationary environment* consists of the fixed coordinates outside the variable blocks; its dimension is the number of those coordinates.

<a id="stmt-prop-selmer-matrix-bound"></a>
<div id="prop:selmer-matrix-bound" class="proposition">

<a id="eq:lm:selmer-nullity"></a>
**Proposition 50** (Nullity forces Selmer dimension). *Fix the curve, support types, a bound for the number of additional constrained places, and a bound for the dimension of a stationary environment. Partition a finite configuration into blocks with zero cross-$M$ entries, and denote their matrices by $M_i$. There is a constant depending only on these fixed data such that $$\label{eq:lm:selmer-nullity}
 \dim_{\mathbb F_2}\mathop{\mathrm{Sel}}_2(E^{(h)}/\mathbb Q)
 \geq\sum_i\dim_{\mathbb F_2}\ker M_i-C.$$ At a unit coefficient symbol the sum of nullities, and hence the number of singular blocks, is therefore uniformly bounded. The bound works for both coefficient sources and is independent of the moving prime $\ell$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-prop-selmer-matrix-bound"><summary>Proof of stmt-prop-selmer-matrix-bound</summary>

*Proof.* On $\bigoplus_i\ker M_i$, impose <a id="eq:lm:type-sums"></a>$$\label{eq:lm:type-sums}
 \sum_{p:\,\mathfrak h_p=\mathfrak h}x_p=0
 \quad\text{for each type }\mathfrak h,$$ using the fixed orientation and basis to identify coordinates of the same type. These equations have codimension at most $\sum_{\mathfrak h}\dim V_{\mathfrak h}$. They kill the correction in every row, since that correction is $$\sum_{\mathfrak h}L(\mathfrak h_q,\mathfrak h)
       \sum_{p:\,\mathfrak h_p=\mathfrak h}x_p.$$ Thus $Bx=0$ at all block positions. Set the environment coordinates to zero and impose its row conditions, losing at most its dimension. The Selmer conditions at $S$ and the additional constrained places have bounded total codimension in local $H^1$. At every remaining good place the classes satisfy the unramified Kummer condition; at a root prime local cohomology is zero.
