Their sums are therefore Selmer classes, and independent inertia coordinates make the map injective. This proves Equation <a href="#eq:lm:selmer-nullity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:lm:selmer-nullity">[eq:lm:selmer-nullity]</a>.

At a unit symbol, Proposition <a href="#prop:unit-symbol-detection" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:unit-symbol-detection">19</a> bounds the Selmer dimension, giving the remaining assertions. The type constraints use only the fixed $S$; a condition at the single moving prime contributes a uniformly bounded local dimension. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-48"></a>
#### Three states on two coordinates

We have obtained two kinds of information from an arithmetic prime configuration: its coefficient symbol and a matrix whose nullity bounds its Selmer dimension from below. To compare configurations, we now vary exactly two coordinates at a time. Both the symbol and the determinant obey one common three-state relation. They remain different functions; the relation gives linearity, not their equality. The bounded number of singular blocks at a unit symbol will be the additional input used in the next section.

A *site* consists of either one split vertex or an ordered pair of simple vertices, and always supplies two matrix coordinates. At a split site use the three states $$\text{absent},\qquad
 \text{present with diagonal }Q,\qquad
 \text{present with diagonal }Q+J.$$ The rational Legendre bit of the aggregate root selects the two present diagonals. At a simple-pair site use absence of both vertices and two present variants differing in their nonmatching cross bit. Replace the second prime by a prime with the same template, self data, norm data, and outside cross bits. Its matching bit with the first prime must also change to keep the rational norm bit fixed; that bit has zero matrix contribution. Thus the two present matrices again differ by the symmetric toggle on their coordinate pair. Require all alternatives to agree against alternatives at other sites. These are finite simultaneous prescriptions allowed by Lemma <a href="#lem:lm:arithmetic-realization" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:lm:arithmetic-realization">49</a>.

In comparing states, keep fixed the total parameter label at the fixed support: the product of the labels of the active sites and the aggregate roots. The aggregate-root label itself changes when a site is deleted, absorbing the deleted labels.

<a id="stmt-lem-lm-site-relations"></a>
<div id="lem:lm:site-relations" class="lemma">

**Lemma 51** (The site relations). *Fix the total parameter label at the fixed support and the diagonal choices at the other present sites. In each state choose aggregate roots restoring this label, compatibly with an order-three residual Frobenius, and preserving those diagonals. For either coefficient symbol, its three values at one site sum to zero. The same holds for $\det M$, with empty determinant one. Consequently both functions extend linearly to the tensor product of one copy of $\mathbb F_2^2$ per site, whose three nonzero vectors represent the three states. These factors encode evaluations, not vectors of $V$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-lm-site-relations"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-lm-site-relations</summary>

*Proof.* For a split site this is the root-deletion rule of Theorem <a href="#thm:symbol-rules" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:symbol-rules">[thm:symbol-rules]</a>. Deletion transfers the removed vertex’s rational labels to the aggregate root. Signed prime discriminants preserve the unit twist, and hence the diagonal, at every remaining prime.

For a simple-pair site, omit the varied second prime from its opposite-parity trace test. In an extension of $G$ by an elementary kernel, two lifts of its transposition $c$ are conjugate by the kernel exactly when their difference lies in the image of $1+c$. Dually, this means agreement on the $c$-fixed radical squareclasses. Besides fixed-support radicals, these are generated by products of the orbit generators $g\pi_p$ over $c$-orbits: their off-support divisors are independent and conjugation permutes them. Singleton orbits test matching bits. A two-element orbit has product in $F^c$; its symbol at the varying degree-one prime is, by the residue norm, the symbol of one factor in $F$, namely the nonmatching bit.

The variants agree on support radicals and the orbit tests for every other vertex. At the first prime they change both matching and nonmatching bits. Modulo the image of $1+c$, their difference is therefore the product of inertia in the matching transposition orientation and inertia in the other orientation. Apply these substitutions successively. The matching-orientation derivative is zero; the different-transposition derivative deletes the pair by Theorem <a href="#thm:symbol-rules" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:symbol-rules">[thm:symbol-rules]</a>. Multiplication by inertia leaves the residual transposition unchanged. The intermediate Frobenius test is realized by Chebotarev; it need not be a site variant. The resulting root has rotation image and transfers the pair’s rational labels to the aggregate. Labels elsewhere are unchanged. At simple vertices root probes are immaterial; at split vertices the common rational labels preserve the diagonals. Matched actual probes, or their aggregate, are available because their discriminant character is trivial. This proves the symbol relation.

For the determinant, reverse every permutation cycle of length at least three. The resulting terms cancel in characteristic two, leaving only involutions. Toggling the symmetric entries $(i,j),(j,i)$ changes exactly the terms containing $(ij)$, whose sum is the determinant with coordinates $i,j$ deleted. This includes the split $J$-shift. Finally, the three-state relation in each factor is precisely linearity on its three nonzero binary vectors. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-lem-binary-tensor-span"></a>
<div id="lem:binary-tensor-span" class="lemma">

**Lemma 52** (Binary tensor span). *Let $W=\bigotimes_{i=1}^rW_i$, where each $W_i$ has dimension two over $\mathbb F_2$, and let $0\ne f\in W^*$. The nonzero pure tensors annihilated by $f$ span $\ker f$. Thus if pure tensors $e,t$ satisfy $f(e)=f(t)=1$, then $t$ is $e$ plus a sum of pure zeros of $f$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-binary-tensor-span"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-binary-tensor-span</summary>

*Proof.* It suffices to show that a functional $g$ vanishing on the pure zeros of $f$ is either $0$ or $f$. Induct on $r$, the case $r=0$ being immediate. Slice at the three nonzero vectors of the last factor, numbering so that $f_3=f_1+f_2$ and $g_3=g_1+g_2$. If $f_i=0$, then $g_i=0$ because the smaller pure tensors span. Otherwise induction gives $g_i=\epsilon_i f_i$ for a binary scalar $\epsilon_i$. If all three $f_i$ are nonzero, $f_1,f_2$ are independent, so the sum identities force all $\epsilon_i$ to agree. If one $f_i$ vanishes, the other two, and their $g_i$, agree. All three cannot vanish. Hence $g=0$ or $g=f$. ◻

</details>

Take $f=\det M$ and let $e$ be the all-absent state. Every invertible state is the empty state plus a sum of singular pure states. Moreover, on any selected set of active sites, some choice of pair toggles makes $M$ invertible: the iterated determinant difference over all selected pairs is the empty determinant, one. These facts turn the Selmer nullity bound into a constraint on symbol evaluations.

<a id="pm-h-49"></a>
#### Making one address singular

The final construction singles out one nonzero vector of a binary cube. Every position is activated by a linear form, as required for interpolation; auxiliary split sites repair the matrix at all other nonzero vectors.

<a id="stmt-lem-lm-address-program"></a>
<div id="lem:lm:address-program" class="lemma">

**Lemma 53** (A block address program). *Let $M_*$ be the singular matrix of a finite site state, and let $D$ be a sum of its pair toggles such that $N_*=M_*+D$ is invertible. For $b\geq2$ and $0\ne x_*\in\mathbb F_2^b$, one can add finitely many primary split sites, each activated by a linear form, so that:*

- *all sites present in the original state have activation $l_0$, with $l_0(x_*)=1$;*

- *no site is active at zero, and at $x_*$ precisely the original state $M_*$ remains;*

- *the matrix is invertible at every other nonzero address;*

- *the active auxiliary matrix is always invertible, and its Schur complement contributes $D$ exactly when the original sites are active and $x\ne x_*$.*

*All entries use the freedoms of Lemma <a href="#lem:lm:arithmetic-realization" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:lm:arithmetic-realization">49</a>.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-lm-address-program"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-lm-address-program</summary>

*Proof.* Choose a basis $y=(y_1,\ldots,y_{b-1})$ for the forms annihilating $x_*$ and complete it by $l_0$. Then $y=0$ exactly at $0,x_*$. For each required toggle and each nonzero $\eta\in\mathbb F_2^{b-1}$, choose a basis of forms all equal to one at $\eta$. Such a basis is obtained from a form $u$ with $u(\eta)=1$ by adding $u$ to a basis of the annihilator of $\eta$. Its unique simultaneous all-one solution is $\eta$.

Construct a path with $r=b-1$ steps, using two new split positions at each step, both activated by the corresponding basis form. In scalar block notation, where a scalar denotes that scalar times $J$, put <a id="eq:lm:path-matrix"></a>$$\label{eq:lm:path-matrix}
 P=\begin{pmatrix}0&T\\T^t&B_e\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad T=I+\text{lower consecutive shift}.$$ The near and far endpoints are steps $1$ and $r$. The matrix $B_e$ has one nonzero diagonal entry at the far endpoint. Restrict both sides to active steps, retaining only the original consecutive edges. The restricted $T$ is triangular with diagonal one, so $P$ is invertible, with scalar inverse $$P^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}
 T^{-t}B_eT^{-1}&T^{-t}\\T^{-1}&0
 \end{pmatrix}.$$ Couple the addressed coordinate pair by $J$ to the first side at the near endpoint. Such a pairing is available also for two simple lines. Solving $Tv=e_{\rm near}$ propagates one to the far endpoint exactly when every step is active; a missing step interrupts the consecutive shift. The Schur contribution is consequently $J$ on a complete path and zero otherwise, including when the near endpoint is absent.

For each nonzero $y$, exactly one path, the one indexed by $\eta=y$, is complete. Their direct sum supplies the toggle when $y\ne0$ and supplies zero when $y=0$. Repeat for each toggle in $D$, with zero mutual cross-$M$ entries. The actual matrices are the scalar matrices tensored with $J$, so the same inverse calculation gives the asserted binary Schur complements. All blocks lie in the permitted spans, and primary diagonals are $0$ or $J$.

At $x_*$ the auxiliary sites are absent and $l_0=1$, leaving $M_*$. At any other nonzero address with $l_0=1$, eliminating the auxiliary sites leaves $M_*+D=N_*$. If $l_0=0$, only the invertible auxiliary matrix remains. Every activation is linear and vanishes at zero. ◻

</details>

<a id="sec:sa:saturation"></a>
### The converse when $E[2]$ is irreducible

The local matrices now supply the families needed for interpolation. We shall arrange that a coefficient symbol is a unit at every nonzero vertex of a binary cube, with all added primes absent at zero. The key observation is that a unit evaluation has only boundedly many singular matrix blocks. A maximal list of such blocks will therefore force all the required unit evaluations. In the odd case, a second construction supplies simultaneous nonvanishing for an auxiliary even symbol.

<a id="stmt-thm-irreducible-converse"></a>
<div id="thm:irreducible-converse" class="theorem">

**Theorem 54** (The irreducible converse). *Let $E/\mathbb Q$ be an elliptic curve for which $E[2]$ is irreducible as a $G_{\mathbb Q}$-module. If $$c_2(E)=\mathop{\mathrm{corank}}_{\mathbb Z_2}\mathop{\mathrm{Sel}}_{2^\infty}(E/\mathbb Q)\in\{0,1\},$$ then $\mathop{\mathrm{ord}}_{s=1}L(E,s)=c_2(E)$.*

</div>

The curve is fixed throughout. Every constant may depend on it and on the finite choices specified below, all made before the cube dimension grows. The result applies pointwise to any quadratic twist by taking that twist as the initial curve.

<a id="pm-h-51"></a>
#### Finite evaluation tables and ordered profiles

A block is a finite set of the three-state sites of Section <a href="#sec:lm:local-matrices" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:lm:local-matrices">8</a>, together with their prescribed matrix entries. A state chooses one of the three alternatives at each site. Its evaluated matrix $M_s$ deletes the coordinates of absent sites and applies the toggles of the chosen active alternatives. The empty state has determinant $1$. We call a state singular when $\det M_s=0$.

The matrix and the coefficient symbol give different information about such a state. The raw matrix $B$ records the active-prime Selmer equations; $M$ is the symmetric matrix obtained after the fixed-support correction. The symbol still depends on the arithmetic realization, even when those matrix entries have been prescribed. What links them is Proposition <a href="#prop:selmer-matrix-bound" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:selmer-matrix-bound">50</a>: a symbol value $1$ permits only boundedly many singular blocks. We shall first stabilize the remaining arithmetic dependence and then use this bound.

Fix a normalized coefficient symbol $A$ on the filter of the parameter $1$. For the odd source retain its condition at the moving detecting prime $\ell$. Consider an actual finite array of blocks, numbered in increasing order, with $M=0$ between different blocks. For chosen indices $i_1<\cdots<i_j$ and states $s_1,\ldots,s_j$, write $$\mathcal E(i_1,\ldots,i_j;s_1,\ldots,s_j)\in\mathbb F_2$$ for its coefficient-symbol value. Each table entry uses its own aggregate-root probe, which restores the total support label of $1$ and gives the chosen diagonals at active split sites. Root substitution makes its value independent of the probe with these data. The calibration below will realize all entries used by a cube with one common set of linearly activated root primes. The total label, rather than the aggregate root’s own label, is fixed: deleting a site transfers that site’s labels to the root. The substitution rules therefore preserve this value when an unused site or an empty block is deleted. In particular, the empty table entry is $A(1)$.

There are two independent indices in these tables. Inside each block, site slots specify where a state and its addressing paths can be put. The indices $i_1<\cdots<i_j$ specify ordered copies of the whole block. We will use a common countable library of site slots in every copy, closed under the finite addressing constructions of Lemma <a href="#lem:lm:address-program" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:lm:address-program">53</a>. A state in this library uses only finitely many sites, with every other site absent. A *word* is an ordered finite list of states from this library, with empty states omitted. An *ordered profile* assigns a value to each such word, consistently with the three-state relations in each block. The next lemma constructs one by stabilizing finite tables: its value depends on the ordered states, but not on which increasing list of block indices carries them. It asserts no invariance under permuting the states.

<a id="stmt-lem-sa-profile"></a>
<div id="lem:sa:profile" class="lemma">

**Lemma 55** (A finitely realizable ordered profile). *For the fixed symbol $A$, there is a countable library of site slots in each block and an ordered profile with the following properties.*

1.  *Every prescribed finite part is realized by an array of distinct primes with the data of Lemma <a href="#lem:lm:arithmetic-realization" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:lm:arithmetic-realization">49</a>. For the odd symbol, it is realized at arbitrarily advanced stages of the prescribed precision stabilization.*

2.  *A word evaluation depends on the states and on their order, and not on the particular distinct block indices used to place them. The tensor relations hold separately in all of its blocks.*

3.  *The site library contains a transferred minimal-weight unit witness and the primary split sites needed for every finite collection of requests in Lemma <a href="#lem:lm:address-program" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:lm:address-program">53</a>.*

4.  *For a constant $C$ independent of the finite array, a unit evaluation contains at most $C$ singular blocks.*

*Couplings to finitely many fixed primes, kept outside the address symbol, may be prescribed in advance. In the even case, all primes may also satisfy a bound on $v_2(p^2-1)$ independent of the finite array.*

</div>

We first derive the consequence of this lemma. Its proof follows the saturation argument and explains how the ordered values retain finite arithmetic realizations, including for the moving odd source.

<a id="stmt-lem-sa-punctured-cube"></a>
<div id="lem:sa:punctured-cube" class="lemma">

**Lemma 56** (Saturation of a punctured cube). *For the profile in Lemma <a href="#lem:sa:profile" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:sa:profile">55</a>, either the empty word has value $1$, or there is a fixed finite word $W$ of singular blocks with value $1$ such that, for every sufficiently large $b$, an addressed family has symbol $1$ at every nonzero point of $\mathbb F_2^b$ and has all sites absent at zero. Every such finite cube is arithmetically realizable.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-sa-punctured-cube"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-sa-punctured-cube</summary>

*Proof.* In the tensor space of a block, every nonsingular state is the empty state plus a sum of singular states, by Lemma <a href="#lem:binary-tensor-span" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:binary-tensor-span">52</a>. Expand the transferred unit witness this way. Some word consisting entirely of singular blocks, possibly the empty word, has value $1$.

The lengths of all such words are bounded by Lemma <a href="#lem:sa:profile" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:sa:profile">55</a><span class="upright">(iv)</span>. Choose one of maximal length $m$. If $m=0$, the empty word has value $1$. Otherwise fix one particular maximizing word $$W=(W_1,\ldots,W_m).$$ Each $W_i$ uses finitely many slots. These slots, and thus their total number, are fixed before $b$ grows. A bound on the number of blocks alone would not give this conclusion.

For each $a\in\mathbb F_2^b\setminus\{0\}$, place a copy of $W$ in its original block order. Address its $i$th block to $a$ using Lemma <a href="#lem:lm:address-program" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:lm:address-program">53</a>. At $a$ the state is exactly $W_i$, with every path site absent. At every other nonzero address the evaluated block is nonsingular, and at zero it is empty. All these finitely many programs are available in the recursive slot list.

At a nonzero address $x$, expand every block outside the copy designated for $x$ as empty plus singular states. Choosing the empty state in every such block leaves $W$ in its original order, hence gives $1$. Every other term contains its $m$ singular blocks and at least one additional singular block, so maximality forces its value to be zero. This includes alternatives involving path slots: maximality was taken over the whole slot profile. Multilinearity therefore gives $1$ at $x$. All evaluations use one finite restriction of the profile, which is realizable by Lemma <a href="#lem:sa:profile" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:sa:profile">55</a>. ◻

</details>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-sa-punctured-cube-2"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-sa-punctured-cube</summary>

*Proof of Lemma <a href="#lem:sa:profile" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:sa:profile">55</a>.* *The witness and available slots.* Begin with the nonroot positions of a minimal-weight unit witness. The minimum-transfer rule in Theorem <a href="#thm:symbol-rules" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:symbol-rules">[thm:symbol-rules]</a> moves them to fresh primes while retaining their fixed-support Frobenius labels. Neither prescribed internal couplings nor couplings to stationary primes change this transfer: the latter primes are outside the coefficient index. The total simple parity is even, so pair its simple positions into sites. Fix admissible generator templates, including support squareclasses and self types, for this pattern.

At each finite stage place a fresh copy of the pattern in every block to be colored. First apply Lemma <a href="#tc:minimum-transfer" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="tc:minimum-transfer">28</a> with matched actual root probes. The nonroot support labels are unchanged, so retaining the aggregate root’s support label restores the same total parameter label. Adjust only its bits at active vertices to give the prescribed diagonals. By Proposition <a href="#tc:irreducible-rules" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="tc:irreducible-rules">27</a><span class="upright">(ii)</span>, a split root-bit derivative deletes weight one and vanishes below the minimal weight, while a simple root-bit derivative is zero. Thus every singleton witness still has value $1$, even after all internal and cross-block entries have been prescribed. For the odd symbol, make the transfer at the actual coefficient level and retain the witness’s labels at the detecting prime. Thus the witness entry of every singleton color is $1$ before taking homogeneous restrictions.

We now enlarge the site library inside each block. For every finite list of earlier site slots and every finite list of addressing requests on it, allocate fresh primary split site slots realizing all those requests. Programs used together receive distinct path slots. Set every undesignated coupling to earlier slots equal to zero in $M$. This gives a countable formal list, since there are countably many finite requests. Any finite set of requested slots, together with its finitely many predecessors, is realizable by Lemma <a href="#lem:lm:arithmetic-realization" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:lm:arithmetic-realization">49</a>. The two simple-pair variants have identical outside bits and the prescribed internal toggle; the aggregate root supplies the split diagonal alternatives. Corresponding types have the same reciprocity correction $L$, so a forward entry $B=M+L$ gives the required reverse entry as well. In every alternative impose $M=0$ between blocks.

*Order-invariant evaluations.* Fix the first $q$ sites of the common library. There are finitely many states on these sites, and their matrix entries have been prescribed. For each $j\le q$, color an increasing $j$-tuple of block indices by the finite table of values $\mathcal E(i_1,\ldots,i_j;s_1,\ldots,s_j)$ on these states. There are finitely many colors. Apply finite Ramsey successively for these finitely many arities. Starting with sufficiently many blocks gives a homogeneous list of any prescribed finite length.

Let the lengths, arities, and slot cutoffs tend to infinity. At each fixed cutoff there are only finitely many possible color vectors. Successive subsequences and a diagonal subsequence make every finite vector constant. These compatible values define the ordered profile. Every finite restriction occurs in an original finite array. The tensor identities, deletion rules, and unit witness survive because each involves only such a restriction.

For the odd symbol, carry out this construction along its fixed nonprincipal ultrafilter of coefficient precisions. The witness has bounded weight, so its fixed-$S$ generator squareclasses and binary self data have only finitely many possibilities; first stabilize these data. Finer ray-neighborhood depths are realization data and need not stabilize. Impose the extra labels at $\ell$ at each actual level. For every fixed weight bound, Lemma <a href="#cs:fixed-weight-uniformity" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="cs:fixed-weight-uniformity">18</a> gives an ultrafilter-large set on which all required lower bounds and smaller-weight vanishing assertions hold. Otherwise one could choose a violating index of that bounded weight at each failing level, contradicting the definitions of the least depth or the least witness weight. More explicitly, let $G_q$ be an ultrafilter-large set on which the witness, cutoff lower bounds, and minimal-weight vanishing assertions needed for the $q$th finite coloring hold. Choose precisions $M_q\to\infty$ in $\bigcap_{j\le q}G_j$, and apply finite Ramsey there. Stabilize the finitely many colors and take the diagonal construction above. The extracted subsequence need not itself be ultrafilter-large: every finite restriction occurs at arbitrarily high precisions, which is the required conclusion. We assert no single level valid at all weight bounds, and choose no infinite array of primes.

*The bound on singular blocks.* Proposition <a href="#prop:selmer-matrix-bound" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:selmer-matrix-bound">50</a> and the uniform unit-symbol bound in Proposition <a href="#prop:unit-symbol-detection" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:unit-symbol-detection">19</a> bound the sum of the block nullities. Each singular block contributes at least one. The type alphabet and its correction cost depend on the fixed support $S$. The moving place $\ell$ and any bounded stationary environment contribute only the bounded additional local cost allowed in Proposition <a href="#prop:selmer-matrix-bound" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:selmer-matrix-bound">50</a>; they do not enlarge that alphabet as the array grows. This proves <span class="upright">(iv)</span> in every finite realization, and therefore in the profile.

For the final even-symbol assertion, choose fixed templates at sufficient $2$-adic precision for the witness and its simple variants, and a fixed sufficiently primary template for the path sites. Refine each rational residue class to a finite precision determining a finite value of $v_2(p^2-1)$. Only finitely many templates occur. Cross-bit conditions at new odd primes do not change these residues. The same argument will apply to the root primes used below. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-52"></a>
#### Local calibration and the even case

The preceding argument determines the symbol values. We next realize all its local twist classes simultaneously, while keeping each prime’s activation linear in the cube coordinates.

<a id="stmt-lem-sa-root-calibration"></a>
<div id="lem:sa:root-calibration" class="lemma">

**Lemma 57** (Calibration by root primes). *The cubes in Lemma <a href="#lem:sa:punctured-cube" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:sa:punctured-cube">56</a> admit realizations by signed squarefree parameters $$h_x=\prod_p(p^*)^{f_p(x)},\qquad x\in\mathbb F_2^b,
 \qquad h_0=1,$$ where each $f_p:\mathbb F_2^b\to\mathbb F_2$ is linear. The prescribed local classes and diagonal choices hold at every assignment. Moreover, $h_x$ may be required to be a local square at any prescribed finite set of stationary primes. Calibration adds only root primes, whose invariant dimension $t_p$ is zero. In the even case, all added primes may satisfy a bound on $v_2(p^2-1)$ independent of $b$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-sa-root-calibration"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-sa-root-calibration</summary>

*Proof.* The address and path programs already give a linear activation form for each nonroot prime. Both primes of a simple site have the same form, so their total simple parity vanishes coefficient by coefficient. For each coordinate $x_j$, add a fresh root prime $q_j$, active when $x_j=1$. Choose its rational radical label at the support to cancel the coefficient of $x_j$ in the total nonroot label. The paired-simple condition makes the residual discriminant obstruction to a rotation label zero. Lemma <a href="#lem:lm:arithmetic-realization" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:lm:arithmetic-realization">49</a> and root substitution in Theorem <a href="#thm:symbol-rules" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:symbol-rules">[thm:symbol-rules]</a> therefore allow these choices.

The same roots supply the diagonal choices. At a nonroot split prime $p$, the unit twist from the other nonroot primes is a linear function of $x$. A desired constant diagonal bit on the active set of $p$ is represented by that constant times $f_p$. The correction needed is therefore linear, say $\sum_j c_{pj}x_j$. Give $q_j$ the Legendre bit $c_{pj}$ at $p$. These bits are independently prescribable for the different $p$; simple positions need no diagonal correction. At each stationary prime, choose the root bits to cancel the existing unit twist coefficient by coefficient. To check compatibility, let $L$ be the compositum of the rational quadratic fields recording these finite tests. The fresh-prime radical classes are independent of the support classes by their valuations. Moreover, $F\cap L=\mathbb Q$ for $G=C_3$; for $G=S_3$ it is at most the residual discriminant field. Thus agreement on the already matched discriminant coordinate is the only additional condition for a rotation in $\mathop{\mathrm{Gal}}(F/\mathbb Q)$. Chebotarev supplies the required roots.

Using signed prime discriminants gives the prescribed quadratic characters at every place, including infinity and $2$. At each $x$, the nonroot states and their internal data are those of its table entry. The product of the active root primes has the support label and the bits at active split primes of the aggregate-root probe in the corresponding table entry. Its bits at simple primes do not change the symbol. Root substitution in Theorem <a href="#thm:symbol-rules" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:symbol-rules">[thm:symbol-rules]</a> therefore identifies $A(|h_x|)$ with that profile value. The same comparison includes $x=0$, where the root collection is empty and all added primes are absent. Finally, root support labels lie in a fixed finite set, so fixed rational $2$-adic residue refinements determine $v_2(q_j^2-1)$. The extra conditions, ramified at fresh odd primes, are compatible with these refinements as in Lemma <a href="#lem:sa:profile" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:sa:profile">55</a>. ◻

</details>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-sa-root-calibration-2"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-sa-root-calibration</summary>

*Proof of Theorem <a href="#thm:irreducible-converse" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:irreducible-converse">54</a> when $c_2(E)=0$.* By Lemma <a href="#pr:invariance" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="pr:invariance">[pr:invariance]</a>, the functional equation has sign $+1$. We use the even coefficient source on the filter of $1$. To obtain its lower bound, choose an auxiliary twist of analytic rank one, with opposite infinity sign and matching local classes at $2N$, by nonvanishing in these fixed local classes (Proposition <a href="#prop:rough-nonvanishing" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:rough-nonvanishing">[prop:rough-nonvanishing]</a>). Exclude its prime support and the exceptional quadratic fields as in Proposition <a href="#prop:even-coefficients" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:even-coefficients">[prop:even-coefficients]</a>. The reverse genus comparison and Theorem <a href="#thm:heegner-genus-bound" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:heegner-genus-bound">13</a> give the lower bound required there. Fix this partner, the exclusions, and the normalized even symbol before choosing the profile or cube dimension.

If the empty word is a unit, Proposition <a href="#prop:unit-symbol-detection" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:unit-symbol-detection">19</a> gives $L(E,1)\ne0$. Otherwise Lemmas <a href="#lem:sa:punctured-cube" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:sa:punctured-cube">56</a> and <a href="#lem:sa:root-calibration" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:sa:root-calibration">57</a> give arbitrarily large cubes with unit symbol at all $x\ne0$. At each such point, $$L(E^{(h_x)},1)\ne0,
 \qquad
 v(\mathcal L(h_x))-2w(h_x)-s(h_x)\le C_A,$$ where $C_A$ depends only on the fixed normalized symbol. The local classes are fixed and the added-prime valuations $v_2(p^2-1)$ are bounded independently of $b$. These are precisely the remaining hypotheses of Theorem <a href="#thm:cyclotomic-interpolation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:cyclotomic-interpolation">8</a>, which yields $L(E,1)\ne0$. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-53"></a>
#### A bounded companion for the odd cube

Assume $c_2(E)=1$. Parity gives functional sign $-1$, so the address symbol $A$ is odd and its filter is the filter of $1$. Choose its fixed genus partner of analytic rank zero, with opposite infinity sign and matching classes at $2N$, by Proposition <a href="#prop:rough-nonvanishing" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:rough-nonvanishing">[prop:rough-nonvanishing]</a>. The irreducible genus bound supplies the coefficient lower estimate. Choose also an even symbol $A_0$ on a fixed filter of negative odd fundamental discriminants $k$ for which $2N$ splits in $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{k})$. It has no condition at the moving prime $\ell$. Its complementary genus partner has analytic rank one and is chosen by the same nonvanishing proposition. Fix these partners, all excluded prime supports and exceptional fields, and both coefficient normalizations.

If $A(1)=1$, unit-symbol detection already gives the desired analytic rank. Otherwise the following construction supplies every arithmetic hypothesis needed for varying-field Heegner interpolation.

<a id="stmt-prop-sa-bounded-companion"></a>
<div id="prop:sa:bounded-companion" class="proposition">

**Proposition 58** (An odd cube with a bounded even companion). *For the fixed symbols $A,A_0$ just chosen, suppose $A(1)=0$. There is a constant $C$ such that, for every sufficiently large $b$, one can find an odd negative fundamental discriminant $k$ and a finite family $$h_x=\prod_p(p^*)^{f_p(x)},\qquad x\in\mathbb F_2^b,
 \qquad f_p:\mathbb F_2^b\longrightarrow\mathbb F_2\ \text{linear},$$ with the following properties.*

1.  *The primes are distinct good odd primes outside the fixed exclusions; $h_0=1$, and every $h_x$ has the local squareclasses of $1$ at the fixed support and at infinity. Each $h_x$ is coprime to $k$. The field $K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt{k})$ satisfies the standing Heegner conditions.*

2.  *The prime support of $k$ has cardinality at most $C$. At every nonroot prime $p\mid\prod_xh_x$, the parameter $k$ is a local square. At every nonroot prime $q\mid k$, every $h_x$ is a local square.*

3.  *The simultaneous symbol values are $$A_0(|k|)=1,\qquad
     A(|h_x|)=A_0(|kh_x|)=1\quad(x\ne0).$$ Consequently $E^{(k)}$ has analytic rank zero and $s(k)\le C$.*

*For the odd source, these assertions mean simultaneous actual tests at arbitrarily high admissible precisions after $b$ and its finite set of tests have been fixed. The constant $C$ is independent of $b$, that precision, and all moving primes. The parameter $k$ may vary with the finite realization.*

</div>

The construction uses the even symbol twice: at $k$ to control the base Selmer group over $K$, and at $kh_x$ to make the product have a simple zero at every nonzero vertex. We first condition $A_0$ by a fixed singular prefix. Only after this conditioning will its later values become determinants.

<a id="stmt-lem-sa-prefix"></a>
<div id="lem:sa:prefix" class="lemma">

<a id="eq:sa:conditioned-determinant"></a>
**Lemma 59** (A determinant-conditioned prefix). *For the fixed even symbol $A_0$, there are a finite list $a$ of singular blocks and an environment consisting of at most one simple vertex with the following property. Fix these vertices and their split diagonal entries. Let $z$ be any further block of tensor sites whose alternatives all have $B=L$ to every block of $a$. Choose aggregate root data preserving the prefix diagonals and the fixed total label. Then $$A_0(a,z)=\det M_z.
 \label{eq:sa:conditioned-determinant}$$ The left side includes the fixed environment. Its couplings need only be compatible with the tensor alternatives.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-sa-prefix"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-sa-prefix</summary>

*Proof.* If the filter of $A_0$ has odd simple parity, retain one simple vertex of a unit witness as the environment; otherwise take the environment empty. The remaining simple positions have even parity, so pair them into sites and put all variable positions of the witness in one block. Allow aggregate roots with the prescribed total class throughout.

Consider all actual finite configurations with this environment and a list of singular blocks, with $B=L$ between blocks, at which $A_0=1$. This collection, allowing an empty list, is nonempty. Indeed, if the witness block is nonsingular, expand it as empty plus singular states by Lemma <a href="#lem:binary-tensor-span" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:binary-tensor-span">52</a>; some resulting term has value $1$. Proposition <a href="#prop:selmer-matrix-bound" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:selmer-matrix-bound">50</a> bounds the lengths of these lists, since the environment has fixed dimension cost. Choose an actual maximizing list $a$ and fix all its primes, singular matrices, and diagonal choices. Only this one finite list is retained; no bound on the sizes of arbitrary maximizing blocks is asserted.

For a proposed further block, fixing the prefix and environment gives a multilinear symbol functional $f$. It vanishes on every singular pure state $z$, for otherwise appending $z$ contradicts maximality. Also $f(\varnothing)=1$, because its aggregate root preserves the total label and the prefix diagonal data of the maximizing evaluation. Singular pure states span the kernel of the determinant functional by Lemma <a href="#lem:binary-tensor-span" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:binary-tensor-span">52</a>, and the empty state has determinant $1$. Hence $f=\det$, proving Equation <a href="#eq:sa:conditioned-determinant" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:sa:conditioned-determinant">[eq:sa:conditioned-determinant]</a>. Maximality here is over actual singular states. It requires no alternative choice for any fixed prefix prime against a later prime. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-54"></a>
##### The number of surviving copies

Fix a nonempty maximal singular unit word $W=(W_1,\ldots,W_m)$ in an odd profile, as in Lemma <a href="#lem:sa:punctured-cube" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:sa:punctured-cube">56</a>. Write $$M=\bigoplus_{i=1}^mM_i,\qquad
 D=\bigoplus_{i=1}^mD_i,\qquad N=M+D,$$ where $D_i$ is a sum of site toggles making $M_i+D_i$ invertible. The matrix $N$ is invertible and $D$ is alternating. Their common coordinate space $U$ has even dimension, fixed with the word.

<a id="stmt-lem-sa-balanced-copies"></a>
<div id="lem:sa:balanced-copies" class="lemma">

**Lemma 60** (Address copies with even total activation). *For every $b\ge2$, the address construction for $W$ may be chosen so that its symbol is $1$ at every nonzero $x$ and all sites are absent at zero. At a nonzero $x$, eliminating its invertible path sites leaves the designated copy of $M$ and an odd number of copies of $N$. The different copies have zero mutual $M$-entries.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-sa-balanced-copies"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-sa-balanced-copies</summary>

<a id="eq:sa:activation-parity"></a>
*Proof.* For every $a\ne0$ choose a linear form $l_a$ with $$l_a(a)=1,\qquad \sum_{a\ne0}l_a=0.
 \label{eq:sa:activation-parity}$$ To obtain these forms, begin with arbitrary choices satisfying the first condition. Allowed changes at $a$ form its annihilator. The annihilators of two distinct nonzero addresses are distinct hyperplanes and span the entire dual space. Changes at those two addresses can therefore cancel the initial sum.

Activate all word sites in the copy designated for $a$ by $l_a$, and use a basis of the annihilator of $a$ for its path coordinates in Lemma <a href="#lem:lm:address-program" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:lm:address-program">53</a>. The saturation proof is unchanged. At a nonzero $x$, the designated copy leaves $M$. Each other active copy leaves $N$, and a copy with $l_a(x)=0$ leaves only invertible paths. Equation <a href="#eq:sa:activation-parity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:sa:activation-parity">[eq:sa:activation-parity]</a> says that the total number of active copies is even. The designated copy is active, so an odd number of other copies remain. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-55"></a>
##### A bounded interface

We will couple every surviving copy to the same fixed collection of split sites. When two $N$-copies are eliminated, their contributions to that collection cancel in characteristic two. Thus the calculation reduces to one $M$-copy, one $N$-copy, and the fixed collection. The following lemma chooses its couplings; its dimension depends on $W$ and not on the number of addresses.

<a id="stmt-lem-sa-interface"></a>
<div id="lem:sa:interface" class="lemma">

**Lemma 61** (Alternating interface repair). *Let $U$ be an even-dimensional vector space over $\mathbb F_2$, let $N$ be symmetric and invertible on $U$, and let $D$ be alternating. There are at most $\dim U$ linear maps $b_i:U\to\mathbb F_2^2$ such that, on writing $J=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and $H=\sum_i b_i^tJb_i$, the matrix <a id="eq:sa:interface-matrix"></a>$$S(H)=\begin{pmatrix}D&N\\N&N+H\end{pmatrix}
 \label{eq:sa:interface-matrix}$$ is invertible. If $U$ has the rotation-field structure $\mathbb F_4^d$ occurring in the cyclic cubic case, the maps may be chosen $\mathbb F_4$-linear from $U$ to the field line $\mathbb F_4=\mathbb F_2^2$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-sa-interface"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-sa-interface</summary>

*Proof.* Start with $H=0$, and write $\pi_2:U\oplus U\to U$ for projection to the second coordinate. For every $H$, this projection is injective on $\ker S(H)$: if $(u,0)$ belongs to the kernel, then $Nu=0$, so $u=0$. The update $H\mapsto H+b^tJb$ adds the alternating form $(b\pi_2)^tJ(b\pi_2)$ to $S=S(H)$. We show how to choose an update reducing every nonzero kernel.

If $\dim\ker S\ge2$, choose $b$ of rank $2$ on $\pi_2(\ker S)$. Take a complement of $\ker S$ and modify its basis vectors by kernel vectors so that $b\pi_2$ vanishes on the new complement. The restriction of $S$ to that complement remains nondegenerate. The update is zero there and in its cross pairings, and has rank $2$ on $\ker S$. Hence it decreases the nullity by exactly $2$.

<a id="eq:sa:diagonal-rank"></a>
Suppose instead that $\ker S=\langle k\rangle$ is one-dimensional. Let $d_S$ denote the diagonal vector. Since $z^tSz=d_S^tz$ for every binary symmetric matrix, $d_S$ annihilates the kernel and lies in the image of $S$. Choose $s$ with $Ss=d_S$. We shall use $$d_S^ts=\mathop{\mathrm{rank}}S\pmod2.
 \label{eq:sa:diagonal-rank}$$ To prove it, restrict to a nondegenerate complement of the radical, with invertible symmetric matrix $A$ and diagonal vector $d_A$. The left side is $d_A^tA^{-1}d_A$. Off-diagonal terms cancel in pairs, leaving $\sum_i(A^{-1})_{ii}A_{ii}$. Applying the same cancellation to $\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(A^{-1}A)$ identifies this with $\dim A$ modulo $2$, proving Equation <a href="#eq:sa:diagonal-rank" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:sa:diagonal-rank">[eq:sa:diagonal-rank]</a>.

Since the ambient dimension is even and the kernel has dimension one, $d_S^ts=1$. The alternating matrices $D$ and $H$ have zero diagonal, so $d_S$ is supported on the second coordinates. Consequently $\pi_2(s)$ and $\pi_2(k)$ are binary-independent: otherwise the former would be zero or equal to the latter, forcing $d_S^ts=0$. Choose $b$ sending them to independent vectors of $\mathbb F_2^2$.

Let $z$ belong to the kernel after this update. Self-pairing gives $d_S^tz=0$. Pairing the updated equation with $k$ gives $$(b\pi_2(k))^tJ(b\pi_2(z))=0.$$ Pairing with $s$ gives the same equation with $s$ in place of $k$, since $s^tSz=d_S^tz=0$. Their independent images force $b\pi_2(z)=0$. The updated equation then reduces to $Sz=0$, so $z$ is a multiple of $k$. As $b\pi_2(k)\ne0$, this multiple is zero. The update has made $S$ invertible.

Both choices of $b$ remain possible under the field-linear restriction. Two binary-independent vectors $u,v\in\mathbb F_4^d$ are either field-independent, in which case a field-linear map can send them to any binary basis of $\mathbb F_4$, or satisfy $v=\alpha u$ with $\alpha\in\mathbb F_4\setminus\mathbb F_2$. In the latter case any field-linear map nonzero on $u$ gives binary-independent images. These maps are allowed by the rotation-field off-diagonal spans, and the preceding argument applies to the underlying binary forms.

Finally, injectivity of $\pi_2$ bounds every kernel dimension by $\dim U$. Each update strictly decreases it, so at most $\dim U$ maps are required. ◻

</details>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-sa-interface-2"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-sa-interface</summary>

*Proof of Proposition <a href="#prop:sa:bounded-companion" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:sa:bounded-companion">58</a>.* Choose the prefix and possible one-coordinate environment from Lemma <a href="#lem:sa:prefix" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:sa:prefix">59</a> and fix all their primes. Build the odd address profile disjoint from them, with $B=L$ to every prefix block. The alternatives at a simple pair have identical compatible outside bits against the environment. Include these stationary primes among the local-square conditions in Lemma <a href="#lem:sa:root-calibration" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:sa:root-calibration">57</a>.

Since $A(1)=0$, Lemma <a href="#lem:sa:punctured-cube" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:sa:punctured-cube">56</a> supplies a nonempty maximal singular unit word $W$. Fix it once. It determines $U,M,D,N$ before $b$ is chosen.

Choose the maps of Lemma <a href="#lem:sa:interface" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:sa:interface">61</a> for this fixed pair $(N,D)$. Let $J_{\mathrm{int}}$ be the direct sum of one standard $J$-block for each map, and let $G$ be the matrix obtained by stacking the maps $Jb_i$. Then $$G^tJ_{\mathrm{int}}^{-1}G=\sum_i b_i^tJb_i=H.$$ For a given $b$, use Lemma <a href="#lem:sa:balanced-copies" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:sa:balanced-copies">60</a> to obtain the address programs and then calibrate their support labels and diagonals by root primes.

Lemma <a href="#lem:lm:arithmetic-realization" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:lm:arithmetic-realization">49</a> realizes these couplings by a fixed number of primary split interface positions, with the field-linear restriction when required.

Only now, for each actual finite address array, construct the auxiliary parameter $k$. Its support consists of the stationary prefix, its possible environment, fresh primes for the fixed number of interface positions, and one fresh root prime. Prescribe $B=L$ between the interface and the prefix blocks. In the matrix $M$ of the further block, couple the interface by zero to the path sites and by the same matrix $G$ to the word coordinates of every address copy. Keep all other bits of the simple variants identical.

Require $h_x$ to be a local square at every interface prime for every $x$. This is compatible with the matrix entries: the rational norm bits against address primes are independently prescribable, so their coefficients against the activation forms can be made zero. Include the already chosen address root primes in these conditions; they need only rational norm bits. Treat them as additional residue places in Lemma <a href="#lem:lm:arithmetic-realization" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:lm:arithmetic-realization">49</a>. The independent matrix and norm prescriptions concern the nonroot primes, and the further norm conditions occur at disjoint root primes. Their quadratic radicals, ramified at those fresh primes, create no relation with the preceding extensions, which are unramified there. Root calibration has already made $h_x$ a local square at the prefix and environment primes.

Choose the last root prime of $k$ to satisfy four requirements: restore the fixed total support class; make $k$ negative and split at $2N$; make $k$ a local square at every nonroot address prime; and give the prescribed diagonals at the prefix and interface. These are simultaneous finite rational radical conditions. Their residual discriminant coordinate is compatible with a rotation, because the environment accounts for any odd simple parity of the filter and the remaining variable simple positions are paired. The arithmetic realization lemma therefore supplies the prime. All new primes can be taken fresh, so $k$ is squarefree, coprime to every $h_x$, and avoids the excluded fields. Address root primes need no splitting condition, since their invariant dimension is zero.

These choices preserve all matrices needed for the two symbols. At every actual assignment, the address matrices for $A_0$ equal those for $A$, since the extra twist by $k$ is a local unit square at every nonroot address prime. The prefix and interface matrices also stay fixed as $x$ varies. In the tensor evaluations used in Equation <a href="#eq:sa:conditioned-determinant" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:sa:conditioned-determinant">[eq:sa:conditioned-determinant]</a>, aggregate roots preserve these same diagonal choices.

<a id="eq:sa:auxiliary-unit"></a>
At zero, the further block is just the interface and has invertible matrix $J_{\mathrm{int}}$. Equation <a href="#eq:sa:conditioned-determinant" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:sa:conditioned-determinant">[eq:sa:conditioned-determinant]</a> therefore gives $$A_0(|k|)=1.
 \label{eq:sa:auxiliary-unit}$$ At a nonzero address, eliminate the invertible paths. There remains one copy of $M$ and an odd number of copies of $N$, each coupled to the interface by $G$. Eliminate the $N$-copies in pairs: each pair has invertible matrix $N\oplus N$ and contributes $GN^{-1}G^t+GN^{-1}G^t=0$ to the interface. Retain the one unpaired copy. Eliminating the interface then reduces invertibility of the further block to invertibility of $$\begin{pmatrix}M+H&H\\H&N+H\end{pmatrix}.$$ The substitution $(u,v)=(u',u'+v')$ transforms this matrix by congruence to $$\begin{pmatrix}M+N&N\\N&N+H\end{pmatrix}
 =S(H),$$ which is invertible by Lemma <a href="#lem:sa:interface" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:sa:interface">61</a>. A second application of Equation <a href="#eq:sa:conditioned-determinant" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:sa:conditioned-determinant">[eq:sa:conditioned-determinant]</a> yields <a id="eq:sa:paired-units"></a>$$A_0(|k h_x|)=1\quad\text{for every }x\ne0.
 \label{eq:sa:paired-units}$$ The odd symbol is also $1$ by saturation. The support of $k$ consists of the fixed prefix and environment, at most $\dim U$ interface primes, and one root prime. Its cardinality is bounded independently of $b$. The symbol $A_0(|k|)=1$ gives analytic rank zero and a uniform bound for $s(k)$ by Proposition <a href="#prop:unit-symbol-detection" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:unit-symbol-detection">19</a>.

For each fixed finite profile restriction, first fix its weight bound and the finite list of symbol and operator comparisons. Choose a sufficiently high actual odd-source level, and realize the address array there as above. Keeping all these address primes fixed, place the required Galois data in a common finite quotient and choose only the fresh interface primes and final root prime of $k$ to meet the remaining matrix and norm prescriptions. All the unit-symbol tests then hold at once. All constants were fixed with the symbols, prefix and word. This proves the proposition. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-56"></a>
#### Completion of the odd case

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-sa-interface-3"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-sa-interface</summary>

*Completion of the proof of Theorem <a href="#thm:irreducible-converse" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:irreducible-converse">54</a>.* Apply Proposition <a href="#prop:sa:bounded-companion" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:sa:bounded-companion">58</a>. It gives $\omega(k)$ and $s(k)$ bounded independently of $b$, with $E^{(k)}$ of analytic rank zero. For $K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt{k})$, Lemma <a href="#lem:h:base-selmer-bound" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:h:base-selmer-bound">11</a> gives $$\mathop{\mathrm{corank}}_{\mathbb Z_2}\mathop{\mathrm{Sel}}_{2^\infty}(E/K)=1$$ and bounds the length of its finite quotient by the divisible part uniformly in $k$. Its hypotheses hold because $E$ is the fixed corank-one curve, the other twist has rank zero with bounded $s(k)$, and $\omega(k)$ is bounded. This step does not assume finiteness of the Tate–Shafarevich group of $E$.

For $x\ne0$, the two unit symbols give analytic rank one for $E^{(h_x)}$ and analytic rank zero for $E^{(kh_x)}$. Their coefficient comparisons also give uniform bounds $$j(P_1(h_*))\le w(h_x)+C_1,
 \qquad
 v(\mathcal L(kh_x))\le 2w(kh_x)+C_2.$$ Here $h_*$ is the fixed genus partner of the odd symbol. The genus point $P_1(h_*)$ is formed over $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{h_xh_*})$, so the point varies with $x$ while $h_*$ remains fixed. Coprimality gives $w(kh_x)=w(k)+w(h_x)$. Proposition <a href="#prop:heegner-comparison" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:heegner-comparison">9</a> first yields $2j(P_{|h_x|}(h_x))\le4w(h_x)+2w(k)+O(1)$. Since $w(k)\le\omega(k)$ is uniformly bounded, this becomes <a id="eq:sa:heegner-upper"></a>$$2j(P_{|h_x|}(h_x))\le 4w(h_x)+C_3.
 \label{eq:sa:heegner-upper}$$ Subtracting the nonnegative finite lengths $s(h_x)+s(kh_x)$ gives the uniform upper bound in Theorem <a href="#thm:heegner-interpolation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:heegner-interpolation">10</a>.

We have also imposed every other hypothesis of that theorem: $K$ is imaginary and split at $2N$; each $h_x$ is coprime to $k$; $h_0=1$; signed prime discriminants are activated by linear forms; the local classes at $2N$ are fixed; and each added prime either splits in $K$ or is a root prime with $t_p=0$. For each fixed finite cube, take a sufficiently high precision from its realization set so that all its unit-symbol tests hold at once. The constants depend only on the already fixed normalized symbols, prefix, and word, not on $b$.

The varying-field uniformity in Theorem <a href="#thm:heegner-interpolation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:heegner-interpolation">10</a> therefore applies to these cubes of arbitrarily large dimension. It gives a simple zero at $1$ for $L(E,s)L(E^{(k)},s)$. The second factor is nonzero by Equation <a href="#eq:sa:auxiliary-unit" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:sa:auxiliary-unit">[eq:sa:auxiliary-unit]</a>, so $L(E,s)$ has a simple zero. This proves the remaining case $c_2(E)=1$. ◻

</details>

<a id="sec:auxiliary-nonvanishing"></a>
### Proof of auxiliary nonvanishing

We prove Proposition <a href="#prop:rough-nonvanishing" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:rough-nonvanishing">[prop:rough-nonvanishing]</a>. The even-sign assertion follows from Hoffstein–Luo after one preliminary twist. For the odd-sign assertion we retain the prescribed local conditions throughout a derivative first-moment calculation.

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-sa-interface-4"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-sa-interface</summary>

*Proof of Proposition <a href="#prop:rough-nonvanishing" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:rough-nonvanishing">[prop:rough-nonvanishing]</a><span class="upright">(i)</span>.* An odd fundamental discriminant is squarefree and congruent to $1$ modulo $4$, so $c_2$ is represented by $u_2\in\{1,5\}$ modulo $8$. For odd $p\in S$, choose a nonzero residue $u_p$ representing $c_p$. The Chinese remainder theorem and Dirichlet’s theorem give a prime $q\notin S\cup B$ satisfying $$q\equiv\sigma u_2\pmod8,\qquad
 \sigma q\equiv u_p\pmod p\quad(p\in S,\ p\ne2).$$ Then $D_0=\sigma q$ is an odd fundamental discriminant in the prescribed filter. Put $A=E^{(D_0)}$ and let $N_A$ be its conductor. Thus $\varepsilon(A)=1$.

The theorem of Hoffstein–Luo (Hoffstein and Luo 1997, 435–36) <a id="pm-cite-77"></a>[[HoffsteinLuo1997](#ref-HoffsteinLuo1997)] gives infinitely many odd fundamental discriminants $h$ such that $$L(A^{(h)},1)\ne0,\qquad \omega(|h|)\le4,$$ and $\chi_h(p)=1$ at every prime in the fixed finite set consisting of $S\cup B\cup\{q\}$ and the prime divisors of $N_A$. The twisting formula for the root number gives $$1=\varepsilon(A^{(h)})=\varepsilon(A)\chi_h(-N_A)
 =\operatorname{sign}(h),$$ so $h>0$. For odd $p$ the condition $\chi_h(p)=1$ says that $h$ is a unit square in $\mathbb Q_p$. At $2$, odd fundamentality and $\chi_h(2)=1$ give $h\equiv1\pmod8$, which has the same meaning. Since $q\nmid h$, the product $D=D_0h$ is squarefree and congruent to $1$ modulo $4$. It retains the prescribed sign and squareclasses and avoids $B$. Finally, $$E^{(D)}\simeq A^{(h)},\qquad \omega(|D|)=1+\omega(h)\le5.$$ Distinct choices of $h$ give distinct $D$. ◻

</details>

<a id="odd:fixed-progression"></a>
#### An odd-sign witness in a fixed progression

We retain the modulus of the local conditions throughout the first-moment calculation. Iwaniec’s derivative moment (Iwaniec 1990, Theorem on p. 367 and Sections 6–10) <a id="pm-cite-78"></a>[[Iwaniec1990](#ref-Iwaniec1990)] treats the negative-discriminant split family. The following argument allows any fixed admissible progression. It makes no uniformity assertion as that progression varies.

<a id="stmt-nv-odd-first-moment"></a>
<div id="nv:odd-first-moment" class="lemma">

<a id="odd:moment"></a>
**Lemma 62** (Odd first moment). *Let $f$ be the weight-two newform of an elliptic curve of conductor $N$, with its $L$-function normalized to have center $1/2$. Fix $H$ divisible by $8$ and $N$, a reduced class $a\pmod H$, and $\sigma\in\{1,-1\}$ with $\sigma a\equiv1\pmod4$. Suppose the twists with $n>0$ squarefree and $n\equiv a\pmod H$ have root number $-1$. For every nonnegative, nonzero $\Phi\in C_c^\infty((1,2))$, there are $c>0$, $c_1\in\mathbb R$, and an absolute $\eta>0$ such that $$\label{odd:moment}
 \sum_{\substack{n>0\ \mathrm{squarefree}\\n\equiv a\ (H)}}
 L'(1/2,f\otimes\chi_{\sigma n})\Phi(n/X)
 =cX\log X+c_1X+O_{f,H,a,\sigma,\Phi}(X^{1-\eta}).$$ Consequently this progression contains arbitrarily large $n$ whose twists have a simple central zero.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-nv-odd-first-moment"><summary>Proof of stmt-nv-odd-first-moment</summary>

<a id="odd:afe"></a>
*Proof.* Write $L(s,f)=\sum_{m\ge1}\lambda(m)m^{-s}$, so $|\lambda(m)|\le\tau(m)$, where $\tau$ is the divisor function, and put $Q=\sqrt N/(2\pi)$. In estimates below, constants may depend on the fixed data in the Lemma; all unspecified power exponents are absolute. The proof separates two issues: preserving the fixed progression while removing the squarefree condition, and controlling the frequencies after Poisson summation. The zero frequency will give a positive main term of order $X\log X$; the other frequencies and the discarded square divisors must together have a power-saving bound. We keep the modulus $H$ fixed throughout these steps. Set $$V(y)=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{(2)}
 e^{z^2}\Gamma(1+z)y^{-z}\frac{dz}{z^2}.$$ The conductor of the twist is $Nn^2$. Its odd functional equation gives $$\label{odd:afe}
 L'(1/2,f\otimes\chi_{\sigma n})
 =2\sum_{m\ge1}\frac{\lambda(m)\chi_{\sigma n}(m)}{\sqrt m}
           V\left(\frac m{Qn}\right).$$ Indeed, shift the defining completed integral across its double pole and use the functional equation. The central value is zero, so the derivative of the completion contributes no additional term. Use the right side of Equation <a href="#odd:afe" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="odd:afe">[odd:afe]</a> to define $\mathcal A(n)$ also for nonsquarefree $n\equiv a\pmod H$.

<a id="pm-h-59"></a>
###### Large square divisors.

<a id="odd:second-moment"></a>
<a id="odd:square-index-bound"></a>
We first record the precise large-sieve input. For every $\rho>0$ and fixed $0<\delta<1/4$, $$\label{odd:second-moment}
 \sum_{\substack{0<t\le Z\ \mathrm{squarefree}\\
             \sigma t\ \mathrm{fundamental},\ (t,2N)=1}}
 |L(1/2+\delta+i v,f\otimes\chi_{\sigma t})|^2
 \ll_{f,\rho,\delta} Z^{1+\rho}(1+|v|)^{C_{\rho,\delta}}.$$ To justify this consequence of the quadratic large sieve, its form in (Heath-Brown 1995, Theorem 1) <a id="pm-cite-79"></a>[[HeathBrown1995](#ref-HeathBrown1995)] is $$\sum_{\substack{t\le Z\ \mathrm{odd, squarefree}}}
 \left|\sum_{\substack{u\le U\ \mathrm{odd, squarefree}}}
 b_u\left(\frac tu\right)\right|^2
 \ll_\epsilon (ZU)^\epsilon(Z+U)\sum_u|b_u|^2.$$ Quadratic reciprocity permits either orientation of the symbol after separating classes modulo $4$. In a Dirichlet polynomial with coefficients $\lambda(m)m^{-1/2}$, write $m=ur^2$, $u$ squarefree. For each $r$, $\chi_{\sigma t}(r^2)$ restricts $t$ to $(t,r)=1$; discard that restriction only after taking absolute squares. Since $|\lambda(ur^2)|\le\tau(u)\tau(r^2)$, Minkowski’s inequality bounds the square root of the moment by $$\label{odd:square-index-bound}
 (ZU)^{O(\epsilon)}
 \sum_{r\le\sqrt U}\frac{\sqrt{Z+U/r^2}}r
 \ll (ZU)^{O(\epsilon)}(\sqrt Z+\sqrt U).$$ The powers of primes dividing $2N$ contribute convergent geometric sums. On a dyadic interval $t\asymp T$, the approximate functional equation has length $U\ll_f T(1+|v|)^C$, apart from rapidly decreasing tails. The main sum’s additional factor $m^{-\delta}$ improves partial summation. The dual sum loses at most $U^\delta$ in coefficients, but its functional-equation multiplier contributes $T^{-2\delta}$, up to a fixed power of $1+|v|$. Thus it incurs no positive power of $T$. Mellin inversion separates the smooth conductor weights; the gamma factors give integrable decay in the Mellin variables. Applying Equation <a href="#odd:square-index-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="odd:square-index-bound">[odd:square-index-bound]</a> with sufficiently small $\epsilon$, and summing dyadic intervals, proves Equation <a href="#odd:second-moment" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="odd:second-moment">[odd:second-moment]</a>.

Expand $\mu^2(n)=\sum_{d^2\mid n}\mu(d)$ and retain $d\le Y$, where $1\le Y\le\sqrt X$. The omitted contribution is <a id="odd:square-tail"></a>$$\label{odd:square-tail}
 O_\rho(X^{1+\rho}/Y).$$ Here are the details for the nonsquarefree terms. Write $n=tv^2$ with $t$ squarefree. An omitted term has $v>Y$, with at most $\tau(v)$ choices of $d$. Also $\sigma t$ is fundamental, $(tv,2N)=1$, and $$\chi_{\sigma n}(m)
   =\chi_{\sigma t}(m)\mathbf1_{(m,v)=1}.$$ On a Mellin line $\Re z=\delta>0$, the series defining $\mathcal A(tv^2)$ therefore uses $$L(1/2+z,f\otimes\chi_{\sigma t})
 \prod_{p\mid v}
 \left(1-\frac{\lambda(p)\chi_{\sigma t}(p)}{p^{1/2+z}}
             +\frac{\chi_{\sigma t}(p)^2}{p^{1+2z}}\right).$$ The product is $O_\epsilon(v^\epsilon)$. By Cauchy’s inequality and Equation <a href="#odd:second-moment" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="odd:second-moment">[odd:second-moment]</a>, the sum of the absolute $L$-values over $t\le2X/v^2$ is $O((X/v^2)^{1+\epsilon}(1+|\Im z|)^C)$. The remaining Mellin factors are bounded by $O(X^\delta)$ times a rapidly decreasing function of $\Im z$. Choose $\delta$ and $\epsilon$ sufficiently small in terms of $\rho$. Absorbing the divisor count and these small powers gives $X^{1+\rho}\sum_{v>Y}v^{-2}\ll X^{1+\rho}/Y$, as claimed. The double pole in the kernel is harmless on this fixed positive line.

<a id="pm-h-60"></a>
###### Poisson summation.

<a id="odd:poisson"></a>
For $(d,H)=1$ put $J=d^2$ and $c_J\equiv aJ^{-1}\pmod H$. Let $T(J)$ be the sum of $\mathcal A(n)\Phi(n/X)$ over $n\equiv a\pmod H$ with $J\mid n$, without a squarefree restriction. Writing $m=m_1q$ with $m_1\mid H^\infty$ and $(q,H)=1$, put $\kappa(m_1)=\chi_{\sigma a}(m_1)$ and $$G_\nu(q)=\sum_{y\bmod q}\left(\frac yq\right)e(\nu y/q),\qquad
 W(z,R)=\int_0^\infty\Phi(x)V\left(\frac z{Qx}\right)e(-Rx)\,dx,$$ where $e(x)=e^{2\pi ix}$. Poisson summation gives $$\label{odd:poisson}
 \begin{split}
 T(J)={}&\frac{2X}{HJ}
 \sum_{m_1\mid H^\infty}\frac{\lambda(m_1)\kappa(m_1)}{\sqrt{m_1}}
 \sum_{(q,H)=1}\frac{\lambda(q)}{q^{3/2}}
                  \left(\frac{\sigma JH}{q}\right)\\
 &\hspace{9mm}\cdot\sum_{\nu\in\mathbb Z}
 G_\nu(q)e(\nu c_J\bar q/H)
 W\left(\frac{m_1q}{X},\frac{\nu X}{HJq}\right),
 \end{split}$$ where $q\bar q\equiv1\pmod H$ and $G_\nu(1)=1$. For clarity, the Chinese remainder theorem evaluates the finite sum as $$\sum_{\substack{x\bmod Hq\\x\equiv c_J\ (H)}}
 \left(\frac xq\right)e(\nu x/(Hq))
 =e(\nu c_J\bar q/H)\left(\frac Hq\right)G_\nu(q).$$ Multiplication by $(\sigma J/q)$ yields Equation <a href="#odd:poisson" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="odd:poisson">[odd:poisson]</a>; this factor vanishes when $(q,J)>1$.

<a id="pm-h-61"></a>
###### The zero frequency.

<a id="odd:zero-integral"></a>
The Gauss sum $G_0(q)$ is zero unless $q$ is a square, when it is $\varphi(q)$. Define $$H_p(z)=1+(1-p^{-1})\sum_{r\ge1}
                    \lambda(p^{2r})p^{-r(1+2z)},\qquad
 F_J(z)=\prod_{p\nmid HJ}H_p(z),$$ $$L_H(z)=\sum_{m_1\mid H^\infty}
          \lambda(m_1)\kappa(m_1)m_1^{-1/2-z},\qquad
 \widehat\Phi_0(z)=\int_0^\infty\Phi(x)x^z\,dx.$$ Mellin inversion expresses the zero-frequency contribution as $$\label{odd:zero-integral}
 T_0(J)=\frac{2X}{HJ}\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{(2)}
 e^{z^2}\Gamma(1+z)(QX)^z\widehat\Phi_0(z)L_H(z)F_J(z)
 \frac{dz}{z^2}.$$ At a good prime, let $\alpha_p\beta_p=1$ and $|\alpha_p|=|\beta_p|=1$. The identity $$\sum_{r\ge0}\lambda(p^{2r})x^r
 =\frac{1+x}{(1-\alpha_p^2x)(1-\beta_p^2x)}$$ shows that $H_p(z)$ is the symmetric-square Euler factor at $1+2z$ times a polynomial $1+O(p^{-2-4\Re z}+p^{-2-2\Re z})$. The correction product converges absolutely near $\Re z\ge-1/16$. To omit a prime dividing $J$, omit its correction factor and insert an inverse symmetric-square Euler polynomial; this introduces no poles at zeros of $H_p$. These omitted factors cost at most $J^B$ on that strip. The finite Euler product $L_H$ is holomorphic there. Symmetric-square continuation, its functional equation, and polynomial strip bounds now allow the shift to $\Re z=-1/16$, with error <a id="odd:zero-error"></a>$$\label{odd:zero-error}
 T_0(J)=R_J(X)+O(J^B X^{1-1/16}),$$ where $R_J(X)$ is the residue of the integrand in Equation <a href="#odd:zero-integral" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="odd:zero-integral">[odd:zero-integral]</a>, including its factor $2X/(HJ)$. For this analytic input see (Gelbart and Jacquet 1978, Theorem 9.3 and Remark 9.9) <a id="pm-cite-80"></a>[[GelbartJacquet1978](#ref-GelbartJacquet1978)]; in the CM case the untwisted symmetric square is a product of nontrivial Dirichlet and Hecke-character $L$-functions, so the same continuation holds near $1$.

<a id="odd:residue"></a>
The sum of the residues, with $d$ extended to infinity, has coefficient function $$M(z)=e^{z^2}\Gamma(1+z)Q^z\widehat\Phi_0(z)L_H(z)
              \prod_{p\nmid H}\bigl(H_p(z)-p^{-2}\bigr).$$ The product is interpreted by its symmetric-square factorization and an absolutely convergent correction. It is holomorphic near zero. Moreover $M(0)>0$. Indeed $$F_p^{\rm ev}:=\frac{1+p^{-1}}
 {(1-\alpha_p^2/p)(1-\beta_p^2/p)}>0,\qquad
 H_p(0)=p^{-1}+(1-p^{-1})F_p^{\rm ev}>p^{-1}.$$ All the fixed local factors in $L_H(0)$ are positive, and $L(1,\operatorname{sym}^2 f)>0$ by the Rankin–Selberg residue formula. The remaining correction factors are positive and form a convergent product. The full residue is therefore $$\label{odd:residue}
 \frac{2X}{H}\bigl(M(0)\log X+M'(0)\bigr),
 \qquad c=\frac{2M(0)}H>0.$$ Extending the residue sum costs $O_\rho(X^{1+\rho}/Y)$: its terms contain $d^{-2}\prod_{p\mid d}H_p(0)^{-1}$, and this product, as well as its differentiated version, is $O_\epsilon(d^\epsilon(1+\log d))$. The resulting $d^{-2+\epsilon}$ tail also justifies differentiating the residue sum.

<a id="pm-h-62"></a>
###### The nonzero frequencies.

<a id="odd:offdiagonal"></a>
The zero frequency has now supplied the positive main term. We next bound the remaining frequencies uniformly in the square divisor $J$ by a fixed power of $J$, so that summation over the retained square divisors will preserve a power saving in $X$. We prove the bound $$\label{odd:offdiagonal}
 T_{\ne0}(J)\ll J^B X^{7/8}.$$ For odd $q$, set $\epsilon_q=1$ or $i$ according as $q\equiv1$ or $3\pmod4$, and $\widetilde G_\nu(q)=\epsilon_q^{-1}G_\nu(q)$. Quadratic reciprocity makes $\widetilde G_\nu$ multiplicative in $q$. As $4\mid H$, the phase $\epsilon_q e(\nu c_J\bar q/H)$ is a function on $(\mathbb Z/H\mathbb Z)^\times$. Expand it in Dirichlet characters $\psi\pmod H$; every expansion coefficient has absolute value at most one. For $\nu\ne0$, consider $$D_{\psi,J,\nu}(s)=\sum_{(q,H)=1}
 \frac{\lambda(q)}{q^s}\frac{\widetilde G_\nu(q)}{\sqrt q}
                 \left(\frac{\sigma JH}{q}\right)\psi(q).$$ At $p\nmid2HJ\nu$, its local factor is $1+\lambda(p)\xi(p)p^{-s}$, where $\xi(q)=\psi(q)(\sigma JH\nu/q)$ is a Dirichlet character. Multiplication by the inverse $\mathrm{GL}_2$ Euler factor leaves $$1+(1-\lambda(p)^2)\xi(p)^2p^{-2s}
     +\lambda(p)\xi(p)^3p^{-3s}.$$ These factors converge absolutely for $\Re s>1/2$.

<a id="odd:gauss-strip"></a>
The exceptional primes cause only a fixed power loss. For an odd prime $p$, put $v=v_p(\nu)$. Direct summation over residue lifts gives $$G_\nu(p^r)=
 \begin{cases}
 \varphi(p^r),&r\text{ even},\ r\le v,\\
 -p^{r-1},&r\text{ even},\ r=v+1,\\
 \epsilon_p p^{r-1/2}
       \left(\dfrac{\nu/p^{r-1}}p\right),
          &r\text{ odd},\ r=v+1,\\
 0,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}$$ For even $r$ this is the Ramanujan sum. For odd $r$, the sum of the lifts vanishes unless $p^{r-1}\mid\nu$, and the primitive quadratic Gauss sum then gives the formula. Thus the local sum is a polynomial; on $\Re s\ge3/4$ its absolute value is at most $\sum_{r\ge0}(r+1)p^{-r/4}\le C_0$. The inverse Euler polynomial is also bounded absolutely. Primes dividing $J$ remove the local sum altogether. Passing to the primitive character underlying $\xi$ introduces only such inverse Euler polynomials. Hence $$D_{\psi,J,\nu}(s)=L(s,f\otimes\xi^{\rm prim})C_{\psi,J,\nu}(s),$$ where $C_{\psi,J,\nu}$ is holomorphic for $\Re s>1/2$ and bounded on $\Re s\ge3/4$ by $(2J|\nu|)^C$. Indeed the exceptional-prime cost is at most $C_1^{\omega(J\nu)}$, and the other corrections have summable $O(p^{-3/2})$ errors there. The conductor of $\xi^{\rm prim}$ is at most $4HJ|\nu|$. The twisted cusp-form $L$-function is entire; its functional equation and polynomial strip bounds therefore give $$\label{odd:gauss-strip}
 |D_{\psi,J,\nu}(3/4+i t)|
 \ll_{f,H}(J|\nu|)^C(1+|t|)^C.$$ The exponents are absolute because the degree and weight are fixed.

<a id="odd:weight-decay"></a>
<a id="odd:ranges"></a>
It remains to sum these bounds without losing the power saving. The kernel and integration by parts in $x$ give, for fixed $r,s$ and every $K>0$, $$\label{odd:weight-decay}
 |(z\partial_z)^r(R\partial_R)^s W(z,R)|
 \ll_{r,s,K}(1+z)^{-K}(1+|R|)^{-K}(1+|\log z|).$$ The logarithm accounts for the double pole when $z$ tends to zero. On the actual sums $z\ge X^{-1}$. For a fixed small $\rho>0$, insert smooth cutoffs $z\ll X^\rho$ and $|R|\ll X^\rho$. The discarded part is negligible: use $|G_\nu(q)|\le q$ and $$\sum_{\nu\in\mathbb Z}
 (1+|\nu|X/(HJq))^{-K}\ll_H1+Jq/X$$ to obtain a polynomial absolute majorant in $X,J$ for Equation <a href="#odd:poisson" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="odd:poisson">[odd:poisson]</a>. More explicitly, its absolute value is $O_\epsilon(X^{3/2+\epsilon}\log X)$, uniformly for $J\ge1$: the $q$-sums contribute $(X/m_1)^{1/2+\epsilon}+(J/X)(X/m_1)^{3/2+\epsilon}$, and the remaining $m_1\mid H^\infty$ sums converge. For $z>1$, absorb the positive logarithm into an arbitrarily small power of $z$ in this calculation. On either discarded tail, increasing $K$ in Equation <a href="#odd:weight-decay" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="odd:weight-decay">[odd:weight-decay]</a> supplies an arbitrarily large factor $X^{-\rho K}$. The retained nonzero-frequency range satisfies $$\label{odd:ranges}
 m_1q\ll X^{1+\rho},\qquad
 0<|\nu|\ll_H JX^{2\rho},\qquad
 q\gg_H X^{1-\rho}/J.$$

Partition the $q$-sum into smooth segments $q\asymp T$. By Equation <a href="#odd:weight-decay" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="odd:weight-decay">[odd:weight-decay]</a>, the finitely many derivative norms needed for Mellin inversion of the segment’s weight are $O(X^{C'\rho})$, uniformly in $m_1,J,\nu,T$. Mellin inversion uses $D_{\psi,J,\nu}(1+s)T^s$. Shift its contour to $\Re s=-1/4$; the factorization above shows that no pole is crossed. Equation <a href="#odd:gauss-strip" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="odd:gauss-strip">[odd:gauss-strip]</a> and the vertical decay of the weight’s Mellin transform give <a id="odd:dyadic"></a>$$\label{odd:dyadic}
 \sum_q\frac{\lambda(q)}q\frac{\widetilde G_\nu(q)}{\sqrt q}
 \left(\frac{\sigma JH}{q}\right)\psi(q)W_*(q/T)
 \ll (J|\nu|)^C X^{C'\rho}T^{-1/4}.$$ Here $W_*$ includes the dyadic and cutoff factors and both arguments of the original weight; their logarithmic derivatives are controlled by Equation <a href="#odd:weight-decay" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="odd:weight-decay">[odd:weight-decay]</a>. The sum over $m_1$ is bounded since $$\sum_{m_1\mid H^\infty}\frac{|\lambda(m_1)|}{\sqrt{m_1}}
 \le\prod_{p\mid H}(1-p^{-1/2})^{-2}<\infty.$$ Equation <a href="#odd:ranges" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="odd:ranges">[odd:ranges]</a> bounds the dyadic sum of $T^{-1/4}$ by $O_H(J^{1/4}X^{-1/4+\rho/4})$, even if its formal lower endpoint is below one. Also $$\sum_{0<|\nu|\ll_H JX^{2\rho}}(J|\nu|)^C
 \ll_H J^{2C+1}X^{2(C+1)\rho}.$$ Multiplying these estimates by $X/J$ from Equation <a href="#odd:poisson" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="odd:poisson">[odd:poisson]</a> proves $T_{\ne0}(J)\ll J^B X^{3/4+C''\rho}$. Choose $\rho$ absolutely small enough that $C''\rho\le1/8$. This proves Equation <a href="#odd:offdiagonal" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="odd:offdiagonal">[odd:offdiagonal]</a>.

<a id="pm-h-63"></a>
###### Conclusion.

Sum the zero- and nonzero-frequency errors over $d\le Y$, with $J=d^2$. Together with the large-square and residue tails, the total error is $$O\left(Y^{2B+1}X^{1-\kappa}+X^{1+\rho}/Y\right),
 \qquad \kappa=1/16,$$ after enlarging $B$. Choose an absolute $\delta_0>0$ with $(2B+1)\delta_0<\kappa/2$, put $Y=X^{\delta_0}$, and choose the tail exponent $0<\rho<\delta_0/4$. Both errors are $O(X^{1-\eta})$ for an absolute $\eta>0$. Equation <a href="#odd:residue" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="odd:residue">[odd:residue]</a> proves Equation <a href="#odd:moment" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="odd:moment">[odd:moment]</a>. Its leading coefficient is positive, so some derivative is nonzero in every sufficiently large dyadic interval. The odd functional equation already forces the central value to vanish, proving the final assertion. ◻

</details>

<details id="proof-stmt-nv-odd-first-moment-2"><summary>Proof of stmt-nv-odd-first-moment</summary>

*Proof of Proposition <a href="#prop:rough-nonvanishing" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:rough-nonvanishing">[prop:rough-nonvanishing]</a><span class="upright">(ii)</span>.* Choose $H$ divisible by $8N$ and by all primes in $S\cup B$. The prescribed squareclasses and sign determine a reduced class $a\pmod H$ with $\sigma a\equiv1\pmod4$, by the Chinese remainder theorem. At a prime in $B\setminus S$, choose any nonzero residue. Then every positive squarefree $n\equiv a\pmod H$ gives an odd fundamental discriminant $D=\sigma n$ in the prescribed filter and prime to every member of $B$. Lemma <a href="#nv:odd-first-moment" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="nv:odd-first-moment">62</a> supplies arbitrarily large such $n$ with $L'(E^{(D)},1)\ne0$. ◻

</details>

<a id="sec:binary-algebra"></a>
### Transfer on a binary cube

<span id="sec:h:binary-algebra" label="sec:h:binary-algebra"></span>

Both analytic arguments will produce one determinant coordinate at each vertex of a binary cube. The following algebra transfers a bounded valuation at every nonzero vertex to the zero vertex. Its essential feature is that the required dimension depends on a bounded number of coefficients, even when the family involves arbitrarily many primes.

Put $\Lambda=\mathbb Z_2[[t]]$ and $O=\widehat{\Lambda_{(2)}}$. Let $G\simeq(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)^b$ and $R=\Lambda[G]$. Index the sign homomorphisms $G\to\{\pm1\}$ by $x\in\mathbb F_2^b$, with $x=0$ the augmentation. For an element or matrix over $O[G]$, a subscript $x$ denotes evaluation at this character. The proofs first control Laurent coefficients, then clear determinant denominators, and finally use the parity of the number of solutions of low-degree equations on the cube.

<a id="stmt-lem-h-laurent-expansions"></a>
<div id="lem:h:laurent-expansions" class="lemma">

**Lemma 63** (Laurent expansions). *For $M\ge1$, $$O/2^MO\simeq(\mathbb Z/2^M\mathbb Z)((t)).$$ Thus an element of $O$ has a unique expansion $\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}a_nt^n$ with $a_n\in\mathbb Z_2$ and $v(a_n)\to\infty$ as $n\to-\infty$. Its $O$-valuation is $\min_n v(a_n)$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-h-laurent-expansions"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-h-laurent-expansions</summary>

*Proof.* If $s\in\Lambda\setminus(2)$, write $s=t^h v_1+2w_1$, with $v_1\in\Lambda^\times$ and $w_1\in\Lambda$. Modulo $2^M$ its inverse is a geometric expansion of length $M$ in $2w_1/(t^h v_1)$. It is a Laurent series with finite negative support. Conversely every Laurent series with finite negative support lies in the localization of $\Lambda$ modulo $2^M$, since $t$ is invertible there. Taking inverse limits proves the expansion statement. Reduction modulo successive powers of $2$ proves the valuation formula. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-lem-h-bounded-poles"></a>
<div id="lem:h:bounded-poles" class="lemma">

**Lemma 64** (A uniform pole bound for Schur elimination). *Let $A_1,\ldots,A_m$ be square matrices over $\Lambda$ with nonzero residual determinants and $\mathop{\mathrm{ord}}_t(\overline{\det A_j})\le h$. Put $A=\mathop{\mathrm{diag}}(A_1,\ldots,A_m)$. If $B=A+2E_1$ with $E_1$ a matrix over $\Lambda$, then $B$ is invertible over $O$. Modulo $2^M$, every entry of $B^{-1}$ has no powers below $-Mh$, independently of $m$ and of the matrix sizes. The same bound holds for a Schur complement $D=P-QB^{-1}S$ when $P,Q,S$ have entries in $\Lambda$.*

*In particular, suppose a block over $R$ augments to $A$. It is invertible over $O[G]$, and the assertion applies uniformly at all sign evaluations. If the lower off-diagonal block $S$ augments to zero, the Schur complement augments to the old block $P$.*

</div>
