<details id="proof-stmt-lem-h-bounded-poles"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-h-bounded-poles</summary>

*Proof.* Write $\det A_j=t^{h_j}v_j+2w_j$, where $h_j\le h$, $v_j\in\Lambda^\times$, and $w_j\in\Lambda$. Put $$C_j=\frac{\operatorname{adj}(A_j)}{t^{h_j}v_j},
 \qquad C=\mathop{\mathrm{diag}}(C_1,\ldots,C_m).$$ Every entry of $C$ has pole at most $h$. We have $BC=1+2F_1$, with every entry of $F_1$ having pole at most $h$. Consequently $$B^{-1}\equiv C\sum_{j=0}^{M-1}(-2F_1)^j\pmod{2^M}.$$ The $j$th summand has pole at most $(j+1)h\le Mh$. The number of summands in a matrix product does not increase a valuation or pole bound. Multiplication by power-series matrices likewise introduces no negative powers. This proves the first assertion.

The ring $O[G]$ is local with maximal ideal generated by $2$ and the augmentation ideal of $G$. The residual determinant of the proposed block is that of $A$, a unit over $\mathbb F_2((t))$, so the block is invertible. Each sign evaluation differs from augmentation by a matrix divisible by $2$ with entries in $\Lambda$. Apply the first assertion to it. The final assertion is the Schur formula with $S_0=0$. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-lem-h-pivot-clearing"></a>
<div id="lem:h:pivot-clearing" class="lemma">

**Lemma 65** (A bounded clearing factor). *Let $D$ be a based bounded complex of finite free $O[G]$-modules, of total graded rank at most $r$, whose augmentation $D_0$ is a complex over $\Lambda$. Suppose that the rational specialization of $D_0$ at $t=0$ has one of the following cohomology patterns:*

1.  *dimension one in degrees one and two, and zero elsewhere;*

2.  *dimension two in degree one, and zero elsewhere.*

*Suppose that the total torsion length in the integral specialized cohomology is at most $h_1$.*

*In case <span class="upright">(i)</span>, take an integral degree-one cycle $z$ and a closed functional $\lambda\in2^{-a_0}(D^2)^*$, and suppose each character constituent over the fraction field of $O$ is either acyclic or has pattern <span class="upright">(i)</span>. Let $u_x$ be the determinant tensor of their cohomology classes, with value zero in the acyclic case. In case <span class="upright">(ii)</span>, take two cycles whose denominator exponents sum to at most $a_0$, suppose each constituent has pattern <span class="upright">(ii)</span>, and let $u_x$ be their wedge determinant coordinate. One may multiply these coordinates by any one element $\eta\in O[G]$.*

*Then there are $f,d\in O[G]$ with $d_x=f_xu_x$ at every character, such that $f$ is $2^{a_0}$ times a polynomial of bounded degree in the differential entries of $D$, the degree depending only on $r$. Moreover $$f_0\in\Lambda,\qquad f_0(0)\ne0,\qquad
 v(f_0(0))\le C(r,h_1,a_0).$$ If, at every fixed precision, the entries of $D_x$ have a uniform bound on negative Laurent support, then so do the $f_x$. No such assertion is required for $d_x$, for the cycles, or for $\eta$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-h-pivot-clearing"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-h-pivot-clearing</summary>

*Proof.* Over $\mathbb Z_2$, put the specialized complex into a sum of free cohomology terms and one-dimensional two-term complexes with differentials $2^{a_j}$, by elementary-divisor decomposition. The sum of the positive $a_j$ is at most $h_1$. Lift the constant integral basis changes to $D$. Cancel the same pivot positions formally, retaining their pivot numerators as denominators. The number of operations is bounded by $r$. Each pivot and basis change is rational in the differential entries. Let $P_1$ be a product of sufficiently high powers of the successive pivot numerators so that every denominator in these changes and in the determinant comparison divides $P_1$. Its degree is bounded in terms of $r$; its specialization $P_{1,0}(0)$ is nonzero with valuation bounded in terms of $r,h_1$. Increase the powers once more if needed to give all final expressions the same denominator.

Over $O[G][1/P_1]$, case <span class="upright">(i)</span> leaves a complex $[O[G]\xrightarrow{\delta}O[G]]$ in degrees one and two. Let $\alpha,\beta$ be the projected cycle and closed functional. Their determinant tensor, including the cancelled-pivot determinant factor, is a rational expression in $D,z,2^{a_0}\lambda$. If a field constituent has $\delta\ne0$, the cycle identity $\delta\alpha=0$ gives $\alpha=0$, so the same expression yields the stipulated zero coordinate. In case <span class="upright">(ii)</span> the remaining complex is $O[G]^2[-1]$ and its coordinate is the determinant of the two projected cycles times the pivot determinant factor. In either case, after denominator clearing, for every constituent on which $P_{1,x}\ne0$ we have $$u_x=2^{-a_0}\eta_x Q_{1,x}/P_{1,x},\qquad Q_1\in O[G].$$ Set $f=2^{a_0}P_1^2$ and $d=\eta P_1Q_1$. This gives $d_x=f_xu_x$ on those constituents. Where a pivot numerator first vanishes, $P_{1,x}=0$, and both sides of the cleared identity are zero. Thus the identity holds on every character. Since $f$ involves only the bounded number of differential entries in the pivot calculation, its degree, augmentation valuation and pole bounds are as asserted. The factor $\eta$ has been placed in $d$, never in $f$. ◻

</details>

The preceding lemmas isolate the denominator problem: after eliminating new blocks, the clearing factor uses a complex of bounded size. The remaining task is to match finitely many coefficients at zero and at some nonzero vertex. The next lemma gives that match once the cube has sufficiently many coordinates.

<a id="stmt-lem-h-boolean-coefficients"></a>
<div id="lem:h:boolean-coefficients" class="lemma">

**Lemma 66** (Finite coefficient congruences). *Let $A_1(x),\ldots,A_q(x)\in\mathbb Z_2$ each be one specified Laurent coefficient of the evaluation of an element of $O[G]$. If $$b>q(2^{M-1}-1),$$ there is $x\ne0$ such that $A_i(x)\equiv A_i(0)\pmod{2^M}$ for every $i$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-h-boolean-coefficients"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-h-boolean-coefficients</summary>

*Proof.* For one coefficient write $$A(x)=\sum_{g\in G}a_g(-1)^{g\cdot x}
     =\sum_{S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,b\}}c_Sx_S,
 \qquad x_S=\prod_{i\in S}x_i,
 \qquad 2^{|S|}\mid c_S.$$ The last divisibility follows by expanding each sign as a product of $1-2x_i$. The $j$th binary digit of $z\in\mathbb Z_2$ is $\delta_j(z)=\binom z{2^j}\bmod2$; this holds on nonnegative integers by binary expansion and then on $\mathbb Z_2$ by continuity. In the ring of functions on the binary cube with coefficients in $\mathbb F_2[[Z]]$, $$(1+Z)^{A(x)}=(1+Z)^{c_\varnothing}
  \prod_{S\ne\varnothing}
    \left(1+x_S\big((1+Z)^{c_S}-1\big)\right).$$ The nonconstant factor indexed by $S$ starts at degree at least $2^{|S|}$ in $Z$. A term contributing to $Z^{2^j}$, for $j\ge1$, therefore has Boolean degree at most $$\sum_S|S|\le\sum_S2^{|S|-1}\le2^{j-1}.$$ The zeroth digit is constant. The congruences in the statement are thus equations over $\mathbb F_2$ of total degree at most $q\sum_{j=1}^{M-1}2^{j-1}=q(2^{M-1}-1)$, all vanishing at zero. For completeness, the number of their common zeros is even: modulo two it is the sum over the cube of the product of $1+Q$ over all defining equations $Q$. Every monomial has degree below $b$, hence omits a variable and sums to zero. This is the Chevalley–Warning argument (Chevalley 1935; Warning 1935) <a id="pm-cite-81"></a>[[Chevalley1935](#ref-Chevalley1935), [Warning1935](#ref-Warning1935)]. The zero solution therefore has a nonzero companion. ◻

</details>

We now apply these coefficient congruences to the cleared identity $d_x=f_xu_x$. Only the bounded negative support of $f_x$ is prescribed; for $d_x$ we will match its constant coefficient alone. This distinction keeps the required number of congruences independent of the numerator’s other coefficients.

<a id="stmt-lem-h-boolean-transfer"></a>
<div id="lem:h:boolean-transfer" class="lemma">

<a id="eq:h:cube-threshold"></a>
<a id="eq:h:central-transfer"></a>
**Lemma 67** (Transfer through a bounded clearing factor). *Let $f,d\in O[G]$ and let $u_x\in\Lambda[1/2]$ satisfy $d_x=f_xu_x$ at each character. Suppose $f_0\in\Lambda$ and $c_0=v(f_0(0))<\infty$. Fix $M>c_0$, and suppose every $f_x\bmod2^M$ has no powers below $-L(M)$. If $$\label{eq:h:cube-threshold}
 b>(L(M)+2)(2^{M-1}-1),$$ some $x\ne0$ satisfies $$\label{eq:h:central-transfer}
 v\bigl(u_x(0)-u_0(0)\bigr)\ge M-2c_0.$$ Consequently, when $c_0$ and each $L(M)$ have bounds independent of the family, a uniform upper bound $v(u_x(0))\le B_1$ at all nonzero vertices forces $v(u_0(0))\le B_1$ for all sufficiently large $b$. The base value itself is allowed to vary with the family.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-h-boolean-transfer"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-h-boolean-transfer</summary>

*Proof.* Apply Lemma <a href="#lem:h:boolean-coefficients" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:h:boolean-coefficients">66</a> to the coefficients of $f_x$ in degrees $-L(M),\ldots,0$ and to the constant coefficient of $d_x$. At the supplied nonzero solution, every negative coefficient of $f_x$ is divisible by $2^M$, and its constant coefficient is congruent to $f_0(0)$. Therefore its constant coefficient has valuation $c_0$, and $v_O(f_x)\le c_0$. Since $d_x\in O$, the identity $d_x=f_xu_x$ gives $v_O(u_x)\ge-c_0$; the same bound holds for $u_0$. By Lemma <a href="#lem:h:laurent-expansions" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:h:laurent-expansions">63</a>, all their coefficients are in $2^{-c_0}\mathbb Z_2$. Both have zero negative coefficients because they lie in $\Lambda[1/2]$.

The convergent constant-term convolution gives $$[t^0]d_x\equiv([t^0]f_x)u_x(0)\pmod{2^{M-c_0}},
 \qquad [t^0]d_0=f_0(0)u_0(0).$$ Combine these identities with the imposed coefficient congruences and divide by $f_0(0)$. This proves Equation <a href="#eq:h:central-transfer" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:h:central-transfer">[eq:h:central-transfer]</a>. For the consequence, choose one integer $M>\max\{c_*,B_1+2c_*\}$, where $c_*$ bounds $c_0$, and then take $b$ above Equation <a href="#eq:h:cube-threshold" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:h:cube-threshold">[eq:h:cube-threshold]</a>. If the base valuation exceeded $B_1$, the transferred nonzero valuation would also exceed $B_1$, a contradiction. The pivot valuation affects the required precision and dimension, but not the transferred upper bound. ◻

</details>

<a id="sec:common-finite-models"></a>
#### Finite cochain models

The arithmetic applications also need finite free complexes that retain maps to the original cochains. The following algebraic construction provides these models and transports their comparison diagrams. It applies before any determinant coordinate is chosen.

<a id="stmt-lem-h-finite-models"></a>
<div id="lem:h:finite-models" class="lemma">

**Lemma 68** (Finite Artin models). *<span id="rl:finite-model" label="rl:finite-model"></span> Let $(A,\mathfrak m,k)$ be an Artin local ring, and let $D$ be a complex of flat $A$-modules. Suppose $H^*(D\otimes_A k)$ is finite dimensional and supported in $[a,b]$. There is a bounded finite free complex $C$, with $$\operatorname{rank}_A C^j=\dim_k H^j(D\otimes_A k),$$ and a strong deformation retraction $$i:C\longrightarrow D,\qquad p:D\longrightarrow C,\qquad
 pi=1,\qquad 1-ip=dh+hd.$$ Thus maps to the original complex, as well as maps between finite models, are available. Any fixed finite collection of chain maps, homotopies, triangles, and perfect pairings can be transported to these models.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-h-finite-models"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-h-finite-models</summary>

*Proof.* Flat modules over an Artin local ring are free, including modules of infinite rank. Here is a useful version of the argument. Lift a basis of $M/\mathfrak
mM$ to a flat module $M$, and map the corresponding free module to $M$. Its cokernel is zero because $\mathfrak m$ is nilpotent. Flatness shows that the kernel has zero reduction, and nilpotence again makes the kernel zero.

Split the residual complex as its cohomology, with zero differential, plus contractible two-term disks. Lift all the graded bases. These lifts are graded isomorphisms: an inverse modulo $\mathfrak m$ lifts to an inverse by a finite geometric series. Let $d_0$ be the lifted disk differential and write $d=d_0+\epsilon$. All coefficients of $\epsilon$ belong to $\mathfrak m$. For the disk contraction $(i_0,p_0,h_0)$, arrange $h_0^2=h_0i_0=p_0h_0=0$ and $1-i_0p_0=d_0h_0+h_0d_0$. The operators $1+h_0\epsilon$ and $1+\epsilon h_0$ have finite geometric inverses. The homological perturbation lemma gives explicit contraction maps; we record the formulas to retain their compatibility with the arithmetic diagrams (Crainic 2004, secs. 2.2–2.4 and 3.2) <a id="pm-cite-82"></a>[[Crainic2004](#ref-Crainic2004)]. The perturbation identities give the differential $$d_C=p_0\epsilon(1+h_0\epsilon)^{-1}i_0$$ on the lifted residual cohomology, and give $$i=(1+h_0\epsilon)^{-1}i_0,\quad
 p=p_0(1+\epsilon h_0)^{-1},\quad
 h=h_0(1+\epsilon h_0)^{-1}.$$ Substitution, using $(d_0+\epsilon)^2=0$, proves the asserted contraction identities. These calculations are valid for infinite disk sums: each operator is a module homomorphism and every geometric series terminates at the nilpotence exponent of $\mathfrak m$.

Transport a map $f$ as $p'fi$, retaining the contraction homotopies for compositions. A quasi-isomorphism between bounded free complexes has a contractible cone and a homotopy inverse. This transports finite diagrams, including triangles and perfect dualities. ◻

</details>

<a id="sec:cy:interpolation"></a>
### Cyclotomic interpolation at analytic rank zero

The cyclotomic argument transfers a nonzero central value across a binary family. Its input is a uniform upper bound for the normalized valuations at every nonzero vertex. Its output is nonvanishing at a corank-zero base. The class used here is Kato’s zeta class, and the additional variable is the real cyclotomic $\mathbb Z_2$-extension of $\mathbb Q$.

Retain $T=T_2(E)$ and put $V_2=T\otimes_{\mathbb Z_2}\mathbb Q_2$. The local weights, finite Sha lengths and period normalization are those of Section <a href="#sec:preliminaries" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:preliminaries">2</a>, and $D(h)$ is defined in Equation <a href="#eq:transfer-normalized-value" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:transfer-normalized-value">[eq:transfer-normalized-value]</a>. We prove Theorems <a href="#thm:cyclotomic-bound" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:cyclotomic-bound">12</a> and <a href="#thm:cyclotomic-interpolation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:cyclotomic-interpolation">8</a> with their stated distinction between the uniform specialization error and the dimension threshold for a fixed base.

For a two-dimensional representation over $\mathbb F_2$, reducibility is equivalent to being an extension of trivial modules. These are therefore the two exhaustive residual cases. The proof has three stages: construct a class in a fixed integral lattice, identify its central determinant, and apply the binary congruences. Residual reducibility makes the cyclotomic complex free after localization at $(2)$; the irreducible case instead uses the bounded clearing factor of Lemma <a href="#lem:h:pivot-clearing" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:h:pivot-clearing">65</a>.

<a id="pm-h-67"></a>
#### The positive cyclotomic complex

At the coefficient prime $2$, the real place must be included in the cochain construction. The positive complex defined below removes the real cochains and retains their connecting invariant line. We will combine this fixed line with the zeta class to form the determinant whose central value detects nonvanishing at a corank-zero base.

Put $$\Gamma=\mathop{\mathrm{Gal}}(\mathbb Q_\infty/\mathbb Q),\qquad
 \Lambda=\mathbb Z_2[[\Gamma]]=\mathbb Z_2[[t]],\qquad
 \mathcal O=\widehat{\Lambda_{(2)}},\qquad
 \Omega=\mathcal O/2\mathcal O=\mathbb F_2((t)),$$ where a generator of $\Gamma$ corresponds to $1+t$. The completion is $2$-adic. An element of $\mathcal O$ has a finite negative Laurent part modulo every $2^M$, but need not have a value at $t=0$. Every central evaluation below is made on a rational Iwasawa class or on an element of $\Lambda[1/2]$ before extending coefficients to $\mathcal O$.

For a family in Equation <a href="#eq:cy:cube" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:cy:cube">[eq:cy:cube]</a>, let $G=(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)^b$ have characters indexed by $x\in\mathbb F_2^b$, and let $\psi:G_{\mathbb Q}\to G$ be its universal quadratic character: evaluation at $x$ is $\chi_{h_x/h_0}$. Put $$R=\Lambda[G],\qquad
 \mathbb T=T\otimes_{\mathbb Z _2}R,$$ with the fixed twist $\chi_{h_0}$, the universal twist $\psi$, and the inverse cyclotomic action. One may replace $G$ by the actual image of $\psi$ and subsequently extend scalars. In a family in Theorem <a href="#thm:cyclotomic-interpolation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:cyclotomic-interpolation">8</a>, a nonzero character trivial on that image already gives the conclusion directly.

<a id="eq:cy:positive-complex"></a>
Let $S$ be the set of primes dividing $2N h_0\prod_{q\in\mathcal Q}q$. For $q\in\mathcal Q$, write $g_q\in G$ for its inertia element, so $x(g_q)=(-1)^{\lambda_q(x)}$. Use continuous cochains with their completed coefficient topology, and set $$\label{eq:cy:positive-complex}
 C_S^+(\mathbb T)=
 \operatorname{Cone}\bigl(R\Gamma(G_{\mathbb Q,S},\mathbb T)
              \longrightarrow R\Gamma(\mathbb R,\mathbb T)\bigr)[-1].$$ The real complex here uses ordinary cochains in nonnegative degrees. There are no imposed local conditions at the finite places. We write $C_S(\mathbb T)=R\Gamma(G_{\mathbb Q,S},\mathbb T)$ for the unmodified complex. Throughout this section, *ordinary global cohomology* means this unmodified cohomology; it imposes no ordinary-reduction hypothesis at $2$.

<a id="stmt-lem-cy-positive-model"></a>
<div id="lem:cy:positive-model" class="lemma">

**Lemma 69**. *The complex in Equation <a href="#eq:cy:positive-complex" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:cy:positive-complex">[eq:cy:positive-complex]</a> is perfect over $R$ and computes derived coefficient specializations. There is a class $a\in H^1(C_S^+(\mathbb T))$ whose rational span is the real-place summand. Its integral index in that summand depends only on $E$ and the fixed real sign.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-cy-positive-model"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-cy-positive-model</summary>

*Proof.* Here are the finiteness and coefficient issues in the use of global cochains. For a finite coefficient quotient of $R$, continuous cochains are filtered unions of finite products of free coefficient modules. Refinement of finite partitions makes these modules flat; over an Artin local coefficient ring they are free. For finite residual coefficients, global cohomology is finite in each degree, and restriction to the real places is an isomorphism in degrees greater than two, by the real-place clause of global duality (Nekovář 2006, vol. 310, sec. 5.7.1.7) <a id="pm-cite-83"></a>[[Nekovar2006](#ref-Nekovar2006)]. Thus the residual fiber has bounded amplitude and finite-dimensional cohomology. The same amplitude bound holds for every finite coefficient module, by a composition series and the cohomology long exact sequence.

This gives a bounded finite free model as follows. Over the residue field split off the acyclic disks, leaving its finitely many cohomology spaces. Lift each invertible disk differential over an Artin coefficient quotient and cancel it. Invertibility of a lifted inverse follows from nilpotence of the maximal ideal. Equivalently one can perform this on a free resolution; a minimal free model cannot have an additional term whose reduction has zero cohomology, because its residual differential is zero. Hence the remaining ranks are the finite residual ranks and are bounded independently of the coefficient quotient. Minimal models identified by a homotopy equivalence over an Artin local ring are isomorphic. Lifting their changes of basis therefore makes these models compatible along $R/\mathfrak m^n$. Taking the inverse limit gives a bounded finite free model over $R$. The cochain construction with finite free coefficients and the same cancellation also proves derived base change. This is a fixed-$S$ argument; it does not assert uniform bounds on the number of generators as $S$ varies.

All the characters of the family have the same real sign, so the action at the real place is the fixed action on $T\chi_{h_0}$ extended to $R$. Choose a nonzero vector in its integral invariant line. Its connecting image in the fiber is $a$. There are no global invariant vectors in the rational elliptic representation, and consequently this connecting map is injective rationally. The choice and its index are fixed. Notice also that $H^1(\mathbb R,\mathbb T)$ is killed by $2$; thus twice any ordinary cohomology class lifts to the positive complex. The real-place global duality input is its corrected form at $2$ (Nekovář 2006, vol. 310, secs. 5.7.1–5.7.5) <a id="pm-cite-84"></a>[[Nekovar2006](#ref-Nekovar2006)]; the invariant line and the lifting assertion follow from the long exact sequence of this ordinary-real cone. Complete real Tate cochains, used in the duality formulation, become acyclic after inverting $2$ and would not retain this invariant line. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-68"></a>
#### Fixed-form zeta classes and the integral coefficient map

To control denominators as the tame support grows, we construct every class in the cohomological lattice of one fixed modular form. Let $f$ be the fixed weight-two form of $E$, and choose its fixed integral cohomological lattice, with the Tate twist making its rational representation $V_2$. Kato’s classes (8.1.2)–(8.1.3), for a fixed symbol $\xi\in\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)$, exist for arbitrary $m$ and any $S$ containing the prime factors of $mN$. The trace in Section 8.9 is a homomorphism into the lattice $$\mathbb Z _2[\operatorname{Gal}(\mathbb Q(\mu_m)/\mathbb Q)]
       \otimes V_{2,\mathbb Z _2}(Y_1(N))(1).$$ Section 8.11 then projects to the lattice of the fixed form. Proposition 8.12 supplies its norm relations. These assertions hold at the coefficient prime $2$ (Kato 2004, secs. 5.1, 8.1, 8.9–8.12) <a id="pm-cite-85"></a>[[Kato2004](#ref-Kato2004)]. In particular, the auxiliary modular-curve level used to define a trace does not become the level of the projected newform.

Choose an isomorphism of the resulting fixed rational representation with $V_2$. A single power $2^{c_E}$ sends its integral lattice into $T$. Choose fixed symbols with nonzero projections on the required period lines; their existence and the construction with both signs are made explicit in (Kato 2004, sec. 13.6 and 13.9) <a id="pm-cite-86"></a>[[Kato2004](#ref-Kato2004)]. Taking a fixed linear combination, if needed, costs another fixed denominator.

<a id="eq:cy:coefficient-map"></a>
The following integral coefficient map encodes the binary family. Choose $m=|h_0|\prod_{q\in\mathcal Q}q$, which is odd and divisible by the conductors of all the tame characters in the family, including $\chi_{h_0}$. At a sufficiently large cyclotomic level write $A_{m,n}=\mathop{\mathrm{Gal}}(\mathbb Q(\mu_{m2^n})/\mathbb Q)$ and let $\Gamma_n$ be its quotient in the real cyclotomic tower. Shapiro identifies the cohomology of the cyclotomic field with global cohomology with induced group-ring coefficients. Push the class along the ring homomorphism $$\label{eq:cy:coefficient-map}
 \mathbb Z _2[A_{m,n}]\longrightarrow
       \mathbb Z _2[\Gamma_n\times G],\qquad
 [\sigma]\longmapsto
       \chi_{h_0}(\sigma)[\sigma|_{\Gamma_n}][\psi(\sigma)].$$ Use inverse actions on both sides if this is required by the chosen Shapiro convention. This is a homomorphism of integral coefficient modules and acts on actual cohomology classes. It requires neither division by $|G|$ nor surjectivity of a cohomological specialization map. The prime $2$ belongs to the fixed omitted support, so Proposition 8.12 gives exact norm compatibility as $n$ increases. The pushed classes therefore give an integral smoothed Iwasawa class with coefficients in $\mathbb T$, up to the single fixed power $2^{c_E}$.

We have placed all character constituents in the lattice of the same modular form. The next normalization issue is smoothing: its removal must be harmless both after localization at $(2)$ and at the central value $t=0$. These are distinct requirements, checked next.

We next remove smoothing. In weight two and with $r=r'=1$, its factors are <a id="eq:cy:smoothing"></a>$$\label{eq:cy:smoothing}
 (c^2-c\sigma_c)(d^2-d\sigma_d).$$ This is the specialization of (Kato 2004, Theorem 6.6 and (4.2.4)) <a id="pm-cite-87"></a>[[Kato2004](#ref-Kato2004)]. Choose a fixed $e\geq\max(2,v_2(N))$, increasing it to accommodate the finitely many fixed symbol levels. The Chinese remainder theorem permits $c,d>1$, prime to $6Nm$, such that $$c,d\equiv1\pmod{3N_{\mathrm{odd}}m},\qquad
 c,d\equiv1+2^e\pmod{2^{e+1}}.$$ Their tame actions in <a href="#eq:cy:coefficient-map" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:cy:coefficient-map">[eq:cy:coefficient-map]</a> are trivial. If $\sigma_c$ acts in $\Gamma$ as $(1+t)^{\kappa(c)}$, then $v_2(\kappa(c))=e-2$. Modulo the maximal ideal of $\mathcal O[G]$ its smoothing factor is $$1-(1+t)^{\kappa(c)}\ne0\quad\hbox{in }\mathbb F _2((t)).$$ It is therefore a unit in $\mathcal O[G]$. Its central value is $c(c-1)$, of valuation exactly $e$. The same statements hold for $d$ and for inverse-translate conventions. Thus unsmoothing introduces neither a $2$-adic denominator at $(2)$ nor a growing central denominator. The integers $c,d$ vary with $m$; the congruences fix the needed valuations, not their exact cyclotomic group elements.

<a id="eq:cy:reciprocity-center"></a>
Denote the resulting rational ordinary class by $z_S$. Kato (2004, Theorem 9.7) applies to $k=2,r=r'=1$. In the character constituent $x$, its central reciprocity formula reads $$\label{eq:cy:reciprocity-center}
 v_2\bigl(\exp_2^*z_{S,x}(0)\bigr)
 =v_2(\mathcal L(h_x))+
  \sum_{\substack{q\in\mathcal Q\,,\ q\nmid h_x}}
       v_2\bigl(\#E^{(h_x)}(\mathbb F _q)\bigr)+O_E(1)$$ when the value is nonzero, and a zero central value gives a zero dual exponential. The omitted primes dividing $2N$ are included in the error. To check the normalization, the character sum in <a href="#eq:cy:coefficient-map" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:cy:coefficient-map">[eq:cy:coefficient-map]</a> is the unnormalized sum, as in Kato’s trace. Its tame quadratic Gauss sum supplies $\sqrt{|h_x|}$ up to a root of unity. Tame conductors and their Gauss sums are $2$-adic units. The period vector is the fixed symbol vector of $f$. More explicitly, in the required sign line write the period represented by $\delta(f,1,\xi)^{\pm}$ as $c_\xi^{\pm}\Omega_E^{\pm}$. The nonzero scalar $c_\xi^{\pm}$ is fixed: the character-sum formula of (Kato 2004, Theorem 6.6) <a id="pm-cite-88"></a>[[Kato2004](#ref-Kato2004)] uses this same $\delta(f,1,\xi)^{\pm}$ for every tame character. The tame character enters through its $L$-value and Gauss sum, not through a newly chosen period vector. The comparison with the minimal differential of $E^{(h_x)}$ at $2$ has bounded valuation, because there are only finitely many local twisting classes there. At a good unused prime the omitted factor is $$1-\frac{a_q(E)\chi_{h_x}(\operatorname{Fr}_q)}q+\frac1q
       =\frac{\#E^{(h_x)}(\mathbb F _q)}q;$$ at a good ramified prime the local $L$-factor is $1$. These account for every varying factor in <a href="#eq:cy:reciprocity-center" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:cy:reciprocity-center">[eq:cy:reciprocity-center]</a>.

<a id="pm-h-69"></a>
#### Rational divisibility and the local Euler corrections

We now exclude poles of the zeta determinant away from $(2)$ and account for every omitted Euler factor. Write $A=\Lambda[1/2]$. Theorem 12.5(3) of (Kato 2004) <a id="pm-cite-89"></a>[[Kato2004](#ref-Kato2004)] is a height-one divisibility over $A$; its possible local $H^2$ correction comes from the arithmetic place $2$. It need not be supported at the Iwasawa ideal $(2)$. The global groups there use $j_*$ outside that prime. The stronger integral assertion of Theorem 12.5(4) is not used. For a non-CM elliptic curve the characteristic-zero image condition is supplied by the open image theorem, independently of the residual image. For CM the required rational statement at every prime, including $2$, is supplied by (A. A. Burungale and Tian 2026, Theorem 2.6 and Remark 2.7) <a id="pm-cite-90"></a>[[BurungaleTian2026](#ref-BurungaleTian2026)]. Neither statement asserts uniform integrality in a quadratic group ring. The rational cohomology statements, including Kato (2004, Theorem 12.4) <a id="pm-cite-91"></a>[[Kato2004](#ref-Kato2004)], give rank one in degree one and torsion in degree two, with no other positive cohomological rank. The real-place modification adds its invariant line. Hence every generic character constituent of the positive complex has rank two in degree one and no other positive rank.

<a id="eq:cy:local-block"></a>
<a id="eq:cy:local-sequence"></a>
Fix a character constituent $h$ and write $V_h=V_2\chi_h$. Let $C_{j_*}$ be the rational Iwasawa complex in Kato’s formulation and $C_S$ the rational full global complex. At an odd prime put $$W_q=H^1(I_q,V_h).$$ The localization triangle has local cone $$\label{eq:cy:local-block}
 Q_q=R\Gamma\bigl(G_{\mathbb F _q},
                   W_q\otimes A(\Gamma^\iota)\bigr)[-1]
   =\left[W_q\otimes A
       \xrightarrow{\ 1-\gamma_q\operatorname{Fr}_{W_q}\ }
             W_q\otimes A\right]$$ in degrees one and two. Here $\gamma_q$ denotes the scalar cyclotomic Frobenius in the chosen convention. Its exponent is nonzero. Consequently $D_q=\det(1-\gamma_q\operatorname{Fr}_{W_q})$ is a nonzero element of $A$, and the map in <a href="#eq:cy:local-block" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:cy:local-block">[eq:cy:local-block]</a> is injective. This remains true after localization at a height-one prime dividing $D_q$: localization does not mean reduction modulo that prime. Thus $$H^1(Q_q)=0,\qquad
 \operatorname{length}_{A_{\mathfrak p}}H^2(Q_q)_{\mathfrak p}
       =v_{\mathfrak p}(D_q).$$ The long exact sequence gives $$\label{eq:cy:local-sequence}
 \begin{gathered}
 H^1(C_{j_*})\simeq H^1(C_S),\\
 0\longrightarrow H^2(C_{j_*})\longrightarrow H^2(C_S)
       \longrightarrow\bigoplus_{q\in S\setminus\{2\}}H^2(Q_q)
       \longrightarrow H^3(C_{j_*}).
 \end{gathered}$$ In particular, the length of $H^2(C_S)$ is at most the length of $H^2(C_{j_*})$ plus the sum of the local lengths. No assertion that $H^3(C_{j_*})$ vanishes is required here.

<a id="eq:cy:local-euler"></a>
At a good unused prime, $W_q=V_h(-1)$, so, on including the quadratic Frobenius sign in $Z$, $$\label{eq:cy:local-euler}
 D_q=P_q(Z),\qquad P_q(Z)=1-\frac{a_q(E)}q Z+\frac1q Z^2.$$ At a good active prime, inertia acts by $-1$ on $V_h$. Its rational inertia cohomology is zero, so $W_q=0$ and $D_q=1$.

At fixed bad primes the general expression is $H^1(I_q,V_h)$ in <a href="#eq:cy:local-block" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:cy:local-block">[eq:cy:local-block]</a>. Replacing it indiscriminately by $V_h^{I_q}(-1)$ would be incorrect. For example, at split multiplicative reduction, $$V_h^{I_q}=\mathbb Q _2(1),\qquad
 H^1(I_q,V_h)=\mathbb Q _2(-1),$$ and the correct determinant is $1-\gamma_q/q$, with nonzero central value. The incorrect replacement would give $1-\gamma_q$. In general $D_q(0)\ne0$ follows from local duality and the Weil pairing: $H^2(\mathbb Q _q,V_h)=H^0(\mathbb Q _q,V_h)^*=0$, since elliptic torsion over a local field is finite. The fixed bad-prime corrections therefore have nonzero central values for every reduction type.

Let $z_{\mathrm{BK},h}$ denote a generator of the rational Kato zeta line in its real cyclotomic component. The rational comparison with the fixed-form class constructed above is made only after taking the character constituent. Both global Iwasawa $H^1$ modules have rank one. Their reciprocity laws at cyclotomic finite-order characters agree up to the omitted Euler factors, a nonzero constant, and a group-like unit. This follows by coprime Gauss-sum factorization and the fixed period comparison; restricting conductor exponents to either fixed parity removes any factor $\chi_h(2)^n$. Infinitely many of these tests have nonzero central value by cyclotomic nonvanishing, as used in (Kato 2004, Theorem 13.5(2)) <a id="pm-cite-92"></a>[[Kato2004](#ref-Kato2004)]. After clearing the finitely many denominators of the scalar ratio, the difference is a power series vanishing at infinitely many finite-order characters. Weierstrass preparation forces that difference to be zero. This proves the generic comparison without identifying the integral lattices of varying twisted newforms. Its nonzero scalar in $\mathbb Q _2$ may depend on $h$ and need not have a uniformly bounded $2$-valuation: every such scalar is a unit of $A$ and does not affect height-one divisibility over $A$. The uniform integral and central bounds instead concern the actual fixed-form class and the fixed period vector in <a href="#eq:cy:reciprocity-center" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:cy:reciprocity-center">[eq:cy:reciprocity-center]</a>.

Equations <a href="#eq:cy:local-sequence" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:cy:local-sequence">[eq:cy:local-sequence]</a>–<a href="#eq:cy:local-euler" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:cy:local-euler">[eq:cy:local-euler]</a> now show exactly how the imprimitive factors enter divisibility. At any height-one $\mathfrak p$ of $A$, enlarging the global complex increases its degree-two length by at most $\sum_qv_{\mathfrak p}(D_q)$, whereas multiplying the rank-one zeta generator by $\prod_qD_q$ adds exactly that quantity to its index. To cover Kato’s coefficient-prime correction, multiply the class also by a fixed element $F_2\in\Lambda$ divisible over $A$ by the characteristic ideal of the relevant local $H^2_{\mathrm{Iw}}$. It may be chosen with $F_2(0)\ne0$. Indeed derived local control gives $$H^2_{\mathrm{Iw}}(\mathbb Q _2,T\chi_h)_\Gamma\otimes\mathbb Q _2
       =H^2(\mathbb Q _2,V_h)=0,$$ so the characteristic ideal has no factor $t$. Local twisting classes at $2$ are fixed, and one element covers their finite set.

<a id="eq:cy:divisibility"></a>
Likewise any additional fixed Euler factors in the rational comparison can be cleared by a fixed product with nonzero central value, using the actual blocks <a href="#eq:cy:local-block" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:cy:local-block">[eq:cy:local-block]</a>. Denote the total fixed multiplier by $F_E$. Multiplying by it only changes the fixed constants in <a href="#eq:cy:reciprocity-center" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:cy:reciprocity-center">[eq:cy:reciprocity-center]</a> and the integrality bound. For the corrected class, still written $z_S$, we have at every height-one $\mathfrak p$ of $A$ $$\label{eq:cy:divisibility}
 \operatorname{length}_{A_{\mathfrak p}}H^2(C_S)_{\mathfrak p}
 \leq
 \operatorname{length}_{A_{\mathfrak p}}
       \bigl(H^1(C_S)/Az_{S,h}\bigr)_{\mathfrak p}.$$

There is an integral convention check for the varying unused primes. In $\mathcal O[G]$, both $P_q(Z)$ and $Z^2P_q(Z^{-1})$ are units: their reductions are nonzero polynomials evaluated at the nonconstant cyclotomic Frobenius. The identity $$P_q(Z)-Z^2P_q(Z^{-1})=\frac{q-1}{q}(1-Z^2)$$ shows that their ratio $r_q$ is $1$ modulo $2$. If $g_q$ is the universal inertia element, then <a id="eq:cy:reciprocal-correction"></a>$$\label{eq:cy:reciprocal-correction}
 U_q=1+\frac{r_q-1}{2}(1+g_q)\in\mathcal O[G]^\times$$ is integral. At an active character it is $1$; at an unused character it is $r_q$. Its unused central value is $1$, since $Z=\pm1$ there. Thus inverse Frobenius conventions can be reconciled before character evaluation, without a denominator for each prime. Products of these units have the same property. The resulting rational character coordinates have the Euler convention in <a href="#eq:cy:divisibility" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:cy:divisibility">[eq:cy:divisibility]</a>.

<a id="stmt-lem-cy-kato-class"></a>
<div id="lem:cy:kato-class" class="lemma">

**Lemma 70** (Fixed-lattice zeta class). *For every binary family and its ramification set $S$, the corrected class $z_S$ satisfies the central reciprocity formula <a href="#eq:cy:reciprocity-center" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:cy:reciprocity-center">[eq:cy:reciprocity-center]</a> and the rational divisibility <a href="#eq:cy:divisibility" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:cy:divisibility">[eq:cy:divisibility]</a>. For some $c_E\ge0$ depending only on $E$, $$2^{c_E}z_S\in
 H^1\!\left(C_S(\mathbb T)\otimes_R^{\mathbf L}\mathcal O[G]\right).$$ The same exponent works for all $S$, binary families, and fixed factors $h_0$ with the specified local classes. Here the displayed cohomology is derived scalar extension of the Iwasawa complex.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-cy-kato-class"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-cy-kato-class</summary>

*Proof.* The integral coefficient map uses the fixed-form lattice and no character averages. Unsmoothing and every varying-prime convention correction are units over $\mathcal O[G]$. The multiplier $F_E$ is fixed. The preceding construction therefore gives the displayed assertion with a fixed exponent, as well as the two stated comparison formulas. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-70"></a>
#### The determinant and its central specialization

The zeta class now has two controls: rational divisibility will exclude poles of its determinant coordinate away from $(2)$, and the fixed lattice bounds the class’s integral denominator at $(2)$. We next identify its determinant coordinate at $t=0$. This is the step that converts those cohomological controls into a statement about $D(h)$.

<a id="eq:cy:rational-integrality"></a>
Choose a basis of the invertible $R$-module $\det_R^{-1}C_S^+(\mathbb T)$; $R$ is local, so such a basis exists. Lift $2z_S$ to rational positive cohomology and take its wedge with $a$. The factor $2$ is fixed, and two lifts differ by a real-place class, which does not change this wedge. Let $u$ be its generic determinant coordinate, including the fixed multiplier $F_E$ above. The real-place summand introduces no height-one torsion over $A$. Thus <a href="#eq:cy:divisibility" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:cy:divisibility">[eq:cy:divisibility]</a> says that $u_x$ has no pole at any height-one prime of $\Lambda$ except possibly $(2)$. Since $\Lambda$ is normal, $$\label{eq:cy:rational-integrality}
 u_x\in\Lambda[1/2]\qquad\hbox{for every }x.$$ The two cycles have a common denominator bounded by a fixed power $2^{C_{\mathrm{int}}}$ after extension to $\mathcal O[G]$. This follows from Lemma <a href="#lem:cy:kato-class" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:cy:kato-class">70</a> and the factor $2$ needed for the lift.

<a id="stmt-prop-cy-specialization"></a>
<div id="prop:cy:specialization" class="proposition">

<a id="eq:cy:determinant-center"></a>
**Proposition 71** (Central determinant formula). *There is a constant $C_{\mathrm{loc}}$, depending only on the fixed curve and local classes, with the following property. Suppose $c_2(E^{(h_x)})=0$. If $L(E^{(h_x)},1)=0$, then $u_x(0)=0$; if $L(E^{(h_x)},1)\ne0$, then $$\label{eq:cy:determinant-center}
 \bigl|v_2(u_x(0))-D(h_x)\bigr|\leq C_{\mathrm{loc}}.$$ The rational positive complex at $t=0$ has cohomology only in degree one, of dimension two, so these are specializations of the same determinant.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-prop-cy-specialization"><summary>Proof of stmt-prop-cy-specialization</summary>

*Proof.* Abbreviate $T_h=T_2E^{(h_x)}$ and $A_h=E^{(h_x)}[2^\infty]$. Use the integral Kummer subgroup $$K_v=\operatorname{im}\bigl(E^{(h_x)}(\mathbb Q _v)^{\wedge}_2
                              \longrightarrow H^1(\mathbb Q _v,T_h)\bigr)$$ at every finite place. For $v\ne2$ it is all of $H^1(\mathbb Q _v,T_h)$. One way to see this integrally is the inverse-limit Kummer exact sequence: its quotient is $T_2H^1(\mathbb Q _v,E^{(h_x)})$, which is zero because local Tate duality identifies the $2$-primary local Weil–Châtelet group with the dual of the finite $2$-completion of the local point group. At $2$ the quotient $$L_2=H^1(\mathbb Q _2,T_h)/K_2$$ is a free rank-one $\mathbb Z _2$-module. The same Kummer sequence and local Tate duality identify it with the $\mathbb Z _2$-dual of the free part of $E^{(h_x)}(\mathbb Q _2)^{\wedge}_2$.

The dual exponential identifies $L_2\otimes\mathbb Q _2$ with the one-dimensional de Rham target. To specify its integral comparison, put $$B_2=E^{(h_x)}(\mathbb Q _2)^{\wedge}_2/\mathrm{tors}$$ and choose a minimal differential $\omega_h$. The Bloch–Kato exponential agrees with the Kummer image of the classical elliptic exponential, which is the inverse of the formal logarithm on a sufficiently small open subgroup. This comparison holds for every reduction type (Bloch and Kato 1990, Definition 3.10 and Example 3.11) <a id="pm-cite-93"></a>[[BlochKato1990](#ref-BlochKato1990)]. The dual exponential is the adjoint of that exponential under local Tate duality (Berger 2003, sec. II and Proposition II.5) <a id="pm-cite-94"></a>[[Berger2003](#ref-Berger2003)]. Extend the formal logarithm to the rationalized local point group and write $\log_{\omega_h}(B_2)=\lambda_h\mathbb Z _2$. The integral identification $L_2=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z _2}(B_2,\mathbb Z _2)$ then gives $$\exp_2^*(L_2)=\lambda_h^{-1}\mathbb Z _2\omega_h,$$ using the Weil-pairing identification of the de Rham target with $\mathbb Q _2\omega_h$. Thus the relative lattice valuation is fixed by the local curve and differential. Since only finitely many local twist classes occur, these valuations are uniformly bounded.

The assumption on the Selmer corank implies that the compact finite Selmer group is torsion and that the discrete finite Selmer group has length $s(h_x)$. Rational Poitou–Tate consequently identifies ordinary global $H^1$ with the singular line at $2$, and gives ordinary global $H^2=0$ rationally. Adding the real invariant line gives the claimed dimension two in degree one. This equals the generic rank, so derived base change of the perfect complex specializes its determinant without a change of rational cohomological rank.

<a id="eq:cy:pt-length"></a>
Here is the integral length calculation. Let $J$ be the image of the free part of global $H^1(G_{\mathbb Q,S},T_h)$ in $L_2$, and put $i=\operatorname{length}(L_2/J)$. The compact/discrete Poitou–Tate sequence for the mutually orthogonal Kummer conditions contains $$\begin{aligned}
 0\longrightarrow L_2/J
 &\longrightarrow \operatorname{Sel}_{2^\infty}(E^{(h_x)}/\mathbb Q)^\vee
 \longrightarrow H^2(G_{\mathbb Q,S},T_h)\\
 &\longrightarrow \bigoplus_{q\in S}H^2(\mathbb Q _q,T_h)
 \longrightarrow H^0(\mathbb Q,A_h)^\vee\longrightarrow0,
\end{aligned}$$ with the usual real Tate-cohomology terms inserted. Those terms are killed by $2$ and have dimensions bounded by the fixed dimension of $T$. Taking lengths and using local duality gives $$\label{eq:cy:pt-length}
 \operatorname{length}H^2(G_{\mathbb Q,S},T_h)
   =s(h_x)-i+\sum_{q\in S}\operatorname{length}H^0(\mathbb Q _q,A_h)
      +O_E(1).$$ This sequence follows from integral Poitou–Tate duality with the finite Kummer conditions and the real Tate-cohomology correction (Nekovář 2006, vol. 310, secs. 5.7.1.6, 5.7.4–5.7.5 and 6.9.1) <a id="pm-cite-95"></a>[[Nekovar2006](#ref-Nekovar2006)]. The free real invariant line is already accounted for by $a$; only the bounded real torsion terms enter the error above. No unramified condition replaces the Kummer condition at a bad prime. Global torsion is bounded by its injection into $E^{(h_x)}(\mathbb Q _2)[2^\infty]$, whose order is bounded by the fixed local twisting classes. The finite terms at $2$ and at fixed bad primes are bounded for the same reason. Passing between ordinary and positive cohomology changes only these bounded real and global torsion terms.

Suppose first that the central value is nonzero. The coordinate of $z_{S,x}(0)$ in the free global line has valuation $$v_2(\exp_2^*z_{S,x}(0))-i+O_E(1).$$ For the inverse determinant, torsion in degree two subtracts its length and torsion in degree one adds its length. This sign can be checked on the complex $[\mathbb Z _2\xrightarrow{2^a}\mathbb Z _2]$ in degrees one and two: its inverse determinant lattice maps to $2^a\mathbb Z _2$ in the rational determinant. A vector’s coordinate thus loses $a$. Using <a href="#eq:cy:pt-length" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:cy:pt-length">[eq:cy:pt-length]</a>, the two appearances of $i$ cancel, leaving $$v_2(u_x(0))=
 v_2(\exp_2^*z_{S,x}(0))-s(h_x)
       -\sum_{q\in S}\operatorname{length}H^0(\mathbb Q _q,A_h)+O_E(1).$$

At an active good prime, quadratic inertia acts by $-1$ on the Tate module. Its invariants on $A_h$ are therefore exactly $E[2]$, and taking Frobenius invariants gives length $t_q$. At an unused good prime, reduction identifies the local $2$-primary torsion with $E^{(h_x)}(\mathbb F _q)[2^\infty]$, of length $v_2(\#E^{(h_x)}(\mathbb F _q))$. These unused terms cancel exactly those in <a href="#eq:cy:reciprocity-center" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:cy:reciprocity-center">[eq:cy:reciprocity-center]</a>. The active terms, including the primes of $h_0$, sum to $2w(h_x)$. All other terms have already been bounded independently of the growing support. This proves <a href="#eq:cy:determinant-center" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:cy:determinant-center">[eq:cy:determinant-center]</a>.

If the central value is zero, reciprocity makes the dual exponential zero. The rational ordinary specialization then satisfies the finite condition at $2$, and it satisfies the finite conditions elsewhere automatically. It lies in the rational finite Selmer group, which is zero. Its wedge with the real-place class is therefore zero. The constant-rank determinant specialization proves $u_x(0)=0$. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-71"></a>
#### Residual freeness and the lower bound

The central formula expresses $D(h)$ through the determinant valuation. When the residual representation is an extension of trivial modules, we can bound that valuation directly: the positive complex becomes a free rank-two module in degree one after extension to $\mathcal O[G]$. The fixed-lattice class then supplies the lower bound without any loss from a growing ramification support.

<a id="stmt-lem-cy-residual-free"></a>
<div id="lem:cy:residual-free" class="lemma">

**Lemma 72** (Residual concentration). *If $E[2]$ is an extension of two trivial $\mathbb F_2$-modules, then there is an isomorphism in the derived category $$C_S^+(\mathbb T)\otimes_R\mathcal O[G]
       \simeq \mathcal O[G]^2[-1].$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-cy-residual-free"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-cy-residual-free</summary>

*Proof.* The ring $\mathcal O[G]$ is local, with residue field $\Omega$ obtained by setting $2=0$ and every $g=1$. Thus the quadratic characters disappear. Since $E[2]$ has a filtration with trivial factors, it is enough first to compute the positive residual complex for the trivial representation.

Let $K_n$ be the real cyclotomic layer of degree $d_n=2^n$. The number of finite primes of $K_n$ above a fixed $S$ is bounded with $n$: at $2$ there is total ramification, and the Frobenius of each fixed odd prime has nonzero image in $\Gamma$. The $2$-ranks of the class groups of $K_n$ are also bounded. Let $X$ be the inverse limit, under norm maps, of their $2$-primary class groups. The unique prime above $2$ is totally ramified in this tower, so class-field-theoretic control gives $$X_{\Gamma^{2^n}}\simeq\mathop{\mathrm{Cl}}(K_n)[2^\infty]$$ (Sharifi n.d., Proposition 3.2.11 and Remark 3.2.12). Ferrero–Washington gives $\mu(X)=0$ for this abelian tower (Ferrero and Washington 1979) <a id="pm-cite-96"></a>[[FerreroWashington1979](#ref-FerreroWashington1979)]. The Iwasawa structure theorem then makes $X$ finitely generated over $\mathbb Z _2$, so all its coinvariants have uniformly bounded $2$-rank. Passing to the quotient $S$-class groups preserves this upper bound.

The signature map of units in $K_n$ is surjective. For $n\geq1$, let $\zeta$ be a primitive $2^{n+2}$th root and put $\epsilon=1+\zeta+\zeta^{-1}$. If $f_1(X)=X^2-2$ and $f_{n+1}(X)=f_n(X^2-2)$, then $f_n$ is the minimal polynomial of $\zeta+\zeta^{-1}$ and $f_n(-1)=-1$. Hence $N_{K_n/\mathbb Q}(\epsilon)=-1$. Its signature vector has odd augmentation. The embeddings form a regular set for the cyclic $2$-group $\operatorname{Gal}(K_n/\mathbb Q)$, whose group algebra over $\mathbb F _2$ is local. A vector with odd augmentation is a unit in this group algebra, so its translates span every signature. For $n=0$ the assertion follows from the unit $-1$.

The signature calculation supplies the real-place surjectivity needed for the positive complex. The class-group and support terms are bounded along the tower. We can therefore identify the one cohomological degree whose dimension grows with the layer degree, and then recover the rank after inverting $t$.

Kummer theory now determines the cohomological growth. Writing $s_n$ for the number of finite support places and $c_n$ for the $2$-rank of the $S$-class group, one has $$\dim H^1(G_{K_n,S},\mu_2)=d_n+s_n+c_n.$$ The real degree-one restriction is surjective by the signature result. In degree two, the Kummer sequence has class-group term of dimension $c_n$ and Brauer term. The Brauer invariants at the real and finite support places have their single sum relation. Since a finite support place above $2$ is present, restriction of the Brauer term to the real places is surjective and has kernel of dimension $s_n-1$. Thus the degree-two kernel of restriction to infinity is bounded. Restriction is an isomorphism in higher degrees by global duality. The degree-zero restriction is injective. The cohomology of the positive fiber is therefore bounded in every degree except one; its degree-one dimension is $d_n+O_S(1)$.

Apply Lemma <a href="#lem:cy:positive-model" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:cy:positive-model">69</a> modulo $2$. Derived specialization to the $n$th layer is specialization modulo $t^{2^n}$. For a perfect complex over $\mathbb F _2[[t]]$, the universal-coefficient exact sequence shows that a rank-$r$ cohomology module contributes $r2^n+O(1)$ to these dimensions; the torsion terms contribute only $O(1)$. It follows that after inverting $t$ the trivial-constituent fiber has dimension one in degree one and vanishes in every other degree. Extensions preserve this concentration, so the fiber for $E[2]$ has dimension two in degree one. A minimal finite free complex over the local ring $\mathcal O[G]$ has zero residual differentials. The concentration just proved forces all its terms except the rank-two term in degree one to vanish. No denominator is introduced by this exact freeness statement. ◻

</details>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-cy-residual-free-2"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-cy-residual-free</summary>

*Proof of Theorem <a href="#thm:cyclotomic-bound" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:cyclotomic-bound">12</a>.* Apply Lemma <a href="#lem:cy:residual-free" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:cy:residual-free">72</a> to the single discriminant $h$. The fixed-lattice construction and the free complex give $2^{C_{\mathrm{int}}}u_h\in\mathcal O$ with $C_{\mathrm{int}}$ depending only on $E$. Equation <a href="#eq:cy:rational-integrality" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:cy:rational-integrality">[eq:cy:rational-integrality]</a> also gives $u_h\in\Lambda[1/2]$. Since $\mathcal O\cap\Lambda[1/2]=\Lambda$, it follows that $v(u_h(0))\ge-C_{\mathrm{int}}$. Analytic rank zero supplies Selmer corank zero by the forward theorem of Gross–Zagier–Kolyvagin. Proposition <a href="#prop:cy:specialization" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:cy:specialization">71</a> now gives $D(h)\ge-C_{\mathrm{int}}-C_{\mathrm{loc}}$. All constants come from the fixed form, the fixed real period line, or the finitely many local twisting classes at $2N$. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-72"></a>
#### Transfer to the base

It remains to prove the missing-vertex theorem. Residual freeness gives a single integral family in the reducible case. In the irreducible case we instead need a bounded clearing factor after eliminating the new local blocks. The bound on $v_2(q^2-1)$ enters precisely here: the next lemma controls the negative Laurent powers in those inverse blocks at each fixed precision.

<a id="stmt-lem-cy-cyclotomic-poles"></a>
<div id="lem:cy:cyclotomic-poles" class="lemma">

**Lemma 73**. *Suppose that $q$ is an added prime and $v_2(q^2-1)\le L$. At augmentation $G\to1$, the inverse singular Frobenius block contributed by $q$ has, modulo each fixed $2^M$, negative Laurent support bounded in terms of $L$ and $M$. This bound is independent of $q$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-cy-cyclotomic-poles"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-cy-cyclotomic-poles</summary>

*Proof.* Identify $\Gamma$ with $1+4\mathbb Z_2$ using a fixed generator. If $\gamma_q=(1+t)^{\alpha_q}$ is the image of arithmetic Frobenius at $q$, then $$v_2(\alpha_q)=v_2(q^2-1)-3$$ when the generator is $5$; changing the generator multiplies $\alpha_q$ by a unit. In particular $\alpha_q\ne0$. The singular quotient is represented by a block of bounded size whose determinant is the Euler polynomial in Equation <a href="#eq:cy:local-euler" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:cy:local-euler">[eq:cy:local-euler]</a>. Modulo $2$, with $z=(1+t)^{\alpha_q}$, it is $$1+\overline{a_q}z+z^2.$$ If $\overline{a_q}=1$, its constant coefficient is $1$. If $\overline{a_q}=0$, it is $(1+z)^2$, whose $t$-order is $2^{v_2(\alpha_q)+1}\le2^{L-2}$. Thus the inverse determinant has uniformly bounded pole order modulo $2$. Lift its inverse modulo $2^M$ by a geometric expansion of length at most $M$. Each term contains only a bounded number of inverse residual factors, and all numerators have nonnegative powers of $t$. The adjugate formula gives the same bound for every entry of the inverse block. ◻

</details>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-cy-cyclotomic-poles-2"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-cy-cyclotomic-poles</summary>

*Proof of Theorem <a href="#thm:cyclotomic-interpolation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:cyclotomic-interpolation">8</a>.* At every nonzero vertex, analytic rank zero gives $c_2(E^{(h_x)})=0$ by the forward rank-zero theorem. Thus Proposition <a href="#prop:cy:specialization" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:cy:specialization">71</a> applies at every vertex.

<a id="eq:cy:universal-integrality"></a>
First assume $E[2]$ is an extension of trivial modules. Lemma <a href="#lem:cy:residual-free" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:cy:residual-free">72</a> and the fixed-lattice construction give $2^{C_{\mathrm{int}}}u\in\mathcal O[G]$. Moreover, the character coordinates of $u$ are in $\Lambda[1/2]$. Fourier inversion, performed rationally, shows $u\in\Lambda[1/2][G]$; intersecting coefficientwise with $\mathcal O[G]$ gives $$\label{eq:cy:universal-integrality}
 2^{C_{\mathrm{int}}}u\in\Lambda[G].$$ The coefficients at $t=0$ therefore obey the bounded-degree Boolean congruences of Lemma <a href="#lem:h:boolean-coefficients" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:h:boolean-coefficients">66</a>. For any fixed precision and sufficiently large $b$, there is a nonzero $x$ for which $u_x(0)$ agrees with $u_0(0)$ to that precision. The fixed multiplier in Equation <a href="#eq:cy:universal-integrality" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:cy:universal-integrality">[eq:cy:universal-integrality]</a> affects the required precision but has no dependence on $b$.

Now suppose $E[2]$ is irreducible. At augmentation, represent the positive complex as the old complex, with ramification set excluding $\mathcal Q$, extended by the direct sum of singular blocks at the new primes. The differential is upper triangular with the old complex as subcomplex. The finite-model argument of Lemma <a href="#lem:h:finite-models" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:h:finite-models">68</a> lifts this model over $R$: stabilize the finite free models and lift their graded changes of basis. These lifts are invertible because the augmentation ideal lies in the Jacobson radical. Cancel all additional lifted unit disks before retaining the old-plus-singular grading; their augmented cross terms are zero, so the remaining augmentation is exactly the prescribed block model. Thus no stabilization disk enlarges the old complex. Lemma <a href="#lem:h:bounded-poles" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:h:bounded-poles">64</a> then applies to this block model. All the new blocks are invertible over $\mathcal O[G]$: modulo its maximal ideal their Frobenius determinants are nonzero in $\Omega$. Schur elimination leaves a complex of bounded size. Its augmentation is the fixed old complex, and its entries have bounded negative Laurent support modulo each fixed $2^M$. Under the determinant-line identification, write $$u=\eta u_{\mathrm{bd}},\qquad \eta\in\mathcal O[G]^\times,$$ where $u_{\mathrm{bd}}$ is the coordinate on this bounded complex and $\eta$ is the determinant factor of the eliminated blocks. No uniform Laurent bound on $\eta$ is needed.

The pole bound remains uniform as primes are added. At augmentation the inverse new block is a direct sum of the inverses in Lemma <a href="#lem:cy:cyclotomic-poles" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:cy:cyclotomic-poles">73</a>. At any character its perturbation has entries divisible by $2$ and no negative powers of $t$. Modulo $2^M$, the inverse uses a geometric series of length at most $M$, independently of the number of blocks. Each product therefore uses a bounded number of inverse entries. Sums of an arbitrary number of such terms cannot decrease the nonarchimedean valuation or the common lower Laurent bound. This is the required bound for Schur elimination.

<a id="eq:cy:cleared-determinant"></a>
At $t=0$ the old positive complex has rational cohomology only in degree one, of dimension two, by Proposition <a href="#prop:cy:specialization" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:cy:specialization">71</a> at $h_0$. Its finite torsion and all old local data are fixed. Choose boundary pivots there, leaving those two free coordinates. Their sizes and valuations may depend on $h_0$ but not on $b$. Apply the determinant clearing argument of Lemma <a href="#lem:h:pivot-clearing" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:h:pivot-clearing">65</a> to the wedge of the two bounded-integral cycles $a,2z_S$ on the remaining complex. Its allowance for an arbitrary factor $\eta$ puts the eliminated-block factor into the numerator alone. It yields $$\label{eq:cy:cleared-determinant}
 d=fu\in\mathcal O[G],\qquad f\in\mathcal O[G],\qquad
 f_0\in\Lambda,\quad f_0(0)\ne0.$$ For each fixed $M$, the negative Laurent support of $f_x\bmod2^M$ is bounded independently of $b$ and $x$. The clearing factor is a polynomial of bounded degree in the remaining bounded-size matrix, with the pivot denominators cleared by adjugates. Neither the eliminated-block unit, the zeta class nor $d$ is required to have a uniform bound on its negative Laurent support.

Equation <a href="#eq:cy:rational-integrality" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:cy:rational-integrality">[eq:cy:rational-integrality]</a> ensures that every $u_x$ has no negative $t$-powers. Thus all hypotheses of Lemma <a href="#lem:h:boolean-transfer" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:h:boolean-transfer">67</a> hold for Equation <a href="#eq:cy:cleared-determinant" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:cy:cleared-determinant">[eq:cy:cleared-determinant]</a>. In particular, for each fixed precision and sufficiently large $b$, some nonzero $x$ satisfies the corresponding central congruence between $u_x(0)$ and $u_0(0)$. The dependence on $h_0$ enters the required precision and dimension, through $v(f_0(0))$, and not the eventual valuation comparison.

In either residual case let $C$ bound the absolute error in Equation <a href="#eq:cy:determinant-center" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:cy:determinant-center">[eq:cy:determinant-center]</a>. The nonzero vertices have $v(u_x(0))\le B+C$. If $L(E^{(h_0)},1)=0$, the central coordinate at zero is zero, and a congruence of precision larger than $B+C$ is impossible. Hence the central value is nonzero. If $D(h_0)>B+2C$, then $v(u_0(0))>B+C$, giving the same contradiction. This proves Equation <a href="#eq:cy:transferred-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:cy:transferred-bound">[eq:cy:transferred-bound]</a> with $C_E=2C$. Only the specialization error determines this final loss; all pivot and pole bounds determine how large a cube is needed. ◻

</details>

<a id="sec:heegner-interpolation"></a>
### Heegner points and transfer

We prove the Heegner comparison, the genus and ring bounds, and the interpolation criterion stated in Section <a href="#sec:transfer-criteria" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:transfer-criteria">3</a>. The point and its paired functional define one determinant coordinate. Its central value measures the point index after the Selmer and local contributions have been subtracted. Local switches then control its divisors. An outer limit supplies the uniform ring bound when residual irreducibility is unavailable; a universal binary family supplies interpolation.

<a id="pm-h-74"></a>
#### Height and base Selmer comparisons

Retain the genus and ring data, character sums $P_c(e)$, and lattice indices of Section <a href="#sec:transfer-criteria" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:transfer-criteria">3</a>. We first justify the two comparisons used there.

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-cy-cyclotomic-poles-3"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-cy-cyclotomic-poles</summary>

*Proof of Proposition <a href="#prop:heegner-comparison" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:heegner-comparison">9</a>.* The explicit Gross–Zagier formula for ring classes (Cai, Shu, and Tian 2014, Theorem 1.1, pp. 2524–2525) <a id="pm-cite-97"></a>[[CaiShuTian2014](#ref-CaiShuTian2014)] applies. Automorphic induction of the quadratic character gives the product in Equation <a href="#eq:h:height" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:h:height">[eq:h:height]</a>. Discriminant and conductor are prime to $N$, and the classical split Heegner hypothesis holds; consequently the shared-prime corrections in the general formula are absent. The unit-index convention is constant in the fields retained here. With a character sum, solving the formula for the height gives exactly $c\sqrt{|k|}$, as in Equation <a href="#eq:h:height" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:h:height">[eq:h:height]</a>. The forward Gross–Zagier–Kolyvagin theorem gives the rank and finiteness assertion (Gross and Zagier 1986; Kolyvagin 1990) <a id="pm-cite-98"></a>[[GrossZagier1986](#ref-GrossZagier1986), [Kolyvagin1990](#ref-Kolyvagin1990)].

For Equation <a href="#eq:h:index-comparison" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:h:index-comparison">[eq:h:index-comparison]</a>, both free points are compared with the free line on $E^{(h)}(\mathbb Q)$. Its regulator cancels from the ratio of their heights, since absolute canonical height is unchanged by twist identification. This height invariance follows from the canonical-height limit and the degree formula for heights under morphisms (Milne 2021, chap. IV, Lemmas 4.1 and 4.5–4.6, and Remark 4.12) <a id="pm-cite-99"></a>[[MilneEC2021](#ref-MilneEC2021)]. The remaining variable factor is $\sqrt{|hk|}L(E^{(hk)},1)$; its infinity sign is that of $h_*$. Period and lattice changes have bounded $2$-valuation. If the rank-one line is instead that of the fixed curve $E^{(h_*)}$, its regulator is fixed and the same calculation gives Equation <a href="#eq:h:reverse-comparison" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:h:reverse-comparison">[eq:h:reverse-comparison]</a>. ◻

</details>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-cy-cyclotomic-poles-4"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-cy-cyclotomic-poles</summary>

*Proof of Lemma <a href="#lem:h:base-selmer-bound" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:h:base-selmer-bound">11</a>.* Restriction, twisting, and addition or subtraction of conjugates give maps in both directions between the Selmer group over $K$ and $$\mathop{\mathrm{Sel}}_{2^\infty}(E^{(h_0)}/\mathbb Q)
 \oplus\mathop{\mathrm{Sel}}_{2^\infty}(E^{(h_0k)}/\mathbb Q)$$ whose composites are multiplication by $2$. They induce isogenies on divisible subgroups. On the finite quotients the kernel of either induced map is killed by $2$: subtract an element of the divisible subgroup to lift a divisible image, and then use the composite. The generator dimensions are uniformly bounded. Indeed the mod-$2$ Selmer group over $K$ is bounded by Kummer cohomology over $K(E[2])$; this is a quadratic extension of a fixed field with a bounded number of ramified primes. Kummer theory bounds the generator number of the corresponding pro-$2$ group over the fixed field, and the index-two subgroup bound preserves a uniform bound. The fixed local support includes that of $h_0$. The finite quotient on the displayed product is bounded by hypothesis; therefore its counterpart over $K$ has bounded length as well. For a finite collection of fields, finiteness of each quotient is enough. ◻

</details>

<a id="rl:section"></a>
#### Integral models and ring-class deformation

<span id="sec:h:finite-models" label="sec:h:finite-models"></span>

The determinant argument uses characters of increasing conductor. We construct their cochain limits together with maps to the original cochains. These maps will let us detect limiting Selmer classes by Galois evaluation and choose local switches. Later we retain the same maps through the outer limit needed for the ring bound.

Write $T=T_2E$ and $\Lambda=\mathbf Z_2[[t]]$. For a quadratic squareclass $h$, put $T^h=T\otimes\chi_h$. The imaginary quadratic field $K$ satisfies the split Heegner hypothesis at $2N$. We omit the two fields with extra units and, when $E$ has complex multiplication, its CM field. A quadratic character $\chi$ comes from a quadratic twist over $\mathbf Q$. We use $$A_i=(\mathbf Z/2^i\mathbf Z)[t]/(t^i).$$ The same constructions work over $A_i[G]$ and $\Lambda[G]$, where $G$ is a fixed finite elementary abelian $2$-group and the additional character has values in $G$. Statements uniform in the number of generators of $G$ will be identified separately; finite-diagram compactness by itself is a statement for fixed $G$.

<a id="pm-h-76"></a>
##### Finite models with their cochain maps

The general finite-model construction is Lemma <a href="#rl:finite-model" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:finite-model">[rl:finite-model]</a>. We apply it to the following arithmetic cochains and retain its actual contractions throughout.

For a profinite group and a finite free coefficient module over an Artin local ring $A$, continuous inhomogeneous cochains are flat: locally constant functions are the filtered union of the modules of functions on finite clopen partitions, and these modules are finite free. Their reduction is the cochain complex with reduced coefficients. The same observations apply to restrictions, mapping cones, and local conditions given by finite free complexes. In the applications below the groups are Galois groups of totally imaginary number fields or nonarchimedean local fields. Their $2$-cohomological dimension and the usual finiteness theorems give the bounded residual cohomology required in Lemma <a href="#rl:finite-model" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:finite-model">[rl:finite-model]</a>.

For an inner limit, the quadratic field $K$, the active conductor support, the finite group $G$, and the number of derivative primes are fixed. The residual representation is $E[2]$: all the scalar characters and group-like coefficients become trivial in the residue field. Put $F=K(E[2])$. The number of places of $F$ in the permitted set $S_i$ is bounded even when its auxiliary primes move. Kummer theory bounds $H^1(G_{F,S_i},\mathbf F_2)$ by the $S_i$-units modulo squares and $\operatorname{Cl}(F)[2]$; their dimensions are bounded by the unit rank, $\#S_i$, and the fixed class-group dimension. Hochschild–Serre for the fixed group $\operatorname{Gal}(F/K)$ then bounds the residual global $H^1$ for $E[2]$. The global Euler characteristic bounds $H^2$, and $H^0$ is already bounded. Local cohomology and the specified local conditions have bounded residual dimensions, since the local degrees of $K$ are at most two and the number of places is bounded. Thus the target Selmer cones over $K$ have uniformly bounded finite-model ranks in this inner limit. This bound may depend on the fixed active support; the stronger outer bound is proved in Lemma <a href="#rl:residual-bound" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:residual-bound">88</a>. No rank bound is asserted for cochains over the growing ring-class fields, or for the induced modules in their Shapiro descriptions.

<a id="stmt-rl-finite-limits"></a>
<div id="rl:finite-limits" class="lemma">

**Lemma 74** (Limits of finite diagrams). *Suppose diagrams of bounded finite free complexes over $A_i$, or over $A_i[G]$, have a common bounded cohomological degree interval and bounded ranks in every degree. Include the chain homotopies and inverses for every asserted identity or equivalence. Along a cofinal subsequence, or a nonprincipal ultrafilter, their matrices converge to the same diagram of perfect complexes over $\Lambda$ or $\Lambda[G]$.*

*Moreover, the contractions into the original cochains may be retained for the evaluation construction in Lemma <a href="#rl:evaluation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:evaluation">[rl:evaluation]</a>. Adding finitely many new objects or maps does not require changing already chosen models for the old objects. Finite-stage arithmetic operations with unbounded source complexes are permitted when only finitely many of their outputs, and the witnesses to their identities, are retained in the bounded target complexes.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rl-finite-limits"><summary>Proof of stmt-rl-finite-limits</summary>

*Proof.* There are finitely many possible graded ranks. Fix them on an ultrafilter-large set. At a fixed precision $j$, all matrix entries belong to the finite ring $A_j$ (or $A_j[G]$), so have unique ultrafilter limits. These limits are compatible as $j$ varies. Matrix identities, including the homotopy-inverse identities, are finite polynomial identities and pass to the limit. New models and maps may be mapped to old models by their already fixed contractions. Passing to any slower cofinal precision has the same old limits. For the all-sequence evaluation statements below, fix this ultrafilter once and for all, and keep the original contraction at every stage. Later arithmetic diagrams must extend these same stages. Restriction to an ultrafilter-large set and passage to slower cofinal coefficient precision preserve every old evaluation on every old group sequence. Thus later operations use the same stage diagrams and ultrafilter, preserving the arithmetic maps already constructed.

Here is the last assertion in cochain terms. Let $D_i$ be an original target cochain complex, with contraction $(\iota_i,\pi_i,h_i)$ onto its bounded finite model $C_i$. Perform transfer and scalar weighting at stage $i$ before applying this contraction. A resulting cycle $z_i'\in D_i^1$ gives $z_i=\pi_i z_i'\in C_i^1$, and $$z_i'-\iota_i z_i=d(h_i z_i').$$ Thus its relation to the original arithmetic cocycle is retained by the original contraction. If an identity in the target is $u_i'-v_i'=d w_i'$, retain the vectors $\pi_i u_i',\pi_i v_i',\pi_i w_i'$; the corresponding identity is still exact. For identities involving maps between target complexes, use the transported maps $\pi_i'f_i\iota_i$ and their contraction homotopies, so that the same assertion includes the required boundary corrections. Local lifts, closed degree-two functionals, and witnesses to specialization, duality and switch identities are treated in the same way. They are finitely many vectors or matrices of bounded size. Their entries, as well as the differentials, therefore have simultaneous limits. Neither a free model of the arithmetic source nor the entire transfer map from that source is included in the limiting diagram. Any precision lost in a finite-stage calculation is accounted for before retaining these vectors; passing to the same slower cofinal precision for the whole diagram preserves all its identities. ◻

</details>

The finite models now retain both the original cochains and their comparison maps. We next specify the local conditions on those cochains. The point is to retain the actual Kummer images at every place dividing $2N$; the determinant comparisons will use their integral orthogonality, not just the rational Selmer ranks.

<a id="pm-h-77"></a>
##### Integral local conditions and duality

<a id="stmt-lem-h-duality"></a>
<div id="lem:h:duality" class="lemma">

**Lemma 75** (Integral Kummer local condition). *<span id="rl:kummer" label="rl:kummer"></span> Let $F$ be a finite extension of a nonarchimedean local field of characteristic zero, and let $B/F$ be any elliptic curve. Put $M_F=B(F)^\wedge_2=\varprojlim_n B(F)/2^nB(F)$. There is a perfect local condition $$U_F=M_F[-1]\longrightarrow R\Gamma(F,T_2B).$$ For every $n\geq1$, derived reduction has $$H^0(U_F\otimes^{\mathbf L}\mathbf Z/2^n)=B(F)[2^n],\qquad
 H^1(U_F\otimes^{\mathbf L}\mathbf Z/2^n)=B(F)/2^nB(F).$$ Its map in degree zero is the isomorphism onto $H^0(F,B[2^n])$, and its map in degree one is the finite Kummer injection. The condition is its own exact orthogonal complement under local Tate duality, for every reduction type and with no hypothesis on $B[2]$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-h-duality"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-h-duality</summary>

*Proof.* The local analytic description of $B(F)$ shows that $M_F$ is a finitely generated $\mathbf Z_2$-module. Its torsion is the finite group $B(F)[2^\infty]$. Consequently $M_F$ has a free resolution of length at most one. Also $H^0(F,T_2B)=0$, since $B(F)[2^\infty]$ has bounded exponent. The integral Kummer injection into $H^1(F,T_2B)$ therefore defines the displayed morphism using the truncation in degrees at most one of $R\Gamma(F,T_2B)$.

Tensor the free resolution of $M_F$ with $\mathbf Z/2^n$. Its two cohomology groups are $M_F[2^n]$ and $M_F/2^nM_F$. The inverse limits of the ordinary Kummer sequences identify their maps as asserted.

For orthogonality, compose cup product and the Weil pairing with the local invariant map. A morphism $$M_F[-1]\otimes^{\mathbf L}M_F[-1]
       \longrightarrow\mathbf Z_2[-2]$$ is determined by its homomorphism $M_F\otimes M_F\to\mathbf Z_2$: the possible $\operatorname{Tor}_1$ is in degree one and gives no extra degree-zero morphism to this target. The indicated homomorphism vanishes, because the finite Kummer image annihilates itself at every level by local Tate duality. Choose a nullhomotopy in free models. The induced morphism $$R\Gamma(F,T_2B)/U_F
       \longrightarrow R\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf Z_2}
                         (U_F,\mathbf Z_2)[-2]$$ is a quasi-isomorphism. This can be checked after reduction modulo $2$: degree one is the perfect pairing of the finite Kummer quotient with the Kummer image, and degree two is dual to $B(F)[2]$. Its perfect cone is therefore zero by derived Nakayama. This proves exact orthogonality and also its compatibility with derived reduction. This is precisely the finite-module duality input of (Nekovář 2006, Proposition 5.2.4) <a id="pm-cite-100"></a>[[Nekovar2006](#ref-Nekovar2006)]. ◻

</details>

Where the scalar deformation is trivial, extend this local condition by derived scalar extension to $A_i$ or $A_i[G]$. At an unramified good prime use the inflated residue-field complex $$U_v=[\,M\xrightarrow{\operatorname{Fr}_v-1}M\,]
 \quad\text{in degrees }0,1.$$ Its quotient in full local cochains is the singular local complex. The full local condition is the identity on local cochains, and its orthogonal strict condition is zero. At a derivative prime the conditions used later are the following specified truncations instead. In its split local model write $$L_v=D^0\oplus(F_v\oplus S_v)[-1]\oplus D^2[-2],$$ where the differential is zero, $D^0$ is dual to $D^2$, and the finite and transverse planes $F_v,S_v$ are each isotropic. Put $$U_{\rm str}=D^0,\qquad
 U_{\rm rel}=D^0\oplus(F_v\oplus S_v)[-1],\qquad
 U_F=D^0\oplus F_v[-1],\qquad U_S=D^0\oplus S_v[-1].$$ Then $U_{\rm str}^{\perp}=U_{\rm rel}$ and each plane condition is its own orthogonal complement. Every displayed condition maps isomorphically onto local $H^0$ and injectively into local $H^1$. Thus they satisfy precisely the detection hypotheses used below. Their finite arithmetic realization and the isotropic-plane nullhomotopies are part of the derivative construction; these truncated conditions are not identified with the full local condition.

<a id="rl:selmer-definition"></a>
<a id="rl:global-duality"></a>
For a finite permitted set $S$ the Selmer complex is, by definition, $$\label{rl:selmer-definition}
 C_S=\operatorname{Cone}\left(
 R\Gamma(G_{K,S},M)\oplus\bigoplus_{v\in S}U_v
 \longrightarrow\bigoplus_{v\in S}R\Gamma(K_v,M)
 \right)[-1].$$ At $2N$ take the Kummer conditions just constructed. Restriction and localization triangles are the triangles of this cone. The finite rings $A_i$ and $A_i[G]$ are Frobenius coefficient rings; alternatively the duality maps may be checked after reduction to their residue field. Exact local orthogonality and global duality therefore give $$\label{rl:global-duality}
 C_S\simeq R\operatorname{Hom}(C_S^{\perp},A_i)[-3],$$ with the appropriate dual representation. This application uses the orthogonality hypotheses of (Nekovář 2006, Theorem 6.3.4) <a id="pm-cite-101"></a>[[Nekovar2006](#ref-Nekovar2006)]; the theorem is not being used to assert the existence of a varying-prime limit. Complex places contribute zero Tate complexes. If the character is inverted by the nontrivial automorphism of $K/\mathbf Q$, conjugate transport followed by the Weil pairing identifies the two representations over the same scalar ring. All maps and nullhomotopies in this paragraph are finite diagrams to which Lemma <a href="#rl:finite-limits" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:finite-limits">74</a> applies.

<a id="sec:h:conductor-direction"></a>
#### The moving conductor character

The conductor character must preserve the local conditions at $2N$ while making the new local terms invertible after reduction modulo $2$ and inversion of $t$. The following proposition supplies those local values. Its separate bounds on Tate Frobenius control the contribution of the moving prime when we later specialize to $t=0$.

<a id="stmt-lem-h-conductor-primes"></a>
<div id="lem:h:conductor-primes" class="proposition">
