<a id="eq:h:r-avoidance"></a>
**Proposition 76** (Ring-class characters with prescribed local values). *<span id="rl:characters" label="rl:characters"></span>Fix finitely many split primes of $K$ above odd rational primes, outside $2N$, and orient one prime in each conjugate pair. There are distinct split rational primes $r_i$ avoiding all the fixed data and characters $$\xi_i:\operatorname{Gal}(H_{r_i}/K)\longrightarrow
                 \mathbf Z/2^{n_i}\mathbf Z,
 \qquad n_i\longrightarrow\infty,$$ such that $\xi_i$ is surjective on the inertia quotient at $r_i$, is zero at the primes above $2N$, and has odd value at each prescribed oriented prime. We can require $r_i\to1$ in $\mathbf Z_2$ and $$\label{eq:h:r-avoidance}
 v_2(2+a_{r_i}(E)),\quad v_2(2-a_{r_i}(E)),\quad
 v_2\det(1\pm\operatorname{Fr}_{r_i}\mid T)\ \leq c_E.$$ The constant $c_E$ is independent of the list and of $K$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-h-conductor-primes"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-h-conductor-primes</summary>

*Proof.* We give the compatibility argument before imposing the Tate condition. Choose prime ideals $\mathfrak p_1,\ldots,\mathfrak p_s$ with pairwise disjoint conjugate pairs, including the oriented prescribed primes and the primes above $2N$, and enough additional split prime ideals to generate $\operatorname{Cl}(K)$. Such additional ideals may avoid any fixed finite set. Put weight $w_j=1$ at a prescribed odd prime and $w_j=0$ at every additional prime and every prime above $2N$. The conjugate weight is $-w_j$. Let $$R=\ker\bigl(\mathbf Z^s\longrightarrow\operatorname{Cl}(K)\bigr),$$ choose a basis $m^{(a)}$ of $R$, and choose $\beta_a\in K^\times$ with $(\beta_a)=\prod_j\mathfrak p_j^{m_j^{(a)}}$.

<a id="rl:kummer-prescription"></a>
Work first over $F_\infty=K(\mu_{2^\infty})$ and adjoin $2^n$-th roots of the finitely many $\beta_a/\overline\beta_a$. Prescribe on these roots the multipliers $$\label{rl:kummer-prescription}
 \zeta_{2^n}^{\,-\sum_j m_j^{(a)}w_j}.$$ The minus sign fixes the choice of connecting map in the ring-class sequence and could be reversed throughout. These prescriptions respect every Kummer relation. Indeed, if $$\prod_a(\beta_a/\overline\beta_a)^{b_a}
                         \in(F_\infty^\times)^{2^n},$$ take its valuation at a prime above each $\mathfrak p_j$ of nonzero weight. These odd primes are unramified in $F_\infty/K$. Thus $2^n$ divides $\sum_a b_am_j^{(a)}$ for each such $j$, proving the required compatibility of <a href="#rl:kummer-prescription" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rl:kummer-prescription">[rl:kummer-prescription]</a>. Primes over $2$ have weight zero and impose no division by a ramification index. Units impose no additional weighted relation. Kummer duality supplies the prescribed automorphism of the radical extension over $F_\infty$.

At a rational prime $r$ split in a sufficiently large finite cyclotomic subfield, the power-residue character of $\mathbf F_r^\times$ is surjective onto $\mu_{2^n}$. The split ring-class exact sequence is $$1\longrightarrow
  (\mathcal O_K/r\mathcal O_K)^\times/(\mathbf Z/r\mathbf Z)^\times
 \longrightarrow\operatorname{Pic}(\mathbf Z+r\mathcal O_K)
 \longrightarrow\operatorname{Cl}(K)\longrightarrow1.$$ The excluded extra-unit fields are the only source of a unit correction. The first group is $\mathbf F_r^\times$, with a principal relation measured by $\beta/\overline\beta$ at the oriented prime over $r$. Consequently <a href="#rl:kummer-prescription" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rl:kummer-prescription">[rl:kummer-prescription]</a> says exactly that its primitive power-residue character extends to the class group with the specified values $w_j$. More explicitly, the inertia group and the chosen ideal classes present the ring-class group, and the basis of $R$ lists its additional relations. We have imposed those relations on the inertia character itself; we have not divided by a class-group order to extend a previously fixed character. Thus this construction introduces no denominator, even when the class number has a large $2$-part. The class group and the number of prescribed primes change the finite Chebotarev extension, but not the integrality of the character. Since the ring-class extension is unramified at $2N$, value zero on Frobenius means that the resulting local character is trivial there. Conjugation acts by inversion.

We now show that imposing these finitely many radical conditions cannot force either forbidden Tate trace. In the non-CM case the image of $G_{K(\mu_{2^\infty})}$ is an open subgroup of $\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbf Z_2)$, by the fixed-prime open-image theorem and the cyclotomic determinant identity (Serre 1968, chap. IV, §2.2, theorem, p. IV-11, and Chapter I, §1.2, Example 2, p. I-4) <a id="pm-cite-102"></a>[[Serre1968](#ref-Serre1968)]: the image is the intersection of the open image of $G_K$ with the determinant-one subgroup. Its index in the corresponding fixed-$E$ image changes by at most two when $K$ changes. Its commutator subgroup contains a fixed open subgroup $U_E$ of $\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbf Z_2)$. One may see uniformity by starting with a principal congruence subgroup in the fixed image: every index-two subgroup contains its squares, and the commutators of the resulting fixed congruence subgroup are open. Because the radical extension over $F_\infty$ is abelian, these commutators act trivially on it. Hence every permitted Tate coset contains a translate of $U_E$.

For completeness, in the CM case let $M$ be the CM field. The image over $KM(\mu_{2^\infty})$ contains a fixed open subgroup of the norm-one Cartan; the index changes by a bounded factor, as $[KM:\mathbf Q]\leq4$. Choose $\gamma\in G_{KM}$ with $\chi_{\rm cyc}(\gamma)=5^4=625$. This is possible uniformly: the cyclotomic image of $G_{KM}$ has index at most four in $\mathbf Z_2^\times$, so contains fourth powers. On the radical Galois group, conjugation by $\gamma$ is raising to $625$, because all the radicands lie in $K$. On the Tate image over $KM$, conjugation is trivial. Therefore $$\gamma u\gamma^{-1}u^{-625},\qquad
 u\in G_{KM(\mu_{2^\infty})},$$ fixes every prescribed radical and acts on $T$ as $\rho_T(u)^{-624}$. Raising to the fixed nonzero power $624$ carries an open subgroup of the one-dimensional norm-one Cartan onto an open subgroup. This proves the required uniform kernel statement also in the CM case. The open Cartan image used here is the CM part of the usual $\ell$-adic image theorem (Serre 1968, chap. IV, §2.2, Remark, p. IV-13) <a id="pm-cite-103"></a>[[Serre1968](#ref-Serre1968)].

On a coset of an open subgroup of $\operatorname{SL}_2$, trace is not identically $2$ or $-2$. The same holds on a coset of an open norm-one Cartan subgroup; on the other Cartan-normalizer component trace is zero. The relevant determinant-one sets are compact and have finitely many cosets modulo the fixed open subgroup. Choose in each coset an element whose trace is neither forbidden value. The largest of the finitely many resulting valuations is a constant depending only on $E$.

Finally restrict the prescribed radical automorphism and such a Tate lift to a finite Galois extension, including as many roots of unity as required. Chebotarev gives infinitely many rational primes with this Frobenius class; choose the place over the prime to realize the chosen representative. They split in $K$ and have arbitrarily high prescribed congruence to $1$. Since $\det(1\pm\operatorname{Fr}_r)=1\pm a_r+r$, a congruence precision larger than the fixed trace bound gives all of <a href="#eq:h:r-avoidance" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:h:r-avoidance">[eq:h:r-avoidance]</a>. All these conditions concern a finite extension at each stage. ◻

</details>

Choose $n_i$ large enough that $1+t$ has order dividing $2^{n_i}$ in $A_i^\times$, and put $\Psi_i=(1+t)^{\xi_i}$. For example $n_i\geq2i$ is sufficient. Orient the inertia generator to act by $1+t$; the prescribed split Frobenius exponents remain odd in the limit. Use global cochains unramified outside $2N$, $r_i$, the active conductor primes and the derivative primes already retained. At $2N$ use the Kummer conditions above and elsewhere outside the conductors use the unramified condition. Reduction modulo $t$, with the unramified condition restored at $r_i$, gives the ordinary fixed-field complex; retain its comparison map at every finite stage.

<a id="stmt-lem-h-relaxed-local"></a>
<div id="lem:h:relaxed-local" class="lemma">

**Lemma 77** (Acyclic relaxed local complexes). *<span id="rl:local-acyclic" label="rl:local-acyclic"></span> For a primitive character constituent, let $C$ denote the limiting Selmer complex with full conditions at $r$ and at its active good conductor primes, and the prescribed Kummer, unramified or derivative conditions elsewhere. The limiting full local complexes are acyclic over every height-one residue field of $\Lambda$ of characteristic zero. At $(2)$, with residue field $\Omega=\mathbf F_2((t))$, the $r$-complex is acyclic, as are the complexes at active split primes with odd prescribed Frobenius exponent of the deformation character and at active primes $q$ with $t_q=0$. At each of these acyclic relaxed places, the full and orthogonal strict conditions agree on the indicated test. If every relaxed place is acyclic at that test and the remaining local conditions are self-dual, global duality makes the Selmer complex self-dual. The Selmer complex has no global invariants on these tests.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-h-relaxed-local"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-h-relaxed-local</summary>

*Proof.* Use tame inertia and unramified Frobenius, or the Hochschild–Serre complex for these two procyclic directions. At $r$, inertia minus one is multiplication by $t$ times a unit. It is invertible on all the indicated fields except the characteristic-zero fiber $t=0$. There, $r\to1$, and the two remaining Frobenius differentials have nonzero determinant by <a href="#eq:h:r-avoidance" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:h:r-avoidance">[eq:h:r-avoidance]</a>, including either sign of the quadratic twist. The bound also ensures that the integral local torsion at this central fiber has bounded length.

At an active odd conductor prime, inertia of the quadratic character acts by $-1$. Its differential is thus $-2$ and is invertible in characteristic zero. In characteristic two the quadratic character disappears. At a split prime the Frobenius action is $zB$, where $B\in\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbf F_2)$ and $z=(1+t)^a$ has odd $a\in\mathbf Z_2$. Its coefficient of $t$ is one, so $z$ is nonconstant. No nonzero polynomial over the finite constant field vanishes at $z$. Thus both Frobenius complexes, with operators $zB-1$ and $q^{-1}zB-1$, are invertible over $\Omega$; here $q=1$ in the residue field. No irreducibility assumption is used.

If $t_q=0$, the rational residual Frobenius $B$ has order three. At a split place the operator is again $zB-1$, invertible whether $z$ is nonconstant or $z=1$. At an inert place the ring-class Frobenius is trivial, since the ideal $(q)$ is principal, and the Tate Frobenius is $B^2$, which also has no eigenvalue one. These observations give the additional $t_q=0$ assertion.

The orthogonal full and strict conditions agree at each place where full local cochains are acyclic. When this holds at every relaxed place and the remaining local conditions are self-dual, Equation <a href="#rl:global-duality" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rl:global-duality">[rl:global-duality]</a> gives global self-duality. Global invariants in characteristic two are excluded by the nontrivial $r$-inertia scalar. In characteristic zero the same argument works unless the scalar is trivial; in that case $T\otimes\mathbf Q_2$ over $G_K$ is absolutely irreducible. For non-CM curves this follows from the open image, and for CM curves from the open Cartan and its nontrivial normalizer component, since $K$ is not the CM field. Lemma <a href="#rl:evaluation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:evaluation">[rl:evaluation]</a> below realizes these actions on the limiting complex as well. On the self-dual tests, duality pairs degrees one and two. ◻

</details>

<a id="sec:h:specialization"></a>
#### The Heegner determinant and its central value

The point index is not itself the quantity transferred across a growing family. Each new conductor prime changes the local Selmer terms as well as the point. We combine these changes in a determinant coordinate. Its central valuation will be twice the point index, less the finite Selmer length and the conductor contribution. This formula reduces the index estimates to lower bounds for the determinant coordinate.

Retain a primitive genus or ring instance from Section <a href="#sec:transfer-criteria" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:transfer-criteria">3</a>, with point $P_c(e)$ over $K$. Use the conductor characters just constructed, taking $n_i\ge2i$, and the representations $T\chi_e\Psi_i$. Retain the same auxiliary primes and the same fixed inner ultrafilter, now denoted $\mathcal U_{\mathrm{in}}$.

The Selmer complex $C$ is a coefficientwise limit of the corresponding finite free cochain models along $\mathcal U_{\mathrm{in}}$. It has the integral Kummer condition at $2N$, the full condition at $r_i$ and the active good conductor primes, and the unramified condition at all other permitted finite places. Here the full condition means that no restriction is imposed on local cochains. Section <a href="#sec:h:finite-models" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:h:finite-models">[sec:h:finite-models]</a> and Lemma <a href="#rl:local-acyclic" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:local-acyclic">[rl:local-acyclic]</a> constructed the local models, their duality maps, and the comparison at $t=0$. We use these concrete complexes and maps; cohomologically equivalent complexes without the comparison maps would not suffice for the later prime choices. Over $\operatorname{Frac}(\Lambda)$, the modified full local complexes are acyclic, so the full conditions agree with their orthogonal strict conditions. Global duality, followed by conjugate transport and the Weil pairing, therefore gives a perfect pairing $$H^1(C\otimes_\Lambda\operatorname{Frac}(\Lambda))\times H^2(C\otimes_\Lambda\operatorname{Frac}(\Lambda))
 \longrightarrow\operatorname{Frac}(\Lambda).$$ Here conjugation in $K/\mathbb Q$ inverts the ring-class character. These are the pairing and identification supplied by Equation <a href="#rl:global-duality" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rl:global-duality">[rl:global-duality]</a> and Lemma <a href="#rl:local-acyclic" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:local-acyclic">[rl:local-acyclic]</a>.

Fix the single integer multiplier $L$ of Lemma <a href="#lem:h:derivative-classes" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:h:derivative-classes">85</a>. It depends on the curve, parametrization and fixed local types, and clears descent and local Kummer ambiguities for the complete conductor. In particular its valuation does not grow with the number of primes. The following construction and formulas include that multiplier throughout.

<a id="eq:h:trace-center"></a>
At each finite stage transfer the Kummer class of $y_{cr_i}$ from $H_{cr_i}$ to $K$ with the specified scalar coefficients, using $Ly_{cr_i}$. Complete the finite coset sum before contracting its target cocycle and local Kummer lifts into the models over $K$. The resulting cycles $P_i$, with their contraction witnesses, give $P\in H^1(C)$ by Lemma <a href="#rl:finite-limits" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:finite-limits">74</a>. Local Kummer conditions at $2N$ are preserved because $\Psi_i$ is trivial there. At the center of the $i$th finite model, the norm relation has the factor $$\label{eq:h:trace-center}
 \begin{aligned}
 b_i&=a_{r_i}-\chi_e(\mathop{\mathrm{Fr}}_{\mathfrak r_i})
            -\chi_e(\mathop{\mathrm{Fr}}_{\bar{\mathfrak r}_i}),
 \qquad r_i=\mathfrak r_i\bar{\mathfrak r}_i,\\
 P_i\big|_{t=0}&=\varepsilon_i b_i\kappa(LP_c(e)).
 \end{aligned}$$ where $\kappa$ denotes the Kummer class in the central comparison and $\varepsilon_i$ is a unit; the equality is taken modulo the finite coefficient precision. Since $\chi_e$ is defined over $\mathbb Q$, its values at the conjugate Frobenius elements agree; explicitly, $b_i=a_{r_i}-2\chi_e(r_i)$. To retain the central identity at the cochain level, let $B_i$ be the reduction of a fixed finite model of the ordinary Kummer complex over $K$, and let $\beta_i:B_i\to C_i/(t)$ be its comparison map to the relaxed central complex. Choose a cycle $q_i$ representing $\kappa(LP_c(e))$. The finite norm relation gives a boundary witness $v_i$ in the target model such that $$P_i\bmod t-\varepsilon_i b_i\beta_i(q_i)=d v_i.$$ Retain $\beta_i,q_i,v_i$, and the target contraction homotopies on the same stages and at the same coefficient precision as $P_i$. Retain these units in the same ultrafilter $\mathcal U_{\mathrm{in}}$ as all the comparison maps. Then $b=\lim_{\mathcal U_{\mathrm{in}}}b_i$ has bounded valuation by Equation <a href="#eq:h:r-avoidance" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:h:r-avoidance">[eq:h:r-avoidance]</a>, and $\varepsilon=\lim_{\mathcal U_{\mathrm{in}}}\varepsilon_i$ is a unit. Thus $P|_{t=0}=\varepsilon b\kappa(LP_c(e))$, with $b\ne0$. The special complex differs from the ordinary Kummer complex only by the active-prime relaxed quotients and the limit of the singular quotient at the single moving prime $r_i$, the latter of bounded length. Inflation from the complexes omitting $r_i$ gives this comparison. All modified local complexes are rationally acyclic at the center, so pairings agree there as well.

If the product has a simple zero, its rational special fiber has one-dimensional cohomology in degrees one and two, and $P$ specializes nontrivially by Gross–Zagier. The generic dimensions are at most these special dimensions. Moreover, the long exact sequence for multiplication by $t$ shows that $H^1(C[1/2])[t]=0$, since the special $H^0$ vanishes. A torsion class that disappeared over the generic field would be killed by a power of $t$ after localization at $(t)$; hence the nonzero special class cannot disappear. Thus the generic ranks are one in degrees one and two, $P$ spans $H^1$, and the rational rank is constant at $t=0$. If only base Selmer corank one is known, the same dimension bound gives generic ranks at most one; a zero generic point is allowed.

<a id="stmt-def-h-determinant-coordinate"></a>
<div id="def:h:determinant-coordinate" class="definition">

**Definition 78**. Choose an integral basis of $\det^{-1}_{\Lambda}C$. In generic rank one, the element formed by $P$ in $H^1$ and the functional $\langle P,\cdot\rangle$ on $H^2$ determines a scalar $u(C,P)\in\operatorname{Frac}(\Lambda)$ in that basis. Put $u=0$ if $P=0$ or the generic rank is zero. Integral changes of determinant basis multiply $u$ by a unit.

</div>

In the simple-zero case, constancy of the rational cohomology rank at $t=0$ makes $u$ regular in the local ring $\Lambda_{(t)}$. Its value $u(0)\in\mathbb Q_2$ is therefore already defined. This specialization takes place at $(t)$; the stronger assertion $u\in\Lambda[1/2]$ will follow from the divisor estimates below.

The determinant has a simple integral interpretation. On a rank-one free Selmer line, the point and its paired functional each contribute the point’s index. Torsion in degree two subtracts its length from the coordinate in the inverse determinant lattice. For example, the complex $[\mathbb Z_2\xrightarrow{2^a}\mathbb Z_2]$ in degrees one and two has inverse determinant lattice mapping to $2^a\mathbb Z_2$ in the rational determinant. The coordinate of a fixed rational tensor therefore loses $a$ in valuation. The next lemma carries out this calculation with the actual local Kummer conditions. It also compares the Selmer length over $K$ with those of the two rational twists.

<a id="stmt-lem-h-central-valuation"></a>
<div id="lem:h:central-valuation" class="lemma">

<a id="eq:h:central-determinant"></a>
<a id="eq:h:weil-restriction-length"></a>
**Lemma 79** (Central determinant valuation). *For a simple-zero instance, $$\label{eq:h:central-determinant}
 \begin{aligned}
 v(u(0))&=2j(P_c(e))
   -\mathop{\mathrm{length}}\mathop{\mathrm{Sha}}(E^{(e)}/K)[2^\infty]
   -\sum_{q\mid c}\sum_{v\mid q}t_v+O_E(1),\\
 t_v&=\dim_{\mathbb F_2}E[2]^{\mathop{\mathrm{Fr}}_v}.
 \end{aligned}$$ Furthermore, $$\label{eq:h:weil-restriction-length}
 \mathop{\mathrm{length}}\mathop{\mathrm{Sha}}(E^{(e)}/K)[2^\infty]
       +\sum_{q\mid c}\sum_{v\mid q}t_v
 =s(e)+s(ek)+\sum_{q\mid k}t_q
                         +2\sum_{q\mid c}t_q+O_E(1).$$ The constants include the one fixed class multiplier and the bounded local contribution at the moving prime $r_i$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-h-central-valuation"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-h-central-valuation</summary>

*Proof.* The ordinary integral Kummer complex over $K$ is self-dual. Its $H^1$ is the compact Selmer module, and the torsion in $H^2$ has the length of the finite quotient of the discrete Selmer group by its divisible subgroup. This follows by derived base change to $\mathbb Q_2/\mathbb Z_2$: the local complexes give exactly the discrete Kummer conditions. In the present simple-zero case that finite quotient is $\mathop{\mathrm{Sha}}(E^{(e)}/K)[2^\infty]$. Duality pairs the free parts in degrees one and two perfectly. Torsion in degrees one and three costs a bounded amount, by global torsion and duality. The uniform torsion bound here comes from a fixed nonidentity Tate scalar acting trivially on every ring-class field in the construction: its scalar minus one annihilates that torsion. Lemma <a href="#rl:kernel" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:kernel">81</a> constructs this scalar, and the descent argument of Lemma <a href="#lem:h:derivative-classes" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:h:derivative-classes">85</a> uses the same bound.

At an active odd conductor place inertia acts by minus identity. All integral $H^1$ is Kummer, and the relaxed quotient contributes only $H^2(K_v,T^e)$ in degree two. Its length is $t_v$, by local duality and the fixed $2$-torsion. At the moving prime $r_i$ the contribution is bounded by Equation <a href="#eq:h:r-avoidance" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:h:r-avoidance">[eq:h:r-avoidance]</a>. The generic pairings specialize to the ordinary Kummer pairing because the modified local complexes are rationally acyclic at the center. Thus the free determinant tensor has valuation twice the point index, whereas torsion in degree two contributes negative length to the inverse determinant. Together with Equation <a href="#eq:h:trace-center" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:h:trace-center">[eq:h:trace-center]</a>, this proves Equation <a href="#eq:h:central-determinant" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:h:central-determinant">[eq:h:central-determinant]</a>. The specialization is at constant rational cohomology rank, so no specialization torsion is being substituted for the point.

For Equation <a href="#eq:h:weil-restriction-length" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:h:weil-restriction-length">[eq:h:weil-restriction-length]</a>, apply the isogeny invariance of the BSD quotient to quadratic Weil restriction and $E^{(e)}\times E^{(ek)}$ (Tate 1966, Theorem 2.1 and the preceding discussion) <a id="pm-cite-104"></a>[[Tate1966](#ref-Tate1966)]. All the groups in this comparison are finite apart from the known rank-one lattices; no BSD equality is assumed. The forward and reverse isogenies have composites multiplication by $2$. Consequently the rank-one lattice indices, height ratios, torsion ratios and period ratios contribute bounded $2$-powers. For periods, the pullback indices of Néron differentials at $2$ are bounded by those composites; real kernels and component ratios are bounded as well.

The remaining terms are the Tamagawa numbers. A ramified quadratic twist of good reduction at an odd prime $q$ has type $I_0^*$ and component number one plus the number of roots of its reduced auxiliary cubic (Barrios et al. 2025, Theorem 4.1, Table 4 and proof, Case 3) <a id="pm-cite-105"></a>[[BarriosEtAl2025](#ref-BarriosEtAl2025)]. To identify this number, write a good integral model as $y^2=f(x)$, retaining the quadratic term, and the twisting parameter as $d=\pi u$. The auxiliary cubic is $\bar u^3\bar f(T/\bar u)$; it is separable and its roots correspond to the nonzero rational two-torsion points. Thus the component number is $\#E[2]^{\mathrm{Fr}_q}$ and its $2$-valuation is $t_q$. This argument also applies in residue characteristic $3$. Its connected reduction is unipotent. Some inertia element acts by $-1$ on the twisted $2$-adic representation, so its local $2$-primary torsion is precisely its Frobenius-fixed $2$-torsion. Over an unramified extension the same formula holds with the Frobenius of the enlarged residue field. At unramified or split places, Weil-restriction component numbers are the products over $v\mid q$. At a prime $q\mid k$ outside $2N$, the curve over $K$ has good reduction and its Weil restriction has connected special fiber. Indeed, Weil restriction of its Néron model is the Néron model of the restriction of the curve (Bosch, Lütkebohmert, and Raynaud 1990, vol. 21, sec. 7.6, Proposition 6) <a id="pm-cite-106"></a>[[BoschLutkebohmertRaynaud1990](#ref-BoschLutkebohmertRaynaud1990)]. Its special fiber has the original connected elliptic fiber as quotient, with connected vector-group layers from ramification. Exactly one rational twist has the ramified component factor. At a conductor prime $q\mid c$, the two rational twists give a combined valuation $2t_q$, and the corresponding contribution over $K$ is $\sum_{v\mid q}t_v$. All places above $2N$ have bounded local contributions. These are precisely the terms of Equation <a href="#eq:h:weil-restriction-length" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:h:weil-restriction-length">[eq:h:weil-restriction-length]</a>. ◻

</details>

In a simple-zero genus instance, the fixed partner absorbs the terms involving $h_*$, while $c=1$ and $k=hh_*$. The displayed formulas therefore identify $$v(u(0))=2j(P_1(h_*))-2w(h)-s(h)+O_{E,h_*}(1).$$ In a simple-zero ring instance with $\omega(k)\le a$, the discriminant term is bounded and the conductor term is $4w(h)$, giving $$v(u(0))=2j(P_{|h|}(h))-4w(h)-s(h)-s(hk)+O_{E,a}(1).$$ The ring identity also applies to the interpolation families in which an added nonsplit prime has $t_q=0$; such a prime contributes no weight. The all-split hypothesis is needed for the uniform ring lower bound. These formulas explain both the lower-bound statements and the normalization in Heegner interpolation. To prove the lower bounds, we must show that $u$ has no negative divisor away from $(2)$ and has a uniformly bounded negative divisor at $(2)$ in the stated cases. We will construct integral local switches that preserve its determinant valuation, and use inner detection to choose switches lowering excess Selmer rank. The uniform ring estimate will require an additional characteristic-zero limit; the universal binary family will instead require a bounded clearing factor after the new local blocks have been removed.

<a id="eq:h:divisor-bounds"></a>
The main intermediate estimate is $$\label{eq:h:divisor-bounds}
 \begin{aligned}
 v_{\mathfrak p}(u)&\ge0
       &&\bigl(\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak p=1,
                         \ \mathfrak p\ne(2)\bigr),\\
 v_{(2)}(u)&\ge-O_{E,h_*}(1)
       &&\text{in genus data with irreducible }E[2],\\
 v_{(2)}(u)&\ge-O_{E,a}(1)
       &&\text{in ring data with }\omega(k)\le a
                         \text{ and all active primes split.}
 \end{aligned}$$ To construct the switches used in these estimates, we first retain enough Galois evaluation data to select their derivative primes.

<a id="pm-h-80"></a>
#### Evaluation and the exact kernel

The determinant estimates require switches that detect the excess Selmer dimension at a height-one test. To choose switching primes, we must still detect a nonzero limiting Selmer class by Galois evaluation. The next two lemmas first retain that detection under coefficient specialization, then restrict it to sequences acting trivially on the full Tate module, all ring-class fields, and the quadratic characters in use.

<a id="stmt-lem-h-evaluation"></a>
<div id="lem:h:evaluation" class="lemma">

**Lemma 80** (Evaluation on arbitrary Galois sequences). *<span id="rl:evaluation" label="rl:evaluation"></span> Fix $K$ and a sequence of the finite cochain constructions above. Keep the contraction maps into the original global cochains. Let $\Gamma_K=\prod_i G_K$ and $\Gamma=\Gamma_K\rtimes\langle\tau\rangle\subset\prod_iG_{\mathbf Q}$, with simultaneous complex conjugation $\tau$. Thus $\Gamma_K$ has index two in $\Gamma$; the larger unrestricted product of rational Galois groups is not used for induction. The matrix limit defines a coefficient action of $\Gamma_K$ on $\Lambda^2$. For every field $L$ receiving a map from $\Lambda$, there is a natural injection $$H^1(C\otimes_\Lambda L)\longrightarrow
 H^1_{\rm abs}(\Gamma_K,L^2),$$ where the right side denotes abstract crossed-homomorphism classes. Here $C$ may be the global complex or a Selmer complex whose local conditions contain all local degree-zero invariants and inject into local $H^1$. The same statement holds for the induced representation of $\Gamma$.*

*The evaluation maps and their degree-two cochain identities exist for every group sequence and commute with coefficient extension.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-h-evaluation"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-h-evaluation</summary>

<a id="rl:eval-boundary"></a>
<a id="rl:eval-cocycle"></a>
*Proof.* Let $C_i$ be a finite model and let $\iota_i$ be its chosen map to the original global cochains, using the projection from the Selmer cone when appropriate. For every $g=(g_i)$ and $h=(h_i)$ define matrices $$e^0_i:C_i^0\to A_i^2,\quad
 e^1_{g,i}:C_i^1\to A_i^2,\quad
 e^2_{g,h,i}:C_i^2\to A_i^2$$ by evaluating $\iota_i$ in degrees zero, one, and two. Their source ranks are fixed and their entries belong to $A_i$. Thus each has a coefficientwise ultrafilter limit, for every choice of $g,h$. The same fixed ultrafilter defines these limits for all $g,h$. Likewise $\rho(g)=\lim_i\rho_i(g_i)$ is a representation. The original cochain identities imply $$\begin{aligned}
 e^1_g d&=(\rho(g)-1)e^0,\label{rl:eval-boundary}\\
 e^2_{g,h}d&=\rho(g)e^1_h-e^1_{gh}+e^1_g.
                         \label{rl:eval-cocycle}
\end{aligned}$$ All identities pass to the limit because their matrix expressions have finitely many terms. A cycle $x\in C^1\otimes L$ consequently gives the crossed homomorphism $g\mapsto e^1_g(x)$, and a boundary gives a coboundary.

We prove injectivity in a way that also controls base change. At each finite stage let $k=\mathbf F_2$ be the residual field. Choose a space of representatives for residual $H^1$. Evaluate pairs $(c,m)$, where $c$ is in this space and $m\in k^2$, by $b_c(g)-(\rho(g)-1)m$. The intersection of the kernels of all these evaluations consists precisely of pairs $(0,m)$ with $m$ an invariant. Since the vector space is finite dimensional, a list of at most $\dim H^1+2$ elements already has this intersection. For these elements evaluation is a chain map $$C_i\longrightarrow D_i=
 [\,A_i^2\xrightarrow{((\rho_i(g_j)-1))_j}(A_i^2)^d\,]$$ in degrees zero and one, inducing an isomorphism on residual $H^0$ and an injection on residual $H^1$. For Selmer complexes this uses the exact sequence of <a href="#rl:selmer-definition" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rl:selmer-definition">[rl:selmer-definition]</a>: the indicated local degree-zero isomorphisms give $H^0(C_i)=H^0_{\rm glob}$ and $H^1(C_i)\hookrightarrow H^1_{\rm glob}$ residually.

Retain these matrices and their chosen group-element sequences. The residual global and local complexes, and the local conditions, have no negative cohomology. The cone definition therefore gives $H^n(C\otimes k)=0$ for $n<0$. Put $Q=\operatorname{Cone}(C\to D)$. The long exact sequence gives $H^n(Q\otimes k)=0$ for $n<-1$; its groups in degrees $-1$ and $0$ vanish because the detecting map is an isomorphism on $H^0$ and injective on $H^1$. Any $H^3(C\otimes k)$ contributes in degree two of this cone, so causes no negative-degree obstruction. Successively cancel the unit differential blocks of $Q$. This gives a homotopy-equivalent bounded free complex starting in degree one. For any $\Lambda$-algebra $L$, its ordinary tensor product computes $Q\otimes^{\mathbf L}_\Lambda L$ and still starts in degree one; no flatness is needed. Thus the long exact sequence makes $H^1(C\otimes L)\to H^1(D\otimes L)$ injective. A crossed cocycle that is a coboundary on all of $\Gamma_K$ is in particular a coboundary on the detecting list, proving the desired injection. For induction the same proof has coefficient rank four and the detecting bound is $\dim H^1+4$. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-rl-kernel"></a>
<div id="rl:kernel" class="lemma">

**Lemma 81** (The exact common kernel). *In the notation of Lemma <a href="#rl:evaluation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:evaluation">[rl:evaluation]</a>, let $H$ be the group of sequences each of whose entries acts trivially on the full Tate module, on all ring-class fields of $K$, and on the quadratic characters in use. Restriction from the crossed classes in that Lemma to $H$ is injective at every characteristic-zero test. It is also injective at the residual $(2)$ test. The characteristic-zero annihilator needed for this assertion can be chosen with a fixed finite $2$-valuation depending only on $E$, also as $K$ varies.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rl-kernel"><summary>Proof of stmt-rl-kernel</summary>

*Proof.* The Tate image contains an open subgroup of scalar homotheties, both in the CM and non-CM cases. Choose once and for all $g\in G_{\mathbf Q}$ with Tate action $u\,1$, where $u\in1+4\mathbf Z_2$ and $u\ne1$. Its square belongs to every quadratic subgroup. Put $$z=g^2\tau g^2\tau^{-1}.$$ The generalized dihedral property of every ring-class extension implies that $z$ is ring-class trivial. It is also trivial on every quadratic character, and its Tate action is the fixed scalar $u^4$. For every sequence in $\Gamma_K$, its commutator with the constant sequence $z$ is in the exact group $H$, since its Tate commutator and all its abelian character images are trivial. Thus $z$ is central in $\Gamma_K/H$ and acts on the coefficients by $u^4$.

Here the elementary central-scalar argument suffices. If a crossed cocycle $b$ is defined on a group with such a central element, comparison of $b(zg)$ and $b(gz)$ gives $$(u^4-1)b(g)=(g-1)b(z).$$ In characteristic zero this makes $b$ a coboundary. Inflation–restriction then gives injectivity on $H$. The valuation of $u^4-1$ is fixed.

In characteristic two choose, at each stage, inertia at $r_i$ mapping onto the chosen generator of $\xi_i$. Its Tate action is trivial and its ring-class images commute, so the resulting sequence is central in $\Gamma_K/H$ and acts on $M$ by $1+t$. Its scalar minus one is invertible in $\mathbf F_2((t))$.

For the induced representation $W$, first restrict to $\Gamma_K$. There $W=M\oplus M^\tau$, and this inertia sequence acts on the summands by $1+t$ and $(1+t)^{-1}$. Hence $W^{\Gamma_K}=0$. Inflation–restriction for the index-two inclusion gives an injection $H^1(\Gamma,W)\to H^1(\Gamma_K,W)$, even in characteristic two. Apply the central-scalar calculation separately to the two summands to obtain injection on restriction to $H$. The same argument works in characteristic zero with the fixed scalar $u^4$. Throughout, $H$ is defined by exact actions at every stage. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-rl-irreducibility"></a>
<div id="rl:irreducibility" class="lemma">

**Lemma 82** (Irreducibility on the characteristic-zero tests). *On an inner characteristic-zero test where $\Psi^2\ne1$, the four-dimensional representation induced from $T\chi\Psi$ is absolutely irreducible. If $\Psi^2=1$ on an inner test, it splits as two inequivalent absolutely irreducible quadratic twists.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rl-irreducibility"><summary>Proof of stmt-rl-irreducibility</summary>

*Proof.* The two induced summands are distinguished by $r$-inertia, whose scalars are $\Psi$ and $\Psi^{-1}$. On either summand, multiplying the Tate matrices by scalars does not alter invariant subspaces. The Tate representation restricted to $G_K$ is absolutely irreducible under the exclusions already specified. These facts give absolute irreducibility of the induction when the two inertia characters differ.

If $\Psi^2=1$, extension across conjugation gives the two quadratic twists. They are inequivalent, since a quadratic self-twist of the Tate representation here would make its restriction to $G_K$ reducible over an algebraic closure. In the CM case this would force $K$ to be the CM field, which was excluded. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-rl-chebotarev-evaluation"></a>
<div id="rl:chebotarev-evaluation" class="lemma">

**Lemma 83** (Simultaneous finite Chebotarev realization). *For any element $u$ of an exact kernel in Lemma <a href="#rl:kernel" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:kernel">81</a>, derivative primes can be chosen, at increasing finite precision, whose rational Frobenius is $\tau u$ on all retained data. Their finite localization is evaluation on $(\tau u)^2$. The assertion is compatible with any fixed finite list of previous derivative operations.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rl-chebotarev-evaluation"><summary>Proof of stmt-rl-chebotarev-evaluation</summary>

*Proof.* At one Artin stage, a coordinate of a cochain in the image of a finite model is a locally constant function. The finitely many coordinates being used factor through one finite quotient of the absolute Galois group. Enlarge it to contain the Tate action at the required precision, the finitely many ring-class fields and quadratic characters currently in use, and all old finite data. Chebotarev realizes the conjugacy class of $\tau u$ on this finite quotient, with a chosen place realizing the desired representative (Milne 2020b, chap. V, Theorem 3.23) <a id="pm-cite-107"></a>[[MilneCFT2020](#ref-MilneCFT2020)]. It gives a rational prime inert in $K$, outside the old finite set. Because $u$ is exactly Tate-trivial, its Frobenius tends to $\rho_T(\tau)$; in particular $a_\ell\to0$ and $\ell\to-1$. Because $u$ is exactly ring-class trivial, the square Frobenius on the $K$-prime is the identity on every retained ring-class field. The unramified local coordinate is therefore the stated Frobenius-square evaluation.

Repeat at each finite stage with increasing precision. All conditions remain finite, and no density bound or prime-size bound is required. Previously imposed finite diagrams are unchanged. ◻

</details>

In induced-module notation, restriction to the exact kernel is additive. For a crossed cocycle $b$ and an exact-kernel element $u$, $$b((\tau u)^2)=(1+\tau)b(u).$$ Indeed $\tau^2=1$, $u$ acts trivially on the coefficients, and the cocycle identity cancels the two occurrences of $b(\tau)$. Projection to either induced summand identifies $\operatorname{im}(1+\tau)$ with a two-dimensional coefficient module, also in characteristic two.

<a id="rd:local-subsection"></a>
#### The local switch and its integral determinant

Fix a complex conjugation $\tau$ and write $C_\tau$ for its action on $T$. The next two Lemmas construct the integral local switches and the classes that pass through them. Their finite-level formulas are needed before applying the limit constructions above.

<a id="stmt-lem-h-switching-pairing"></a>
<div id="lem:h:switching-pairing" class="lemma">

<a id="rd:local-cohomology"></a>
<a id="eq:h:local-coordinates"></a>
**Lemma 84** (The split local model). *<span id="rd:local-model" label="rd:local-model"></span>Let a sequence of inert good primes $\ell$ have rational Frobenius lifts tending on $T$ to a fixed complex conjugation $C_\tau$. At the unique prime of $K$ above $\ell$, the limiting local complex has $$H^0=M,\qquad H^1=F\oplus S=M\oplus M,\qquad H^2=M,
 \label{rd:local-cohomology}$$ with zero differentials in a free split model. Here $M=T\otimes\Lambda$ with the relevant scalar coefficient structure. The two degree-one coordinates of a cocycle are $$f(c)=c(\gamma^2),\qquad s(c)=c(\sigma),
 \label{eq:h:local-coordinates}$$ where $\sigma$ is an oriented pro-$2$ tame generator. The plane conditions $F=\{s=0\}$ and $S=\{f=0\}$ include $H^0$ and exclude $H^2$. Each is its own orthogonal complement for conjugate-Weil duality. The strict condition $H^0$ and the relaxed condition $H^0\oplus H^1[-1]$ are mutually dual. All four inclusions can be equipped with compatible integral duality triangles.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-h-switching-pairing"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-h-switching-pairing</summary>

*Proof.* The prime-to-$\ell$ local cochains are computed by the tame inertia and residue-field directions. In these two directions the differentials are formed from inertia minus one and Frobenius minus one, with the usual Frobenius action on tame inertia. On $M$, inertia is trivial at the derivative prime. The square of a rational Frobenius is trivial on every ring-class character. In the limit it is also the identity on $T$, while $\ell^2$ tends to one. Thus both differentials become zero, giving <a href="#rd:local-cohomology" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rd:local-cohomology">[rd:local-cohomology]</a>.

Here is a finite-precision check of the pairing, needed at $2$. At a retained quotient killed by $2^a$, impose also $q=\ell^2\equiv1\pmod{2^{a+1}}$, as well as trivial Frobenius-square action on the coefficient module at this quotient. The tame two-generator complex then has zero differentials, with the coordinates in <a href="#eq:h:local-coordinates" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:h:local-coordinates">[eq:h:local-coordinates]</a>. Its degree-one scalar generators are the unramified and tame characters. More explicitly, use the presentation $\phi\sigma\phi^{-1}\sigma^{-q}=1$. After augmentation with trivial coefficient action its Fox resolution has terms of ranks $1,2,1$, with $d^0=0$ and $d^1=(0,1-q)$, in the ordered finite and tame coordinates. The diagonal from the same resolution has zero pure-finite term, unit mixed terms, and pure-tame coefficient $\pm\binom q2$. The latter coefficient is the augmented second derivative of $\sigma^{-q}$ together with its adjacent $\sigma$ in the relation. Both $1-q$ and $\binom q2$ vanish modulo $2^a$ under the imposed congruence. Thus this is an actual split complex and an actual pure-plane zero pairing at the retained precision. The field contains the $2^{a+1}$-st roots of unity, so $-1$ is a $2^a$-th power. The norm-residue identity $(x,x)=(x,-1)$ for the $2^a$-Hilbert symbol therefore makes the square of each scalar generator zero. The two generators form a basis; local Tate duality makes their cross pairing a unit. The same calculation applies coefficientwise to the free Artin coefficient module, including its nilpotent $t$ and quadratic variables. Thus the pure plane restrictions are already zero at every retained quotient. All these congruences can be imposed simultaneously with the derivative Frobenius conditions by increasing their precision. Taking the compatible limit proves integral vanishing of the pure squares. It is not deduced from skew symmetry in characteristic two.

<a id="eq:h:cross-pairing"></a>
Equivalently, in the limiting tame presentation $\phi\sigma\phi^{-1}=\sigma^q$ with $q\to1$, the rank-$(1,2,1)$ resolution specializes to the exterior resolution for two procyclic directions. The finite Hilbert-symbol calculation specifies the cup product on its split cohomology and rules out a hidden square term. Conjugation transports the finite Tate coordinate by $C_\tau$ and the singular coordinate by $-C_\tau$, with possible scalar units coming from the orientations. Consequently the cross pairing is $$\beta(x,y)=\epsilon\,\langle x,C_\tau y\rangle,\qquad
 \epsilon\in\Lambda^\times,\quad x\in F,\ y\in S,
 \label{eq:h:cross-pairing}$$ where $\langle\, ,\,\rangle$ is the perfect alternating Weil form. This proves the assertions about orthogonal complements. Since the restrictions of this explicit pairing to either pure plane are zero as maps of the split complexes, their isotropy homotopies may be chosen to be zero. Only a product of two degree-one terms could map to the degree-two local invariant target; the degree-zero terms introduce no additional restriction. These zero homotopies agree on the strict subcomplex. These are the actual orthogonality data required in the Selmer duality construction (Nekovář 2006, Theorem 6.3.4) <a id="pm-cite-108"></a>[[Nekovar2006](#ref-Nekovar2006)]; the compatibility assertion is therefore an assertion about these displayed complexes and maps. Lemma <a href="#rl:finite-limits" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:finite-limits">74</a> is used to retain this finite diagram together with the unchanged local data. ◻

</details>

For a finite set $I$ of derivative primes, let $C_I$ be obtained from $C$ by replacing the finite plane condition $F$ by $S$ at each prime of $I$, retaining all other local conditions. The classes below use the same multiplier $L$ already included in $P$; in particular, $P_{\varnothing}=P$.

<a id="stmt-lem-h-derivative-classes"></a>
<div id="lem:h:derivative-classes" class="lemma">

<a id="eq:h:finite-singular"></a>
**Lemma 85** (Descent and the switch at $2$). *<span id="rd:derivative" label="rd:derivative"></span>Suppose that the finite ring-class transfers are performed before retaining their target cycles and witnesses as in Lemma <a href="#rl:finite-limits" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:finite-limits">74</a>. There is one integer $L\ne0$, depending on the fixed curve, parametrization and fixed local types, such that the classes obtained from the Heegner derivatives of $L$ times the point satisfy, for every finite switched set $I$, $$P_I\in H^1(C_I),\qquad
 f(P_{I\cup\{\ell\}})=0,\qquad
 s(P_{I\cup\{\ell\}})=C_\tau f(P_I).
 \label{eq:h:finite-singular}$$ The same $L$ works for every number of active and derivative primes. The previously imposed singular conditions are retained.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-h-derivative-classes"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-h-derivative-classes</summary>

*Proof.* We first descend the derivative classes using one multiplier for the complete conductor, and verify their Kummer conditions at $2N$. We then compute both local coordinates in Equation <a href="#eq:h:finite-singular" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:h:finite-singular">[eq:h:finite-singular]</a>. The last step retains these classes and identities in the same bounded target cochain diagrams used for evaluation.

<a id="rd:derivative-identity"></a>
<a id="eq:h:heegner-norm-reduction"></a>
Choose the orientations coherently. The relative ring-class group at an inert prime $\ell$ is cyclic of order $\ell+1$. For distinct new primes these groups form a product: the ring-class exact sequence has kernel the product of the local residue-unit quotients, and the only global units here are $1,-1$, whose images in these quotients are trivial. Set $$D_\ell=\sum_{i=1}^{\ell} i\sigma_\ell^i,\qquad
 D_I=\prod_{\ell\in I}D_\ell.$$ Direct multiplication gives $$(\sigma_\ell-1)D_\ell=(\ell+1)-
             \sum_{i=0}^{\ell}\sigma_\ell^i.
 \label{rd:derivative-identity}$$ The Hecke correspondence and reduction of its CM isogenies give, for every class-group translate, $$\operatorname{Tr}(y_{c r n})=a_\ell y_{c r n/\ell},
 \qquad
 \widetilde y_{c r n}=\operatorname{Fr}_\ell
                       \widetilde y_{c r n/\ell}.
 \label{eq:h:heegner-norm-reduction}$$ These are the point relations, not an application of a residual irreducibility theorem. A fixed multiple of the parametrization removes cuspidal terms.

There is a uniform bound on the $2$-primary torsion over the union of the ring-class fields in use. To see this, choose a fixed nonidentity scalar homothety of infinite order in the $2$-adic Tate image. Square a lift so that it belongs to every quadratic subgroup under consideration. Multiply it by its conjugate under complex conjugation. Its action on each ring-class field is trivial, because conjugation inverts the abelian ring-class action, while its action on $T$ is still a fixed nonidentity scalar. If $2^e$ annihilates its scalar minus one up to a unit, then $2^e$ kills the torsion in question. The existence of this fixed scalar, including the CM case, is the Tate-image input used in Lemma <a href="#rl:kernel" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:kernel">81</a>.

Work first with coefficients modulo $2^a$. Require $a_\ell$ and $\ell+1$ to vanish to a precision substantially larger than $a$. Equations <a href="#rd:derivative-identity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rd:derivative-identity">[rd:derivative-identity]</a> and <a href="#eq:h:heegner-norm-reduction" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:h:heegner-norm-reduction">[eq:h:heegner-norm-reduction]</a> then make the derivative Kummer class invariant under the relative ring-class group. In the inflation–restriction sequence, both the obstruction to descent and the ambiguity of descent are killed by $2^e$, since their coefficient module is killed by $2^e$. Multiplication by $2^{2e}$ therefore gives a descent independent of this ambiguity: descend $2^e$ times the class and multiply its lift by $2^e$. There is no repetition of this factor for individual primes; descent is performed once from the field with the complete conductor.

The global descent has cost only the fixed factor $2^{2e}$, regardless of the number of derivative primes. It remains to ensure that the descended class satisfies the Kummer condition at every fixed bad place; this is a separate local descent issue.

At a place over $2N$ these descent extensions are unramified. Here is the local descent argument, valid also for even extension degree and for toric or additive reduction. Let $F'/F$ be a finite unramified extension with group $G$, and write $k'/k$ for its residue extension. The successive formal-group quotients $E_j(F')/E_{j+1}(F')$ are additive copies of $k'$. The normal basis theorem makes each a cohomologically trivial $G$-module, without a restriction on $|G|$. Every finite quotient $E_1(F')/E_j(F')$ is therefore cohomologically trivial. The inverse systems of these finite groups and their invariant groups satisfy the Mittag–Leffler condition. Taking inverse limits in finite $G$-cochains consequently gives $H^1(G,E_1(F'))=0$. Let $\mathcal E/\mathcal O_F$ be the Néron model and put $\widetilde E^0=\mathcal E_k^0$, a smooth geometrically connected commutative algebraic group over the finite field $k$. Lang’s finite-extension cocycle theorem (Lang 1956, Proposition 3, p. 559) <a id="pm-cite-109"></a>[[Lang1956](#ref-Lang1956)] gives $H^1(G,\widetilde E^0(k'))=0$. The smooth reduction sequence then gives $H^1(G,E^0(F'))=0$. Let $\Phi=\mathcal E_k/\widetilde E^0$ be the finite étale component-group scheme. Each fiber over a point of $\Phi(k')$ is a torsor under $\widetilde E^0_{k'}$, and hence has a $k'$-point by Lang (1956, Theorem 2, pp. 557–558) <a id="pm-cite-110"></a>[[Lang1956](#ref-Lang1956)]. Smooth lifting therefore makes $E(F')\to\Phi(k')$ surjective. Hence $$H^1(G,E(F'))\lhook\joinrel\longrightarrow
 H^1(G,\Phi(k')).$$ Existence of the smooth finite-type model and smooth lifting follow from Bosch, Lütkebohmert, and Raynaud (1990, vol. 21, sec. 1.3, Corollary 2, and Section 2.3, Proposition 5) <a id="pm-cite-111"></a>[[BoschLutkebohmertRaynaud1990](#ref-BoschLutkebohmertRaynaud1990)]. The right side is killed by the exponent of $\Phi(\overline k)$. By inflation–restriction, the left side is exactly the kernel of $H^1(F,E)\to H^1(F',E)$. Thus the same fixed exponent makes a class in $H^1(F,E[2^a])$ Kummer whenever its restriction is Kummer. Néron models commute with unramified base extension (Bosch, Lütkebohmert, and Raynaud 1990, vol. 21, sec. 7.2, Theorem 1 and Corollary 2) <a id="pm-cite-112"></a>[[BoschLutkebohmertRaynaud1990](#ref-BoschLutkebohmertRaynaud1990)], so their geometric component groups are unchanged. Only the finitely many fixed local twisting types at $2N$ occur, so the product of these component exponents is bounded independently of the conductor and of the extension degree. Include this product, the single descent factor $2^{2e}$, and the parametrization factor in $L$. Thus the descended class has the integral Kummer condition at $2N$. No good-ordinary or semistability condition was used. Transfer with the scalar character preserves this condition because $\Psi=1$ there.

The single multiplier $L$ now gives descent with the required Kummer conditions. We next prove the finite-to-singular identity itself. Both coordinates matter: the singular coordinate must become $C_\tau f$, while the new finite coordinate must vanish at the retained precision.

Here is the local calculation, including the division by two. Apply the derivatives at all primes other than $\ell$, and write $X,Y$ for the resulting lower and upper points. Put $F_\ell=\operatorname{Fr}_\ell$. The lower field splits at the $K$-prime $(\ell)$, since that ideal is principal. Reduction therefore gives $F_\ell^2X=X$. The following Frobenius-polynomial identities are taken on the reduction; good odd-prime reduction is injective on the $2$-primary torsion coordinates being compared. If $Q$ is a $2^a$-division point of $LX$, the finite coordinate of its Kummer class is <a id="rd:finite-formula"></a>$$f=(F_\ell^2-1)Q=
       \bigl(a_\ell F_\ell-(\ell+1)\bigr)Q.
 \label{rd:finite-formula}$$ We give the descent-cocycle calculation of the other coordinate. Choose $Z$ with $2^aZ=LD_\ell Y$, and choose the descended cocycle $b$ so that on the upper-field Galois group it is $b(g)=(g-1)Z$. A change by the already bounded descent ambiguity has no effect on the eventual limit. The crossed identity gives $$U=(\sigma_\ell-1)Z-b(\sigma_\ell)
                  \in E(H_{crn}).$$ For $g$ in the upper-field Galois group, compare the two expansions of $b(g\sigma_\ell)$; they give $gU=U$. Moreover, $$2^aU=L\bigl((\ell+1)Y-a_\ell X\bigr).$$ Both integers $\ell+1,a_\ell$ are divisible by $2^a$. Consequently $$U_0=L\frac{\ell+1}{2^a}Y-
                      L\frac{a_\ell}{2^a}X$$ is an actual upper-field point with the same $2^a$-multiple as $U$. Thus $U-U_0$ is upper-field torsion of bounded exponent. This comparison with an actual integer quotient is what bounds the ambiguity; arbitrary division points would not give this bound. Reduction makes $\sigma_\ell$ act trivially and $\widetilde Y=F_\ell\widetilde X$. Therefore reduction of $b(\sigma_\ell)=-U$ gives its singular coordinate <a id="rd:singular-formula"></a>$$s=\bigl(a_\ell-(\ell+1)F_\ell\bigr)Q
 \label{rd:singular-formula}$$ up to the uniformly bounded descent torsion already described. The Frobenius polynomial yields the exact operator identity <a id="rd:exact-frobenius"></a>$$(F_\ell-a_\ell)
     \bigl(a_\ell F_\ell-(\ell+1)\bigr)
       =a_\ell-(\ell+1)F_\ell.
 \label{rd:exact-frobenius}$$ Thus $s=(F_\ell-a_\ell)f$; when $a_\ell$ vanishes at the retained torsion precision, this is $s=F_\ell f$. Taking the Frobenius limit gives $s=C_\tau f$.

If $\gamma$ is the chosen rational Frobenius lift, its image in the generalized-dihedral ring-class Galois group lies outside the abelian subgroup, so $\gamma^2$ acts trivially on the full upper ring-class field. The same lift therefore computes the descended finite Kummer coordinate from the reduced point over the common residue field $\mathbf F_{\ell^2}$. For the new finite coordinate, reduction of the derivative point is <a id="rd:half-factor"></a>$$\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}iF_\ell X
       =\frac{\ell(\ell+1)}2F_\ell X.
 \label{rd:half-factor}$$ The finite Kummer coordinate consequently vanishes modulo $2^a$ if $v_2(\ell+1)\ge a+1$. The additional $1$ is essential at $2$. It is imposed in the choice of the next precision, and does not multiply the class by a new denominator. Bounded torsion ambiguities disappear on passing from $E[2^a]$ to $E[2^m]$ with $a-m\ge e$. Choose $a$ and the Frobenius precision successively faster than $m$.

The calculation is compatible with every translate in the transfer: transport the place and its Frobenius before applying that translate. The scalar weight on the lower and upper class is identical. Applying the same calculation at each $\ell\in I$ proves the earlier singular conditions as well.

The local formulas now give the switch. To use it in the rank-reduction argument, we must retain more than its cohomology class: the transferred target cycles, local lifts and degree-two cochain identities must extend the original finite diagrams. We record this compatibility next.

Here the transfer itself is integral at the cochain level. For a finite Artin coefficient ring $A$, let $\Delta=\operatorname{Gal}(H_{cr}/K)$, through which the finite scalar and quadratic characters factor. Shapiro’s cochain map and the coefficient homomorphism $$A[\Delta]\longrightarrow A,\qquad
 [\sigma]\longmapsto\chi_e(\sigma)\Psi(\sigma)$$ send the descended class to the desired twisted class. For a universal quadratic family, replace the quadratic value by its group element in $A[G]$, also including the fixed base character. Choose inverse actions on both sides when using that Shapiro convention. Explicitly, these are the finite coset sums with the indicated scalar weights; there is no division by $\#\Delta$. These maps and their degree-zero and degree-two compatibility formulas are used at this finite stage, before passage to a bounded target model. Naturality of restriction and Kummer corestriction supplies the local lifts. At $2N$ the scalar character is trivial, so these are precisely the Kummer conditions of the indicated quadratic twist.

More explicitly, in the universal case let $\nu:\Delta\to G$ be the additional quadratic character. Perform the coefficient map $$A_i[\Delta]\longrightarrow A_i[G],\qquad
 [\sigma]\longmapsto
 \chi_{h_0}(\sigma)\Psi_i(\sigma)[\nu(\sigma)]$$ and the finite coset sum before any character evaluation. This gives one cycle over $A_i[G]$, with its local lifts. Every sign evaluation $A_i[G]\to A_i$ sends this cycle and these lifts to the corresponding weighted construction, because it commutes with finite sums and differentials. After contraction, compare an evaluated target model with its already chosen scalar model using their maps to the same original target cochains. Retain these comparison matrices and their contraction homotopies for all the finitely many characters of this fixed $G$. No character idempotent or division by a class-group order is used. At $t=0$ the split-prime norm multiplier on this universal cycle is $$a_{r_i}-2\chi_{h_0}(r_i)[\nu(\mathop{\mathrm{Fr}}_{\mathfrak r_i})].$$ The two conjugate Frobenius values of $\nu$ agree because each quadratic character comes from $\mathbb Q$. Evaluation at the character corresponding to $h$ therefore gives exactly $a_{r_i}-2\chi_h(r_i)$, with the central boundary witness described above.

Finally contract only the resulting target cycles, local lifts and boundary witnesses into the models over $K$. Retain the target comparison maps, the split local Fox complexes, their zero isotropy homotopies, and their duality and switch identities in degrees zero, one and two. The proof of Lemma <a href="#rl:finite-limits" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:finite-limits">74</a> shows explicitly how to transport these identities and their witnesses. In particular the unbounded cochains over $H_{cr}$ and the full Shapiro maps are not objects or maps of this limiting diagram. When a further derivative prime is selected, extend the same original finite-stage diagram and its contraction maps, using the same inner ultrafilter. Do not construct an unrelated cohomologically equivalent old complex. The earlier evaluations, including all degree-two cocycle identities, are consequently retained by the same contraction maps after each new switch. For a fixed finite set of switches and fixed $G$, the target rank bounds above apply. Lemma <a href="#rl:finite-limits" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:finite-limits">74</a> therefore applies to these extended target diagrams at their common retained precision. Their limiting classes give <a href="#eq:h:finite-singular" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:h:finite-singular">[eq:h:finite-singular]</a>. The displayed local formulas agree with the calculation underlying (Howard 2004, Proposition 1.7.4) <a id="pm-cite-113"></a>[[Howard2012](#ref-Howard2012)]; Howard’s odd-prime global hypotheses are not being asserted at $2$. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-lem-h-determinant-switch"></a>
<div id="lem:h:determinant-switch" class="lemma">

<a id="eq:h:switch-equality"></a>
**Lemma 86** (Preservation of the determinant coordinate). *Let $\mathcal O$ be a height-one discrete valuation ring at which the complexes and switching conditions are self-dual. Suppose the generic Selmer group for a set $I$ has rank one and is spanned by $P_I$, and $v_0=f(P_I)$ is nonzero at the next derivative prime. Then the switched generic group has rank one and is spanned by $P_{I\cup\{l\}}$, and $$\label{eq:h:switch-equality}
 v_{\mathcal O}(u_I)=v_{\mathcal O}(u_{I\cup\{l\}}).$$ This assertion does not require a primitive localization in either integral plane.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-h-determinant-switch"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-h-determinant-switch</summary>

*Proof.* Compare the strict condition and the relaxed condition of Lemma <a href="#lem:h:switching-pairing" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:h:switching-pairing">84</a>. Their complexes are dual. Over the fraction field, the image of relaxed $H^1$ in $F\oplus S$ is self-annihilating by Poitou–Tate, hence two-dimensional. Strict $H^1$ is zero because the original rank-one group localizes nontrivially. The relaxed image meets $F$ in the line spanned by $v_0$ and, by Equation <a href="#eq:h:finite-singular" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:h:finite-singular">[eq:h:finite-singular]</a>, meets $S$ in the nonzero line spanned by $C_\tau v_0$. Its intersection with either plane is therefore exactly a line. This proves the rank and spanning assertions.

For the integral determinant comparison let $A=P_I$ and $B=P_{I\cup\{l\}}$ be a field basis of relaxed $H^1$. The dual basis $A^\vee,B^\vee$ belongs to strict $H^2$. In the triangle adding $F[-1]$ to the strict complex, the map $F\to H^2_{\mathrm{str}}$ pairs a vector $x$ against the relaxed localization. By Equations <a href="#eq:h:cross-pairing" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:h:cross-pairing">[eq:h:cross-pairing]</a> and <a href="#eq:h:finite-singular" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:h:finite-singular">[eq:h:finite-singular]</a>, it is a unit times $\langle x,v_0\rangle B^\vee$. The remaining $H^2$ quotient maps to $A^\vee$. Choose $x$ mapping to $B^\vee$. Although $v_0$ and $x$ need not be integral separately, the volume of the ordered basis $(v_0,x)$ of $F$ is a unit of $\mathcal O$, precisely because its symplectic pairing is a unit. For $S$ use $C_\tau v_0$ and a preimage of $A^\vee$; its volume is again a unit. The two determinant tensors thus map, up to units, to the same tensor in the strict determinant, using $A^\vee\wedge B^\vee$. All triangles and plane lattices in this comparison are integral. Their determinant isomorphisms consequently give Equation <a href="#eq:h:switch-equality" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:h:switch-equality">[eq:h:switch-equality]</a>, including any torsion or localization-index contribution. ◻

</details>

<a id="sec:h:rank-reduction"></a>
#### Rank reduction and nonnegative divisors

The derivative-prime reduction follows the Kolyvagin-system argument of Howard (2004, Lemmas 1.5.3 and 1.6.4) <a id="pm-cite-114"></a>[[Howard2012](#ref-Howard2012)]. We carry its switches through integral Selmer complexes and preserve their determinant coordinate. The local calculation and descent above supply the characteristic-two pairing and one fixed multiplier; the argument below supplies the uniformity as the conductor varies.

We now prove the first two bounds in Equation <a href="#eq:h:divisor-bounds" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:h:divisor-bounds">[eq:h:divisor-bounds]</a>. A height-one specialization can have larger Selmer dimension than the generic rank-one line. Local switches will remove that excess dimension while preserving the determinant valuation. At test dimension one, integrality is immediate. At the coefficient prime $(2)$ this argument uses residual irreducibility and therefore applies here to genus data.

Use the sequence groups $\Gamma_K\subset\Gamma$ of Lemma <a href="#rl:evaluation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:evaluation">[rl:evaluation]</a>, and write $\mathcal H$ for the exact kernel of Lemma <a href="#rl:kernel" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:kernel">81</a>. Over the relevant test field, put $W=\operatorname{Ind}_{\Gamma_K}^{\Gamma}(T\chi_e\Psi)$. Lemma <a href="#rl:chebotarev-evaluation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:chebotarev-evaluation">83</a> realizes finite localization as the projection of $(1+\tau)b(u')$, for $u'\in\mathcal H$, to one induced summand. Restriction to $\mathcal H$ is injective by Lemma <a href="#rl:kernel" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:kernel">81</a>, and evaluation there is additive and Galois-equivariant. The image of $1+\tau$ is a copy of the two-dimensional summand, also in characteristic two.

<a id="stmt-lem-h-height-one-reduction"></a>
<div id="lem:h:height-one-reduction" class="lemma">

**Lemma 87** (Rank reduction at a height-one prime). *Suppose a primitive instance has generic cohomology of rank at most one in degrees one and two, zero elsewhere, and $P$ spans $H^1$ when it is nonzero. Then the first line of Equation <a href="#eq:h:divisor-bounds" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:h:divisor-bounds">[eq:h:divisor-bounds]</a> holds. These hypotheses hold in every simple-zero instance and also at the base of Theorem <a href="#thm:heegner-interpolation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:heegner-interpolation">10</a>. The second line holds in genus data with irreducible $E[2]$, with a bound independent of the number of active or derivative primes.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-h-height-one-reduction"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-h-height-one-reduction</summary>

*Proof.* There is nothing to prove if $u=0$. Otherwise the generic rank is one and $P$ is nonzero. Localize, and if convenient complete, at a height-one prime. Test its residue field; at $(2)$ do this argument only in genus data with irreducible residual representation. Suppose first that $\Psi^2\ne1$ on the field. Then $W$ is irreducible. Inertia at $r$ distinguishes its two induced summands. On one summand, irreducibility of $T$ over $K$ comes from open image or the CM normalizer in characteristic zero, and from the assumed residual irreducibility at $(2)$. In the latter case we have omitted the fields meeting $\mathbb Q(E[2])$ nontrivially. The cyclic cubic residual case remains irreducible over $\mathbb F_2((t))$, with a possibly quadratic commuting field. Constant Tate matrix images are realized on the sequence group; scalar character twists do not change this irreducibility.

Let the test Selmer $H^1$ have dimension $s\ge2$. Include the reduction of a primitive generator of the generic free $H^1$ lattice among two independent classes. We can arrange that their localization has rank two. To see this, if the classes are independent over the commuting field of $W$, simplicity and the injective restriction in Lemma <a href="#rl:kernel" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:kernel">81</a> imply that the field span of their joint evaluations on $\mathcal H$ is the whole of $W\oplus W$. Otherwise a nontrivial equivariant linear relation would vanish on restriction, and hence on the original classes. Projection by $1+\tau$ therefore spans all pairs in the two-dimensional localization space. Some actual evaluation pair has nonzero determinant: a homogeneous quadratic vanishing on an additive group vanishes on its field span, since its polar form vanishes on every pair from the group. This argument is valid in characteristic two as well. If the classes are dependent over the commuting field but independent over the ground field, projection commutes with that field action on the graph of $\tau$. At the residual prime $(2)$, in the cyclic cubic case, this commuting field is $\mathbb F_4((t))$: rational complex conjugation has trivial residual image, so the commuting-field action is the same on the two induced summands. If the second class is $\alpha$ times the first, with $\alpha$ outside $\mathbb F_2((t))$, a nonzero projected evaluation $v$ gives the ground-field-independent pair $v,\alpha v$. Thus this case also gives rank-two localization.

Choose the derivative prime realizing that evaluation. Its localization is nonzero on the primitive generic generator. The relaxed image on the test fiber is self-annihilating of dimension two, and contains all of $F$ because the finite localization has rank two. It is therefore $F$. Switching to $S$ lowers test $H^1$ dimension by two. Generically, Lemmas <a href="#lem:h:derivative-classes" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:h:derivative-classes">85</a> and <a href="#lem:h:determinant-switch" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:h:determinant-switch">86</a> keep rank one, a nonzero class, and the same determinant valuation.

It remains to treat $\Psi^2=1$, which occurs here only in characteristic zero. Extend $\Psi$ across $\tau$ and split into the two conjugation signs. Conjugation on the cochains includes $1+t\mapsto(1+t)^{-1}$, which is trivial on this fiber. The fixed Kummer conditions and relaxed conditions are preserved. At previously switched places the split local model has diagonal conjugation action on $f,s$, so its plane conditions are preserved too. The induced representation now splits into two nonisomorphic absolutely irreducible twists. Finite and singular localization each have one line per sign. Within a sign the pairing is a symmetric hyperbolic pairing of those two isotropic lines; the signs are orthogonal.

If both Selmer signs occur, the restriction argument just used gives rank-two localization by choosing one class of each sign, with a nonzero component of the primitive generator among them. If only one sign occurs and $s>1$, choose rank-one localization nonzero on that generator. The relaxed image has a self-annihilating line in each sign. In the sign hit this is the finite line; in the other it must be the singular line, since a symmetric hyperbolic plane in characteristic zero has exactly these two isotropic lines. The switch preserves the total dimension but introduces the other sign: the old strict kernel has dimension $s-1\ge1$ and the new singular line contributes the second sign. A subsequent rank-two switch reduces dimension. Iteration reaches test rank one; it cannot pass below one, because the generic rank-one class has been retained throughout.

At test rank one the minimal self-dual complex over the DVR has one free term in each of degrees one and two and zero differential; there are no invariants. An integral class and its integral dual functional therefore give an integral determinant coordinate. Reversing the switches gives the first assertion. At $(2)$ the initial fixed descent and local multiples cost a bounded valuation, independent of every subsequent switch. This proves the second assertion with the stated uniformity. ◻

</details>

<a id="sec:h:uniform-ring-bound"></a>
#### Uniformity without residual irreducibility

Only the ring-data bound at $(2)$ remains. Residual irreducibility is not assumed, so the preceding argument on that residue field does not cover every instance. We first bound the model sizes and retain evaluation through a second limit. These constructions turn a hypothetical sequence of unbounded negative determinant valuations into a characteristic-zero outer limit. There the retained evaluation maps permit rank reduction and force a bounded denominator, giving a contradiction.

<a id="stmt-rl-residual-bound"></a>
<div id="rl:residual-bound" class="lemma">

**Lemma 88** (Uniform residual sizes). *Suppose $\omega(\operatorname{disc}K)\leq A$, the local twisting classes at $2N$ belong to a fixed finite list, and all active conductor primes are split with odd Frobenius exponent of the deformation character. After localization and completion at $(2)$, the minimal free ranks of the Selmer complexes are bounded in terms of $E,A$, and the number of retained derivative primes. They do not depend on the number of active conductor primes.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rl-residual-bound"><summary>Proof of stmt-rl-residual-bound</summary>

*Proof.* Reduce first over $\mathbf F_2[[t]]$. The quadratic character is now trivial. Removing the active conductor primes from the permitted ramification set changes the global complex by their singular local complexes. These, and their unramified local complexes, are acyclic after inverting $t$, by Lemma <a href="#rl:local-acyclic" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:local-acyclic">[rl:local-acyclic]</a>. The resulting smaller-support complex, including its comparison maps, can be constructed at the original Artin stages before taking the limit. Its support consists of $2N,r$, and the retained derivative primes. Its $\mathbf F_2((t))$ cohomology dimensions are bounded by those at $t=0$: choose a minimal finite free model over $\mathbf F_2[[t]]$.

Here is a uniform bound for the latter residual cohomology. Put $F=\mathbf Q(E[2])$, a fixed field. Then $FK/F$ is at most quadratic. Enlarge the allowed set of primes of $F$ by those ramified in $K$. Its cardinality is bounded by a constant depending on $E,A$ and the number of derivative primes. Kummer theory bounds the number of generators of the maximal pro-$2$ Galois group over $F$ unramified outside this set, using the fixed unit group, the fixed $2$-class group, and the allowed valuations. The subgroup defining $FK$ has index at most two; the elementary Schreier bound bounds its generator number. Every finite Galois $2$-extension of $FK$ with this ramification has Galois closure of $2$-power degree over $F$, so this subgroup indeed controls the required pro-$2$ extensions of $FK$.

Over $FK$ the residual Tate module is trivial. Restriction and inflation–restriction therefore bound the residual $H^1$ over $K$. The $H^0$ bound is immediate, and the global Euler characteristic or global duality bounds $H^2$. The local terms at the remaining bounded set have bounded dimensions, with degrees of the local fields at most two over the fixed rational local fields. At $2N$ there are only finitely many local quadratic twisting classes. The same bounds apply to the Selmer cone. Lemma <a href="#rl:finite-model" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:finite-model">[rl:finite-model]</a> now bounds the minimal ranks. Determinant valuations will require a separate argument. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-84"></a>
##### Evaluation through the outer limit

The preceding evaluation argument concerns one inner construction over a fixed $K$. The ring bound must also be uniform when $K$ and the conductor vary. When all active primes split and $\omega(k)$ is bounded, Lemma <a href="#rl:residual-bound" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:residual-bound">88</a> bounds the model sizes after any fixed number of derivative operations. The next proposition shows that passing to a second limit of such models preserves detection, including classes represented only by approximate cycles before that limit.

<a id="stmt-rl-outer-evaluation"></a>
<div id="rl:outer-evaluation" class="proposition">

**Proposition 89** (Integral evaluation through the outer limit). *Let $C_j$ be any family of the preceding limiting complexes, completed over $\mathcal O_j=\widehat{\Lambda_{(2)}}$, possibly for different quadratic fields $K_j$. Suppose their minimal ranks are bounded. Assume a common bounded cohomological degree interval. Keep the actual evaluation matrices and transport them to the minimal models through integral contractions. For a nonprincipal ultrafilter $\mathcal U$, put $$\mathcal O_\infty=
 \left(\prod_{\mathcal U}\mathcal O_j\right)/\mathfrak a,
 \qquad
 \mathfrak a=\{(x_j):
    \{j:v_2(x_j)\geq n\}\in\mathcal U\text{ for every }n\}.$$ Then $\mathcal O_\infty$ is a DVR with uniformizer $2$ and a characteristic-zero fraction field $L_\infty$. The outer $H^1$ over $L_\infty$ injects into crossed classes on the inner quadratic sequence group product, or its extension by one simultaneous complex conjugation for the induced representation. Its restriction to the product of their exact common kernels is injective. All arbitrary-sequence degree-two evaluation identities survive. These conclusions also hold after retaining any fixed finite collection of additional integral diagrams.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rl-outer-evaluation"><summary>Proof of stmt-rl-outer-evaluation</summary>

*Proof.* A nonzero element of the quotient has a representative whose valuations are bounded on an ultrafilter-large set. A finite partition then makes its valuation equal to a single integer $n$ on such a set. It is $2^n$ times a unit. Products add these finite valuations, so the quotient is a domain, and every nonzero ideal has an element of smallest valuation. It is consequently a DVR. The integer $2^n$ is nonzero for every $n$, so its fraction field has characteristic zero.

For each $j$, all-sequence evaluation maps originally have entries in $\Lambda$. Extension to $\mathcal O_j$ and composition with an integral contraction still give integral matrices. Thus evaluation on any sequence of inner group elements has an entrywise image in $\mathcal O_\infty$. Equations <a href="#rl:eval-boundary" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rl:eval-boundary">[rl:eval-boundary]</a> and <a href="#rl:eval-cocycle" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rl:eval-cocycle">[rl:eval-cocycle]</a> survive for all such sequences. In particular, if an outer cycle is represented by vectors $x_j$ for which $d_jx_j$ has valuation tending to infinity, the evaluation of $d_jx_j$ does too: the degree-two evaluation matrix is integral. Thus an outer cycle gives an exact crossed cocycle even when its representatives are only approximate inner cycles.

Over the inner residue field $\Omega_j$, choose a detecting list as in Lemma <a href="#rl:evaluation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:evaluation">[rl:evaluation]</a>; its length is at most $\dim_{\Omega_j}H^1(C_j\otimes\Omega_j)+\operatorname{rank}M$. These lengths are bounded. Include in the integral diagrams the evaluation map to its two-term complex and a contraction of its cone to a complex starting in degree one. Such a contraction uses only unit pivots over $\mathcal O_j$ and has bounded graded sizes. All its matrices, including inverses and homotopies, are integral and pass to the quotient.
