Its cone still starts in degree one after extension to $L_\infty$. This proves injectivity just as in Lemma <a href="#rl:evaluation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:evaluation">[rl:evaluation]</a>.

Let $H_j$ be the inner exact kernel. In the product of the quadratic sequence groups, the central elements of Lemma <a href="#rl:kernel" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:kernel">81</a> give a central element modulo $\prod_jH_j$ with scalar $u^4$. Since $u^4-1$ remains nonzero in $\mathcal O_\infty$, the same calculation gives restriction injectivity. For the induced representation first restrict to the quadratic subgroup, as in Lemma <a href="#rl:kernel" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:kernel">81</a>. Additional finite diagrams pass through the same entrywise operations. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-rl-outer-irreducibility"></a>
<div id="rl:outer-irreducibility" class="lemma">

**Lemma 90** (Irreducibility in the outer limit). *On the outer characteristic-zero test, $\Psi$ has infinite order and the four-dimensional representation induced from $T\chi\Psi$ is absolutely irreducible.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rl-outer-irreducibility"><summary>Proof of stmt-rl-outer-irreducibility</summary>

*Proof.* The inner irreducibility argument requires a uniform finite witness to survive this limit. The images of the quadratic subgroups have index at most two in the fixed compact $2$-adic Tate image. A compact $2$-adic analytic group is topologically finitely generated and hence has only finitely many closed subgroups of index at most two. Choose one on an ultrafilter-large set. Its absolutely irreducible representation has finitely many matrices spanning $M_2(\mathbf Q_2)$; the determinant expressing this spanning property is a fixed nonzero $2$-adic number. Every one of these Tate matrices is realized by choices of Galois elements in each component. Their accompanying character scalars are units and do not change the spanning assertion. Its determinant remains nonzero in $L_\infty$. This proves absolute irreducibility in that field. Also $1+t$ has infinite order already in every $\Omega_j$: for a nonzero integer $n$, the first nonzero term of $(1+t)^n-1$ occurs in finite degree. It remains a unit modulo $2$ in every component, so no such power becomes one in the outer field.

The two induced summands therefore have different inertia scalars, $\Psi$ and $\Psi^{-1}$, and the induction is absolutely irreducible as in Lemma <a href="#rl:irreducibility" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:irreducibility">82</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-rl-outer-chebotarev"></a>
<div id="rl:outer-chebotarev" class="lemma">

**Lemma 91** (Prime realization through the outer limit). *The finite Chebotarev realization of Lemma <a href="#rl:chebotarev-evaluation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:chebotarev-evaluation">83</a> is compatible with Proposition <a href="#rl:outer-evaluation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:outer-evaluation">89</a> and with any fixed finite list of previous derivative operations.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rl-outer-chebotarev"><summary>Proof of stmt-rl-outer-chebotarev</summary>

*Proof.* Apply Lemma <a href="#rl:chebotarev-evaluation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:chebotarev-evaluation">83</a> at each finite stage. For an outer sequence do this separately for each inner sequence, retaining the relevant finite evaluation matrices and degree-two identities before taking the outer quotient. Approximate inner cycles cause no problem, by the integrality calculation in Proposition <a href="#rl:outer-evaluation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:outer-evaluation">89</a>. Previously imposed finite diagrams are unchanged. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-rl-limit-evaluation-package"></a>
<div id="rl:limit-evaluation-package" class="theorem">

**Theorem 92** (Compatibility of the limit constructions). *The finite free models, ring-class characters, local conditions and pairings constructed above can be retained simultaneously. Their inner limits have the stated height-one acyclicity and all-sequence cohomology detection. For all-split ring data with bounded $\omega(\operatorname{disc}K)$, the residual model sizes are bounded independently of the active conductor support. Their outer limits retain arbitrary evaluations, exact-kernel injectivity and finite Chebotarev realization after any fixed number of additional integral arithmetic operations.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rl-limit-evaluation-package"><summary>Proof of stmt-rl-limit-evaluation-package</summary>

*Proof.* Use Lemma <a href="#rl:finite-model" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:finite-model">[rl:finite-model]</a> at each finite stage and keep the same contractions and ultrafilter as in Lemma <a href="#rl:finite-limits" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:finite-limits">74</a>. Perform the finite ring-class transfer and weighting first, retaining only the resulting bounded target cycles and witnesses as in that lemma; no limit of the growing Shapiro source is taken. The local assertions and uniform residual sizes are Lemmas <a href="#rl:kummer" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:kummer">[rl:kummer]</a>, <a href="#rl:local-acyclic" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:local-acyclic">[rl:local-acyclic]</a> and <a href="#rl:residual-bound" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:residual-bound">88</a>; the required characters come from Proposition <a href="#rl:characters" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:characters">[rl:characters]</a>. Lemmas <a href="#rl:evaluation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:evaluation">[rl:evaluation]</a> and <a href="#rl:kernel" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:kernel">81</a> give inner detection. Proposition <a href="#rl:outer-evaluation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:outer-evaluation">89</a> and Lemma <a href="#rl:outer-chebotarev" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:outer-chebotarev">91</a> preserve it through the outer limit and later finite operations. Every retained identity is an identity of actual integral matrices. The finite derivative classes and local identities of Lemma <a href="#lem:h:derivative-classes" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:h:derivative-classes">85</a> are among the integral arithmetic target diagrams retained in these operations, including the central norm relation before and after sign evaluation. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-lem-h-uniform-ring-determinant"></a>
<div id="lem:h:uniform-ring-determinant" class="lemma">

**Lemma 93** (Uniform determinant bound in ring data). *For simple-zero ring data with every active conductor prime split in $K$ and $\omega(k)\le a$, the coordinate of Definition <a href="#def:h:determinant-coordinate" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="def:h:determinant-coordinate">78</a> satisfies $$v_{(2)}(u)\ge -C_{E,a},$$ where $C_{E,a}$ is independent of $h$ and $K$. There is no residual irreducibility assumption. This is the last line of Equation <a href="#eq:h:divisor-bounds" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:h:divisor-bounds">[eq:h:divisor-bounds]</a>.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-h-uniform-ring-determinant"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-h-uniform-ring-determinant</summary>

*Proof.* Put $O=\widehat{\Lambda_{(2)}}$. By Lemma <a href="#rl:residual-bound" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:residual-bound">88</a>, after any fixed number of derivative switches the minimal $O$-models have bounded size in terms of $E$, $a$ and that number, independently of $h$. The full local complexes at $r$ and the active split primes are contractible over $O$, and the switched planes are integrally self-dual. Thus the class and its paired closed functional have a common bounded clearing exponent, supplied by the fixed descent multiplier and the retained global duality map.

Suppose the asserted lower bound fails. Choose instances with $v_O(u)\to-\infty$. Cancel disks over $O$ and take an outer limit of their bounded free models. Transport the class, closed functional, evaluations and the retained comparison and switch maps through these integral contractions, applying the same contractions to their boundary witnesses. Only the resulting bounded target vectors and matrices enter the outer diagram; the eliminated list of active-place complexes does not. Concretely, take the ultraproduct of their valuation rings and quotient by the ideal of sequences whose valuation tends to infinity. The resulting ring $\mathcal O_\infty$ is a DVR with uniformizer $2$: a nonzero sequence has a finite valuation on an ultrafilter-large set and is that power of $2$ times a unit. Its fraction field has characteristic zero. All integral matrix identities, duality diagrams, and the local switch diagrams pass to this limit.

Proposition <a href="#rl:outer-evaluation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:outer-evaluation">89</a> gives injective evaluation on the outer sequence group and on its exact common kernel. This includes outer cycles represented by approximate inner cycles, since their coboundaries are evaluated by integral degree-two matrices. The fixed central scalar remains different from one in the outer field. Lemma <a href="#rl:outer-irreducibility" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:outer-irreducibility">90</a> gives absolute irreducibility of the induced representation there: the scalar $1+t$ has infinite order and distinguishes the two summands.

Each individual minimal $O$-complex is a square complex in degrees one and two, by self-duality and the absence of residual invariants. Choose a primitive vector in its generic kernel. Such vectors survive the outer limit, so outer $H^1$ has rank at least one. If its rank exceeds one, choose rank-two localization by the absolutely irreducible evaluation argument in Lemma <a href="#lem:h:height-one-reduction" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:h:height-one-reduction">87</a>, making it nonzero on one of these primitive vectors. The inner Chebotarev construction realizes the corresponding sequences of derivative primes. At each original Artin stage retain the old contractions and evaluations, adjoin the new local and derivative diagrams, and pass through the same inner and outer ultrafilters. Slower cofinal coefficient precision is permitted; independent reconstruction of the old diagrams is not. For an ultrafilter-large set of instances the localization is generically nonzero. Lemma <a href="#lem:h:determinant-switch" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:h:determinant-switch">86</a> preserves the valuations tending to minus infinity, while the outer rank falls by two. The new complexes and integral classes obey the same bounds, with only the now fixed finite number of added derivative primes.

The process must reach outer rank one: ranks are finite and cannot fall below one while the primitive kernel vector is retained. At this stage some maximal boundary minor is nonzero over the outer fraction field. Its valuation is consequently bounded in the individual DVRs on an ultrafilter-large set. Split that minor over their fraction fields. The entries of the class and duality maps are integral and their common initial multipliers are bounded. The formula for their determinant coordinate, or the elementary-divisor decomposition, then has a lower valuation bound depending on this minor and the bounded complex size. The Heegner classes themselves need not survive the outer limit: a numerator tending to zero only increases its valuation. It is the primitive kernel vector that preserves rank, and the boundary minor that bounds the denominators. This contradicts $v_O(u)\to-\infty$, and proves the uniform estimate. ◻

</details>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-h-uniform-ring-determinant-2"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-h-uniform-ring-determinant</summary>

*Proof of Theorems <a href="#thm:heegner-genus-bound" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:heegner-genus-bound">13</a> and <a href="#thm:heegner-ring-bound" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:heegner-ring-bound">14</a>.* By Lemmas <a href="#lem:h:height-one-reduction" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:h:height-one-reduction">87</a> and <a href="#lem:h:uniform-ring-determinant" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:h:uniform-ring-determinant">93</a>, the element $u$ has nonnegative valuation away from $(2)$ and a uniformly bounded negative valuation at $(2)$. Normality of $\Lambda$ implies that a fixed power of $2$ times $u$ belongs to $\Lambda$. Its central value therefore has the same lower valuation bound.

In genus data, $s(h_*)$ and the weight of $h_*$ are fixed, $c=1$, and $k=hh_*$. Equations <a href="#eq:h:central-determinant" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:h:central-determinant">[eq:h:central-determinant]</a> and <a href="#eq:h:weil-restriction-length" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:h:weil-restriction-length">[eq:h:weil-restriction-length]</a> give Equation <a href="#eq:h:genus-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:h:genus-bound">[eq:h:genus-bound]</a>. The excluded intersection fields are finite in number, since an irreducible two-division field has at most one quadratic subfield. In ring data, the sum over $q\mid k$ is bounded by $2\omega(k)$, whereas $2\sum_{q\mid h}t_q=4w(h)$. The same equations give Equation <a href="#eq:h:ring-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:h:ring-bound">[eq:h:ring-bound]</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="sec:h:universal-class"></a>
#### The universal Heegner class

For interpolation we combine the non-$(2)$ divisor estimate and the central valuation formula with a universal binary family. The characterwise coordinates must have a uniformly controlled clearing factor. We first remove the norm and local determinant factors belonging to primes unused at a character, then eliminate the new-prime blocks before choosing that clearing factor.

Recall the binary coefficient rings: $$G\simeq(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)^b,\qquad R=\Lambda[G],\qquad
 O=\widehat{\Lambda_{(2)}}.$$ We work with the universal quadratic character over $R$ for the family in Theorem <a href="#thm:heegner-interpolation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:heegner-interpolation">10</a>. At a new prime $q$ let $g_q\in G$ be its inertia bit: at a character $x$, it evaluates to $-1$ when $q$ is active and to $1$ when it is unused. Choose the conductor character of Proposition <a href="#rl:characters" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:characters">[rl:characters]</a> with odd exponents at all the new split primes. In the universal complex relax at every new prime and at the old active primes, and take the trace class $p$ from the conductor containing all new primes, together with $r$ and the old conductor. As in the proof of Lemma <a href="#lem:h:derivative-classes" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:h:derivative-classes">85</a>, form its $A_i[G]$-weighted target cycle at each finite stage, together with its local lifts and boundary witnesses, before evaluating any sign character. Apply the limit construction for this fixed $G$ to those target data; the source ring-class cochains do not enter the limiting diagram. Choose an integral determinant basis and write $u_{\mathrm{rel}}$ for the characterwise determinant coordinate.

<a id="stmt-lem-h-unused-prime-correction"></a>
<div id="lem:h:unused-prime-correction" class="lemma">

<a id="eq:h:normalized-vertex-bound"></a>
**Lemma 94** (Removing the unused-prime factors). *There is $\eta\in O[G]$ such that $u=\eta u_{\mathrm{rel}}$ agrees at each character with the primitive determinant coordinate up to a $\Lambda$-unit. In particular, $u_x\in\Lambda[1/2]$. If the base product derivative is zero, then $u_0(0)=0$. At the nonzero vertices, $$\label{eq:h:normalized-vertex-bound}
 v(u_x(0))\le B+O_{E,h_0,a}(1),$$ where $a$ bounds $\omega(k)$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-h-unused-prime-correction"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-h-unused-prime-correction</summary>

*Proof.* At an unused prime, the norm relation multiplies the primitive point class by $$e_q=\begin{cases}
 a_q,&q\text{ inert in }K,\\
 a_q-z-z^{-1},&q\text{ split in }K,
 \end{cases}$$ where $z=\chi_{h_0}\Psi$ times the universal quadratic scalar at an oriented Frobenius. The relaxed singular quotient contributes $$l_q=\prod_{v\mid q}
  \det\left(1-q_v^{-1}\eta_v(\mathop{\mathrm{Fr}}_v)\mathop{\mathrm{Fr}}_v\mid T\right),$$ where $q_v$ is the residue cardinality and $\eta_v$ denotes the full scalar character. Thus $u_{\mathrm{rel}}$ differs from the primitive coordinate by $e_q^2/l_q$, up to a $\Lambda$-unit. This follows from the localization triangle with its integral determinant isomorphism; the pairing comparison is made over the fraction field. Choose conjugate-compatible Frobenius lifts in these formulas, taking the square of rational Frobenius at an inert place, and extend the expressions universally over $O[G]$.

<a id="eq:h:group-ring-correction"></a>
Both $e_q$ and $l_q$ are units in $O[G]$. At a split prime, the odd Frobenius exponent gives a nonconstant scalar in $\mathbb F_2((t))$; at an inert new prime, the hypothesis $t_q=0$ gives an odd trace. Moreover, already in the group ring, $l_q\equiv e_q^2\pmod2$. In the split case the residual identity is $$(1+a_qz+z^2)(1+a_qz^{-1}+z^{-2})
       =a_q^2+z^2+z^{-2}=(a_q+z+z^{-1})^2.$$ In the inert case the Frobenius-square polynomial gives $a_q^2$. Here the group-like quadratic scalars have square one, so the identities hold before sign evaluation. Consequently $$\label{eq:h:group-ring-correction}
 \eta=\prod_{q\ \mathrm{new}}
  \left(1+\frac{l_q/e_q^2-1}{2}(1+g_q)\right)
       \quad\text{belongs to }O[G].$$ Its factor is $l_q/e_q^2$ at unused characters and $1$ at active characters. It makes the required correction without an idempotent denominator for each prime.

For all the primitive constituents, generic cohomology has rank at most one. At nonzero vertices this follows from the simple-zero assumption. At the base it follows from Selmer corank one; a nonzero generic class then spans the possible rank-one group. Hence Lemma <a href="#lem:h:height-one-reduction" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:h:height-one-reduction">87</a> applies to every nonzero primitive determinant coordinate. Its nonnegative valuations away from $(2)$ imply membership in $\Lambda[1/2]$, by normality. The same assertion is automatic for a zero coordinate.

If the base derivative vanishes, Equation <a href="#eq:h:height" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:h:height">[eq:h:height]</a> makes the specialized point torsion. Either its generic determinant coordinate is zero or the specialization is at constant rational rank one and its degree-one class is zero there. In either case $u_0(0)=0$. At a nonzero vertex use Equations <a href="#eq:h:central-determinant" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:h:central-determinant">[eq:h:central-determinant]</a> and <a href="#eq:h:weil-restriction-length" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:h:weil-restriction-length">[eq:h:weil-restriction-length]</a>. Subtracting the two Sha lengths and $4w(h_x)$ leaves precisely the expression bounded in Equation <a href="#eq:h:interpolation-hypothesis" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:h:interpolation-hypothesis">[eq:h:interpolation-hypothesis]</a>, together with bounded terms at $k$, the old support and $r$. This gives Equation <a href="#eq:h:normalized-vertex-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:h:normalized-vertex-bound">[eq:h:normalized-vertex-bound]</a>. ◻

</details>

The corrected coordinates have the required upper bounds at nonzero vertices and vanish at the center if the base derivative vanishes. To apply binary transfer, we still need $f,d\in O[G]$ with $d_x=f_xu_x$ at every character. The required controls are a bound on $v(f_0(0))$ and, at each fixed precision, a bound on the negative Laurent support of every $f_x$. The next lemma obtains those bounds from the old complex, whose size is bounded, rather than from the full growing conductor.

<a id="stmt-lem-h-family-clearing"></a>
<div id="lem:h:family-clearing" class="lemma">

**Lemma 95** (A uniform clearing factor for the Heegner family). *For the element $u$ of Lemma <a href="#lem:h:unused-prime-correction" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:h:unused-prime-correction">94</a>, there are $f,d\in O[G]$ with $d_x=f_xu_x$ at every character, $f_0\in\Lambda$, and $v(f_0(0))$ uniformly bounded. For each fixed $M$, the negative Laurent support of every $f_x\bmod2^M$ has a bound independent of $b$ and of the number of new primes.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-h-family-clearing"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-h-family-clearing</summary>

*Proof.* First make the pairing functional integral up to a bounded multiplier. The class $p$ is integral. Lift $2^{a_0}p$ to the complex strict at the relaxed places and use integral duality against the relaxed complex. At $r$ and every new prime the full local complex over $O[G]$ is contractible: its reduction at the maximal ideal is acyclic, by the local calculation in Lemma <a href="#lem:h:relaxed-local" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:h:relaxed-local">77</a> and the root-type alternative. At the old active primes its cohomology is killed by a bounded power of $2$, because inertia is minus identity. The old support is fixed. Thus $a_0$ is bounded independently of the new primes. After inverting $2$, lifting is canonical. We obtain a closed representative of the paired functional over $2^{-a_0}O[G]$.

At augmentation, present the complex as the old complex, with no new primes, extended by the direct sum of their singular complexes. Each singular complex is a bounded-size block in degrees one and two, with differential $A_q$ and determinant $l_{q,0}$. The differential is upper triangular with the old complex as a subcomplex. This graded free model lifts to $R$: stabilize the finite free models, identify their augmentations, and lift the corresponding graded changes of basis. The lifts are invertible because the augmentation ideal lies in the Jacobson radical. Cancel the additional lifted unit disks before retaining the old-plus-singular grading. Their augmented cross terms are zero, so cancellation leaves precisely the displayed augmented model; the added disks do not enlarge its old part. The old model has bounded size, since $h_0$ is fixed and $\omega(k)$ is bounded. Indeed, the fixed-field Kummer and Schreier argument in Lemma <a href="#rl:residual-bound" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rl:residual-bound">88</a>, now retaining the fixed primes of $h_0$, bounds the residual global and local dimensions uniformly for $\omega(k)$ bounded. This size bound is separate from the central torsion-length bound used below.

Over $O[G]$ the entire new-prime block is invertible. Schur elimination leaves a complex $D$ of the bounded old size, with augmentation exactly the old complex. For each $A_q$, the order of its residual determinant at $t=0$ is bounded uniformly. At a split prime this follows from the odd Frobenius exponent and the degree-two Frobenius polynomial; at a root-type prime the constant term is already nonzero. Every sign evaluation of the lifted block is its augmentation plus a matrix divisible by $2$ with power-series entries. Therefore Lemma <a href="#lem:h:bounded-poles" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:h:bounded-poles">64</a> bounds the negative Laurent support of the entries of every $D_x$ modulo each fixed $2^M$, independently of the number of blocks.

The integral central specialization of the old complex is controlled by the ordinary base Kummer complex, the fixed old conductor primes, and the bounded singular contributions at $r$. Its rational $H^1$ and $H^2$ both have dimension one. Its torsion lengths are bounded by the finite Selmer quotient assumed in Theorem <a href="#thm:heegner-interpolation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:heegner-interpolation">10</a>, together with bounded global torsion and these local contributions. Choose its elementary-divisor bases at the center and lift. Apply case <span class="upright">(i)</span> of Lemma <a href="#lem:h:pivot-clearing" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:h:pivot-clearing">65</a> to $D$, the projected cycle and paired functional. The eliminated large block contributes an $O[G]$-unit to the determinant, and the multiplier in Equation <a href="#eq:h:group-ring-correction" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:h:group-ring-correction">[eq:h:group-ring-correction]</a> belongs to $O[G]$. Include both in the allowed factor $\eta$ of that lemma, so neither enters the clearing factor $f$. The lemma gives $d=fu$, a bounded central valuation for $f_0$, and the asserted pole bounds for $f_x$. ◻

</details>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-h-family-clearing-2"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-h-family-clearing</summary>

*Proof of Theorem <a href="#thm:heegner-interpolation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:heegner-interpolation">10</a>.* The primitive ring-class product has odd functional-equation sign under the standing Heegner conditions. Suppose the base product does not have a simple zero. Its first derivative then vanishes. By Lemma <a href="#lem:h:unused-prime-correction" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:h:unused-prime-correction">94</a>, $u_0(0)=0$, whereas every nonzero vertex has central determinant valuation bounded by one constant $B_1$ independent of the family. By Lemma <a href="#lem:h:family-clearing" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:h:family-clearing">95</a>, the hypotheses of Lemma <a href="#lem:h:boolean-transfer" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:h:boolean-transfer">67</a> hold with uniform central and pole bounds. Choose its fixed precision larger than $B_1$ plus twice the central bound, and then take the cube dimension sufficiently large. It supplies a nonzero vertex whose central valuation exceeds $B_1$, a contradiction. Thus the base product has a simple zero. ◻

</details>

<a id="sec:conclusions"></a>
### The unrestricted converse and Goldfeld’s densities

The two residual constructions now give the pointwise theorem. The density statement then requires only Smith’s Selmer distribution and an elementary change of counting convention.

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-h-family-clearing-3"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-h-family-clearing</summary>

*Proof of Theorem <a href="#thm:main-converse" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:main-converse">1</a>.* By Lemma <a href="#pr:residual-cases" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="pr:residual-cases">6</a>, either $E(\mathbb Q)[2]\ne0$ or $E[2]$ is irreducible. Theorem <a href="#thm:rational-converse" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:rational-converse">48</a> proves $a(E)=c_2(E)$ in the first case, and Theorem <a href="#thm:irreducible-converse" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:irreducible-converse">54</a> proves it in the second. Both use the local Kummer conditions defining the corank in the statement. The isogeny choices in the rational-torsion proof preserve that corank and the $L$-function by Lemma <a href="#pr:invariance" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="pr:invariance">[pr:invariance]</a>. Thus every curve in the theorem has analytic rank zero or one. Lemma <a href="#pr:ranks" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="pr:ranks">4</a> supplies the Mordell–Weil rank equality and finiteness of the whole Tate–Shafarevich group. ◻

</details>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-h-family-clearing-4"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-h-family-clearing</summary>

*Proof of Corollary <a href="#cor:finite-descent" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="cor:finite-descent">3</a>.* Lemma <a href="#pr:finite-descent" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="pr:finite-descent">7</a> gives $c_2(E)=d_2(E)$ and shows that $\mathop{\mathrm{Sha}}(E/\mathbb Q)[2^\infty]$ is divisible. Theorem <a href="#thm:main-converse" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:main-converse">1</a> gives the rank equalities and whole-Sha finiteness. A finite divisible $2$-group is zero, so its $2$-primary part vanishes. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-lem-squarefree-density"></a>
<div id="lem:squarefree-density" class="lemma">

**Lemma 96** (From integer to squarefree parameters). *Let $\mathcal P$ be a property of nonzero signed integers unchanged by multiplication by an integer square. Suppose $$A(X)=\#\{n\in\mathbb Z:0<|n|\le X,\ \mathcal P(n)\}
      =2\delta X+o(X).$$ Then $$S(X)=\#\{d\in\mathcal D(X):\mathcal P(d)\}
      =\frac{2\delta}{\zeta(2)}X+o(X).$$ In particular the property has density $\delta$ among signed squarefree parameters ordered by absolute value.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-squarefree-density"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-squarefree-density</summary>

*Proof.* Every nonzero integer has a unique expression $n=m^2d$ with $m>0$ and $d$ signed squarefree. Thus $$A(X)=\sum_{m\le\sqrt X}S(X/m^2),\qquad
 S(X)=\sum_{m\le\sqrt X}\mu(m)A(X/m^2).$$ The second equality follows by substituting the first and using $\sum_{m\mid r}\mu(m)=\mathbf1_{r=1}$. For a fixed integer $M$, the terms with $m\le M$, divided by $X$, tend to $2\delta\sum_{m\le M}\mu(m)/m^2$. The remaining absolute contribution is at most $$2X\sum_{m>M}m^{-2},$$ because $A(Y)\le2\lfloor Y\rfloor\le2Y$. First let $X$ and then $M$ tend to infinity. The absolutely convergent series $\sum\mu(m)/m^2=1/\zeta(2)$ proves the formula. Applying it to the property always true gives $\#\mathcal D(X)\sim2X/\zeta(2)$, proving the density assertion. ◻

</details>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-squarefree-density-2"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-squarefree-density</summary>

*Proof of Theorem <a href="#thm:main-density" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:main-density">2</a>.* Smith’s theorem states that, for every fixed elliptic curve $E/\mathbb Q$ and $j=0,1$ (Smith 2025, Theorem 1.1) <a id="pm-cite-115"></a>[[Smith2025](#ref-Smith2025)], $$\#\{n\in\mathbb Z:0<|n|\le X,\ c_2(E^{(n)})=j\}=X+o(X)
 .$$ Quadratic twisting depends only on the squareclass, so Lemma <a href="#lem:squarefree-density" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:squarefree-density">96</a> gives density $1/2$ for each corank among the signed squarefree parameters.

For $j=0,1$, Theorem <a href="#thm:main-converse" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:main-converse">1</a> gives $c_2(E^{(d)})=j\Rightarrow a(E^{(d)})=j$, while Lemma <a href="#pr:ranks" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="pr:ranks">4</a> gives the converse implication. The analytic-rank counts therefore equal the corresponding corank counts exactly. The two densities sum to one. Their complement, the twists of analytic rank at least two, has density zero, and Lemma <a href="#pr:ranks" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="pr:ranks">4</a> gives the final rank and finiteness assertions on the density-one union. ◻

</details>
